Title: Sentimental Value
Comment:
this year marked a decade since my parents got divorced, putting an end to a marriage that had already been dead for a decade itself after beginning a decade prior. and yet today, they, my sister, and i will all celebrate thanksgiving together in the house we grew up in, and the one they had built from the ground up just two years before things took that first terrible turn - an event that once seemed unfathomable to me under the weight of all that came before. much like the memories our house holds, my emotions today are mixed, but mostly warm, as the pain of the past has finally given way to steady and quiet contentment only occasionally interrupted by reflective melancholy. today, however, sentimental value has sparked one of those interruptions.
though this isn’t the first house my family owned, most of my young life was lived here, as i was only three when we moved and can’t remember anything of my childhood before the house i now call home. i don’t have many memories of its construction, but countless pictures of my sister and i running through its unfinished halls fill my mom’s photo albums and subsequently fill in the gaps in my remembrance as well. one thing i do inexplicably and clearly recall is how excited my parents, and especially my mother, were to be making this home together. there was so much thought put into its design to make it the perfect place to raise my sister and i and truly start their life together, and i still feel that care and consideration to this day. in many ways, i almost see it as my parents’ third child. and, much like its siblings, it would come to bear the trauma of the next ten years right alongside my sister and i.
with distance, i’ve been able to accept the emotional complexity of my memories in this house and adjust to the cognitive dissonance of the place i always have and always will call home simultaneously holding so much hate and fear in its very foundation, but as a child, that mental gymnastics eludes us. we haven’t lived enough life yet to see things as anything but what they immediately are in the moment. and for most of those moments in my childhood, our house was more of a battlefield than a home - and as a result, its entire identity was characterized more by cruelty than calm as well. initially, my parents kept the arguing confined to their bedroom, and in my head, that helped me keep their simmering resentment trapped in this room too. but it was only a matter of time before it spilled out and began to take place anywhere at any time, infecting every last inch of our house’s skeleton until it was as integral to its structure as the wood that supported its framework.
likewise, with this spillage, it would’ve been impossible for me to stay out of the fights forever, seeing as i was the older sibling my mom trusted me with stories my sister was too young to know at the time, and my own strained relationship with my father growing up was the spark that lit the fuse for many of these arguments. throughout it all though, even as i became a regular member of the near-daily grudge matches, i did my best to keep my sister away from it all, so they wouldn’t derail her life the way this endless stress did mine. i’d do whatever i could to distract her from the chaos in our kitchen, isolating her to my room with one of our pets for comfort so she could focus on her homework while mine remained incomplete until midnight. we had our fair share of disagreements as kids, as all siblings do, but when it came to our parents’ failing marriage, all those petty squabbles perished. i never wanted her to share the ire i’d inherited from impact on the frontlines.
my dad left a few times before finally moving out for good in the spring of 2015, and though the peace and quiet that remained in his absence helped our house heal some of its wounds, much of the pain it - and now i, by association - bore proved permanent, and its oppressive presence was exacerbated by the countless roles and responsibilities i now had to take on while my father was gone too. naturally, as a 15-year-old who was simultaneously struggling with an identity crisis in the midst of all this mess, i drowned in my despair instead of rising to the occasion and often became the next problem for my mom after she thought she was finally free. even while being broadly known by many as a “good kid” who got good grades and stayed involved in school in almost every way i could, i was constantly a basket case to my mother and sister behind closed doors and i couldn’t even articulate why most of the time.
for a while there, it almost ruined my relationship with my sister, as she remembered me less by what i did for her when we were younger and more for how mean and angry i was as a teenager, usually seemingly for no reason. there was so much i wanted to say and just didn’t know how, and because of that, i shared less with the people who loved me most and instead sought quick hits of attention and affection from friends and lovers instead, falling fast and trusting too easily but justifying it all as worth it in the end for that first high. heading into college i began to brutalize my body as well, starving it almost past the point of no return as my inability to process the chaos of my childhood and my intense unhappiness with who i was and the life i led manifested into violent self-mutilation. only when these actions started to seriously threaten my life was i forced to wake up to the truth of my identity and face the entirety of my adolescent anguish head on at long last.
coming out of this, i moved home halfway through college, switched schools, and started to finally accept what my life had to look like in the future if i still wanted to live. and i didn’t know if i did at the time, but i knew i wanted to try. and that began with coming out to my sister as trans in a target parking lot towards the end of the summer of 2019. it wasn’t something grand or planned, it was just something i couldn’t keep from her any longer. our relationship had improved somewhat since the start of my recovery over the past year, but one wall still divided us, and i couldn’t stand it anymore. so, even though this didn’t excuse all of my anarchy when we were younger, i thought that, at the very least, it could offer one explanation and help her understand what i’d been hiding underneath all that anger all this time.
i think a part of me always resented my sister for seemingly making it out of my parents’ marriage without any scars back then. even still, as i’ve watched her follow “The Right Path of Adulthood” and finish college on time with no hiccups, find a boyfriend her freshman year who’s she been with for five years and will probably marry, and consistently work Real Adult Jobs that root her life in stability i’ve never known, i continue to struggle with that envy. for obvious reasons, our lives will never look the same, but that doesn’t stop me from feeling like a failure in comparison, constantly hopping from place to place and person to person and profession to profession while saddling her and my mother with my psychosis simultaneously. and of course, aside from our different identities, the main explanation for this contrast i return to is the vastly opposite ways we experienced our childhood.
but in that moment i shared this thing i’d kept stored under lock and key in my heart for so long it’d almost killed me, it was like the last two decades of our life didn’t matter at all. i finally let her see me - all of me - and in response, she let me know the side of her i never knew when i was away in active combat with our parents all those years ago. this perfect girl i’d built up in my mind - my parents’ dream daughter i’d never be - was suffused with just as much sadness as me, she just had a better poker face. and, because i already claimed the problem child title when we were teens, she took up the part of mediator i’d played for a decade prior, and this was a role she hadn’t given up until that conversation where we laid everything ugly bare and watched something beautiful bloom in its place.
it took a little more time for my dad and i to find each other again. after he moved out, he was still around my life from time to time, but while my sister remained in contact with him, i maintained only the faintest communication, and the conversations we did have were almost entirely arguments. however, i started to see him more when my self-flagellation forced me to move home halfway through college so my mom could keep an eye on me, and over time, we built a new bridge to each other bit by bit, brick by brick, until the day i finally came out to him as well. given that much of our strained relationship when i was younger was due to not being the son he’d envisioned i’d be, it’d be an obscene understatement to say i was merely “dreading” this disclosure - in actuality, i almost puked on my phone.
however, the call in question - which came in the spring of 2022 - only took about ten minutes. i think he’d known for some time and simply been waiting for me to say the words aloud, but instead of responding with the enmity i’d long expected, he plainly told me he just wanted me to do whatever made me happy, and he wanted to be a part of whatever my life looked like going forward. i think, after taking a considerable amount of time to "work on himself," he’d realized how much he’d ruined when we were younger, and he didn’t want to waste any more time without me. but i also know that, with that call, he could finally give up mourning the son he never had and focus solely on loving and getting to know the daughter he’d gained.
for most of my life, my father and i’s relationship had been defined by that incompatibility of who we wanted each other to be vs. who we really were - and also recognizing undesirable traits we shared in each other but we’re simultaneously ashamed to possess, such as our often unruly rage (usually spurred by aforementioned incompatibility in our expectations for each other). i wasn’t what my dad originally wanted, nor was he my dream father growing up either. but we got stuck with each other nevertheless, and only when i was finally and fully open with him were we able to accept what we had here instead of wishing for something else. it hasn’t always been easy, and as with my sister, these revelations don’t remove the struggles we’ve shared from our memories, but now, we get to make new ones to replace them with. and in a way, i think those new memories are to my dad and i what movies are gustav and nora. they’ve helped us heal, and they say what can’t be said.
today, when i sit down for thanksgiving dinner with my family, i won’t be thinking about all these things. i rarely actively do anymore. but nonetheless, they’re still there, just as the house we’ll eat in holds all these memories alongside me. i used to view them as an affliction, as things that had permanently disfigured me emotionally and rendered me unable to ever live a normal life. now, however, i know that these experiences aren’t a flaw in my or my house’s foundation but instead integral to who we are, and who we’ve become. we’ve weathered wild storms together, but we’ve been showered in so much sunlight too, and memories on both sides have affected and altered us equally. this isn’t “for better” or “for worse” - it just is, and that’s all there is to it. but we can’t come to that place of understanding on our own. because sometimes, the people who hurt us most - or those who we hurt most - are the only ones who can set us free.

Title: Marty Supreme
Comment:
Like many great actors and virtually all legitimate movie stars, Timothée Chalamet is a salesman at heart. But where most of them prefer to keep that like something of an open secret, the razor-cheeked Lisan al-Gaib — who’s become a brand unto himself, despite showing up at a time when Hollywood remains far more invested in franchises than faces — has embraced his entrepreneurial zeal with the same winning commitment that he brings to literally everything else he does.
It’s baked into the most basic essence of his image. Chalamet doesn’t co-own a mobile phone company or do an inordinate amount of commercial work (his ads are limited to Super Bowl spots and Scorsese collaborations), but whether accepting an award or simply delivering a turn worthy of one, he never shies away from the sense that he’s selling himself on screen. In that light, it’s no coincidence that his status as both a great actor and a legitimate movie star has grown increasingly undeniable the more that his performances have started to seem like pitches. Magic chocolates. Ancient prophecies. Electric folk songs. Limited edition track jackets. Whatever the product they’re trying to move, Chalamet’s recent characters don’t feel like roles so much as fences for his infectious self-belief. The poor kid was born with the hustle of a champion but saddled with the soul of an artist; Michael Jordan didn’t need an audience to affirm his greatness, but Chalamet’s legend requires us to buy him all over again with every shot.
The ecstatic tension at the heart of the world-beating “Marty Supreme,” in which Chalamet makes one of the most colossal movie performances of the 21st century seem as natural as a lay-up, is that it encourages modern Hollywood’s ultimate striver to sell his heart out, just so it can interrogate why anyone would bother trying so hard. It challenges — and rewards — his outspoken pursuit of greatness by casting him as a character who’s pathologically driven by the same thing.
Which isn’t to suggest that Josh Safdie’s A24 epic is best appreciated as a metatextual commentary on its star (much as it was obviously written both for and about him), or that a generational classic this overflowing with life should be reduced to another cautionary tale of someone flying too close to the sun, but rather to emphasize how thoroughly it suffuses Chalamet’s singular eagerness into a film as propulsive, quicksilver, and electrifying as he is. The result is a roman candle of a movie that feels like it was shot out of a cannon, despite being burdened with the gravity of an implausible dream; a totemic Jewish-American odyssey about where such dreams come from, where they might lead to, and where they’re liable to come apart at the seams along the way.

Title: Train Dreams
Comment:
A gentle poem about time, loss, and reaching for meaning. Joel Edgerton gives his best performance as a logger working to build a life for his family. Felicity Jones is wonderful as always, and William H Macy gives a performance of surprising power despite its limited screen time.
This is a delicate story about a man clinging to a small corner of the world as it turns and turns beneath him. The landscape changes, technology advances, time moves along, and at some point we each realize we aren't at the front of the wave, but behind it.
The movie is quiet and gentle, even in its violence. It takes the time to point out that forest valleys were once under thousands of feet of ice, the landscape carved by receding glaciers, growing green with now ancient trees, only to be burned to ash... and grow again. Against that enormity, both of time and of nature, human lives are lived, lost, and forgotten, and the great machine lurches ever on. We're here too briefly to understand it.
At some point we each must realize that the world has crashed over us and moved ahead, and we are left to wonder why we're still here, and what the hell any of it means. This is the story of a life that aches, quietly and in solitude, and then is gone - but not before a contemplative moment that reaches skyward for some kind of meaning. That ultimate meaning is elusive - or perhaps we won't understand it until we disconnect from the earth, and look down at it from a far remove. Maybe only then will we feel connected to it all... maybe the answer to the riddle is only clear to us in our final moments. Until then, we love, we learn, we yearn, and we mourn.
One of the very best films of the year.

Title: Marty Supreme
Comment:
More than anything, a movie about being an actor. About lies being more real than the truth, about refusing to believe in a future with failure, about being more in love with the concept of greatness than you are with any person. Marty even introduces himself to Gwyneth Paltrow by laying the movie’s theme bare, and admitting he’s something of a performer himself. He mythologizes his own story at every turn because it’s all he knows how to do, and he pushes away the things that tether him to reality because he knows he can’t make it without delusion. The hustle is the life– and for
better and for worse, there’s not much on the other side.
After viewing two, I’m team Chalamet Best Actor this year. He’s delivering such a confident and unwavering performance that is so well-tuned it feels like he’s been living in it for years. (And  based on his greatness speech at the Golden Globes, I think he has!) I’m also team supporting actress nom for Odessa A’zion but fuck it’s a stacked year.

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
Miles better than Glass Onion and, while I liked the first one more and probably nothing will ever top its slick perfection, this movie is doing a lot more. 
As a sequel it references itself in clever ways, plays with your expectations and does a lot of Benoit edging. As a new story it works on a shocking amount of levels—a capably complex mystery is explored, meta-referential to the genre, it riffs a lot on our current societal nightmare and it’s generally funny as hell but what really carries this movie into the stratosphere is the empathic depiction of faith. 
Yeah, I didn’t expect that either. There’s a conversation between an atheist detective and a priest that had me in tears. Wake Up Dead Man took me to church.

Le film à soutenir en salles cette semaine est La Voix de Hind Rajab : un call center en Palestine reçoit un appel d'une enfant de 6 ans coincée dans une voiture constamment mitraillée par l'armée israélienne.
Les enregistrements téléphoniques sont authentiques, c'est la vraie voix de l'enfant que vous entendez, le film va brouiller les pistes entre réalité et fiction en montrant aussi des vidéos des vrais événements.
C'est à la fois un huis clos efficace qui utilise beaucoup les projections à l'image (carte, son, photos, dessins) mais qui crée aussi des conflits entre personnages qui veulent tous bien faire. C'est une critique de la lenteur et inefficacité du système mais surtout et évidemment des rouages mis en place par Israël pour continuer de massacrer les populations locales.
Le film se concentre sur la résolution de problème et l'incapacité des gens qui ont toutes les bonnes intentions du monde face à l'oppression hiérarchique.
C'est peut-être un peu too much en termes de pathos à certains moments mais en toute sincérité, je pense qu'on peut s'identifier à tous les personnages de l'œuvre et surtout à leur réactions qui agacent mais qui sont compréhensibles.
Visionnage très difficile et les 1h30 sont longues vu la difficulté du sujet mais c'est très poignant et la salle était en larmes tout le long.
Soutenez aussi ce genre de cinéma qui est à la fois bien fait mais aussi qui dénonce aussi l'armée d'occupation génocidaire israélienne.

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
Better than the first film, and even better than the second, this one operates as Johnson’s most coherent refinement of the contemporary mystery format. For those attuned to the grammar of classic detective fiction, the film will feel immediately legible, Johnson demonstrates once again his capacity to construct genre as both homage and critique. If earlier entries used the “old style mystery” template to examine American greed (the first) and pervasive stupidity (the second), this film shifts its thematic centre toward the phenomenon of charismatic authority, the way individuals, despite supposedly knowing better, abdicate judgment in favour of a figure who offers certainty.
Part of Johnson’s strategy involves situating this fascination with authority within a broader critique of social values. The narrative repeatedly exposes how certain attitudes (misogyny, hostility, generalized culture of resentment) continue to circulate under the protective language of “tradition.” This extends to an examination of religion's ambivalent position, which the film treats as a source of emotional investment and a mechanism for legitimizing exclusion.
Beyond those sociological observations, the film also functions as a deliberate rearticulation of the classical mystery. Johnson’s reconfigures the mechanics of these classic stories while preserving their pleasures. Anyone who has spent time with the narrative architectures of Sherlock Holmes, for example, will recognize the structural echoes and, perhaps, feel the faint nostalgia embedded in the film’s pacing and puzzle-work.

Title: One Battle After Another
Comment:
After two months and a lot of work, my big essay on One Battle After Another is finally live on Vulture.
“After seeing One Battle After Another for the first time, I walked out of Chicago’s Music Box Theatre into an unseasonably balmy fall afternoon and learned that Assata Shakur had died. Shakur was a legendary revolutionary with the Black Liberation Army who in May 1977 was convicted of killing a New Jersey state trooper in a shoot-out that left her wounded and another comrade dead. Two years later, Shakur, aided by other BLA members, escaped from prison and was granted political asylum in Cuba in 1984, where she resided until her death. During Barack Obama’s presidency, she was added to the FBI’s Most Wanted Terrorists list, and her bounty doubled to $2 million. She long proclaimed her innocence.
Teyana Taylor cited the complicated, controversial Shakur as a touchstone for her performance as Perfidia Beverly Hills in Paul Thomas Anderson’s tense, propulsive, and heartfelt One Battle After Another. The movie opens on the steely gaze of Perfidia as she canvasses an immigration holding facility along the U.S.-Mexico border. Perfidia is a leading member of the French 75, an incendiary far-left group whose raid on the facility and its fallout composes the first 30 or so minutes of the film. While the rest of the French 75 help the immigrants escape, Leonardo DiCaprio’s bomb expert “Ghetto” Pat lights up the twilight sky as an announcement of their revolution and, more importantly, to impress Perfidia. She’s preoccupied though, training a gun on the facility’s head officer, Colonel Steven J. Lockjaw (Sean Penn), whose RFK Jr. rasp and licentious focus on Perfidia sets him up as a comedic draw and a convincing picture of America’s sanctioned white violence.
Anderson breezes through monumental shifts from there — Perfidia’s deepening romantic relationship with Pat, her subsequent pregnancy and postpartum depression, the beginnings of a psychosexual dynamic with Lockjaw, the downfall of the French 75, and the splintering of the lives associated with it. Perfidia rats out her group in order to stave off a prison sentence after a bank robbery goes awry, and she kills a Black security guard. (Shakur may have been an inspiration for the character, but she was never a rat in life.)
The story picks up 16 years later after Perfidia has escaped witness protection. Not much has changed in the world, she says in voice-over. Ghetto Pat now goes by Bob, who is less a dutiful parent to 16-year old Willa (Chase Infiniti) and more a frustrating and paranoid obstacle in her small-town California life. DiCaprio is hilarious in the role of a burnout revolutionary without much of an internal compass, bringing slapstick physicality to the drama he inhabits. He’s perennially high, whether he’s hitting a vape or nursing the remnants of a joint held precariously between scissor blades. But Anderson punctures his weed haze with the bright light of a past that in actuality never dimmed, when Lockjaw begins to hunt Pat and Willa.
One Battle After Another is a full meal in ways so few films of this scale and budget (by most accounts, more than $130 million) these days are. It is expertly directed and lensed, brimming with aesthetic prowess. At the same time, it makes a spectacle out of its philosophical ideas. It’s a quicksilver film, shifting and melding solemn character reflections with amusing internecine conflicts. At its worst, the humor, enlivening on the level of entertainment, undermines the horror we’re otherwise witnessing. At its best, the discomfiture paves the way for charged performances — none more crucial than Teyana Taylor’s Perfidia.
Perfidia is a contradiction nestled in thorns, selfish and prickly and bold. Taylor brings to life a kind of flawed rendering of Black womanhood that I have longed to see in cinema. Not aspirational, but something more meaningful. Genuinely complex, authentically inhabited. The image of Perfidia swollen deep in her pregnancy, firing off an automatic machine gun, says it all. There’s nothing simple and warm and sacrificially maternal about this woman. She’s jealous of her baby daughter, racked with hormones and memories of a complicated birth. Every image and voice-over carry the friction of expectation that she should be something more upstanding and easy to root for. Taylor’s performance doesn’t ask you to root for Perfidia so much as be galvanized by her.
Watching Taylor (who physically occupies only a slim portion of the two-hour-40-minute film) as well as Infiniti and Regina Hall (playing the most mature and committed member of the French 75), it becomes evident that the Black women of Anderson’s ensemble are the MVPs. They ground the most contested segments of the emotionally and intellectually ambivalent story. If you don’t know Anderson’s work, from the capacious Boogie Nights to the deliciously austere Phantom Thread, you might expect a movie about revolutionaries to be interested in what it only glances at: liberation. Perfidia ultimately is a frame for the portrait Anderson is more interested in: a father-daughter story that considers what elder generations are leaving behind and what their children must navigate when a parent’s sins come crashing into their lives. Any time the film coheres into a robustly realized depiction of the mood of this present American moment, as absurd as it is violent, it’s a testament to the abilities of its cast. The Black women of the film are lightning rods for the most forceful conversations the film can bear, and it’s thrilling to watch them embody what Anderson’s script can only loosely hold.” - An excerpt from my big essay on One Battle After Another, the black actresses in the film, what we expect film to show of the current historical moment, the racialized libidinal contradictions of the film and more. Now available to read on Vulture.

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
“God has a sense of humor.”
“Will you pray for me?”
praise and glory be! I’d been joking for months now that this movie was “genetically engineered in a lab for me specifically,” but deep down I think I’d worried my expectations might be too high. not so! I was beaming from ear to ear, on the verge of applauding and shouting “amen” from beginning to end, jaw on the floor with each twist and turn, and I left feeling satisfied and moved and seen in ways I’d never anticipated.
this is going to be a cinematic cornerstone for me. Rian somehow broke the polite Thanksgiving dinner rule and talked about religion and politics in a way that, I believe, will feel genuinely honest and good-faith to nearly everyone from believer to skeptic and generate rich conversation between both. a worthy and provocative double feature with Conclave, among other things!
above all, it is easily the densest movie thematically that Rian has made since The Last Jedi, and the two actually have a lot in common: namely, wrestling with the negative consequences of broken institutions while simultaneously resurrecting the potentially transcendent and transformative power of believing in their foundational myths. Rian’s movies have always been what Flannery O’Connor might call “Christ-haunted,” and here it feels like he’s entering that haunted House of God genuinely interested in asking questions and wrestling with the paradoxical tensions of faith rather than giving didactic answers.
needless to say, I resonated profoundly with Josh O’Connor’s Father Jud; the purity of his faith, his frustration at the distortion of it, the desire for things to be done better (even to the point of reckless pride and resentment), the acknowledgement that this is an inescapable part of his purpose and lens of viewing reality. even the yearning for imperfect members of his community to be known and given the care they need rather than false solutions. and the way Jud and Blanc play off one another brings out nothing but riveting thematic foil; this is Benoit Blanc at his most dynamic, challenged not necessarily just by the impossibility of the case but by what it confronts about who he is and how he engages the world. Blanc’s philosophy since the first Knives Out has been following “Gravity’s Rainbow,” using his intellect and perception to arrive unerringly at the truth—but, this film posits, what if mere truth is not enough? I shan’t spoil the thematic conclusions it offers instead, but of course I was deeply moved. 
while Glass Onion was just as technically stellar as Knives Out, I did feel that it lacked the “kind heart” of the original (carried primarily by the relationships of Marta and Harlan, and Marta and Blanc) and instead opted for pure satire above all. what Onion lacked in human emotion, though, Wake Up Dead Man makes up in spades; I found myself crying several times, and subsequently consoling a friend in the movie theater lobby as she full-on sobbed about the brokenness of the church and all the ways it has excluded instead of welcomed. a scene involving prayer is probably my favorite in the whole movie; both convicting and touching. and in the midst of all this emotion, it’s worth hammering home just how good it looks (Yedlin is f*cking unleashed here) and how funny it all is; I was almost hyperventilating in moments from sheer laughter, including when a character says that their book is “my one way ticket out of Substack hell.” I’ll need to see this a dozen more times and then I’ll be quoting it for the rest of my life, as with the first film.
I don’t know how Rian comes up with these mysteries. this one does feel a tad more convoluted than the others, and I’ll need to see it again just to unpack all the moving parts. but it bears repeating: this is a whodunnit where the truly rapturous and edge-of-your-seat mystery lies most on a thematic and character level, rather than plot. when I watch it again, which will be very soon, I will be basking in the rich layers of everything it is saying and exploring. Rian has made a film here that is ripe for vulnerable discussion and reflection with others, particularly about one’s personal experience with religion and spirituality. so, ya know, the kind of movie I’ve always wanted to make and keep making. I wish it would have been given the wide and lengthy theatrical release it deserved—the crowds would have eaten it up, and knowing it will be largely buried on streaming makes me wanna go full First Reformed on Netflix HQ. but alas, Father Jud would not approve. in this stead, I will be Wake Up Dead Man’s biggest evangelist to the ends of the earth. call me a believer.

Title: Train Dreams
Comment: Back in September, a friend visiting the city for TIFF pressed a copy of Denis Johnson's novella into my hands—his copy, as it turned out. He wanted me to have it and to read it before I saw the movie version. I'm grateful for that, even though it's as a direct result of reading the book— really good; a swift, impressionistic account of a life of no real consequence—that the film failed to impress me as it did him. Not that it's bad, exactly; the spare, glancing style is derivative of you-know-who (the opening shot uses a (falling) Tree to symbolize all Of Life) but still well suited to Johnson's prose, a lot of which is faithfully reproduced and nicely read by Will Patton. The cinematography is, you know, nice, and there are some passages where Clint Bentley and his editor Parker Laramie work up a (you guessed it) nice coruscating rhythm, and some where they show a lot of patience by just sticking with Joel Edgerton and his face. I like Edgerton, in general, and very much here; he's believably rugged as an avatar of the early 20th Century, and has right reticence for a man who doesn't expect to be listened to, and isn't sure he has much to say anyway. His performance is good: it pushes, gently but firmly, against the sanitized vibe of the proceedings. But about that sanitized vibe... it really isquite remarkable how thoroughly the filmmakers have worked to superimpose a contemporary, progressive perspective on the story and to efface (or simply erase) the grotesquerie that gives Johnson's prose (and his protagonist's experiences) their vital life force. Their reasons for doing so are their own; it's a shame those impulses align with the prevailing tendency for so many literary adaptations to simplify—and, however well-meaningly, betray— their source material in the nnam of accesibility. Train Dreams: The Movie scrubs Robert Grainer's hands and conscience clean even as it covers him in ashes; it swaps out the bad things he's done for things beyond his power that he feels bad about.And: it surely sentimentalizes (and, yes, more or less Instagram-ifies) his memories of fatherhood, especially when one of the details that brought me up short in the book was how Robert didn't really remember much about his late daughter, and took comfort in how little she'd ever seen or understood of the world before leaving it. The idea that we can't truly control or curate our memories, in waking life but especially not in dreams, and that in forcing meaning on them we only distort them, is frightening and profound. Bentley's film, which I don' think is either of these things, operates more schematically in the home stretch as a kind of psychic highlight reel. To paraphrase Johnson, it sees Robert as connected to all things, but in a way that mainly makes those connections legible -- and sympathetic, and relatable -- to us. That's nice. Beneath all its dutifully rendered melancholy, Bentley's movie is peddling reassurance, and it can keep it.

Comment:
Everyone on here seems desperate to decode this movie as some kind of MeToo parable or moral reckoning, as if the film is secretly ashamed of its own ambiguity. But that’s the joke, you dopes - it’s ABOUT having nothing to say and the frantic social performance of pretending otherwise. It’s a gonzo comedy of manners dressed up as a discourse film, a send-up of people who can only experience art as a public demonstration of their good politics - that is, of all of the Letterboxd reviewers here taking a break from launching tired Twitter one-liners to gravely tut tut at Luca Guadagnino for not Doing A Serious when it comes to sexual misconduct. The whole point of the movie is that IT IS NOT making the commentary you're all accusing it of making poorly! It doesn't think it has a grand, cutting message; it is about not having a message. To function as a critique of MeToo would violate its basic ethos - it's not a critique of MeToo's philosophy but a joke about how there is no philosophy once basic self-preservation is involved. These characters could not be more directly invested in the concept of ethics and moral responsibility, the conflict is over the most serious of moral dilemmas, and all they can do is worry about department politics and their tenure cases. THAT is this movie's message. It has no interest in celebrating or indicting MeToo. It merely suggests that such high-minded considerations disappear in the face of naked self-interest.
It's perfectly legitimate to see this whole enterprise as offensive, stupid, pointless, or insufficiently serious. But half of the reviews on here are reacting to a critique of MeToo that simply isn't in this movie. That's not what it's about! It's about how feeble principle is in the face of self-interest.
You’re not supposed to nod gravely and post your syllabus; you’re supposed to laugh at how everyone in it (and, yes, in this reviews section) is auditioning for moral clarity in a world that has none. You are the mark, dour liberal Letterboxd reviewers who feel panicky about not having the right MeToo politics. You are the mark. The joke is on you.

Life isn’t any more complex than the simple passage of time. But time doesn’t pass us by; it passes through us. The moments, the people, the small collisions and big connections—they move straight through us. And it’s only when enough of them have vanished that you can finally look back and see what your life has actually been about. Life might be lived in the present, but it’s understood by the past, and the past is always what’s no longer with us.
What a painful paradox.
Train Dreams is an absolute ache of a movie. The quiet of it somehow hits loudly. We watch a man who has had so many moments and people move through him that, in the end, all he’s left with are his memories and himself. There’s no connection anymore—just the residue of everything that once mattered.
The film tries to leave us on a high note, to suggest that connection is still possible, that something or someone might still reach him… but I don’t think the story achieves that. It’s not nihilistic, but beneath all the beauty there’s an unresolved sadness that’s left me awfully pessimistic.
This is one of the most beautifully sad movies I’ve seen in an age.

Title: Frankenstein
Comment:
ever since i read frankenstein for the first time my senior year of high school, it’s been my favorite book for reasons i couldn’t always explain. all i knew at the time, while still denying certain aspects of my own identity to myself, was that i felt an instant kinship with the creature - this tragic being that didn’t ask to be alive or have any say in the body he was born into or the way he looked and only ever wanted to be loved and no longer alone, but because of the things he had no control over, the world wouldn’t let him. because no matter what he did, they’d only ever see him as a monster first and foremost. because no one ever gave him the chance to be anything else.
yeah, it’s a wonder why i identified with a character like that.
but, almost a decade later, i no longer solely see myself in the creature’s sadness. i see myself in the way he initially finds beauty all around him at all times - whether he’s actively trying to or not - when finally free to move through the world on his own in this new life, experiencing it all through virgin eyes. i see myself in the way his weary heart is healed by human connection, especially with those rare few who treat him as someone deserving of compassion and consideration and remind him of his worth that no reconstructed exterior can erase. and i do sadly also still see myself in the way he struggles against the inevitability of violence and anger in this cruel world too, despite his inherent belief system being defined by innocence and optimism - qualities he desperately tries to defend until they’re savagely stripped from his soul, leaving an empty husk of hate behind.
but the true treasure of del toro’s take on this story to me is the message that, even if you do find yourself at one point seduced by the occasionally attractive pull of unrestrained spite and self-despair, it’s never too late to change course and choose love again. it’s never too late to forgive those who have hurt you and also yourself for giving into enmity at a time when almost everything and everyone around us is eagerly campaigning for cruelty. our lives are not defined by who we’re born as, nor are they set in stone by any one singular choice we make throughout the turbulent years that follow - they’re defined by how we respond to unavoidable strife, and how we evolve from our inevitable stumbles along the way.
we will fall, and we we will fail - it’s who we are. it’s human. but it’s never too late to start a new life. there’s still time until there’s not.

Comment:
RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL
So there’s a universe where I would’ve been reviewing this film from a CAM rip or had to wait a month or so because last week I got the news that my theater couldn’t work out a deal with the distributor and was not going to release the film in theaters here. This is not much of a novelty, as earlier this year, we were supposed to have Jurassic World: Rebirth playing here, but at the last minute, the same thing happened. However, I guess they managed to resolve whatever problem they had, and well, here I am.
But was all the hassle worth it?
Hmm, kinda. It was great to see the incredible and immersive production design displayed on the big screen. Again, top-notch work and arguably one of the best elements of both films. I know many people keep complaining about the cinematography, especially the backlighting. I don’t know; many of the day scenes are a little too bright, which makes some scenes look a little artificial, but it wasn’t something I was terribly bothered by. The score was decent; I liked the little nods to some of the great songs from the first one, especially using “Defying Gravity” as a motif/theme song. The CGI was solid, if a little spotty at times.
In terms of the performances, Ariana and Cynthia are great together. They manage to get back into their characters’ skins effortlessly, delivering really good performances with the material they are given (more on that later), and the vocals, man, the vocals were fantastic. Grande especially gets to show off her range, particularly in the ending. Their dynamic was solid; I wished we had gotten more. That fight scene got me and my crowd laughing. Bailey was a pretty good romantic lead. It’s always fun to see Goldblum. Michelle should avoid singing like the plague. Also, her character promised a lot, but I feel she got the short end of the stick.
As for the negatives, where do I start? This one honestly didn’t get close to the greatness of the first one. It toyed with some pretty good ideas and had so much potential, but it didn’t live up to it, at least for me. I liked the way they played around with the iconic characters like the Tin Man and Scarecrow; I wasn’t expecting one of them to become this sadistic individual, lol. I know they did their best in selling me on the animal abuse and the truth behind Oz, but I never felt a connection with this cause, and therefore the whole evil Oz thing left me underwhelmed. Much of the film left me feeling that way, if I am being honest. The music, which was fun like “Popular,” and in the case of “Defying Gravity,” it was awesome; here, other than the Kame Kame Ha song, the music felt repetitious sonically, and none of them left much of an impression on me. Some great displays in terms of the vocals, but I honestly can barely remember any of them. And you know? For a musical, that’s a big problem. It’s like a comedy film that doesn’t make you laugh—a musical where you walk out of the theater unimpressed. You know, it’s troublesome, to put it lightly. And there were other things they did with some of the characters that were laughable in execution. This character dies, and not only is there a whiplash of a tonal shift, but also the way it was executed—instead of having me gasping, I almost burst into laughter. And speaking of laughs, they handle Dorothy so poorly here. Like, couldn’t they get the rights or what? Because I don’t think we even get to see her face; she just (literally) flashes by. I know the focus is Galinda and Elphaba, but I don’t know, man, that whole thing didn’t land for me and got me chuckling.
All in all, by no means a clusterf—k of a film, but when compared to the first one, this simply paled in comparison. The writing and characterization left a lot to be desired. The music was pretty forgettable. The acting had its highs and lows. I had a nice time and can’t say I regret watching this, but it’s not the great follow-up I was hoping for.

Title: Back to the Future
Comment:
if you put your mind to it you can accomplish anything
I saw this film when I was about four or five years old and it shaped the entire course of my life. My destiny. Up until that point, I had only seen The Jungle Book, Mary Poppins, and maybe a few other Disney movies. I had seen commercials for BTTF. It was to be playing on ABC or something that week. I begged my mom and dad to let me watch it (I was obsessed with “Family Ties” and Michael J Fox gayyyyy). They finally relinquished and taped it for me (my bedtime was 8pm after all). I don’t remember the first time watching it. I just know that I watched that tape and then I watched it again and then I watched it again and again and again. That next year, they released the trilogy on VHS and my parents bought me a proper, commercial free version. I don’t remember which time I watched it that the following fact was cemented within my consciousness (after all…my brain was still forming when I was watching this movie)…i just know that seeing this movie made me want to make movies.
Why? I don’t really know why. It could just be that it was the first movie I ever saw that wasn’t specifically a “kids movie.” It could be that the movie is, I would argue, a perfectly constructed film in terms of narrative setups and payoffs. Or maybe it’s because the medium of film itself is true time travel. Perhaps this present version of myself - the woman who just saw this movie at Vidiots, the filmmaker trying to heal her inner child - she’s sending vibrations of dreams-come-true to that little kid from the midwest who wanted to tell larger than life stories. Saying, “hey kid: watch this film and study it and make it your mission to make this kind of art at all cost.”
I adore this movie. It’s a part of me. The neural pathways in my brain that know what love is supposed to feel like were formed when I saw the way Marty and Jennifer look at each other with Huey Lewis and The News blasting or the way Laraine looks up at George after he slugs Biff. The maximalist approach I can’t help but take in my art - much to the chagrin of my reps and my producers and my bank account and my fans who can’t stop asking me why making my next film is taking so long - all comes from the complexity of that opening oner… the palindromic narrative of novelty Harold Lloyd wall clocks in act one mirroring a tense third act where Christopher Lloyd hangs from a clock tower. My entire concept of what a film is supposed to be was watching a movie with 25 year old actors in old age makeup and flying DeLoreans. 
Maybe the whole reason I struggle with regret…constantly obsessing and trying to remember a different past…one where all my dreams came true and the rest of me was somehow magically fixed…one where I didn’t lose [redacted]…maybe I just grew up thinking time travel was possible and now this faulty way my mind developed is creating so much suffering and ruminating and I gotta just move the fuck on and accept that relationships end one way or another. That making movies is hard, even (especially?) after you win Gotham Awards and win legal battles against multimedia conglomerates. 
I can’t go back in time and teach my dad how to be a man who fights for what he believes in. I can’t retroactively invent rock n roll at a high school dance. I can’t skitch behind a car and ram the town bully into a manure truck. Maybe, just maybe, with the help of community/breathwork/sobriety/healthy living, I can teach my nervous system to trust me. Maybe someday I can learn to love myself into a sense of authenticity and womanhood, instead of relying on the love of others. Maybe soon I’ll be able to focus less on what I’ve lost, and finally see, feel, know, and soak in the gratitude of all that I have and all that is in front of me. I’ll enjoy the Question. I’ll embrace it…it’s God. It’s Possibility. Not knowing the future, not trying to control it. Having hopes and goals is fine but finally appreciating the process. Not manipulating it. Taking the ride. The journey. This is my dream. What I can aim for. Most days I wake up feeling like I’m late for something. A hole in my soul that says I am not enough…
If five year old me could see the woman in bed writing this letterboxd review, she’d know how that’s all bullshit. That the doubt and fear and regrets that haunt me are illusions. Nevermind that all her dreams came true, she’d just look at me know the truth of the Eternal Then, Now, and What’s to Come. She’d see the Flux Capacitor tattoo on my arm and say “oh thank god this is me.” That kid, watching the same worn down vhs copy of Back to the Future would see me and say, “you’re right on time.”

Title: The Godfather
Comment:
It’s almost impossible to say something new about The Godfather, a movie so deeply woven into our cultural bloodstream that even people who have never watched it can quote or reference it. Yet, every time I return to it, I understand again why this movie became legendary in the first place. The movie’s lasting power comes from a devastating truth about human nature: a single moment, a single crisis, can pull a person across an invisible threshold and transform them into someone they never imagined becoming. The movie traces that change with such inevitability that it feels both mesmerizing and frightening. The shift is subtle and gentle until you realize you are watching a soul reshape itself. It is honestly shocking that there are still people in the world who have not watched The Godfather, because witnessing that transformation is watching cinema understand humanity at its most delicate and dangerous.
What makes this masterpiece essential viewing, even today after endless parodies, quotes, references, and imitators, is that beneath the iconic scenes and legendary performances lives a story that understands how families shape us, protect us, and define who we become. There is a universal heartbeat under all of its grandeur. You don’t need to care about crime sagas or mid-century America to be moved by it; you only need to know what it feels like to grow, to choose, to lose, and to stand at a moment where the person you once were quietly steps aside. The reason people should finally sit down and watch The Godfather is simple: few movies let you experience transformation, with all its tragedy and clarity, the way this one does. It is not just a classic. It is a reminder of how stories can reveal the parts of ourselves we rarely have the courage to face.

Title: Task
Comment:
RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL
Task is a tale of two halves.
One of the things that moved me to give this one a shot was the raving reviews this miniseries from the mastermind behind Mare of Easttown kept receiving. All the 5-star ratings, the 96% on Rotten Tomatoes—this critical acclaim was baffling. Baffling because, for the first three or four episodes, it honestly felt like a bit of a chore to get through. The pacing was slow; between any truly eventful moments, nothing much seemed to happen. It was all buildup, with no apparent payoff in sight. Then, starting with episode five, things finally pick up, with episode six delivering one of the most exciting and thrilling moments I’ve seen on TV this year.
Now, I think the real problem with my initial enjoyment came from my own expectations. Despite what the poster might suggest—it certainly did in my case—this is not an action-packed crime procedural. Ultimately, it’s a heartfelt tragedy: traumatized souls navigating a world that demands empathy and kindness, yet stumbling through the shadows of their own pain, striving to do right but caught in the delicate web of human frailty and failure. All of this is wrapped in a crime procedural style very much in line with Mare of Easttown, taking its time to unfold, reaching its height in episode six and wrapping up incredibly well, full circle.
The performances resonate with quiet power, each actor painting their character’s inner world with subtle brushstrokes rather than bold declarations. Tom Periphrey’s Robbie Prendergrast is a portrait of a man caught in the delicate balance of desperation and denial—a family man trying to hold the pieces together, unaware that the cracks beneath will soon shatter everything. His shades of gray invite both sympathy and unease, a complex soul navigating a storm he can’t fully see.
Ruffalo’s weary FBI agent carries the weight of his own battles; every glance and twitch tells stories words cannot capture. The silent dialogue between these two men creates a haunting parallel, a dance of fate and consequence that lingers long after the scene fades. The supporting cast weaves seamlessly into this tapestry, their performances threading the story with emotion—sometimes fierce, sometimes fragile—pulling the audience into a world where every feeling counts, whether it’s sympathy for the flawed or disdain for the villains.
All in all, this slow-burning show rewards your patience with a truly satisfying payoff. The performances shine brilliantly, with standout work from Tom that captivates and moves. Title: Bugonia
Comment:
A movie filled with heavy-handed metaphors and shallow social critique elevated by a bombastic style and brilliant performances. As I watched, I was reminded of the toothless, "we get it guys, rich people suck" sentiment reflected in movies like Good Fortune and The Menu, only to learn that this movie was written by the screenwriter of The Menu. Like that earlier, less flashy movie, Bugonia can identify the problems, but doesn't have much to say beyond "shit sucks, right? kina funny tho." Amazon sucks, CEOs, girl boss culture, big pharma, it's all making people crazy. And as much as the movie goes to great pains (black and white fantasy sequences) to sympathize with the working-class characters, it nevertheless results in another Lanthimos freak-show, because at the end of the day these guys think Emma Stone is an alien, and they are doing bad things. 
I've see comparisons to Eddington, and there are interesting comparisons, sure, but Eddington succeeds at specificity, Eddington isn't afraid to get into the weeds, which you have to do to have genuine empathy for these conspiracy-brained people on the fringes. At the end of the day, Lanthimos and screenwriter Will Tracy can't help making it all a big joke. 
(SPOILERS FOR BUGONIA) 
Because of course she's actually an alien, why not? It's the obvious, necessary punchline. She eradicates human life as her final act, and we get to glibly admire the beautifully composed corpses of all these bad humans who (we must admit) have destroyed the planet. What's the point? One feels the director grinning self-satisfied, just beyond each eerily-composed frame.
Admittedly, Lanthimos is not a filmmaker I've ever loved. I will admit that the 2nd act of this movie is effective, there's tension and a few thrills, but it's undercut at every moment by this style and screenplay that refuses to take it all too seriously, lest we empathize too much with these weirdos. It all feels too easy, exactly what you'd expect Hollywood's favorite weird auteur to make out of America's polarized political climate.

Title: Happiness
Comment:
"Everyone has their pluses and minuses," says Philip Seymour Hoffman near the end of this movie - a line that serves as the film's ironic thesis statement. This movie is unsettling less for the horrors that happen mostly offscreen, and more for the way it presents a group of differently flawed characters in the same tonal register. Dylan Baker is a suburban dad who is secretly a child molester; his wife (Cynthia Stevenson) is smug, casually cruel, and an enthusiastic player of her role in the patriarchal capitalist order; and nothing in Solondz's flat, prosaic style directs you to despise one more than the other. In this way, Solondz gets at something very real about the world. When you were growing up, did you ever find out that a certain member of your school staff was dismissed for... reasons? There was never any ominous music to underline they were a villain.
To the extent that Baker's character garners empathy, it's because he lives in a sick and hypocritical society (which finds its living embodiment in his wife), and because he is recognizably human. Is there a side of you that you keep hidden from the world? Have you ever compartmentalized actions that contradict your self-conception as a Good Person? But acknowledging this doesn't redeem Baker, who really is a monster. Also, while Hoffman's sexually-maladjusted obscene phone-caller is pathetic, he's not some kind of misunderstood "loveable loser" either. He channels his self-loathing into terrorizing women. We see very little evidence of goodness in him. 
Watch this movie on mute and, save for a couple of moments, you might assume it's a normal Sundance indie. Most of the horror is implied, or introduced through jarring dialogue in scenes that otherwise look or feel like any other scenes. This is not to say that Solondz is a strictly hands-off observer - he's often nudging you in the ribs with cruel little bits of irony. This movie is a comedy, and not afraid to be funny, or to traffic in feelings beyond the obvious revulsion and disapproval. The scene where Baker drugs his family plays with our emotions the way that Hitchcock does; when the little boy declines to eat his sandwich, it's like when Marion Crane's car briefly stops sinking in the swamp in Psycho. And instead of ending on a note of transcendence/epiphany, like the similarly-themed American Beauty does, the movie ends on a couple of sick jokes. If you haven't taken anything from the previous two-plus hours, you're not going to be spoon-fed anything in the last minute. Forget about any reassurance that you're a good person for watching this.
I should be careful about big declarations like this, but Dylan Baker gives one of the greatest performances of all time here. The thing about compartmentalizing parts of your personality is, you can never really do it. Those parts exist, and will eat you up from the inside. Baker's character is paralyzed by the role he has to play, and so never veers too far from a studied placidity. He communicates so much in micro-gestures and small shifts in tone, like the little "Oh!" he lets out when his wife tells him that a certain boy's father is on the phone.

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
“Grace for the guilty.”
The healing power of belief in doing good. Of finding God in service to others on our road to Damascus. Of redemption through love. And finally, in forgiveness and acceptance. 
The best Rian has ever been. The best Yelden has ever been. A bleeding heart of faith and desire for peace in a broken world fueled by fear and division. Guilt isn’t just brushed off or played for plot points, rather, it’s handled from beginning to end with the heavy gravitas it deserves. 
Need to see it again to really breakdown and dive into every little detail, it’s so thematically dense and rich I decided to just soak it up this time. To feel that sunlight on my face. To have my moment on the road to Damascus. Recently, as recently as last night, I have been plagued with thoughts of despair. Of how division is impossible to overcome, and how our world of misinformation and bad faith community built on exploitation and hatred of an enemy can never be fixed. 
But when the final title card appeared, and its difference from how it looks at the beginning…I felt it all wash away. Not because the movie has some heavy handed “life is worth living” ending, but because we can do the hard thing. We can forgive. We can forgive ourselves, each other, and we can find the strength to keep going.
The world isn’t a wolf. I love you Rian. I would’ve been so pissed if I watched this on my TV for the first time.

Title: Cinema Paradiso
Comment:
RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL
ON THE ROAD - LE STRADE ITALIANE: PASTA, GRANDE IMPERO E LA TERRA DEI MIEI ANTENATI
What’s left to be said about this film that hasn’t been said before? It is undoubtedly the greatest love letter to cinema ever to grace the screen. It tells a tale of an endearing friendship anchored by cinema. Even when we reach the romance, we see Salvatore using a camera to film his source of affection, and we get that final scene in which movies and love literally come together, full circle, in one of the most moving moments in cinema, elevated by Morricone’s minimalist but powerful score that captures distinctive tones and often becomes a character on its own. There’s even a scene where Alfredo manages to have a film screened in the plaza, showing the passion this small village had for cinema, where they would find joy just by seeing the film, even with no audio. The picture is where the magic resides, and just seeing their favorite movie is enough for their spirits to be uplifted.
Another thing that makes this film so brilliant is the collection of characters. As I said, the friendship between Salvatore and Alfredo is just beautiful—an old man with no children and a child who has lost his father both create this missing bond in a way that warms my heart. Cascio, as the kid version of Salvatore, was such a cutie; he brought out that sense of wonder and innocence capable of breaking the shell of our initially grumpy old man. Noiret, as Alfredo, was fantastic as well—you can see through his eyes and expressions the passion and love he had for cinema. Every time he watched a film, his face would light up like sunshine. I even enjoyed the small characters who served as great comic relief, such as the priest who can’t stand people giving a kiss (though, to be honest, there were some spicy scenes) and got disturbed whenever a scene of romance popped up.
If I had any negatives, I’d say the second half wasn’t as strong as the first. Other than the ending, everything with Salvatore and his newfound love with this girl was fine, but I honestly didn’t care that much. Though this is redeemed by the final scene where, as I said, romance and love for cinema are intertwined, and Perrin’s physical performance and the score make the scene work so well.
All in all, this is a film that grabs you from the very first second, bolstered by some incredible performances, a really great script, and technical work that will surely leave a lasting impression after the film ends.

Title: GoodFellas
Comment:
"Now go home and get your fucking shinebox."
If Scorsese's career were a cathedral, Goodfellas would be the stained-glass window. I think this is his most effortlessly rewatchable film. He has this ability to take stories of moral decay and make them feel exhilarating without ever losing sight of their cost. I know that he has a lot of mob movies and I understand the sentiment that many of his films can feel like the same thing. 
With all due respect, you're wrong.
As far back as anyone can remember, Henry Hill wanted to be a gangster. Ray Liotta, to me, fits so well between De Niro's cool menace and Pesci's feral volatility. Henry isn't the toughest guy or the craziest or, quite frankly, the most ambitious. He is the most relatable guy and his eyes tell us exactly what he's thinking constantly. I love his eyes. 
Behind all of the excited bravado that he has in this life, his eyes are always saying, "I hope I don't die today." His arc is so organic too. He goes from this confident young man to someone more grounded in the world to finally detonating in a coked-out panic.
Scorsese follows the rhythm of Henry's heartbeat with his signature kinetic camerawork. It looks so good and it's further developed by the unforgettable editing. Thelma and Scorsese don't really transition between scenes. More glide or snap depending on where Henry is psychologically. 
The cocaine sequence is just fucking magnificent. I feel this building anxiety every time I watch it, even though I know what's coming. The helicopter overhead, the time jumps, the switches between drugs, cooking sauce, paranoia.
Opposite that anxiety is Robert De Niro being cool, calm, and collected. He's too cool to lose his shit (most of the time). Each time I watch him in something, I'm amazed at the command that he has. He doesn't need to explode to be terrifying. He just needs to exist in a room. Few actors can turn a friendly wave into a murder attempt. 
"Go pick up some dresses at the store around the corner." 
Fuck.
Joe Pesci is doing what Joe Pesci does best: being fucking crazy. Pesci is obviously small in stature, but gigantic in presence. Tommy talks fast, moves fast, loves fast, kills faster. He has the emotional logic of a child, but it's unbelievable how Pesci makes so much uncertainty feel real. He's the king of gaslighting. I have to admit though that it is very satisfying to see him get what he deserves.
Can't forget Lorraine Bracco. Karen Hill is the character in this that makes what could be a regular mob film into a tragedy. I feel like there are two points of view here. We have Henry's narration of course, but Karen is the seismic shift that happens. 
The man inside it and the woman drawn in from the outside. Ray Liotta and Bracco match each other so well and at no point is she overshadowed. She carries her own weight and does a hell of a job.
A moment that stands out to me every time is when Henry breaks the fourth wall in the courtroom. This buildup just keeps coming and he's finally like, "You know? Fuck this. Let's talk to you fuckers directly." The mob gave him purpose and excitement. Anonymity gives him nothing. He doesn't learn a lesson, but just loses the life he loved. It's his own personal purgatory.
Thirty-five years later, Goodfellas still remains one of the best mob films of all time. I love films that are long, but don't feel long. Where you're completely and utterly sucked in entirely.
Five stars hardly seem enough.

Title: The Lady Vanishes
Comment:
Well, I have to say, that was disappointing. Disappointing for two reasons: the book being a masterclass in suspense and Alfred Hitchcock being considered the "Master of Suspense". And bearing that in mind, I believe that creating expectations for a film adaptation in his hands, wasn't entirely my fault. Especially since my experience with "Psycho" a long time ago, I remember finding it a masterclass in filmmaking. But while one holds this title for me, The Lady Vanishes is a masterclass in resilience, in how not to give up halfway through and go all the way to the end. Even if it's unaffectedly boring.
Drawing parallels initially with the original material, we had: A beginning that contextualized us well regarding the peculiarities and characteristics of each of the guests of that hotel (which was the initial basis to be used later in the train sequence). We had a much more detailed and prolonged dialogue between Iris and Miss Froy before her disappearance, giving us much more substance to develop our theories. And the entire unfolding of events, from Iris's certainty, her distrust of those people, and the mystery, made for an excellent read that didn't let up until the last page.
Many of the things I read created considerable expectations in me, imagining how they would be reflected in the adaptation, also taking into account that the reading was quite short - which, in my opinion, wouldn't be a big problem. But The Lady Vanishes brought an extremely fast-paced narrative rhythm, and ironically, also very slow. Given that the mystery is solved in less than 30 minutes, subsequently leading to an hour of something unnecessarily unstimulating and tiring, since what gave meaning to the narrative was completely revealed to us.
Still regarding the pacing, even with the mystery solved, the film's persistence in including scenes that try to suggest the theory that it's all in Iris's head, for some reason, even after the early confirmation that it's not, is still present.
In the end, I went to brush my teeth to try get rid of the bad taste in my mouth after such a waste.

Title: The Others
Comment: Filmed in Sepia and almost complete darkness, the film builds tension slowly, as if the air were getting harder and harder to breathe. Amenábar clearly didn’t choose to make this tension through some crazy horror spectacle, but through deprivation: the deprivation of clarity, of certainty, of sunlight, and even of loved ones. What we cannot see becomes the engine of fear; what is missing becomes louder than what remains. Nicole Kidman, perfectly chosen for this brittle, haunted role, gives the story its emotional stability. And while Amenábar occasionally inclines too heavily on atmosphere as if it could fully replace thematic depth, there’s no denying the craft behind it all. A work that feels meticulously orchestrated; stylish, eerie and undeniably clever.

Title: Wolfwalkers
Comment:
A mythical painting brushed with a prehistoric touch, carrying its own nature-(wolf)-forged tale, whispered legends etched into bark. Such an amazing animation.
A powerful story that hides within it surprising layers of history and a whole constellation of viewpoints, shifting depending on which direction you approach it from. Moore and Stewart have crafted a world for me that feels inherited, where both the style and the story speak in their own ancient dialect, and that demands genuine admiration. And that’s exactly why I’m sitting here on my couch, smiling like an idiot.
And the animation style itself is wonderfully odd. It leans heavily on the spirit of 70s–80s animation, yet it carries this modern touch that slightly warps the vibe, in a good way....maybe. What I loved most is how the film keeps bending itself, changing its visual rhythm in subtle ways, creating a kind of symmetrical imperfection that feels alive, as if the world were breathing past the edges of the frame. At the same time, this shifting design helps its rewatch value, some scenes genuinely look like old, hand-painted tapestries that tilt their perspective. I can’t fully explain it, but there’s this perfect artistic roughness intertwined with a sense of absolute polish. Or at least that’s how it feels🤔
The music is chef's kiss. The voice acting flows naturally, and the characters sit at the very top, the fierce protectiveness of parenthood, the wild rebellion of childhood, and the cold, structured cruelty of authority all collide in a surprisingly emotional balance. World that breathes, its rules, its forest, everything feels alive in a way that connects us closer to the idea of returning to nature and recognizing its fragile beauty. Outwardly, it’s simple, but the entire thing could’ve collapsed into overacting or heavy-handed directing. But, they hold it together with an instinctive sense of balance.
So, in the end, this is a "masterpiece" in its own strange, defiant way. A film that refuses to stay inside the lines, and I mean literally and that rebellion shows through its animation. It remembers an older era while rooting itself in a modern gaze that somehow clicks perfectly. The film takes a risk, leaps without hesitation, and the final result is exactly the creature it wants to be.
And now, if you’ll excuse me, I’m going to go run with the wolves while listening to it, because sometimes I just want to feel what perfection feels like.
89/100

Title: The Tragedy of Macbeth
Comment:
That witch needs some lip balm, and fast.
Hmmmm… It’s not a leap into madness so much as an existential form of embellishment, a distortion that lights itself from all the wrong angles. Coen carries a strange vision here, an extremely controlled and beautifully monochrome work that reminds me of something specific, yet I can’t quite place my finger on it, so it will likely haunts somewhere in the back of my mind for the rest of the week. But in its own peculiar way, this is a bold film. Coen seems determined to strip away every unnecessary layer, and what ultimately remains is something people are bound to interpret in different ways. And I mean will you like it or not.
The story itself is familiar, the good old erosion of morality. Visuals shows the amplification of personal hallucinations clothed in archaic costume yet housed within starkly modern architecture. The tragic impulse grows from an inner toxicity, a self-corroding force no one is capable of restraining once it has been unleashed. There are fragments scattered throughout of something impossible, destruction a nihilistic worldview sustains through its own strange, almost mystical gravity.
And extremely difficult to follow because, well… you know… and yet, somehow, this still manages to be a deeply gripping experience, especially if you surrender to the beautifully dissonant dialogue you struggle to decipher. The visuals completely overtake the film, and for good reason, expressionism filtered through a Bergman-esque severity of light and shadow. And maybe that is exactly what the imagery keeps reminding me of 🤔 There’s a sense of “clinical holiness” here, a purified, sterilized sacredness that feels ominous no matter how safe you think you are. The film reflects itself through its characters, most intensely through Macbeth’s inner landscape and I think Coen accomplishes that mirroring with remarkable precision.
So I don’t really know… I didn’t enjoy this in the conventional sense, not as something comforting or emotionally accessible, but it absolutely triggers my Shakespearean fascination at its best, because this is something wholly its own, an eerily symbolic cradle rocked by a raven darker than black itself, silently watching every move you make.
There’s a timeless energy radiating from it, because it refuses to anchor itself to any single era or setting. It exists in a kind of purgatory, where the beauty of the human mind is slowly devoured by greed and by whatever end your personal fate ultimately bares its teeth toward, whether you witness it through your own eyes or are compelled to look through someone else’s. The trinity is an unnatural, visibly chapped creature that never leaves anyone in peace, because this tragedy has no ending.
Eh… four stars.
78/100

Title: Ludwig
Comment:
35mm | Italian dubbed
Luchino Visconti’s Ludwig feels like stepping into someone’s memories rather than a straightforward historical biopic. The four-hour version is not just preferable but essential because it allows Visconti to build a world where grandeur is both intoxicating and suffocating, where palaces look like gilded mausoleums and every gesture carries the weight of doomed ideals. This is a meticulous study of opulence rotting from the inside out, a portrait of a king whose romantic visions outpace the world’s patience. Helmut Berger plays Ludwig II with a mixture of fragility and stubbornness, turning him into a man who seems to be drifting between eras even while standing in the center of his own kingdom. The movie’s conversations rarely feel like filler. They’re windows into a man’s slipping grip on beauty, power, and himself.
It’s admittedly a long watch, and Visconti makes no attempt to hide that. The pacing isn’t slow for the sake of it. It’s slow because the story is about time stretching and bending around a lonely ruler who keeps chasing a dream that refuses to exist. The camera dwells on faces and architecture until you feel the chill of those empty halls, the stillness of a life increasingly defined by isolation. Yet even with its length and its occasional indulgence, the movie never feels hollow. It’s too beautiful for that, too invested in showing how ideals can collapse when the world refuses to meet them halfway. For anyone willing to settle in and truly watch it, Ludwig becomes a strangely moving experience. It’s a meditation on a life caught between fantasy and responsibility, showing that even the grandest visions can crumble in the quietest ways.

Just some quick initial thoughts! That was peak Disney they honestly cooked, not only is the film better than the original but it maintains the spark that got them to this point. The voice cast are all on their A games and I’m a huge Jason Bateman fan so I’m gonna be biased but he makes the film with his Nick Wilde character. All the returning cast feel authentic and developed, and the new additions are so welcome; Ke Huy Quan and Fortune Feimster being my favorites but there’s an infinitely stacked cast list ranging from wrestlers to Crocodile Hunter Robert Irwin playing a damn Koala, its elite. 
The world building in the first Zootopia was already so inventive, and the sequel truly elevated it. New vibrant locations and different terrains for all of these characters, it was meticulously designed and executed how they integrated new species. It made Zootopia feel like an even bigger, more lived-in metropolis, I already cannot wait to revisit the film to see all these amazing locations. 
The marsh market being one of my favorite new locations; it’s a water based town on the swampy outskirts. It features buildings above and below water, swim up bars, and a unique transportation system that uses water filled tubes for water animals to zoom across country through, it’s a stunning sight when we do see it in operation. 
I love how the city's infrastructure is central to the plot, exploring how the famous weather walls and urban planning itself created segregation between neighborhoods like the Marsh Market, giving the world a real world resonance. It’s well executed and appeals so well to both children and adults alike, there’s something in this film for everyone. 
The relationship between Judy and Nick is the emotional core that holds the sequel together. We have seen them go from learning to trust each other, to now learning to work together, and of course they face trials and tribulations that deepens their undeniable chemistry, I’d love to see more of them. 
The vibrancy and detail is immaculate, there feels like another level has been achieved with an enhanced depth of field and richer color palettes that make everything so appealing to gaze at, its fantastic stuff. There’s scenes that are so heavily occupied I was curious how many animals they actually got on screen at times; I’m reading they managed to render some shots featuring as many as 50,000 unique animals on screen at the same time, all with individual fur and costume details.
