Title: Sentimental Value
Comment:
Monumental. After the success of The Worst Person in the World, Joachim Trier could’ve easily taken the guaranteed funding of his follow-up to do something huge in scale, as most filmmakers in his position would do. And in many ways he did, but instead of scale of things, he gave us scale in the form of emotion. I lived a dozen lives while watching Sentimental Value, it held a mirror up to me from all angles. In it I saw my many selves, and how they reflect similarly off of those I love. I saw my past, future and present, as foggy as they are clear. And I saw the storyteller I want to be within the storytelling I admire, even if the stories I do tell take a different shape.
By and large cinema feels quite lost right now, and subsequently I often feel quite lost when engaging with contemporary work in the medium. I simply don’t think we have found a way to tell modern stories yet. In particular stories set in the present, but also more broadly stories about humanity from the perspective of the present. Everything is either slavishly indebted to the past, or caught up in technological musings that’ll be dated within a year. To run you must first stumble, though perhaps having something to stumble towards is a nice start. If you’re stumbling for too long, maybe sit down and look around for a second.
This is all to say, of our contemporary directors, I think Joachim Trier has found something truly “now”. Each of his films could not be removed from their present context. Like all the best stories they speak to humanity as a whole, but also capture so specifically what it means to be human in our world today. Things like cellphones, laptops and streaming services aren’t distracting nuisances like they are in most films that try to incorporate them, but they also aren’t ignored outright. They are there, plain and simple, as they are in our lives, for better and worse. Same goes for the feelings and struggles of modern life, depicted so earnestly, without the slightest exaggeration. 
Sentimental Value reaches the rare esteem of a film I will aim to revisit many times in my life, not just because I want to, but because I feel I must to better understand myself.

This is the only time in my entire life that I have sat through the credits all the way until the very end. First, I could hear the birds, then the crickets, and then a thunder rolled in — a storm broke out and the calming rain followed.
The credits were the best thing about this film. I happened to catch a late screening, and there were maybe one or two other people in the cinema with me. I just sat there at the end with my eyes closed, listening.

Apart from the peaceful outro, Bugonia was a bit of a panic attack. A panic attack that I honestly found myself enjoying very much. I loved the bees, I loved their meaning, I love what they do on earth — I fucking love bees. Next time I encounter a bee, I’ll just sit there and let it walk all over me, because I know it is one of God’s most beautiful creations.

I just really liked this film. I thought it was very relevant to where we are in the world. Ordinary, humble, honest lower- and middle-class workers are used and overshadowed by the higher ranks. Their hard work gets overlooked, just like the innocent, thankless hard work of bees.
We forget what will happen after we go extinct. Just like the bees emerged from the corpse of a dead ox (according to the old myth), the bees will emerge from our dead bodies too. It brings me peace to know that life will go on. Maybe not human life — but the bees will keep buzzing.

And so, while Teddy and his dear cousin Don are completely psychotic, I somehow found myself standing by their side. This CEO woman who tells people to do this and that — and never takes a single second out of her day to think about how much fatigue and sweat her subordinates endure just to keep her on her pedestal — deserved to realise what she was doing with her life. And while kidnapping her and torturing her in a basement might not have been the best method… they got there in the end, didn’t they?

Maybe I’ll become a beekeeper? I mean, I put honey in my yoghurt every morning, and the only real way to repay them for their hard work would be to work hard alongside them, wouldn’t it?

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
"That poor girl."
“Start fighting wolves, and before you know it, everyone you don’t understand is a wolf.”
"I have to do it of my own free will, or it won't mean anything."
As a former youth group kid, Rian Johnson’s Knives Out movies have always been, whether implicitly or explicitly, about God.
It started with the lightning-in-the-bottle of the first movie: a film already chock-full of references to Johnson's evangelical childhood, from a 90s Christian rock needledrop in the background of a bar scene to the name of Chris Evans' character Ransom, inspired by CS Lewis's Space Trilogy. But these undercurrents go deeper than being simply (as Blanc might say) ornamental. The very eschatology of Knives Out's climactic ending comeuppance is one of the upside down kingdom of Christ: the last shall be first, and the meek and lowly shall inherit and dwell in the House of God with the rich left outside gnashing their teeth. My house, my rules, my coffee.
Who could be said to represent "God" in the first Knives Out film? A compelling argument could be made for Christopher Plummer's Harlan Thrombey. Harlan is the one who wills everything he owns to his lowly caregiver Marta, not unlike the father who freely gives away his fortune in the Prodigal Son narrative or Christ's various parables about a "master of the house" in which the master often gives more generously or openhandedly than the story’s audience would have found remotely reasonable. The Thrombey family's appalled reaction to Harlan's generosity toward Marta could be compared to the way Christ's most scrupulously religious listeners reacted toward his suggestion that Gentiles might have more purehearted faith than themselves, and that the "unclean" might inherit the heavenly reward that the supposedly "clean" had taken for granted as belonging to them.
In all of these ways, and as the benevolent enactor of this turning-of-the-tables, Harlan Thrombey works as a sort-of God the Father surrogate. With emphasis on the "father" component, because Harlan is also dealing out "tough love" to each of his children right before his death, giving and taking away in ways that none of them fully comprehend but that he knows as a parent will be for their ultimate good. As a great writer and storyteller (another parallel with the divine) Harlan is blessed with the sight and perception to love each child in his house with both affection and knowledge of their selfish brokenness. He wants what is best and most dignity-giving for them all, even if it means pain and confusion in the short term: “Please accept my decision with grace and without bitterness,” Harlan says in his will, “but do accept it, it’s for the best.”
Speaking of sight and perception, however, we've been overlooking another reflection of God before us in the first film: Benoit Blanc himself, of course. The character of Benoit Blanc, and much of detective fiction more broadly, fulfills a certain longing within mankind: namely, the desire for a good and righteous judge to correctly see what was done in the dark and bring it to the light. In this way, Blanc's pursuit of justice and truth throughout all of his outings takes on a profoundly spiritual layer; as a master detective, he is doing what we ordinary mortals cannot, and playing the role that deep down we hope the almighty might play someday too: "For there is nothing done in secret that will not be revealed."
Blanc, in all three movies, seems to see the human heart in ways that ordinary "law" enforcers often overlook, and frequently finds himself breaking the "rules" to defend characters who have been deemed guilty. I will never not be moved by Blanc telling Marta that “you are a good nurse,” and part of what makes it so heart-rending is the way that Blanc rightly perceives Marta's “kind heart” from the moment he meets her—much as Harlan does—even though he knows she's somehow mixed up in the crime. Not unlike the “ransom” atonement theory—in which God is made flesh in Christ to free humanity from the Accusation of Satan—Blanc sees through Marta (who has even declared herself guilty) and shows that because of her heart and her devotion to Harlan, she is actually innocent.
Much else could be extrapolated, of course, about Glass Onion. Though broadly excellent and cleverly-crafted and all the things, most people seem to agree this movie is ever-so-slightly the weakest of the three—and I think it might have something to do with the way it lacks the benevolence and kind heart of the original, more prominently focused on skewering the elite without reserve. If Harlan Thrombey was a flawed-but-noble patriarch and selflessly sacrificial representative for God the Father in the first Knives, Edward Norton's Miles Bron in Glass Onion is everything an atheist might say God really is: an egomaniac who thinks himself more worthy of worship and respect than he is, easily outsmarted by logic and reason once you stop affording his "grand plan" the benefit of blind faith. He's also, of course, just a brilliant commentary on billionaires like Musk and Zuckerberg who fancy themselves sort-of gods in the first place. And in this way, Benoit Blanc's final tearing-to-shreds of Bron's supposed brilliance could be viewed alternatively as either a dismantling of God himself or simply a deconstruction of the shallow men who play God in their arrogance and ego. Either way, the upside-down kingdom comeuppance of Knives Out is maintained in this entry by Janelle Monáe's Helen—though this comeuppance is less about the disinherited receiving good things and instead about watching the false idols of man burn to the ground in retributive spectacle. In the context of a Judeo-Christian framework, that desire to watch the shallow glass kingdom of the wicked go up in flames is far from uncommon. In many ways, it is the very foundation of the imprecatory Psalms, and John’s Apocalypse of Revelation.
But finally, we find ourselves at Wake Up Dead Man—where without a doubt, the spiritual subtext of previous entries is now text. All three Knives movies have a patriarch at the center of the crime, from Harlan Thrombey to Miles Bron to Jefferson Wicks. And if Miles Bron represented the wealthy elites who want to be gods, Wicks is clearly an indictment of those who would cynically use a religious platform to speak for God—all the while serving their own interests and ego. If Wicks were interpreted alternatively as God, it would be a very grim picture of the almighty indeed.
But despite all the ways it lambastes Wicks, Wake Up Dead Man's heart is not quite as vicious as Glass Onion—or, in some ways, even the first Knives Out. Much like Marta and Helen, Josh O'Connor's Father Jud Duplenticy stands out as a touchingly sincere center of good throughout the film, and an alternative to the version of faith presented by Wicks and his congregation—which Jud argues quite directly is "not the true church." And even in the fallibility of Wick's congregation, Johnson seems to have more empathy and tenderness than he did with the Thrombeys or the "Disruptors" in the previous two films. Fairly early in the movie, Father Jud pleads with Wicks to see the vulnerable humanity of his "flock" the way that he does; Jud is generous enough to perceive that Andrew Scott's Lee Ross is a deeply talented writer who has tragically gone down the conspiracy rabbit hole and needs help—much like Jeremy Renner's lonely Dr. Nat needs help, too. And Cailee Spaeny's Simone and Kerry Washington's Vera are largely purehearted people misguidedly putting their faith in Wicks when they should be putting it in God—a predicament that Wicks, of course, does not discourage. The only character in the “flock” whom Johnson unreservedly blasts is Cy Draven, a shallow political opportunist who seems to have no sense of moral compass or real faith beyond desire for power—and never once speaks about Christ as anything other than a political mascot. Cy, it might be noted, echoes the entitled attitude of the Thrombeys which views inheritance as deserved birthright.
Johnson’s critique of politically-motivated religious nationalism and wealth-obsessed cult-of-personality is, as always typical for him, extremely well-timed. Among other things, Brolin’s Wicks and the pathetic bootlicking devotion of his followers is a brilliant Trump commentary without being too on the nose. But what makes Wake Up Dead Man feel so personal, and so powerful, is the well-rounded picture of religion it paints in all its perversions and purities.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, we learn early in Wake Up Dead Man that Benoit Blanc is a skeptic toward religion and the almighty in every sense of the word. “I kneel at the altar of the rational,” he says, with a loaded monologue about every ill that the church has perpetuated because of a “fairy tale.” But the pairing of Father Jud and Blanc brings out profundity and growth from both of them. Jud allows Blanc to say his piece, if only because honesty is a virtue he holds highly—and it’s one that the film will continue to press throughout, with most of the mishaps and errors occurring because characters were not honest enough, either with others or with themselves. Even as much as Jud decries dishonesty, he gives into it when he hides the flask—and therefore, a crucial piece of evidence—to prevent others from finding out that Wicks was drinking. It’s an act of foolish grace for his enemy, and just as Glenn Close’s Martha will later say, “it started with good intentions.” But this is a detective story, where what is hidden cannot heal and truth must be brought to the light.
But then: what is truth? Jeremy Renner’s Dr. Nat clumsily asks this question midway through the film, which might seem like an offhanded joke, but the astute will know that it is the very question Pontius Pilate asks Jesus when he is on trial, knowing not that he is speaking to the very cosmic essence of truth made flesh.
Like most mysteries, much of the Knives Out series thus far has been focused on getting to the bottom of what “really” happened, and this makes up Benoit Blanc’s whole philosophy. But Father Jud’s perspective on truth is somewhat different: ”You're right. It's storytelling. The rites and the rituals...costumes, all of it. It's storytelling. I guess the question is, do these stories convince us of a lie? Or do they resonate with something deep inside us that's profoundly true, that we can't express any other way except storytelling?”
Later in the film, Blanc says outright that to solve this case, “I had to look at the myth that was being constructed, not to solve whether it was real or not, but to feel in my soul the essence of that which it strove to convey.”
Rian Johnson, then, views truth not necessarily as the simple logistical reality of “what happened” but as the deeper and more resonant human quality of “what it meant,” and “what it inspires.” It’s not so different from his interpretation of the Myth of Luke Skywalker in The Last Jedi, where Luke willfully steps into the realm of a “legend” to inspire people around the galaxy with his heroism and sacrifice, despite the fallibility of himself and the Jedi in general. Here, Rian seems to implicitly present the idea that regardless of whether all the things in The Bible “really happened,” purehearted faith and the way it can hearten a person and help them to love others (like “daily bread”) is undeniably beautiful and real, and that’s what matters most. For my part, I was deeply touched by the picture of embodied, welcoming, sustaining faith Rian paints with affection.
In some sense though, a non-believer's ode to the merits of religion can only go so far. We can talk about whether overtly poetic narratives like Genesis or Revelation are valuable regardless of whether they “really happened” or not; in that area, I tend to fit snugly with Blanc’s assertion that the “real truth” lies in what the story seeks to convey about the human condition and the broader character of God. I’ve often said myself that The Garden of Eden narrative is “true” regardless of whether it was “real.” But at the same time, crucially: The Apostle Paul said that Christians are fools to be pitied above anyone else if Christ was not really raised from the dead in the most literal and factual sense of the word. And so therefore, ultimately, any attempt to view Christianity as a "nice blanket" for the individual folks who happen to get something helpful out of it—regardless of whether it’s actually true or not—stands in some contradiction with the claims of Christianity itself. I think often about Flannery O'Connor's words: "What people don't realize is how much religion costs. They think faith is a big electric blanket, when of course it is the cross.” It could be argued that Rian is trying to have his cake and eat it too; he no longer necessarily believes Christianity is true, but he still sees the beautiful fruit of what it represents, and doesn’t want to let that go. I’m highly sympathetic toward this perspective, and altogether, I think his wrestling with what to take and leave from faith makes this film one of his most vulnerable and personal to date, and it's better for it. In a sense, it feels like Rian’s real conviction is torn between Jud and Blanc, made manifest in their butting heads onscreen. And here, Blanc’s pursuit of certain truth as “checkmate” is challenged by a novel contrast: the transcendent value of grace.
One of the most compelling moments in the movie is a scene where Jud—having just smashed a statue of Jesus while frantically looking for a secret Swiss bank account number—is asked by a stranger, Louise, to pray for her over the phone. Suddenly, his true purpose and conviction are made strikingly clear, and his frenzied search for “answers” is challenged by the reverence of his faith. I will always remember the way the theater went completely silent during this sequence, the woman’s humble need and vulnerability calling forth a palpable spiritual reality in the midst of the noise and the hunt for “the truth.” In the aftermath of this prayer, Jud tries to call it quits solving the crime with Blanc; he observes that if he is focused solely on “winning” or “beating” others with “finding answers,” then he is no different than Wicks, “making it all about myself and not Jesus.” It’s one of several moments that seems to take Blanc aback and rattle his worldview ever-so-slightly. And it’s a profound instance of self-critique, not just about this case but about religion in general; just a few scenes later, Spaeny’s Simone pleads, “can’t you just tell us the answer, isn’t that what all of this is for?” But Jud is right: when you approach God looking only for “answers” and “truth” and “rightness,” you make things about yourself and ignore the importance of relationship with both the divine and others. Father Lawrence from Conclave would probably have a word here: ”If there was only certainty, and no doubt, there would be no mystery…and therefore no need for faith.”
This isn’t the only moment that seems to rattle Blanc. Later, Father Jud is convinced that he needs to turn himself in for seemingly killing Samson: “I have to do it of my own free will,” he says, “or it won’t mean anything.”
This, of course, is the ethos of not just the Gospel but the entire Bible. God gives humanity free will because he wants us to be able to come to him of our own accord—real love, real repentance, and real grace would not be possible any other way. Christ used that same free will to freely give his life for us, while we were yet guilty, not out of obligation but out of genuine affection, adoration, and desire for reconcile.
The most ironic paradox in the film’s conclusion is that despite his lack of belief, Blanc ultimately becomes a surrogate for the almighty once again—calling everyone to attention from the pulpit with his final monologue and forcing them all to sit in reverent silence. But Blanc has learned a different kind of justice and truth from Father Jud, and the further he gets into his “laying bare the sins of the wicked,”—something he had little problem doing in Glass Onion—the more he realizes that this charade is more about his own ego and intellect and “right”ness than anything else, fighting wolves not unlike Wicks himself. In his “Damascus moment,” Blanc does not suddenly come to believe in God, but he does decide to lay down his arms of his own free will and accept defeat—at least in public—for the sake of reconcile. In this way, Blanc—previously a surrogate for God’s righteous exposing judgement—now becomes a representative of Christ in his mercy and sacrifice. Like Christ being willingly mocked and scorned on the cross, Blanc plays the “holy fool,” allowing the world to think that he has been unable to crack the case when in fact he is giving the guilty party free will to confess of their own accord. It’s a stunning portrayal of the Gospel, made all the more ironic by the fact that Jud’s prayer for God to help him through this trial has been answered in the form of an atheist who haphazardly takes on the role of Christ.
And Blanc’s sacrifice to play the fool and afford the guilty free will pays off. Martha, convicted by his example, repents and confesses her sin to Father Jud, allowing him to fully embody his role as a priest (“do what you were born to do,” Blanc urges him) for the first time in the film. In finally repenting, Martha is able to reframe her shame-laden version of the “harlot whore” and see her as she really was: ”that poor girl.” Through being given grace, Martha finally sees Grace—and in laying down her arms and answers, she rightly understands truth.
What is truth? Perhaps, truth is found through grace. Seeing the heart with grace. And grace itself is a divine mystery—a mystery that even the world’s greatest detectives will never quite crack.

Title: Resurrection
Comment:
Cinema continues to amaze me. Just when I think I’ve seen everything a film has to offer, a film like this comes along and surprises me with its boldness, its innovation, and the shocks it delivers through purely cinematic means. This film contains many things I’ve never encountered before: images and techniques that feel entirely new, as if someone is stretching cinema’s skin from the inside. Watching it was an experience unlike any other, much like the journey of one hundred years of film history through various films and styles. Each chapter of the film has a different body, a different mood, and a different rhythm than the previous one. Like a rollercoaster, the film keeps moving forward through every possible direction in art, design, and music, and in some instances, overwhelms me as I’m being immersed in a sensory orgy that pulls me in before I even have the chance to leave.
At this late stage in my life, and having been exposed to different styles, languages, and formats of filmmaking over the years, I sometimes reflect on what the future of cinema will be like long after I am gone. This movie gives me an odd kind of comfort and reassurance and reminds me that cinema will go on after me, evolving in ways that I won't be here to see but which I can sense building up. As part of the intense experience I had watching this, it also helped answer a question I’ve long carried: cinema doesn’t die-it resurrects.
There are always people questioning if cinema will eventually die. This seems to happen every few years or so, much like some superstition that we cannot shake. Each time a new technology is created, a change occurs within people's viewing habits, or the cinema industry goes through one of its periodic moments of crisis, there are those that fear cinema is slowly disappearing from existence.
Cinema has been 'dead' many times over in people's imaginations. People worried that cinematography would be diminished by the use of sound back when sound was first introduced to film. With the introduction and success of television, studios believed that no one would ever leave their homes again to watch movies on the big screen. With the advent of the internet and streaming platforms, we saw a shift towards customers being drawn to the ease and convenience with which they could access film, and there were many theorists speculating that the ritual surrounding people going out to the movie theatre would eventually disappear. Yet every time, cinema continues on.
Every time, cinema resurrects itself, taking new forms and discovering new shapes. At times, it may expand into spectacle, at other times it may decrease into intimacy and at some points, it will travel into weird, experimental areas as the film has a right to do. This film demonstrates just how this principle manifests. Each of the six chapters in this film (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch and mind) has a different cinematic manifestation. One chapter flickers like a silent film, fragile and dreamlike; another sinks into noir shadows; another leans into expressionist distortion; another unfolds in a long, unbroken take that stretches time itself. This film thus demonstrates that while film continues to be one medium, it continues to demonstrate the potential of many forms living within that single medium, and repeatedly surprises me with what film will become next.
Through all these changes, cinema has never stopped existing. It continues as long as humans have the urge to create, to dream, and to remember. Humans will always want to make records of their lives and, in turn, turn those records into moving images that other human beings can feel.
Cinema won’t die. It will resurrect itself, as it always has. Theaters may shrink, technologies may rise, the formats we cherish may drift to the margins. But somewhere, someone will still feel the need to pick up a camera, not for content, not for trend, but because they have something burning inside them, their dreams, that can only be expressed on the silver screen through light and movement.
And as long as there are people like Bi Gan who dare to dream, who dare to see cinema as a language of emotion and sensation, who believe cinema is alive and will survive us all, filmmaking continues to be resurrected.
As long as people need to dream, as long as people let art set their dreams on fire, letting it burn through the night and into the sunrise, refusing to dim even when the world changes around it, cinema remains alive. not frozen in the shape we once knew, but shifting, restless, and still carrying that flicker of humanity that no machine, no platform, no cultural shift has ever managed to extinguish.

Title: Die My Love
Comment:
Far more conceptual than it's getting any credit for - that last shot-reverse shot between Jennifer Lawrence and the house interior, my god! Totally unapologetic about its manic energy and its rapid swings between devastating and hilarious: lesser filmmakers will find tension in making every shot a handheld close-up, but here the tension emerges out of a late 30s couple moving into a parents property as they struggle with reconciling basic domestic life, raising a child, and yet unexplored sexuality. It's like the first film that's actually *about* millennials. Actually kind of dazzling because there's no judgement from Ramsey on her characters, which allows the core subtext to emerge virtually immediately; a dichomity that's realized within seconds of the movies opening, which is between the process of taking a care of a baby with the carnal sexuality that produces one. The hyper-stylized register that the film is operating in is all about making this tension visceral - the actors have to exaggerate, because it has to relate the intensity of feeling and experience in conjunction with the form of the film itself.
Jennifer Lawrence is out of this world good here - one of the best performances in any movie this decade, and she manages a remarkable balance in both naturalism and this exaggerated approach. Conversely, it appears Pattinson is holding all the cards close to his chest - at first. It almost seems like Pattinson is working with substantially weaker material until you realize this too is central to the films tension: he's like the comedic "straight man" archetype - Dean Martin to Lawrence's Jerry Lewis. Anyways, this is wearing everything on its sleeve - what's not to like? Unpopular opinion (for now?) but this is my favorite of Ramsey's films.

Title: It Was Just an Accident
Comment:
From The New Republic: newrepublic.com/article/201114/jafar-panahi-just-accident-revenge-road-trip-masterpiece

“I’m not that brave,” the Iranian director Jafar Panahi told Film Comment in an interview earlier this year. “I’m just doing my job. I’m making my films…. I feel a bit embarrassed when this is seen as courage.”
Such humility is becoming in any filmmaker, especially one clutching a Palme d’Or. The citation, bestowed at Cannes upon Panahi’s new film, It Was Just an Accident, gave the 65-year-old director a lifetime sweep of the world’s top film festival prizes, along with a Golden Bear from Berlin and a Lion from Venice. Panahi’s modesty serves as an extension of the humane sensibility that suffuses his films—an empathy that transcends simple technique. It also belies the obvious and lamentable fact that Panahi has had a very hard time doing his job for some while now.
The 1979 Islamic Revolution didn’t just transform the Iranian film industry. It rendered it a shadow of its former self, with directors forced to observe strict limitations on form and content in the name of religious purity. Panahi began working as an army cinematographer in the early 1980s, enrolling in film school after his military service and producing a series of television documentaries before shooting his beguiling, child’s-eye debut, The White Balloon, in 1995. He is a fluid, intuitive storyteller and a conscientious social critic; he has a gift for crafting deceptively conceptual story structures and for making the quotidian signify beyond itself.
Rather than submit to the dictates of Iran’s Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance—where the buck stops for filmmakers in search of official support or theatrical distribution—Panahi has continually striven for creative freedom, whether via procedural ruses like submitting fake scripts for committee approval or else by ignoring the authorities’ input entirely. The extravagant praise bestowed on his films by international critics has, predictably, served to exacerbate his perceived enemy-of-the-state status at home; in 2010, following a series of increasingly public skirmishes with the authorities, Panahi was detained and imprisoned by the Iranian government on charges of disseminating propaganda against the regime. He was sentenced to six years in prison (a stretch eventually reduced to house arrest) and also a 20-year ban on travel, foreign media interviews, and filmmaking of any kind. The latter, it seemed, was a cruel and unusual punishment: an edict designed both to staunch a fearless artist’s output, and also to break his spirit.
It didn’t work—at all. Throughout the 2010s, Panahi conjured up a series of small, clandestinely shot films that dramatized, fictionalized, and allegorized his experiences, often with a wry sense of humor. The Magritte-inspired title of Panahi’s 2011 masterpiece This Is Not a Film, a ruefully funny video diary primarily shot on an ­iPhone in the director’s apartment, precisely annotated the nature of its maker’s resistance: It proclaimed that he was following the rules set down from on high even as he was breaking them, an act of cinematic sleight of hand in manacles, and with his fingers crossed slyly behind his back.
“Nothing can prevent me from making films since when being pushed to the ultimate corners I connect with my inner self,” said Panahi in 2015. “Despite all limitations, the necessity to create becomes even more of an urge.”
That urgency can be felt throughout It Was Just an Accident, which is the first movie that Panahi has made on the other side of his filmmaking ban, as well as his first since being released from a seven-month stint in Tehran’s notorious Evin prison in 2023. (He was jailed for inquiring about the status of a fellow anti-establishment director, Mohammad Rasoulof.) Technically, It Was Just an Accident is the work of a free man, but it feels more obsessive than liberated, as it plunges deeply into the minutiae and metaphysics of imprisonment. In formal terms, it might be Panahi’s most conventional piece of work since the 1990s, but accessibility shouldn’t be mistaken for compromise. It’s a bristling, brilliant piece of work: a swift and rollicking comic thriller whose autobiographical subtext lies under the surface, like an engine beneath a chassis, or a body stowed in the trunk.
Things begin innocuously enough. We open on a prosperous-looking family puttering their way back to the city down a country road at night, their car’s interior illuminated from within by the glow of a little girl’s iPad. The driver, Eghbal (Ebrahim Azizi), is middle-aged and handsome, framed head-on through the car’s windshield, a camera setup nodding directly to Iranian art-film tradition (including Panahi’s own Taxi). Suddenly, there’s a bump in the road. Eghbal has driven over a dog. He doesn’t seem too broken up about it. “What will be will be,” sighs his wife. “God surely put it on our path for a reason.” “He killed a dog,” replies her daughter evenly from the back seat. “God has nothing to do with it.”
Like his wife—who, it turns out, is pregnant with their second child— Eghbal may be a true believer, but he isn’t given any opportunities of his own to opine about divine intervention. Rather, he’s swiftly reduced to a prop: drugged, battered dead weight, trussed-up and locked away in the back of a van driven by Vahid (Vahid Mobasseri), the film’s true protagonist. Vahid was working the late shift at a roadside warehouse when Eghbal brought in his wrecked car for repairs; watching from the shadows, Vahid recognized the interloper’s voice—and the squeaking of his prosthetic leg—as belonging to the notorious torturer at Evin known colloquially as “Peg Leg.” Vahid is a quiet man with no desire to revisit his past, but one accident begets another. What will be will be. The question: Did God put Peg Leg in Vahid’s path for a reason? Or does God have nothing to do with it?
There is one obvious precedent for Panahi’s scenario: Chilean writer Ariel Dorfman’s acclaimed play Death and the Maiden, in which an ex-political radical suffering PTSD reencounters—and then abducts—the Pinochet stooge who brutalized her behind closed doors. That play was adapted for the screen (very effectively) by Roman Polanski in 1994, but the movie that came to mind more for me during It Was Just an Accident—a good deal of which is set inside Vahid’s vehicle as it winds its way through town, taking on passengers at regular intervals—was Abbas Kiarostami’s Taste of Cherry, which stands at the very apex of the New Iranian Cinema. In Kiarostami’s film, a man named Mr. Badii drives around in search of a stranger who will agree to quietly bury him after he commits suicide; his peregrinations provide a microcosmic glimpse at the surrounding society. The same picaresque principle applies to Panahi’s film, but where the hitchhikers and bystanders in Taste of Cherry are reluctant to abet a religiously forbidden act of self-negation, Vahid’s fellow passengers—a bookseller, a bride-to-be, a wedding photographer, and a construction worker—are all ex-detainees like himself. They express a shared desire to dance on Peg Leg’s grave, which has already been dug in the middle of the desert, much like the one for Mr. Badii.
It is a thin line between parable-like simplicity and outright contrivance, and It Was Just an Accident circumnavigates its chosen route smartly; the slight bumpiness of the dramaturgy works in a story where the man at the wheel isn’t always sure where he’s headed. Panahi has written the script to have a sense of the absurd; at one point, a character name-checks Beckett, and there are various satirical threads woven through the storyline. Vahid pays off a pair of skeptical security guards via a portable card reader—a bit of business that gets repeated later on at a hospital. At least the bribery is convenient: no cash required. Throughout, Panahi cultivates a strain of mordant comedy around the problems of transporting a body through a busy city (this is surely the first Palme winner to evoke Weekend at Bernie’s). There’s also humor in the group’s sputtering, fractious interactions, but it’s rooted in authentic trauma. “He made me feel his rotten leg with a blindfold on, to prove his exploits in their fucking holy war,” moans Hamid (Mohamad Ali Elyasmehr), the construction worker, after examining the unconscious Eghbal’s body. “I’ve been running my hand over his leg for five years, in my nightmares.”
Hamid is ready to wring Eghbal’s neck where he lies and stands appalled by the idea of offering mercy to a man who destroyed so many lives. Others are more cautious, whether out of guilt, or doubt, or a sense of self-preservation. Shiva (Mariam Afshari), the wedding photographer, cannot be sure that the man in the van is Peg Leg. Like Vahid and Hamid, she never saw his face in prison. Moreover, she doesn’t know what should be done with him even in the case of a positive ID. Their captive is, after all, a husband and a father; when Eghbal’s cell phone inevitably rings, it’s his daughter—the little angel who mourned that poor dead dog—calling with news of an emergency that reroutes the movie’s plot (and the audience’s sympathies) while spiking the tension about whether or not the group has passed the point of no return.
There’s an element of gauntlet-dropping to Shiva’s character: Afshari is the first woman to appear in one of Panahi’s films without a mandatory hijab, and her vibe—thoughtful and cosmopolitan beneath a fashionable shank of silvering hair—makes her a complex avatar of social change, especially in a movie that maps the collateral damage of principled resistance. (In a nicely calibrated irony, Vahid’s van resembles those of the so-called morality police, whose remit is to enforce religious dress codes.) It’s Shiva who tries the hardest to pump the brakes on Vahid’s plan, and yet she also ends up delivering the film’s most harrowing speech, an outburst of pure fury that gives the impression of Panahi—who has necessarily had to play himself on-screen, for the last 15 years or so—addressing his captors through a distaff surrogate.
This penultimate sequence—lit expressionistically by deep-crimson brake lights and captured in a single, static, unblinking take—represents some of the most remarkable staging and direction of Panahi’s career; it sears through the screen, and lifts the veil, already thin and fluttering, on the film’s fiction. The coda, meanwhile, suggests a different kind of exposure, a gaping psychic wound that neither time nor distance will ever quite suture shut. The final moments find a key character paralyzed with fear and doubt, rooted to the spot as his past creeps up on him, one creaky footstep at a time. We’ll never know if he’s able to move on; the bravery of Panahi’s film lies in its maker’s own refusal to be overtaken. The movie is evidence of his mobility. He pushes forward, with his camera in hand: another job well done.

I noticed it was snowing quite heavily outside, decided it was only right to turn Batman Returns on. That decision was justified about 10 seconds in when the snowy WB logo appeared on my screen just before peak Batman business commenced. 
Tim Burton went crazy with this one, with the film deviating from the traditional superhero film structure and tone with it often feeling more like a dark, expressionist fable than a standard comic book sequel. They really do feel like lonely monsters attempting to connect in a world that has rejected and scarred them, it’s poetic and makes for a compelling two hours of entertainment. 
It’s one of the few comic book films that actually feels like a comic strip has been brought to life; from the characters to the world built it feels like it was ripped straight from the comics. The Penguin and Cat-woman with some unforgettable costume and makeup design, and the performances from both Pfeiffer and DeVito are second to none, perfect character’s for this special world, and I can imagine the costumes for both were incredibly uncomfortable! 
Tim Burton’s mind and Gotham go together so effortlessly, his vision for the world is full of distorted and claustrophobic architecture with an abundance of depth and smart lighting choices; the contrast between deep, inky shadows and bright highlights is expertly done.  
I love the snowy and Christmas setting, I forgot just how complete a Christmas film it is, tying the narrative all together with the relighting of the Christmas tree. I’ll definitely be adding this to my yearly Christmas rotation and I think you should too, it’s got the snowy Gotham backdrop, the Christmas lights and decorations, the Christmas trees; the one in Wayne’s Manor is a stunner, really can’t be denied as a Christmas film. 
The film is cool because it manages to be entertaining and accessible on the surface while simultaneously being complex and thematically rich underneath. I watched this with peskymason and he had a great time and probably didn’t understand much of the plot but the action and interactions are absolutely entertaining, really strong filmmaking from Burton and the acting across the board was solid, everyone understood the assignment. 
Only visited this film a couple of times but it’s rising in my superhero rankings, it’s truly a special film. It’s even got imo the greatest Batman theme song, I think it’s the one that played in the Lego Batman games so it’s nostalgic and awesomeness makes for a phenomenal combo. Such a great comic book film, and although Keaton isn’t my favorite Batman his portrayal is so great and I’d take these films over Batfleck all day.

Comment:
This really was a beautifully sad, languid film that captures a sombre tone that also has such rich imagery and is full of evocative music. It really is a haunting movie that stays with you while showcasing the beautiful northwest. Bentley gently portrays a simple mans life from boy to death full of happiness and loss. It deals a lot with sadness and being tortured by memories of regret and anguish but ends on one of hope in discovering the world and humanity in an unjust world.
Joel Edgerton(Robert Grainier) is really excellent here playing a quiet lead character observing the world in all it's facets and taking it in at times and rejecting it in other moments. It'd really smartly orchestrated as we follow his life with the occasional time jump to know that the story is not entirely dower. I was fascinated by the friendships and connections along his life and have to remark that it is kind of an opposite version of "Forest Gump" in which our protagonist takes his lumps.
I must admit that this is the first movie I've seen this year where I was getting a little misty viewing but I think it was well earned and heartfelt. I would totally recommend it if you like some amazing shots of forested hills and introspection.

Title: Hala
Comment:
Moment of breath, a small pause in the noise, a story about a Pakistani-American teenage girl, a coming-of-age tale where religion and identity collide beneath the surface.
Baig’s film may not draw me in the way it hopes to. It’s a story I can’t fully connect with because A) I’m not Pakistani living in America, and B) I’m not a teenage girl 🤔.
The film is softly intimate, yet also a quietly heavy experience, showing how suffocating a place can become when parental pressure, their past mistakes, and the confused turbulence of youth all fold into one seemingly simple narrative. The movie doesn’t really take risks, though it doesn’t have to. It just feels a little bit incomplete...
And these certain moments feel unfinished, not in a good way but I also sense what Baig is reaching for, because she positions us directly inside Hala’s uncertain footsteps. The film stumbles, yet when everything clicks… I somehow liked it. Not much, just a little, but enough to stay with me. So it becomes a film that is, in its own way, lost, its central soul drifting somewhere within that quiet storm. Baig understands how to shape emptiness, how to capture the struggle of searching for a direction in a world where that direction is already chosen for you.
So in the end, the movie rebels, but only with the fragile force of someone still young, still figuring themselves out. A stumbling piece of work, not groundbreaking or "earth-shattering", but undeniably a window into the life of someone whose experience I’ve never lived. And that’s exactly why films like this matter. A good movie, overall. Also Wiswanathan is great.
59/100

Title: Timecop 2: The Berlin Decision
Comment:
191st Review for The Collab Weekly Movie Watch
This film is like a better movie adaptation of Assassin’s Creed than the Fassbender film. Also it’s kind of like Assassin’s Creed before there was Assassin’s Creed.
But seriously, for a direct-to-video sequel, this turned out surprisingly entertaining. The CGI and visual effects haven’t aged gracefully, yet in this case, that adds a certain nostalgic charm—especially during that memorable transporting scene. There’s a body horror/gore moment that caught me off guard; I didn’t expect that from a Timecop movie. Lee isn’t exactly a thespian, but then again, neither is JCVD—and this film doesn’t demand it. What it needs is a capable actor who can deliver the lines but, more importantly, nail the action and fight sequences—and in that regard, the lead succeeds. There’s a bit more martial arts flair here, with people flying through the air from kicks and punches. We get some cool action set pieces, like the opening and the prison riot. The score also carries a lot of weight; while it does date the film in some ways, it amplifies the excitement and cool factor of many scenes.
All in all, this is a solid follow-up to the original, delivering what’s necessary while expanding the film’s universe, supported by some solid lead performances, action, and story. It does lose some steam towards the end, but it still a good time.

Title: Zodiac
Comment:
“Are you okay?” — “No, but thanks for asking.”
Another classic and one of my favorite films I’ve got to see at the cinema. I’m so happy with the amount of classics I’ve seen in theatres lately, it’s truly so cool.
Zodiac is just an amazing film, and it got even better on a rewatch. The cast is stacked, the direction is flawless, and the cinematography creates a suspenseful and eerie atmosphere that fits the story of the film perfectly.  
It also captures perfectly how the people who are involved in this case all slowly lose their minds and lives over it by descending into an unhealthy obsession. In the end, all three of our main characters ruin their personal (and professional) lives because of their obsession with this case in different ways. Paul Avery (Robert Downey Jr.) loses his career and his health by descending into alcoholism. Robert Graysmith (Jake Gyllenhaal) loses his marriage and time with his kids because he isolates himself just to investigate this case. David Toschi (Mark Ruffalo) loses his confidence and his reputation, since he can’t solve the case as the lead detective. It’s very interesting to watch, but also terrifying, since their personal lives begin to fall apart more and more — and despite these sacrifices there is no definitive answer to who the Zodiac killer is in the end.
Another little thing I noticed is that it spans a narrative arc between the first and the last scene of the film by connecting these two scenes thematically, which I really appreciate too since the film feels very well rounded because of that — despite the fact that the case is still unsolved.
Also, Jake Gyllenhaal is such a cutie patootie here, he’s so adorable (especially in the beginning). I also love RDJ’s ass when he sits on the desk (who said that?), and he’s so fine here too…I need him.

Title: Eddington
Comment:
I thought this was absolutely hysterical. I’m not sure what it means that my three favorite movies of the year so far (though I’m still holding final rankings until after Avatar and Marty Supreme) feature extreme violence mixed with moments of juvenile humor in desert settings. Who knows, but it’s clear that South Park, Jackass and video clips of people getting killed in the GWOT had as big of an impact on Ari Aster as they did on me. 
Maybe I need to rewatch Raising Arizona? This movie definitely feels indebted to that film in particular, though I honestly feel like Miller’s Crossing was actually a big influence on this, at least the gun stuff. I was reminded of both the Danny Boy sequence and the giant shootout at the end (if this has been directed by the Coens, Sam Raimi would’ve played an Antifa terrorist) during the last stand of PATRIOT Sheriff Joe Cross.
Ari Aster is clearly a massive Coen Brothers fan (of course, who isn’t) in general, but also Looney Toons and Thomas Pynchon. Obviously, One Battle After Another is the big Pynchon movie this year, but I’m currently reading V. and there were numerous moments that kind of reminded me of it. Not in anything specific, but more so that I could’ve imagined Benny Profane drinking in the bar when Sheriff Cross fights with the crazy bum (who I imagined was preaching to rats in the sewers before showing up in Eddington), or Pig Bodine being a member of the crew that shows up with Vernon Jefferson Peak. 
I completely understand why this movie probably pissed off a lot of people, but Aster just loves being a little stinker. The final knife to the head confirms that. Getting mad is kind of a self own when the opening shot of the movie is of the SolidGoldMagikarp Data Center.

Title: One Battle After Another
Comment:
The adrenaline of the chase. It's been far too long since a film got my heart pumping as much as One Battle After Another. It is a film of action, of movements and momentum, not just physically but also as revolutionary acts. Revolution is for the young, for those who can run and keep on running.
With One Battle After Another Paul Thomas Anderson has crafted a alternate contemporary reality as immersive as his historical settings, one of cycles of revolution that go beyond words into warfare. But as each generation fails the next one emerges to try to do better. In the middle of which One Battle After Another places the story of a father searching for his daughter, a fallen revolutionary playing catch-up. The film may have a cynicism towards the failing cycles of eternal revolution, but it depicts care as a virtue, where trust can be life-saving and the quiet community-based activism of Benicio del Toro's character is the most effective we see. In contrast to which we have the white supremacists and their dorky fantasies of having a desk in an office. One Battle After Another is a film of two losers, Lockjaw and Bob, but while the one with power and confidence can mask himself behind displays of masculinity it is actually the drug-taking nobody who has a community willing to help him.
One Battle After Another is the finest film in many years. It has so many perfectly crafted stretches, where every edit and shot is perfect. It captures the generational fight against oppression interconnected with the personal relationships that drive people forward. A recent cinematic experience above and beyond almost any other.

Title: Train Dreams
Comment:
One Mississippi, two Mississippi, three Mississippi...
Take a deep breath and look out the window. Time moves in the blink of an eye. A story where you walk into it wearing someone else’s boots, and step by step it draws closer to its end, changing you while its nostalgic landscape reflects a transformation you might no longer recognize at all. But at its core, nothing will ever truly change as long as you hold on to that hope that reminds you of the quiet flame that keeps burning even when the world around you decays/changes and moves on without you and just like in the film, where even the smallest memories... bad or good can become the final anchors of an entire life.
Absolute poetry✋️, visual storytelling done in the truest, most honest way, able to touch that quiet corner of the soul that holds our humanity. A place where the ordinary is guided by natural light and the freedom of the surrounding world, yet constantly reminding us how small we really are in its presence. Bentley’s direction radiates something familiarly nostalgic and assured, something that feels both refreshing and almost like an homage. A beautiful film that moves at its own pace and only for the simple reason that we allow it to tell its story in its own time, without rushing a single moment.
So let's keep going slowly "four Mississippi, five Mississippi, six Mississippi....
The acting is flawless, nothing to complain about, Edgerton is a master of understatement, a man of his time, guilt weights on him, trying to sustain himself with the beauty of the world around him, and that beauty is reflected back to us through Jones’s performance. A warmth of its own, a touch under the summer sun, and a gaze into that burning soul that reminds us why we’re alive. And of course, Macy’s incredible addition to the protagonist’s world, serving as that anchor that reminds us of something important.
The film is simply brilliant because its humanity is so deeply connected to the nature in which it all takes place. One of those films that makes me despair so much about the modern world, how immersed everyone is in the virtual while the real beauty lies entirely outside of it. And if it were up to me, Letterboxd should be the only thing you’re allowed to watch on your phone. And no, I’m not biased at all… I’m based.
Final Mississippi. Rhythmed in a way that is never boring, tragically hopeful, crafted with incredible subtlety. A very surprising film in how moving it is, because after all, it’s just the story of one among billions leaving their mark on the world.
So...perhaps, in the end, up in the heights, we realize its significance as we approach it, becoming a new star in the sky, shining simply by existing. Grief repeats itself, joy is a fleeting celebration, and that’s why every single second matters, because it might be one of the most important “Mississippis” on your own reel of life. An amazing film, a prime example of how this kind of movie works at its very best. Even if the narration might be twisting itself a bit too tightly into a corner, I’ll forgive it😊
88/100

My favorite movie among the three, and without a doubt one of the best films ever made.
Masaki Kobayashi created the greatest trilogy ever put on screen!
Nearly ten hours of pure Masterpiece filmmaking. This was remarkable and unforgettable. Taking this journey was genuinely one of the best things I’ve ever done in my life, and I truly mean that.
This is such an important piece of art, and everyone should experience it! At least watch the first film, and if you like it, then you can continue with the second and third films, but at least try!
This journey is, of course, accompanied by many emotions. It’s not easy to watch, that’s for sure, because horrible things happen. I mean, this is war. But the realism throughout these three films is honestly shocking and incredibly impressive. There were moments when I had to pause just to get some air... ! It’s a complete immersion.
The cinematography, framing, and all the composition of all the scenes are completely astonishing and perfect.
There are also some amazing close-ups throughout the 3 films that give so many emotions due to the amazing acting, mainly from Tatsuya Nakadai as Kaji, who gives one of the best acting performances ever.
On November 8th, 2025, we lost an icon of Japanese cinema and cinema in general. May Tatsuya Nakadai rest in peace, while all of his work will live on forever!

While Rian Johnson's return to the whodunit genre delivers a fairly entertaining spectacle, it is a clear step down from its predecessor. The film successfully navigates the complex structure of a modern murder mystery, offering solid location work and a host of engaging new suspects, yet it ultimately struggles to match the narrative depth and substance of the original hit.
The new ensemble cast proves to be one of the film’s major strengths. They deliver lively and compelling performances, driving the action forward even as the stakes feel slightly diminished. Unlike the tightly-knit, crumbling family unit of the first film, this group shares a unique, chosen-family dynamic.
This bond, however, is heavily defined by a clear power divide, with many characters acting as pawns in the game of the central host. This differentiated dynamic is fresh, but it contributes to the film's overall intimacy issue; the connection to the characters and their motives is simply less visceral than it was with the Thrombey family.
The plotting remains ingenious, with the introduction of a key twin plot working effectively. However, much like the overall substance, this twist feels less well-rounded and impactful compared to the intricate reveals of Knives Out. I know, I shouldn’t just be comparing this film to Knives Out but when you set the bar so incredibly high it’s hard not to pick up on these lapses in quality. 
Even the climactic resolution, while enjoyable and delivering necessary fireworks, highlights the jump in emotional intimacy. When placed side by side with the original, the emotional payoff here feels glaringly smaller. I do think the ensemble do great work for a fair payoff and I’m always got to enjoy Benoit Blanc breaking down the evidence, Craig sells it so well. 
The ensemble cast are great, albeit not the same level as the original, they work well and provide a strong dynamic. I think Dave Bautista delivers one of his better performances, and still goes down as my favorite wrestler turned actor(John Cena a close second). Madelyn Cline is insane as Whiskey and a reason to tune into the film, Ethan Klein and Hugh Grant getting two second cameos feels like a wasted opportunity they would do fantastic work as part of the films murder mystery narrative.
Daniel Craig could do these for the rest of his days and I’d be tuning in, no questions asked. He’s perfected the aura and essence of the character of Benoit Blanc, heck I’d even tune in for episodes of him in the bath playing games. He’s got some bathroom set up by the way, the entire film again has incredibly rich set dressing; every room has personality and style, again though I prefer the confined space of the Thrombey manor but this was still a well crafted set up. 
Ultimately, Glass Onion is a good film anchored by excellent production design, beautiful Greek locations, and a committed cast. But whilst I still think it’s a highly watchable and satisfying entry into the franchise, one can’t help but hope that for the third installment, Johnson finds a way to return to the intricate level of character-driven mystery and substantive intimacy that defined the originals excellence.
I’m so ready for Wake Up Dead Man, I’ll be getting into the cinema for that one soon. Zootopia 2 with the gang for today though, fair to say Zootopia 2 won’t be the last we see of them with 500m+ in the opening weekend.. ridiculous business by the mouse.

Title: The Butterfly Effect
Comment:
“UMA COISA TÃO SIMPLES, QUANTO O BATER DE ASAS DE UMA BORBOLETA, PODE CAUSAR UM TUFÃO DO OUTRO LADO DO MUNDO.”
Efeito Borboleta poderia ser só mais uma história sobre viagem no tempo, mas não o é pelo tratamento dado à sua narrativa. O longa é um dos grandes filmes de ficção científica dos anos 2000, nos guiando através de um roteiro inteligente, dinâmico, para uma curiosa trajetória de conflitos de um jovem que por uma inusitada circunstância do destino consegue voltar no tempo e reviver situações emblemáticas de sua vida. Escrito e dirigido pela dupla Eric Bress e J. Mackye Gruber, o projeto bate na tecla das incontroláveis variáveis de um olhar para a teoria do caos, percorrendo as alterações de eventos e os desdobramentos imprevisíveis. Uma das grandes sacadas do longa, que faz com que nenhuma das sequências chegue remotamente perto de repetir a qualidade deste, é o engenho com que alia a apresentação das regras e do recurso implicados em viajar no tempo ao elemento humano. A narrativa liga o turbo na não linearidade, algo que faz com que o espectador precise ter atenção já que praticamente uma sequência influencia a outra. Essa construção é feita de maneira brilhante tendo como norte as incontroláveis variáveis de um olhar composto por linhas temporais, física e toda a problemática que gira em torno. Quase um lopping reflexivo sobre crise existencial. Parece que estamos montando um quebra-cabeça onde peças novas entram e desmontam as já montadas. O universo incontrolável do sentimento também é uma mola propulsora da história . Há espaço para explorar temas como a importância da amizade, dos sonhos e também do amor, esse último talvez o ponto fixo e estopim da trama. Efeito Borboleta também é uma história sobre um amor obsessivo. Entre tantos tópicos abordados, os diretores conseguem retratar esse amor com sutileza, sem irritar em nenhum momento, apresentando-o em ações dinâmicas, não em desamparo desmedido. É uma película que depois de assistido faz o espectador pensar sobre muitas coisas e o que talvez poderia se mudar havendo possibilidade. É importante alertar que Efeito Borboleta tem um final alternativo, que, segundo consta, é preferido dos diretores. Obviamente, há quem discorde, mas aqui defende-se ferrenhamente que, por sorte, o preferido não foi o escolhido. Inquietante, diferente, sem apelar para uma solução tão fácil, que implica em viver com marcas de um sacrifício, o final original é a cereja do bolo. Para quem desejar conferir o final alternativo, no entanto, este está disponível no YouTube.

Cillian Murphy you can't just be flaunting your balls, d*ck and ass in front of my screen like that (you should be doing so in the comfort of my own room 🫦). The setup of this movie reminded me a lot to this one story my cousin told at a family gathering about a man who woke up from a coma during the height of the pandemic/quarantine 😰, same goes for those monkeys who reminded me of the ones The Fireflies were experimenting with at that university in The Last Of Us. And what did we learn ladies, gentlemen and they/thems? Men's biggest weakness will always be their penis.
I'd always known about the signature look of this movie but i honestly didn't know what to expect. It kinda takes a while to get used to at first but once you do it sucks you completely in, i think world building and atmosphere is what helped this movie stand out from the rest within the zombie genre the most. The camera that it was shot in paired with that amazing rock score set against the empty desolate streets of London and The UK countryside, it gave the movie a documentary/found footage feel almost as if the world was stuck and time had stopped moving after the out break happened.
As for the script at first i thought it presented us with a pretty average zombie apocalypse story, yes it was a very realistic look at how humanity would react to a situation like this which has a new added layer meaning after what we all went through in 2020 but as it was going it just kept getting better and better. For starters i really liked how it touched upon a sentiment that i've always had yet i'd never seen any other zombie piece of media tackle head on which is that, in a scenario like this, the only thing that'd be worth clinging onto in order to keep going would be the possibility of building human connection.

"I was thinking I was wrong.
About what?
All the death. All the shit. It doesn't really mean anything to Frank and Hannah because... well, she's got her dad, and he's got his daughter, so - I was wrong when I said that staying alive is as good as it gets.
See, that's what I was thinking.
Was it?
Hmm. You stole my thought."
Jim and Selena's romance wasn't very well developed in my opinion, it felt very rushed and i honestly thought they'd be better off as friends but they grew on me as a couple, i look at them as 2 people who have been trauma bonded which one could argue isn't very healthy but hey it's the best kind of relationship one can hope for after the fall of society. The look of The Infected and the gore was very good, hard to look at enough to make you uneasy while not being so explicit or in your face.
The final act especially blew me away, once our characters arrive in Manchester everything started to click for me. I really wasn't expecting Danny Boyle to go there! 😳 while clichéd in the sense that at its core every zombie story is about how we as humans can commit bigger atrocities than literal monsters, it was a very raw depiction of how men would react when posed with the issues of handling their lust and addressing how to repopulate the world (it honestly carries the whole film for me). Jim turns into a complete badass, Selena is willing to make a very noble sacrifice and Hannah steps up to the plate and saves the day at the last minute! I especially liked the detail of the rain after Frank mentioned it earlier in the movie.

While 28 Days Later seemed like it was gonna turn out to be overrated/overhyped in the end it totally lives up to its reputation, as always i think it should've ended after its first installment but it's no surprise why it gained a cult following and became a franchise. It has now become one of my favorite pieces of media within the zombie genre and i can't wait to find out what the sequels have in store 👀.

"That was longer than a heart beat."
Overall score: 9.6/10
P.S: The scene where we arrive at Frank's apartment really helped me start getting into the holiday spirit 🎄

Title: Carol
Comment:
the world is cold in december, but not as cold as pretending. in a city humming with loneliness—taxi lights flickering like half-hearted stars—two women meet in the quiet way storms begin: gently, then all at once.
therese is a shutter click, a girl made of observation and almosts. she drifts through her days like a ghost looking for a moment to solidify. her longing is small, careful, folded into the corners of her gaze. she wants more than what the world has handed her, but she doesn’t yet know the name for that hunger.
and then—carol.
carol, with her fur coat trailing winter behind her and a cigarette balanced like a secret between her fingers. carol, who walks into a department store and turns the air electric. she is a woman built from elegance and ache, equal parts tenderness and armor. she looks at therese as though she’s reading the beginning of a story she has waited years to find.
their connection is not an explosion but a slow thaw. it melts in glances. it murmurs between shared silences on long drives. it settles in the soft space where fear becomes desire and desire becomes truth.
but the world has rules for women—rules carved from coldness—and every step toward each other feels like trespassing. love becomes surveillance. affection becomes evidence. their hearts—suddenly alive—are held hostage by hands that will never understand them.
still, they reach for each other. not recklessly, but bravely. like two birds discovering their wings in the middle of winter.
therese finds her voice in the shape of carol’s name. carol finds her freedom in the steadiness of therese’s gaze. together, they become something rare: a possibility.
and in the end—across a crowded room, in a moment suspended like a breath held between heartbeats—carol looks at therese with that soft, devastating yes. a look that says i choose you, openly, finally, without fear.
carol is a winter hymn to longing, to the quiet revolution of being seen, to the kind of love that doesn’t crash but glows. it reminds us that some connections aren’t loud—they’re luminous. that sometimes, all someone needs to change your life is a glance that refuses to look away.
and when the scene fades, you can still feel it: the warmth of a love strong enough to survive the cold.

Title: Bugonia
Comment:
"Greetings. Welcome to the headquarters of the human resistance."
I swear, the moment I started watching Bugonia, I realized how much I missed seeing a new Yorgos Lanthimos film. That deliciously wild, proudly "weird," utterly idiosyncratic cinema... God, I was starving for this. If only he would just keep adding new characters and worlds to his freak show every year and never take a break. His view of the world is so unapologetic, so perverse, yet so normal in the face of a world that is turning to shit every day. The moment the movie started, I felt that old, familiar jolt and HE'S DONE IT AGAIN!
The film is one of Lanthimos's angriest films. In its bitterness, it feels a bit like the fourth installment in Kind of Kindness. It's a brutal mix of escalating paranoia, eroding trust, environmental anxieties, a growing hatred of big business and the wealthy, and the slow decay of rural America. Teddy's obsession with Andromedan aliens isn't really about aliens; it's a rebellion against a poisoned, corporatized world. And underlying it all is the fundamental question: Who is the real monster here? Michelle, Teddy, or humanity itself? Or the systems we've built and now treat as victims? And there's a psychosexual element to the film, as if these characters are cleaning up their own spiritual filth while refusing to confront their own egos. It's a stark reference to human laziness: we resist change because it scares us. Where Poor Things has a strange optimism, Bugonia is nihilistic, and we constantly find ourselves musing on a line from another character—despairing musings.
And Jesse Plemons, I've finally put this man among my favorite actors. He was practically exploding on screen! Sweaty, tense, dirty, unstable, yet strangely still endearing. It's deeper and more pathological than anything he did in Kind of Kindness. He makes you swing between disgust and empathy like you're on an emotional trampoline. Only Plemons could convince a conspiracy theorist that there are aliens living on Earth. Emma Stone, meanwhile, has entered the Lanthimos era like it's a lifetime commitment, and I hope she doesn't cancel it. Michelle is a shaved-headed, wide-eyed nightmare boss who wields corporate jargon with terrifying grace. And the way she maintains that perfect ambiguity "is she an alien or is she capitalism in human form" is truly unreal.
To those who ask, "Why does Lanthimos keep casting the same actors?" I'm baffled. Because when Jesse Plemons and Emma Stone give a two-hour acting masterclass, you don't question it; you thank them. He knows these two can reach exactly the level of freaky he envisions, and that's why he won't give up on them. And if Jesse Plemons and Emma Stone don't at least get Oscar nominations, I'll take to the streets in protest.
Also the "transformation" scene is as wild as it gets: Teddy shaves her head, creams her skin, and gradually transforms her into the alien she believes herself to be. And suddenly, Stone does indeed appear otherworldly. Her beauty becomes eerie, primal, but her voice, like the only tether that ties her to Earth, remains true to life. But one of her best moments comes right before the chaos: her singing along to Chappell Roan’s “Good Luck, Babe!” in the car. It is such an Emma Stone moment! I could watch that 30 seconds on loop forever. And I'm currently writing this review while listening to Chappell Roan's album.
And I'm sorry, but I also reject the "predictable ending" criticism. That's not the point, and anyone who's seen more than two Lanthimos films should know exactly what a Lanthimos ending will look like. The destination is never a shock; the disruption, the discomfort, the journey itself. Bugonia isn't trying to fool us, after all; it's trying to make us uncomfortable.
And the final sequence left me breathless. It was simply AMAZING! I need to see more films from The Holy Trinity (Lanthimos, Stone and Plemons)

Title: Different from the Others
Comment:
I write this still feeling the film’s gravity in my chest. I’m in awe and quite furious at how brave a thing it is to make a moral and political argument with images when the world around you is still learning how to look. This film is not just an early narrative about desire; it’s a public act of courage, a piece of social surgery performed on screen. Watching it, even in its fragmented survival, I sense a filmmaker and a thinker who refused to let law and prejudice speak for what is human.
Richard Oswald’s direction feels like the work of someone who understands cinema as a civic instrument. The fact that Magnus Hirschfeld co-wrote the screenplay, appears on camera, and helped finance the production through his Institute for Sexual Science gives the film a feeling of urgency. This is cinema as testimony, as petition, as clinical testimony turned into compassion. They were not only telling a story; they were staging an argument against Germany’s Paragraph §175, which at the time criminalized homosexuality. That legal shadow is the pressure under the film because everything the characters live through is measured against that law, and the film’s rhetoric is as much juridical as it’s cinematic.
It matters to me that the premiere was not a small private showing but a public claim: a special performance at the Berlin Apollo-Theater on May 28, 1919, followed by the Prinzeß-Theater screening on May 30, 1919. Those dates are anchor points in the film’s life, markers of the moment when an Aufklärungsfilm, a “sexual enlightenment film,” dared to step into the light with forty prints in circulation, a remarkable number for 1919, and proof that the film crew expected, and hoped for, an audience and a debate.
What I paid more attention to when I was watching was the film’s hybrid making. It’s part fiction, part didactic documentary, and part photography (although some are placed because the film is partly lost), but that blending I see as a strategy. By interweaving narrative drama with documentary elements and expert testimony, Oswald and Hirschfeld refuse the simplistic binary of morality versus pathology. They propose, instead, that education and empathy belong at the heart of public life. To see Hirschfeld, a pioneering sexologist and an activist, on screen is to witness knowledge insisting on its right to be visible and to be humane.
“Love for one of the same sex is no less pure or noble than for one of the opposite. This orientation can be found in all levels of society and among respected people. Those that say otherwise come only from ignorance and bigotry.” — Doctor played by Hirschfeld.
And then comes the betrayal of history: the censorship that followed. By May 1920 a new censorship program was being shaped in direct reaction to films like this, and by August 1920 the film was effectively banned except for private educational viewings. The film’s prints (many of them) were later consigned to flames in 1933 during the Nazi book and film burnings. The original version is gone; much of the film was lost beyond recall. That erasure is part of the film’s wound but also part of its meaning: what they tried to destroy refuses to be fully extinguished, and its fragments speak louder for having been nearly silenced.
I also have to mention the intensity of the backlash the film provoked. Conservative Catholic and Protestant groups, reactionary political forces, and organized antisemitic circles set themselves against the screenings, sometimes by disrupting them in public. There were also ugly accusations that Hirschfeld and Oswald (both Jewish) were somehow trafficking in a “Jewish vice,” a claim so weird and absurd that it makes me think about how hatred often wraps itself in the language of moral panic. To understand that reaction is to understand the stakes: this was not only a cultural debate about film content; it was a fight over who gets to define citizenship, normality, and the reach of state power into private lives.
The critiques leveled at the film claimed it was biased against Paragraph §175, that it offered a one-sided presentation, and that it might “confuse” or “recruit” youth. Those charges says a lot more about the accusers than the accused. The film’s clarity of purpose was interpreted as propaganda because a humane stance toward homosexuality threatened entrenched legal and moral orders. I find it heartbreaking and humanly intelligible that a film arguing for dignity should be read by opponents as a kind of menace.
There is also a generational irony in the film’s fate. The very visibility it demanded made it a target for censorship; the very attention it sought ensured it would be remembered enough to be destroyed. But destruction doesn’t erase influence. Even in its damaged state, the film became an emblem: an early cinematic plea for LGBT civil rights, a document from a moment in which science, law, politics, and art collided in public
I return, in thought, to the figure of Magnus Hirschfeld. To fund a film through the Institute for Sexual Science was to believe that knowledge could be a weapon against cruelty. To write for the screen was to recognize cinema’s capacity to reach people in ways that pamphlets and lectures could not. I feel gratitude, almost filial, for that risk.
Finally, I want to say this plainly, my affection for this film is not purely sentimental, since I can’t “like” properly a film that is not complete, but my affection is a form of political reverence. I am moved by how it places ethics into the circuitry of image and soundless motion. I am in awe of its historical courage and of the stubborn tenderness with which it treats its subjects. I feel respect for Oswald and Hirschfeld, not only as creators, but as honest interlocutors with their society; they turned cinema into a courtroom for compassion.
Everyone should watch it because it teaches how art can speak against unjust law, how knowledge can be a form of love, and how even fragments of a film can be a living testament. To watch it is to be educated in humility and to feel, alongside outrage, a fierce gratitude that such an act of seeing was ever carried out.
“You have to keep living; live to change the prejudices by which this man has been made one of the countless victims. [...] You must restore the honor of this man and bring justice to him, and all those who came before him, and all those to come after him. Justice through knowledge!”
