Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
Comment:
Not only one of my favourite films of all time, but one of the films that fundamentally changed me - I still have such a vivid memory of seeing this at the cinema on release, as my dad was a big fan of the books. It blew my 10 year old mind. In the year between this and the Two Towers releasing I watched it on VHS countless times, as well as reading the books. It’s probably what set me down the path of films, books and video games - prior to this film I was all about football - watching it, playing it, talking about it. It all seemed pretty boring to me after watching LOTR.
The Fellowship of the Ring is such a remarkable achievement - just getting the thing made was an epic journey in itself. (I recommend the podcast ‘What Went Wrong’ for anyone interested in behind the scenes information on films). It manages to have so much heart, without sacrificing plot, or action. It’s funny, sad, exciting and inspiring. Every single character is perfectly cast. It’s shot to perfection. It’s so long and yet not a second of the film drags. The music is incredible. The special effects still largely hold up, and the practical effects are some of the finest on film - the orc makeup, incredible miniatures and luscious set design.
I think one of the films biggest successes is condensing so much lore and history from the books and streamlining it in such a way that can be easily digested - from the incredible prologue to the exposition peppered throughout the rest of the film. Lots of adaptations of similar properties struggle with this, and get too bogged down in explaining everything - or don’t explain enough, leaving anyone not familiar with the novels wondering what’s going on. 
While I love all three of the films so much, this one probably remains my favourite, although it’s incredibly close. I like to cheat and count the entire trilogy as one film when listing favourites of mine.

Title: Left-Handed Girl
Comment:
as a leftie myself, this has become an instant favorite. you can definitely see Sean Baker’s fingerprints everywhere on this, all the way from the iPhone cinematography to the coloring. it reminded me of The Florida Project in the way it captures themes of motherhood and class. what felt new to me here though, and something that Shih-Ching Tsou added, is was how the film shows the infrastructure of a family and the unspoken hierarchies that end up shaping the kids’ worldview. take I-Jing’s left-handedness for example, the words her grandpa says get under her skin, and she begins to see her left hand as truly something evil and even tries to police herself by wrapping it with a cloth.
and while yes, this is about cultural superstitions, i see it more so as a metaphor for the way society projects fear onto natural behaviors or traits that don’t fit the “norm.” it’s about taboos, and about what is considered unacceptable (like early or nontraditional motherhood, which comes back full circle by the end). this is made even clearer when the meerkat GooGoo dies (🙁), and I-Jing immediately takes the blame because she thinks that it was her left-handed throw that caused it. even though her logic is obviously flawed, to a young kid, who emotionally absorbed the idea that anything “different” is dangerous, it would feel real, and this is exactly how society conditions people who do not conform. this internalized shame builds up in different characters for different reasons throughout the story, which is why the ending, and I-Jing’s simple “look, mom!” carries so much meaning, because it immediately breaks that weight of shame

Title: Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio
Comment:
“GAROTOS DE VERDADE NÃO VOLTAM”.
 "Pinocchio" não leva o nome de seu diretor à toa, já que carrega consigo alguns dos pontos mais fortes da trajetória e das peculiaridades de Del Toro. O compromisso de toda a vida do cineasta em transformar os frutos de sua imaginação em realidades físicas torna sua decisão de optar pela estilo stop-motion para seu primeiro longa-metragem de animação uma escolha óbvia e perfeitamente adequada. Com um tom decididamente mais maduro do que as versões animadas anteriores da fábula do século XIX de Carlo Collodi, embora não menos comovente ou cativante, esta versão escrita por Guillermo del Toro e pelo co-roteirista Patrick McHale, apela tanto para crianças quanto para adultos com suas temáticas que até chegam a assustar, mas sem nunca perder um verniz humorístico e leve, o longa promove uma releitura do tom moralista da história original para apresentar a insurgência como o único caminho possível para se lidar com o autoritarismo e o fascismo. Além de explorar temas sobre pais e filhos imperfeitos, personificando a fusão de narrativa e técnica em uma unidade filosófica coesa. Tudo isso é amparado na magia do stop-motion, que ajuda a distinguir o filme dentre as várias versões de Pinóquio, sendo uma aula magna de como se adaptar material base já extensamente adaptado, e se firmando como a releitura definitiva da obra no audiovisual.

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
These movies are like magic tricks: Rian Johnson introduces an elegant premise, blows it all up, and then you watch sexy Forghorn Leghorn rebuild the puzzle.
For nearly 2 hours it’s just Rian stacking up this incredibly tall Jenga tower by jumping into different POVs, character vignettes, and flashbacks, poking his murder mystery with holes, contradictions, and impossibilities. And the finale is the prestige, it's what we're all waiting for, Benoit Blanc, always the showman, meticulously puts the tower back together, and against all odds it all makes sense, the tower is complete and stands on its own. It reminds me of Vince Gilligan's ethos during Breaking Bad, where he would intentionally put the characters into a hopeless situation and challenge himself and the writers to find the best solution.
We've gotten three different flavors of Benoit Blanc and Wake Up Dead Man's focus on religion is the most thematically rich one yet, every character has a different motivation through their own distinct relationship with their faith. Daniel Craig is great as usual, but we spend more time with the two Joshes which make the rest of the supporting cast less well-rounded than the one in the previous two.
The whodunnit genre has blown up since the first Knives Out, there's been more movies and shows that play with these tropes, but I’ll take more of these Benoit Blanc mysteries — the formula isn’t stale, and there’s just very few folks doing it like Rian Johnson and Steve Yedlin when it comes to making movies that actually look like MOVIES.
With that said, I’m looking forward to Johnson taking a break and stepping into something new… or you know, just give the man his much-deserved blank check and let him do his Star Wars trilogy, his nuanced take on religion makes me even more interested in what he can cook up in that universe.

Title: Pale Rider
Comment:
“i asked for a miracle.”
Pale Rider isn’t that deep, but it’s thoroughly intriguing because its grand, almost spaghetti-Western spectacle is anchored by a grounded, warm core that gives it real heart. The stunning cinematography of the Idaho mountains lifts the whole thing into something mythic right from the start. It’s a classic Western setup, almost comfortingly familiar in its shape: a rough riverside mining camp, the town pushing up against it, and the company men blasting into the mountains for gold, squeezing out the last small claims and the people holding on. Into this comes, almost out of nowhere and just when they need a miracle, a mysterious stranger with a supernatural aura stepping into the conflict. He befriends the camp folks and takes up the fight against the local mining baron and his deputy. He’s clearly out for revenge, but for some reason he moves slowly, folding into the rhythm of the community. It's as if he sees his former life in these people, the life the same greedy men once took from him. He’s already a ghost, the bullet holes prove it, helping the version of himself he can’t save anymore.

“he’s a good man.”
So tucked inside all of that, much like the camp set deep in the woods, is something real, almost soft. It's a story about finding room to yearn and dream in a world that’s cruel, where pragmatic choices are the only way to survive those who hold power. What pulled me in was the transitional space that opens between them, the way this fragile, accidental patchwork family forms around the preacher: the widow trying to rebuild something steady, the daughter struggling to shape her feelings after losing her father, and a stubbornly resistant man who genuinely loves them both. The preacher steps into all of their lives at once, stirring a whole string of conflicted emotions, never easy, and the film handles it all with remarkable gentleness. Even the daughter’s affection for him is drawn with subtlety: he lets her feel what she feels, but he sets boundaries with care, never harsh, never misleading. It never felt uncomfortable to me, aside from that brief late-night moment in the woods that lands a bit heavy at first, but even that ultimately feels sincere. And it was her despair that summoned him in the first place, praying for a savior after losing someone yet again, burying her dog alone in the woods.
The villains sit exactly where they should, giving the intimacy of the story its framing and its pressure. And guided by this spiritual figure, they find the courage to move on, less abandoned, more heartened – they were right to believe in him. By the end it becomes less about romance and more about letting go of the past and finally seeing what’s right in front of you. Or maybe what’s waiting for you in the future. Something that’s real. And good. There’s a tenderness in the way they keep each other from breaking, a sense of care that shows. And that’s everything in a world like this.

“i’ll be around.”

To me the showdown at the end didn’t feel gritty. It’s more camp, really. The way he keeps slipping out of those increasingly absurd hiding spots, killing Stockburn’s men one after the other, made me laugh more than anything. And come on, it’s a simple tale of good versus evil. The outcome is obvious – it was finally time for redemption. And that’s fine, because the real weight lies in what follows. It’s about saying goodbye for them, and for him. First there’s that quiet, lightly humorous goodbye between the two men – Clint making that little joke about the long walk ahead, a gesture that lands as both teasing and respectful. Then we see him leaving, slowly vanishing into the vast openness. The daughter misses him so she shouts into the sky, finally able to voice everything she’s been holding: the goodbye, the thank you, even the i love you that now finally finds its right form. Her echoes carry into his final ride toward the mountains stretching out ahead of him. That’s cinematic perfection, leaving me with that fuzzy feeling you only get from something this sincere. And honestly, it’s just that darn beautiful. Comfort movie unlocked.

Title: The Mastermind
Comment:
Starring Josh O’Connor in arguably his most challenging role to date, The Mastermind is about J.B Mooney, an unemployed father who organizes an art heist that goes terribly wrong. The rest of the movie concerns itself with J.B.’s struggle to evade punishment. On the surface, it looks as though Reichardt has sketched J.B in the likeness of a Bresson character—toying, moody, lonely, and amoral, like Michel from Pickpocket (1959). But, where in Pickpocket (1959) where we marvel at the technical ability of Michel’s sleight-of-hand, watch him train his fingers like Rocky running the stairs, in The Mastermind we marvel at J.B’s inability.
The Mastermind is a film about the shitty dads who ran out on our elders, long gone and trapped inside tales shared around the dinner table. My alcoholic grandfather, my other grandfather, a yeller, my great grandfather, a philanderer—it’s a story about the men of our pasts who sucked at providing, but we choose to love them, or the ghosts of them, anyways, despite ourselves.
What is daddy up to right now? The reality, says Reichardt, is not so alluring. Moving against genre, she turns the entropy of J.B.’s life - what could easily become the coked-out third act of Goodfellas - into a careful character study. Her’s is a movie composed of interstices, its power lies in the moments of inbetween, where human behaviour reveals itself most lucidly. Title: Secretary
Comment:
the world teaches girls like her to fold themselves small. to be neat, obedient, quiet—an origami version of humanity. but lee is all paper cuts and tremors, a bruise pressed into a blouse, walking through life like she’s holding her breath. she moves through rooms as if she’s apologizing for taking up space, her heart stitched together with trembling thread.
then she steps into his office.
gray walls. perfectly arranged pencils. a man carved from precision and silence. mr. grey is a storm disguised as stillness, a man who fears the mess of feeling so deeply that he’s organized the world into submission. his voice is a gavel; his gaze, an inventory.
and yet—something in her unraveling calls to something in his restraint.
their connection begins the way a match meets a dark room: quiet, then inevitable. he sees her—really sees her—in the places others dismissed as weakness. he reads the tremble in her hands like scripture. and she learns that obedience can be chosen instead of expected, that surrender can be a language of desire, not humiliation.
in his office, lined with rules and paper and the hum of unspoken longing, she discovers a strange new truth: that control can be a cradle. that being held firmly is not the same as being confined. that some boundaries are soft, and some commands are doors.
he teaches her how to stand still. she teaches him how to feel without flinching.
their tenderness is a quiet rebellion, a love letter written in discipline and permission. it is not the kind of romance the world understands—or even wants to. but it is theirs: sharp, deliberate, intimate. a choreography of trust. a devotion built not on breaking her, but on uncovering her.
and when she finally sits in that chair—waiting, unmovable, steadfast—it becomes clear: she is not empty or fragile or lost. she is choosing. she is claiming. she is becoming.
secretary is a fairy tale wrapped in shadows, a story about two broken shapes finding the form they were always meant to take. it whispers that love doesn’t have to be soft to be kind, and that some hearts bloom only when given structure strong enough to hold them.
and in the quiet after, when the papers have settled and the world returns to its noise, you can almost hear it: the sound of two people who finally, impossibly, fit.

Title: Nightmare Alley
Comment:
Vision in Darkness and Light
Guillermo del Toro has always been a filmmaker enthralled by monsters. Not just as spectacles, but as mirrors reflecting the fragility, longing, and ache inside his characters. From Pan’s Labyrinth to The Shape of Water, his tales often feel like fables dipped in moonlight, where the inhuman reveals what is most human. Nightmare Alley, however, turns that fascination inward, stripping away the comfort of mythic creatures and asking instead what happens when the monster wears a man’s face. Del Toro focuses on how pride, longing, and self-deception can twist a person into something far more frightening than any fairytale beast.
For my viewing, I opted for the black-and-white extended director’s cut, having read it deepens the noir atmosphere and sharpens the moral edges. However, much to my disappointment, I’m not in love with this version or the movie overall. There is supposed to be a great story buried in here, but the movie struggles to uncover it. The pacing drags, especially in the first hour, where scenes go on without building tension or momentum, and the narrative feels like it’s circling itself rather than digging deeper. Del Toro’s signature touches (normally enchanting) end up muddying the clarity of the story instead of enhancing it, leaving the movie caught between grounded noir and something dreamlike that never fully lands. There are moments where the movie brushes against something truly harrowing, especially as it spirals toward what might be del Toro’s bleakest ending yet, but those moments feel like islands in a long, uneven sea. It’s an interesting experiment from a filmmaker I admire, but for me, Nightmare Alley is haunting in moments but hard to fully embrace.

Title: Elevator to the Gallows
Comment:
"I lost you in the night, Julien. I should have left you alone. I shouldn't have kissed you or caressed your face."
Nervous Breakdown The Movie:
The first half hour of the movie completely pulled me in. From the start, there was that mounting tension and uncertain rhythm of classic noirs. Julien sneaking into Carala's office just after the romantic yet instantly identifiable phone call between two lovers, his quiet, calculated steps, his sudden shift from self-assuredness to pure panic when he realizes he's trapped in the elevator. These were the moments that truly got my pulse racing. Meanwhile, Florence, wandering the rainy streets of Paris, moving from bar to café, searching for any trace of Julien, creates this beautiful, somber noir atmosphere. Everything is foggy, a little hopeless, and strangely exciting.
But when the film included the Louis and Véronique storyline, my mood plummeted. I couldn't stand them. Every decision they made was so absurd that I found myself getting annoyed and losing interest in the film. I especially prayed for Louis's death, seriously. Not only that, but after a while, the "elevator escape" theme and Florence's endless wanderings became tedious. What started out tense and intriguing gradually became tiring, almost repetitive; it felt like the film was dragging on for far too long.
Still, there's a charm to Louis Malle's approach to film noir. Instead of relying on the classic archetype of the cold, manipulative, self-centered femme fatale, he focuses on a woman unraveling not by ambition, but by love. Florence isn't exploiting anyone for her own personal gain; she's simply a woman caught up in her own longing, drifting through the city using her heartbreak as her compass. Amidst this tangle of bad decisions, crimes, and misunderstandings, the story keeps returning to love as its quiet center. But I can't say I'm a big fan of "French love stories," but that's entirely my problem.
So, what I appreciated most about the film was its excellent title choice, its noir atmosphere, its original main female character, and the first half hour. Other than that, it unfortunately left most of my expectations unfulfilled.

Title: Wicked: For Good
Comment:
"Perhaps...a change in the weather."
Fair warning: This isn't going to be one of my better reviews. There's a lot that I have to get out and it may not come nicely.
As most musical theatre fans know, Act II is never quite as good as Act I. Jon Chu has made some interesting choices here, not all of them for good. I think when something is evolved from a novel to a musical to a film, each medium demands different priorities. In most cases, the book is going to be better than the film.
If you've read Wicked, then you'll know that it is a much darker story with lots of complex themes and characters. What's lost for me in the film is that complexity or even just a sense of coherent direction. In adaptations like this, you are going to have two different audiences: the individuals like me who want to dive deeper into the novel's original intention of questioning who gets labeled as "evil" and how prejudices and power distort truths.
Then, you have the general audience who want the strong friendship themes and the magical spectacle. I'm not knocking those people at all, but it's a big reason why this film didn't work for me nearly as well as Wicked: Part One. In the novel, Elphaba isn't just misunderstood. She's shaped by oppression and a lifetime of being used or ignored by systems far bigger than she is.
Besides her little scene where the animals go under the Yellow Brick Road and she sings about how this is their home and they should stay and fight, what else is she against? Do I think that Cynthia Erivo was perfect casting for Elphaba? Hell yes. Whether she is silent or belting, she brings an incredible depth to the character. I adore her voice.
Tangent: THE SEX SCENE! Why? Why was this necessary? Jonathan Bailey is absolutely gorgeous, but did we really need all of that? Couldn't things be implied? When she said, "For the first time, I feel wicked," I almost walked out of the theatre. 
I kid you not.
Opposite Ariana Grande, she is the grounding force of the story. I truly just feel that the writing for this second part is...not good. It seems throughout the film that there are no real stakes and what really is the Wizard doing that is extremely evil? Okay, he has the animals in cages for a scene. And? Is that all that we're supposed to play with?
Ariana Grande is doing the best that she can with her character, but again, there's not much there. Most of the time, we're checking off boxes to make sure that "The Wizard of Oz" lore is being adhered to. Why? Did Bok really have to turn into the Tin Man? I'll put him going apeshit on the witch to the side for a moment. What was the Lion's motivation for hating the Witch again? Because she released him from a cage? That's why he's cowardly?
There's just so much here that falls apart. It's one example of a film that I do wish locked into its source material even a bit more. Do we really have to treat our audiences as dumb constantly? Speaking of odd performances, I can't forget about Jeff Goldblum and Michelle Yeoh. I will give him some credit: Jeff Goldblum is a fun, whimsical guy. I understand why he was cast as the Wizard. 
Michelle Yeoh, tho? Nope. Please know that this is an actress that I adore. I think Yeoh is incredible in everything she does. But this? She's just here to collect a paycheck.
Also, for a musical, the music here is bad. For Good and No Good Deed are the only good songs in this. The rest are trash. Why did we have to add more?
I could go on for days. Why does the outside of Oz look like the sandworm planet from Beetlejuice? Why does Elphaba live at the end? She just abandons all of her ambitions and goes off with Scarecrow Fiyero? 
I'm happy for those that enjoyed this, but for me, Wicked: For Good is a bewildering misfire. The emotional beats rarely connect and the magic that once defined the story seems drained of color and conviction. I am rather concerned for Jon Chu's future.

Title: Left-Handed Girl
Comment:
As a leftie and former spawn of Satan myself, I have lots of thoughts.
Tsou’s Left-Handed Girl encapsulates centuries-worth of male dominance through a common cultural superstition about left-handedness’ association with the devil. In a way, this myth opens the first door to a patriarchal structure built on walls of obedience and subjugation. To veer off the path of “normalcy” (a.k.a. being left-handed) becomes a silent notion that shakes the patriarchy down to its knees.
This conformity then becomes a learned habit that’s too difficult to shrug off, with each generation of mothers carrying responsibilities far heavier than what they can endure. It becomes even more apparent in sequences where the most obvious choice is to ask for help, but the female characters just don’t budge, because it has been instilled that women are to suppress all forms of emotion, be it desire, grief, embarrassment, or vulnerability (hence the inevitable, but highly effective, dinner sequence). That’s why sorry’s are rarely uttered (if ever) in Asian households: because an apology might shatter the status quo long built on emotional self-regulation.
There’s also beauty in the way the film captures Taipei’s nightscapes through an intimate verité approach (a Sean Baker touch) and in the constant shift to I-Jing’s (Nina Ye) perspective (and its accompanying whimsical score) to evoke as much authenticity to the topic at hand as possible. In the end, I’m glad Tsou is finally shedding light on one of the most underrepresented, oppressed factions on the planet: left-handed folks.

Title: The Life of Chuck
Comment:
🇺🇸 in english: Wow — what an interesting and quietly captivating film. Mike Flanagan takes Stephen King’s story and turns it into something gently cosmic and unexpectedly intimate, a kind of life portrait told in three movements that each feel like a self-contained universe on the verge of disappearing. What makes it so compelling isn’t a single twist or revelation, but the way Flanagan reframes an ordinary man’s existence with a sense of wonder, melancholy, and tenderness. It’s the end, the middle, and the beginning looking at each other through a cracked mirror, every shard reflecting its own strange light.
The first section throws you straight into a soft, melancholic apocalypse — not chaos, but the eerie quiet that comes when the world is unraveling in slow motion. Empty streets, subtle glitches in routine, people trying to hold onto normal life even as it slips away. And in the middle of all that, Chuck appears not as a savior or a mystic figure, but as someone whose simple kindness feels almost supernatural against the fading backdrop around him. Flanagan has always understood the horror of the inevitable, but here he uses it in the gentlest way possible.
As the film folds back and lets us get closer to Chuck, everything becomes even more rewarding. What’s striking is how Flanagan avoids turning him into a symbol. Chuck is just Chuck: a shy kid, a man shaped by small fears, tiny victories, fleeting joys, and a solitude that never quite hardens him. Every detail of his life — mundane on paper — gains weight, texture, and meaning. Nothing feels like a perfunctory flashback; everything
beats with a kind of sincerity that only clicks when you recognize the fragile beauty of a life that could easily have gone unnoticed.
Flanagan, usually more literal, finds here a rare harmony between memory, fantasy, and emotional truth. The editing stitches these fragments together with a gentle musicality, and even when the film leans into melodrama, it does so with a disarming honesty. You end up feeling like you’re watching a gesture of affection — a filmmaker quietly embracing a character who might otherwise be invisible.
In the end, The Life of Chuck doesn’t just want to move you. It wants you to pay attention. To breathe with it. To notice the beauty in things that fade without spectacle. It’s a film about endings, yes, but even more about the small, luminous moments that justify everything before the lights go out.
A delicate, soulful piece of work.

🇧🇷 em português: Uau, que filme interessante e cativante — e não apenas pelas promessas que um título como esse carrega, mas pela maneira como Mike Flanagan desmonta a vida de um homem comum em três movimentos que parecem, cada um à sua maneira, um pequeno universo em colapso. Flanagan pega o texto de Stephen King e o transforma numa experiência estranhamente íntima, quase cósmica, ao mesmo tempo mundana e profundamente emocional. É como se a vida de Chuck fosse vista através de um prisma que distorce e amplia o que normalmente deixamos passar: o fim, o meio e o começo convivendo num espelho quebrado, onde cada fragmento brilha por um motivo diferente.
A primeira parte já te joga de cabeça numa atmosfera de mistério melancólico, esse fim-do-mundo silencioso que Flanagan filma tão bem. Não é sobre caos, é sobre a quietude que antecede o último suspiro — ruas vazias, pequenas falhas de rotina, pessoas tentando manter a normalidade enquanto o mundo escorre pelos dedos. E é justamente aí que o filme pega: Chuck surge como uma presença quase mística, não por fazer algo extraordinário, mas por existir com uma gentileza tão deslocada do cenário que você sente que há algo maior por trás. Flanagan sempre soube trabalhar o horror do inevitável, e aqui ele usa isso de forma mais terna do que trágica.
Quando o filme recua e te coloca mais perto de Chuck, ele te recompensa com uma sensibilidade enorme. O interessante é que Flanagan evita transformar Chuck num símbolo grandioso — ele é só ele, com sua infância tímida, seus medos, seus pequenos triunfos, sua solidão e suas pequenas alegrias. É quase estranho como cada detalhe banal da vida dele vai ganhando peso, significado, textura própria. Nada é tratado como mero flashback explicativo: tudo vibra com uma sinceridade que só faz sentido quando pensamos na beleza efêmera de uma vida qualquer.
E Flanagan, que costuma ser mais literal, aqui encontra um equilíbrio raro entre fantasia, memória e sentimento. A montagem vai costurando essas peças com certa musicalidade, e mesmo quando o filme arrisca melodrama, ele o faz com uma honestidade que desarma. A sensação geral é de estar assistindo a um gesto de carinho — um diretor abraçando um personagem que, à primeira vista, parecia invisível.
No fim, A Vida de Chuck não quer simplesmente emocionar. Ele quer que você observe. Que você respire junto. Que você perceba a beleza em algo que desaparece sem estardalhaço. É um filme sobre o fim, mas também sobre todas as coisas pequenas que justificam a existência antes dele.
Um trabalho delicado, cheio de alma e textura, que mostra Flanagan num registro mais simples, mas surpreendentemente maduro.

Title: Train Dreams
Comment:
Robert Grainier cresce sem conhecer sua família e atravessa a juventude praticamente sozinho, até encontrar Gladys, seu grande amor, com quem passa a dividir uma pequena cabana de madeira às margens de um rio. Dessa união nasce uma filha que, por causa do trabalho sazonal construindo ferrovias ou derrubando árvores, ele vê com menos frequência do que gostaria. Grainier fala pouco, mas guarda uma afeição sincera pelos raros vínculos que cria, seja com a esposa e a criança, seja com os companheiros de ofício que, de tempos em tempos, voltam a cruzar seu caminho em outros cantos. Entre alegrias intensas e perdas dolorosas, sua existência avança como todas as outras. Basicamente, "Train Dreams" se dedica justamente a isso: aceitar a vida tal como chega, encontrar pequenas centelhas de felicidade no cotidiano mais simples e carregar, quando necessário, o peso das culpas e responsabilidades que surgem. A proporção de tela menos usual reforça a sensação de vastidão diante das árvores antigas que desmoronam uma após a outra, sacrificadas por um ideal de progresso que já não faz sentido ao protagonista, sobretudo quando ele passa a sentir o acolhimento da família que formou.
As paisagens são deslumbrantes, marcadas por sutis indícios da passagem do tempo e do avanço da modernidade, que denunciam não apenas a obsolescência do árduo ofício de lenhador, mas também a perda gradual de propósito na trajetória de Robert, criando uma atmosfera mais lenta e contemplativa. A sequência do avião funciona como uma espécie de visão totalizante da existência, um instante em que tudo retorna à memória quando se está mais perto do sublime. É como estar parado na entrada de uma porta e, ao olhar para trás, ver um filme dos melhores e piores momentos de uma vida inteira desfilar diante de olhos solitários e desgastados. Um ponto que me causou certo estranhamento no filme foi o uso constante da narração, que acaba assumindo um peso maior do que deveria. Em vez de deixar o espectador apenas observar a vida em suas várias formas, seja a própria, a de Grainier ou uma noção mais ampla, a narração, por vezes excessivamente presente, antecipa sensações, entrega conclusões prontas e impede que o tempo trabalhe por si. A intenção é boa. Sem esse recurso, o filme talvez se tornasse mais enigmático do que deveria. Mas a frequência com que Patton aparece explicando o que está diante de nós é maior do que o necessário.
A vida não é algo para ser decifrado a cada passo, e sim algo para ser sentido. E "Train Dreams", como reflexo dessa própria vida, também funciona melhor quando pode simplesmente existir. Quando uma voz externa nos orienta sobre o que sentir ou entender em determinadas passagens, nossa liberdade de interpretação diminui, nossa possibilidade de apenas respirar o momento se estreita, e nem tudo precisa ser compreendido imediatamente ou mesmo compreendido. Ainda assim, não é uma interferência que comprometa a experiência como um todo. É apenas um obstáculo leve, superável, mas que acaba afastando o filme da plenitude que poderia alcançar caso confiasse mais no silêncio e no próprio fluxo da narrativa.

Title: Wicked: For Good
Comment:
“They need someone to be wicked, so that you can be good.”
I walked into the second chapter with all the glow of the first film still buzzing in my head, and while this follow up delivers a satisfying and emotional conclusion, it never quite reaches the spellbinding heights of its predecessor. The story picks up right where things left off, diving deeper into Elphaba’s journey as she fully embraces her power and the consequences that come with it, while Glinda is forced to confront what leadership really demands once the wizard’s lies begin to collapse around her. The themes are still strong, especially in the way the film explores responsibility, corruption, and the cost of trying to fix a world that refuses to fix itself, but the pacing is noticeably choppier and some major moments don’t hit with the weight they should.
“For the first time, I feel, Wicked.”
Jon M. Chu still brings plenty of magic and a good sense of great filmmaking, but his direction doesn’t flow with the same confidence or energy as before. The musical numbers this time are more inconsistent, though still memorable. “No Good Deed” comes roaring in with raw power thanks to Cynthia Erivo, and the reprise of “For Good” hits the emotional beats it needs to. But other sequences feel oddly staged or visually muted, missing that sweeping energy that made the first film’s numbers pop. There’s less consistency in the visual rhythm overall, and the movie occasionally struggles to maintain momentum as it jumps from one big moment to the next. It’s good, ambitious, but not the same fluid, polished experience the first film delivered so effortlessly.
“But I know I’m who I am today because I knew you.”
The cast, however, remains the backbone of the entire production. Cynthia Erivo is once again incredible , giving Elphaba’s emotional arc depth, strength, and real heartbreak. Ariana Grande continues to be exceptional, and she brings both comedic spark and genuine warmth to Glinda’s evolution. Michelle Yeoh, Jeff Goldblum, and Jonathan Bailey all return and continue to fit their roles well, even if they aren’t given as many standout moments this time. The songs, even when the staging falters, remain beautifully performed. And by the finale, the film sticks the landing with enough power and heart to make the whole journey feel worthwhile, even if it can’t quite replicate the magic that made the first installment so unforgettable. The Wicked Witch of the West shall live on forever, a truly hopeful ending.

Title: Belén
Comment:
"Todas somos Belén."
De las mejores implementaciones de Gangnam Style que he visto en mi vida. De nuevo MUCHÍSIMAS gracias a @Mateo por recomendarme esta película! 🥰🫶🏻
Usualmente prefiero no hablar sobre cosas que no se pero en mi humilde opinión como mexicana, esta película llega en un momento muy importante para la historia de Argentina, un momento en donde al igual que en muchos otros paises del mundo, su gobierno esta viendo un ascenso en ideologías políticas de extrema derecha. A pesar de estar basada en un caso de hace más de 10 años se siente muy actual ya que la seguridad y autonomía corporal de las mujeres sigue siendo un tema de debate en muchos rincones de Latinoamerica.
Nos presenta la historia de Julieta alias Belén, una chica que fue utilizada como chivo expiatorio por la administración conservadora de su provincia, la abogada valiente que decidió tomar su caso y todos los obstáculos que tuvieron que superar para conseguir su libertad. Más allá del mensaje que quiere transmitir con el cuál estoy TOTALMENTE de acuerdo creo que mis aspectos favoritos fueron los leves toques de comedia, siento que lograron darle un sentido de ligereza sin quitarle la seriedad a lo que es una historia devastadoramente esperanzadora y como abordó el tema de la religión.

No es un secreto que muchxs pro-vida utilizan sus creencias religiosas como una justificación de lo que ellxs creen que es y no es moralmente correcto y es una de las muchas razones por las cuales, a una muy corta edad deje de creer en lo que se le llamaria un "poder mayor" pero aqui, una de nuestras protagonistas es una mujer católica. La escena de la cena con su familia me hizo mucho ruido ya que pese a las dudas de su hija, la perspectiva de Soledad demuestra que hay MUCHAS maneras de practicar la fé de unx mismx y su razonamiento sobre Dios siendo lo que le da un sentido de propósito a su vida me hizo mucho sentido.
La dirección de Dolores Fonzi es super buena, la manera en la que retrato la época fue muy acertada, esta llena de simbolismos, hubo 2 secuencias en específico que se me hicieron muy originales y de su actuación ni se diga, lo mismo para Julieta Plaate como Belén. Se la recomendaría mucho a todas esos hombres que no entienden la importancia del feminismo como movimiento o a las personas que (como yo) necesitamos un recordatorio que la lucha por la igualdad nunca termina de vez en cuando 💜💚.
En un mundo ideal la nominarian a un Oscar por Mejor Película Internacional y si es que termina siendo el caso tiene completamente mi apoyo. No creo poder hacerle justicia con mis palabras más de lo que otras personas seguramente ya lo han hecho asi que lo último que dire es, dejemos de deshumanizar a las mujeres asignandoles titulos como "madre" cuando el embarazo no las convierte automáticamente en una y que chinguen a su madre Beatriz Camaño y todas las personas en poder que se aprovechan de fallos sistemáticos para impulsar sus agendas a costa de mujeres como Julieta Gómez 🖕🏻.

Puntuación general: 8.9/10

It's no secret that many pro-lifers will use their religious beliefs to justify what they deem is and isn't politically correct which is one of the many reasons why i, at a very young age stopped believing in what you would call a "higher power" but in here, one of our protagonists is a catholic woman. The scene with her family stood out a lot for me since in spite her daughter's doubts, Soledad's perspective is proof that there's MANY ways to practice one's faith and her reasoning of God being what gives a sense of purpose to her life made a lot of sense to me.
Dolores Fonzi's directing is so good, the way she portrayed the era was very accurate, it's full of symbolisms, there were 2 sequences specifically that i thought were very original and don't even get me started on her performance, the same goes for Julieta Plaate as Belén. Title: The Nightmare Before Christmas
Comment:
'Just because I can't see it all... doesn't mean I can't believe it!'
A skeleton, the structure of a living being, a collection of bones and cages, born only for the purpose to carry a body around and keep up its shape, and to die with that fulfillment, too. Jack is a skeleton, a clump of bones and cages with the goal to keep not just his town's shape up, but his own, too, a double job he isn't payed extra for, an act of entertainment he etches onto his skull which he cannot hide, but can cover up with a smile. His life goal, to scare and terrify, set not by himself but by everyone around him, has already been succeeded time and time again, a yearly routine rather than a challenge, a form of torture done for joy and laughter. A permanence of terror on Halloween, a never-appearing day without light and a never-ending emptiness of darkness at night. And despite being arguably the most important and providing part of the body, Jack doesn't have anything he needs, living a dull life of monotonous greys and blacks with the backdrop of a pasty moon that struggles to lighten any of his days, acting rather as a reminder of his lack of happiness than giving him any.
And instead of waiting on that gift, Jack decides to go and get it himself. He starts to lose a mind that was never there, to anticipation and curiosity, an adventure he'd never been on, a place he'd never discovered. He was a skeleton without a mental backbone, a lack of persverance to carry on in the worst of times, and instead of dealing with his problems, got himself the gift of a distraction, not a cure. Stealing Christmas was the joy he had needed, a time of community with family and making angels in the snow, something he never could have had back at home. When someone's life becomes devout on finding happiness, the thing you fight so hard to get is often pushed away or stolen by other people, the urge for fulfillment cannot be found by looking for it, but by waiting for it to come to you, or rather by making it with what and who you have.
'My dearest friend, if you don't mind... I'd like to join you by your side. Where we can gaze into the stars...'
'And sit together, now and forever. For it is plain, as anyone can see. We're simply meant to be.'
Or perhaps happiness is always there, you're just not able to see it. In Jack's case it's Sally, a love he didn't know he had, but was always there from the beginning. She seems to be the only sane on in town, holding a true desire for a true life with the man she's in love with, away from her appearence of stitches and stuffing and happy being with a person just as imperfect as her, both in desperate need of care and affection, and both have none. While trying to create a perfect dream world in Christmas, Jack isn't able to see past his own nose, making an even worse version of Halloween when he tries to steal it, he creates a duplicate holiday where what was once snow has turned into a field of pumpkins, as he becomes a prisoner to his own perception of reality. Sally helps Jack understand where the true joy lies, she can see the truth, for not just herself, but for Jack, too.
Jack tried to find a soul in his soulless structure in Christmas, something he felt he missed in Halloween, it was the thing he thought he needed, and in a way it was, but on his journey to find his spirit he instead got something better; a heart inside his ribs. For a soul is useless if you aren't able to love it, but so much better when others can actually see it beating inside of you, a kind of love a skeleton shouldn't be able to feel. But when finally touched by love, Jack became more than just a skeleton providing for everyone else, but a skeleton managing to provide for himself and the one that he loves.

i watched this a couple days ago and had high hopes: while i did enjoy the first one it drags on a little bit, but the sequel is basically better in almost every way. i think it’s really rare to find a franchise where the original movie isn’t the best one, as sometimes sequels just either rehash the same ideas or go completely off track to the point they don’t feel connected: this is a great example of how a sequel should be like. it’s similar to evil dead ii in the way that it keeps the premise basically the same: it has the time travel, robotic elements of robots from the future trying to kill a human from the past before she gives birth to her son who was the leader of the resistance against robots, a fun thing here is there’s quite a time jump and her son is now born, so the target is now moved onto john o’connor, rather than sarah. making the terminator the good guy was probably the best choice this movie made: he’s basically the face of the franchise so it would be weird not to include him, but i’m also glad he isn’t the villain because that would feel too similar to the original, and also the new villain they produce here holds more power which truly heightens the vulnerability of the lead characters, which allows more suspense whether they live or die. i think one main highlight was 100% the visuals, mainly the use of cgi. i’m not gonna lie, i’m not silent about my dislike over cgi in the movie industry: as it usually lacks authenticity and makes everything look artificial and cheap. but there’s some expectations, and this is one of them. saying the cgi here was groundbreaking would be an understatement. the liquid metal effects of t-1000 look immaculate and were decades ahead, i would even go as far as saying they still hold up in 2025. i think that was the main thing that differentiates this film from every other action flick from the 90s: as the metallic goop on the villain is great on the eye. another thing i usually dislike is constant action, but for some reason i love it here. the action sequences are beautifully crafted and sometimes unpredictable. it’s a constant chase scene, it’s complete adrenaline filled,  which makes the 2 hour runtime go past swiftly. the narrative flip is amazing, as the terminator goes through some major character development as he gains some emotional depth as he fathers the son of sarah, as he understands human connection and consciousness. sarah o’connor is such a badass here, plus t-1000 was really nonchalant which makes his character more ominous. despite its great style, it also has some substance underneath. it has some clear messages of the dangers of technological advancements (which is even more relevant today, with the alarming amount of ai) and also human nature.

Everything else sinks into this sort of streaming-service purgatory, the kind that refuses to take any real risks and instead hides behind the glossy surface of green-screen make-believe. The story doesn’t reach for anything, and because of that, the almost two-hour runtime starts to feel like it’s stretching itself thin just to stay upright.
Sooo...flight from the past, a road trip that acts like it cares, but only in the way someone absent-mindedly pats their own head and says, yeah, this’ll do. And it does but it leaves behind nothing more than the aftertaste of a one-evening distraction. So, two and a half stars, not actually bad because this is just “enough” in the most bare-minimum, self-satisfied way.

Title: All Quiet on the Western Front
Comment:
35mm
All Quiet on the Western Front is one of those movies that makes you wonder how human hands, limited by the technology of the era, could craft something so emotionally devastating and technically daring. Words can’t even comprehend how a movie made nearly a century ago still feels so spiritually alive with those sweeping battlefield sequences, the close-ups of young faces already carved by fear, and the sound design that feels like a distant echo of real suffering. There’s absolutely no doubt filmmakers have used this movie as a blueprint, consciously or not; its fingerprints are visible across decades of war cinema. Yet, despite its towering influence, we can’t allow it to fade into existence simply because of its age. It remains as impactful and relevant as ever, a reminder that early cinema wasn’t primitive. It was often bold, unflinching, and ahead of its time.
When I compare it to the 2022 adaptation, the movie’s legacy only feels richer. I genuinely see both versions as masterpieces, but they speak to me in completely different emotional registers. The 1930 version feels intimate, almost tender in the way it portrays innocence being worn down. I can feel the closeness of WWI in every frame, its wounds still fresh enough to feel. The 2022 version, on the other hand, strikes me as colder and more unrelenting, leaning into the industrial brutality of war (the mud, the metal, the machinery of death). One devastates me with its simplicity, the other with its sheer, crushing force. Instead of overshadowing one another, both movies coexist beautifully in my mind and they both form a powerful conversation across generations about the cost of conflict and how easily humanity forgets its own lessons.
I watched All Quiet on the Western Front on a gorgeous 35mm print and it made the entire experience feel almost sacred. Sitting in the theater, I couldn’t stop thinking about the audiences who first saw this only twelve years after the war ended. What must it have felt like for them to confront these images so soon after the world had torn itself apart? Maybe some of them believed the movie’s message would be heard, that something like this wouldn’t happen again. Unfortunately, just nine years later, history repeated itself with even greater fury.

Title: Kill Bill: Vol. 1
Comment:
Kill Bill chegando no fortnite, e é claro que eu tinha que assistir o mais rápido possível pela primeira vez.
“Kill Bill Vol. 1” é como se Tarantino tivesse decidido transformar pura adrenalina em cinema. O filme já começa com aquele clima de vingança sem rodeios, e dali pra frente é só um desfile de cenas perfeitas, cortes rápidos e coreografias tão boas que dá vontade de aplaudir antes mesmo do filme acabar. A Noiva é simplesmente icônica - cada passo dela parece dizer “vocês escolheram a pessoa errada pra mexer”.
O melhor é que o filme não tenta ser profundo; ele abraça a própria loucura com orgulho. Mistura anime, kung fu, faroeste, tudo embalado por uma trilha sonora que deixa cada cena dez vezes mais legal. No fim, Kill Bill é aquele filme perfeito pra quando você quer ver cinema sendo cinema: exagerado, divertido e com personalidade de sobra. Uma experiência sangrenta, estilosa e totalmente única.

Title: Weapons
Comment:
I love my mom, but I forgot the mental strength it takes for me to watch a movie with her. I'm visiting my hometown for Thanksgiving and wanted to show her a film I liked from this year. I thought she would be hooked on the true crime / mystery of this missing kids story. But within the first five minutes, during the opening narration, she tells me to lower the volume so she can ask “how many stars should I rate your new mattress from Amazon?”.  
Weapons is great, watching Weapons with my mom was not. Every time I show her a movie I think it will go better, but it actually feels like a mental battle for me not to crash out from the near-constant interruptions. I’m pretty sure I had to pause the movie approximately 30 times for her to get up or for me to explain what was happening. I like spending time with her and try not to be the bossy cinephile who tells her to put her phone up and pay attention, but this Weapons watch really tested me lol. 
I know she liked it when “the kids ripped up that evil old bitch” (her words), but I’m not sure what she thought of the movie overall, or what she would rate it, at least I know she rated my new mattress five stars on Amazon for sure.

Title: Lolita
Comment:
"I don't want you around them. they're nasty-minded boys."
"you're a fine one to talk about someone else's mind."
definitely a weird choice for a first stanley kubrick (for the controversial subject matter, and is generally just less acclaimed) but was one of the first movies i put on my watchlist and had a spare three hours on friday so i honestly just why not. i’ve never read the book before, i had thoughts of listening to it on audiobook but never really got round to it: but after watching the 1997 film adaptation already (i know, criminal for that to be the first lolita themed thing i saw, but it was the only one on a streaming service at that time) i struggled to find this anywhere, but was just determined to watch because of that vintage americana cover with the heart shaped sunglasses (the thing that lana del rey kinda builds her aesthetic on, also having a song revolving this story which was another thing that brought my interest towards it) but yeah, i did prefer it over the 1997 film and is one of those types of movies that will probably stick with me. this is very much a love-hate type of flick: and i fully understand why. the subject matter is really disturbing and probably not one an average viewer would take much pleasure in. the main concept of the middle aged step-father having sexual, romantic obsessions over his adolescent stepdaughter ‘lolita’ may seem exploitative on first glance, but i love when taboo ideas get thrown into film, as i think this type of thing happens a lot more than a person; would really realise. i think this movie is clearly effected by censorship of its era: as while i haven’t read the book, i’ve heard about how the highly transgressive the explicit parts of the book were, and this movie seems to have a little bit of a lighter tone just because it was harder to show more explicit scenes during the hays code era. despite this, it still had the main premise of it’s psychological manipulation through the weird power dynamic. while this obviously isn’t going to win any awards for being feel-good, it has quite a lot of humour within. it mixes dramatic scenes of social satire, and black humour which may seem a little jarring in contrast to its themes: but i honestly think it works surprisingly well and allows ‘lolita’ to lighten the mood a little bit. i could understand why someone would think this movie goes slow, but i honestly enjoy it enough that i thought this movie went by swiftly. it’s highly dialogue heavy, which may not be for everyone but i'd take a good script over action any day. this was definitely a well-made movie, which was nothing less than what i was expecting. i think the main reason this works so well as a book film adaptation is because of the performances by the main cast, which are noticeably better than the later movie. the portrayal of humbert humbert was honestly powerful. it leans into his more obsessive side. charlotte may seem a little bit over the top with her constant screaming, but i kinda think it fits her character and also lolita was also great with the actresses breakout film. the direction of the film is also great, using minimalist cinematography and heavy dialogue which makes me more intrigued to this movie. this is also quite a bold movie being made in the era of censorship: where almost everything slightly out there received major cuts by the mpaa. this gets credit from me for being boundary breaking and a true statement. not gonna lie and say this is one of my favourite movies, but has aged quite well and i would be open to a rewatch.

Title: Train Dreams
Comment:
Like being able to sit down and ask your great great grandpa for an epic life story one last time. The history is lost but still forever there underneath time. The internalized stoic greatest generation who could barely show emotion, just focus on work and life and getting things done.
This is Robert's story but every character they come across adds little pieces to them. Entire cast is spectacular. This movie highlights how real these locations and characters are. As if you were looking through a history picture book, and the last remnants of the American frontier came alive. 500 year old trees, 500 year old ghosts. All coming and going through a breezy hypnotic score that keeps you locked deep inside the middle of a forest.
This a beautiful movie wrapped up in religious quotes, the spiritual force of nature in the trees and floods coming alive, and more humanism in the second half surrounding this film. Robert finds himself on a renewed journey to understand life and faith through connecting with people and the world. I thought the lengths they went to show the simple shared moments through the future were touching even if they were on the nose. Although the last portions of this don't have as much spirituality compared to endearing grounded moments it still feels like it landed on spiritual humanism. As if he hasn't found the answers to his faith but he is still content with his life and what comes afterwards for him and everyone he knows. All things must pass.

Title: I’m Not Scared
Comment:
RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL
ON THE ROAD - LE STRADE ITALIANE: PASTA, GRANDE IMPERO E LA TERRA DEI MIEI ANTENATI
This is an interesting beast—not exactly your conventional coming-of-age story, as these films normally lean into drama, humor, and whatnot, whereas this one takes a bit of a paranoid thriller direction. We follow a young kid who finds himself in a big predicament when he stumbles upon a hole in the ground where he encounters a poor young kid who has been kidnapped. Slowly, a kind of friendship born out of curiosity flourishes between the two. However, his rescuing would prove to be quite challenging when he has no one to trust, as any of the adults is a suspect. Here’s where we get some of the aforementioned paranoid elements.
The performances are all around pretty solid, especially our lead played by Giuseppe Cristiano. His story arc was great to see—the way it evolves from not being the most likable kid due to an action that happens at the beginning, to playing the hero and only hope for this other kid. He brings a good amount of innocence that gets cracked as he becomes embroiled in all of these situations. The rest of the cast all do their respective jobs really well, especially in selling the ambiguity in their characters, where you yourself don’t know who to trust.
Another element that caught my attention, and I was not expecting it to be this good, was the cinematography. The use of lighting, namely in those scenes in the hole with the dark background, helps highlight the characters and visually create this sense of unease. Also, those scenes in the open field were beautiful. There’s a great contrast between the beauty of the field and the darkness underneath the ground.
All in all, I’d definitely call this a gem that should be seen. It takes a while to get interesting and sometimes can feel somewhat redundant, like I could have easily cut a few minutes, but overall this one was a pretty suspenseful cinematic ride.

Title: Red One
Comment:
This is the second film from my 2025 The 12 Days of Christmas Films list.
It is not destined to be a yearly Christmas classic, but I found Red One to be a fairly entertaining, action packed holiday film. I think that the thing the film suffers most from is identifying its audience. It's not an obviously for grown-ups movie--like Bad Santa, Violent Night, or Rare Exports. It's not really a film for the Elementary crowd or a Christmas Family film.
Red One is a "save Santa, and save Christmas" movie that was given a healthy dash of the Fast and Furious treatment. This is not at all surprising since it stars The Rock and was adapted by Chirs Morgan, who wrote or co-wrote 7 of 8 of the F&F films.
The star power in the film is also impressive: Dwayne Johnson, Chris Evans, J.K. Simmons, Lucy Liu--but no one really shines. JK Simmons makes an interesting, jacked version of Santa Claus and the Rock, the Rock--the same persona that he plays in nearly all his movies. Kristofer Hivju (Tormund Giantsbane from Game of Thrones and the Scotts Miracle Gro fertilizer guy) stands out but his role as Lord Krampus doesn't get enough screen time.
The most impressive part of this film is the special effects and the practical effects. I loved the fighting Snowmen, the Christmas worlds look amazing, and I loved the Rock 'em Sock 'em Robots. The makeup on Lord Krampus and every character in that world was amazing.
If you know what you're getting in to, you're looking for a Christmas film, and you are a fan of highly revved action films, you could do worse.

Title: Lady Bird
Comment:
"We're afraid that we will never escape our past. we're afraid of what the future will bring. we're afraid we won't be loved, we won't be liked. and we won't succeed"
Lady bird feels fresh and original because it doesn’t seem to care about whether or not it delves too deep into the realm of adolescent introspection, or if it plays into the dominant tropes of the genre, it isn’t every day you see a film so attuned to the outsized drama of adolescent life. the film is bursting with life and rich in observations both large and small. saoirse ronan plays a catholic high school senior in sacramento, california who has given herself the name lady bird. she “hates” her home town, but what she actually hates is living on the wrong side of the tracks and being an outsider at school.
There is a kind of gender-less universality about the character of lady bird, this makes her truly unique and she transcends the typical seen-it-a-thousand-times struggling teenager, the universal experience is much more lush for the picking, the opportunities for contrasts and comparisons with ones life alone make this narrative very multifaceted. gerwig knows this and she plays into it through the experiences lady bird is put through. while I do believe that the highest value should be placed on the exploration of the human experience, a film does need embellishments beyond this, and gerwig uses her dialogue to offer some comic relief just at the proper moments. what I took from this film right away was that it really is a story about growing up (not exactly coming-of-age however) and how our relationships change during that process, we see relationships between parents, friends, mother-daughter, father-daughter, and romantic relationships, for those of us that can relate to the situation, going away to college, that period between your last days in high school and the transition to college is when everything changes. family and romantic relationships especially go through huge changes. you are forced to see life in a very different light as well. gerwig really captures this feeling, it permeates the whole film.
Gerwig’s films are a reflection of who she was as an adolescent. she explores themes such as friendship, complex relationships with parents, the journey of growth and maturation of a woman. gerwig is able to facilitate a sense of realness and authenticity when capturing the complexity of the family and its dynamics, as well as portraying flawed individuals in a way that resonates with our own internal dialogues and struggles. especially in the process of growing up, we may have found ourselves in lady bird’s shoes one way or another.
Enough can’t be said about the incredible performances across the board in this film but principally from the two leads,saoirse ronan and laurie metcalf, whom both from the first frames of the movie share a believable, loving, and somewhat painful mother-daughter bond. they are so alike in so many ways but too strong willed to notice the amount of themselves in one another. even if we think we don’t want it, especially when we’re teens, we all spend a good part of our lives striving to win our parents’ approval and while doing so wondering if they even “like” us. honestly, maybe sometimes they don’t and just want us “to be our best selves,” whatever they might perceive that to be. the struggle between these two characters lies therein: marion just wanting the best but not wanting to let go, and lady bird needing to be understood and to be herself.
I’m lucky to have a uniquely close relationship with my dad, and i didn’t get my driver’s license until two weeks before I left for college, which helped build that relationship much more quickly, it was up to my dad to get me to and from school, friends’ houses, and sports practices as well as the occasional road trips, more or less, any part i saw was through the passenger-side window. you get familiar with the way things look on that side of the road: the trees that line the roads, sidewalks, bike paths that never seem wide enough for the people that travel in them, remaining mostly ignorant of what’s in front as well as what’s available from the driver’s side. naturally, we bickered, being the only child, i took notes on how to dance around lectures when I could, but I still became a teenager. i scoffed whenever my dad tried to get me to notice the mountains at sunset. my eyes occasionally glazed over as my dad pulled a life-lesson from his past. we’ve all been in that seat or at least sat in the back of the car while our friend endured a similar situation. now, I, like lady bird, feel emotional driving through my hometown. maybe it’s because I think about my dad making the same drive without me there, knowing I’ve grown beyond needing a ride anywhere. there’s a reassuring but annoying feeling that creeps in when you realize people who tried to teach you something were, in fact, right. now, when I drive around my hometown, I cannot help but enjoy the layers of mountains surrounding the city, or how a cloud’s colors shift with the sunlight.
At the end of the movie, we see lady bird struggle less to denounce aspects of herself and reach a greater level of self-acceptance, and in a scene towards the end where she has earned her driving license and is driving alone for the first time on the bridge of Sacramento, we see her mom mirrored, driving on the same bridge. she concedes for the very first time in her life that sacramento is beautiful, and realizes what her mother sees and loves about the place that lady bird has been desperately trying to flee. she had never taken the time to look thoroughly herself. she can never ‘leave’ sacramento as it is a part of her, and unconsciously, she will always, her final phone call to her mother gives us hope, that even if marion continues to struggle to see eye to eye with her daughter, at least lady bird will take initiative to forge that connection with her mother and move their relationship to a place where they can accept each other, even if they want different things. after all, life is a work in progress, and as lady bird shows us, you may make a ton of mistakes along the way, but the important thing is to never give up. most people, at some point, realize that their parents or guardians were right about at least a few things growing up, the lessons taught aren’t always pulled from an argument, or a clunky speech, but rather in presence or observation, and all of a sudden, all a child can do is look back and say, “thank you.”
My life will be black to the white rind of the old and fading moon. my life will be like water over the cracked floor of these desert years. i will land on my feet this time, knowing at least two languages and who my friends are, i will dress for the occasion, and my hair shall be whatever color I please. everyone will go on celebrating the old birthday, counting the years as usual, but I will count myself new from this inception, this imprint of my own desire, my life will be swift, past leaning fence posts, a gravel shoulder, asphalt tickets, the beckons of the open road. my life will be wide-eyed, fingers shifting through fine sands, arms loose at my sides, wandering feet, there will be new dreams every night, and the drapes will never be closed. i will toss my string of keys into a deep well and old letters into the grate, my life will be ice breaking up on the river, rain soaking the fields, and a hand held out a fire and smoke going upward, always up!!
(P.S- watching this film on my birthday every year is more like a ritual now, and a big thank you to all the lovely people here, who makes this place feel like a home, i love you all so so much, i feel so lucky i got to share my love for art with y'all!!! <3)

Title: Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning
Comment: The big submarine sequence is probably the one thing people will remember from this movie, and it stands well for it, as impressive a feat as it is lugubrious. Physically satisfying filmmaking of the kind only big pockets allow,  operating under a drama drowned in its failed intimations of heaviness. The first hour is so turgid, it is almost surprising when the film at least starts to move some when it hits the sub. The whole movie does suffer from a serious case of screenwriter brain, not only with all the effort to tie things up, but also with how overdesigned everything feels. The good McQuarrie entries can also feel very mechanical, but they at least manage to convert all the strings into the flow of action. In this one, every magic trick is exposed with little dramatic satisfaction. The big airplane action is a solid return to the kind of stunt the series later entries do well, big and exciting, but it is telling that its stabs at crosscutting simply go dead the moment it goes away from Cruise. For all the talk about the IMF team (these movies were better when the supporting cast was Ving Rhames and whatever recognizable, disposable faces the producers bring on), this is probably the entry that serves its supporting cast worse.  So many scenes of people talking and explaining story and meaning while Cruise does things, none of it works. Considering this runs near three hours, it is impressive it spends so much time in Basset’s scenes. What is left is the enormity of Cruise’s narcissism; if the movie has any value, it is by how overblown its superstar worship is allowed to become. It is so large, the cracks and emptiness of it end up visible enough to allow for some fascination. The first three stunt-heavy Mission Impossibles stand for a certain big-scale awe that studio filmmaking of the time was hardly able to conjure; the general creakiness of Final Reckoning, from Cruise worship to the labored scenes, suggests a machinery that finally reached an end. There's nothing left for this kind of Hollywood cinema, blow up the whole thing. It is finally dead.

Title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
Comment:
Ustaca islenmis bir film ki, bundan daha iyi bir tanim var mi bu film icin, emin degilim. Keske sinemada deneyimleme sansim olsaydi; bos koltuklar, karanlik, daha yuksek sesli muzik, daha dikkatli bir gozle izlemek… Su an hissettigimden cok daha fazlasini hissederdim, biliyorum.
Filmin bir kadin elinden cikmis olmasina o kadar sevindim ki. Bir kadinin, kadinlarin askını anlatırken onları cinsellestirmemesini, izleyici cekmek icin degil, aralarindaki bagi anlayalim diye sevistirmesini gormek tarifsiz bir rahatlikti. Tesekkurler Céline Sciamma. Oyle ustaca yonetmissin ki…
İnsanı masal dunyasına alip goturen, soluksuz birakip son sahnesiyle buruk bi gerceklige carpan, izledigim en ozel filmlerden biriydi bu. Sessizlik dolu sahnelerde bile her sey konusuyordu. Bakislar, nefesler, duygular.. Hepsi abartisiz ama gucluydu. Umutsuzlugun icinde hayatta kalmaya calisan aski, oyuncularin son derece gercek performansiyla hissetmek inanilmazdi.
Film boyunca aklima kosmayı, ruzgarı hissetmeyi, kitaplarla iyilesmeyi bana ogreten kadinlar geldi.
Bazi sahneler aklimdan hic cikmiyor: Atesin basinda Heloise’in askini kabul ettigi o an, tabloda '28' yazisi, unutulmaz son sahne; Sessizlikle müzigin birlestigi o unutulmaz son sahne. Heloise’in ilk defa bir senfoni dinlerken yuzunde beliren onlarca duyguyu seyretmek tarifsizdi.
Marianne’in resmi yaparken verdigi emegi adim adim izlemek, memnun olmadiginda en bastan yapmayi goze almasini gormek cok etkilenesiydi. Çogu filmde ressam iki cizgi atip bir tabloyu bastan sona yaratmis gibi gosterilir. Burada fircanın her dokunusu, her duzeltme, her katman… Hepsi Marianne’in ruhunu tasiyor gibiydi.
Heloise’in hayatinda hic senfoni duymamis olmasini konusmalari, hayatimin kolay oldugunu tekrar ve tekrar fark etmeme sebep oldu. Simdi bir senfoni acacak olsam, buna on saniyemi ayirmam yeterli. O donemde insanlarin hayatina hic girmeyebilecek bir mucizeydi. Marianne’in ona nasil bir sey oldugunu anlatmaya calisirken kelimelere sigdiramayip calıp gostermeye calismasi, izledigim en naif seylerden biriydi.
Birlikte yasadiklari kisa tatli anlar, uyusturucu sahnesinde Heloise’in buyumus goz bebekleri.. Hic kitap okumayan Heloise'in okudugu kitabin tek bos sayfasi olan 28. Sayfayi ezbere bilmesi, Bunun sergi sahnesinde karsimiza cikmasi, o son sahnede Heloise'in duygu yogunlugundan ve etkilenisinden kiminle ayni yerde oldugunu bile fark edemeyisi, daha onlarca detaya bile deginsem bu filmin guzelligini kelimelerle anlatamayacagimi fark ettiriyor. Iyi ki dogru zamanda izlemisim. Kotu aksamimda izleyip klasik ve basit bir lezbiyen filmi yorumu yapmis olmayi dusunemiyorum bile.

Title: Knives Out
Comment:
Knives‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌ Out [2019] – Yesterday marked the sixth anniversary of Knives Out and I thought it would be good idea to watch the movie again with my dad. In fact, this was only my second viewing of the film, and I had almost no recollection of anything that happened during the first. I suppose I didn’t focus too much when I saw it initially, so it was almost like my first time watching it. That made me pretty much fall in love with the movie again. After some time away from it, I can really see how much effort and detail went into making the film.
First of all, the aspect that most impressed me during my viewing of the film was the main storyline being told with utmost conviction. The manner in which Rian Johnson presents the mystery is very exact, and to be honest, even if you know the major twists, it is still very gripping. All of the dialogue, every joke, every little visual detail — it all matters. This time I was also very much aware of how the film’s elements of humor, suspense, and dysfunctional family dynamics are perfectly interwoven. In addition, it is not only very clever but also quite enjoyable to watch.
Daniel Craig is still great as Benoit Blanc, but this time around, I found myself appreciating the entire cast more. Particularly, on a second viewing, Ana de Armas’ performance seems to be the most real and the strongest. The other characters, through their subtle moments, which most people do not notice, also, really help the story to deepen. The film invites the viewer to be an active participant and certainly, I was not getting most of it during my first viewing.
I have been a big fan of the Knives Out universe and I was made even more of a fan by Glass Onion. Rian Johnson alters the mood and style in between the two films but keeps that which makes them so great, and that is actually one of my favorite things about the series. Watching the original again made me realize why these movies are so different from other modern mysteries.
Now that I’ve seen the first one again, I’m even more excited for Wake Up Dead Man. If the first two are any indication, the third one will be smart, unique, and packed with surprises. I am really looking forward to what Benoit Blanc will be up to ‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌next!

Title: Back to the Future Part II
Comment:
Enriching Sci-Fi Film…
Back to the Future Part II is an exciting thought provoking follow-up with numerous story twists and an engrossing examination of the intricacies of time travel. Marty, Doc, and Jennifer fly to 2015, picking up where the previous film left off. Marty and Doc traveling back in time to 1955, as we see in the classic Back to the Future scenes, was a clever move. Biff is a character that is simultaneously likeable, humorous, aggravating, and hateful. The VFX and tempo were superior to the original. The film offers an unforgettable combination of action, cleverness, and adventure while skillfully balancing humor and depth. It’s an introspective and unique film that tells an interesting story while leaving questions for Back to the Future Ill to address with a suspenseful conclusion.
Memorable Scene: The final sequence is so flawless and wonderful; the guy's sudden appearance is so powerful that it convinces you that time travel is real since, from Marty's point of view, that is precisely how things would unfold.
Marty McFly: “2015? You mean we're in the future?”
Biff: “Hello? Hello? Anybody home?”
Biff: “Why don't you make like a tree and get out of here?”
Doc: “The time-traveling is just too dangerous. Better that I devote myself to study the other great mystery of the universe: women!”

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
Comment:
“Spear shall be shaken, shield shall be splintered!
A sword-day, a red day, ere the sun rises!
Ride now, ride now, ride!
Ride for ruin and the world's ending!
Death! Death! Death!”
A remarkable conclusion to quite possibly the best trilogy ever made. 
The scale is incredible - sweeping battlefields, massive towers and cities, huge armies, cavalry charges, apocalyptic stakes and a gigantic amount of heart. 
It’s no surprise this film swept the Oscars (11!) - although it’s disappointing that they didn’t put anyone forward for the acting categories. Sean Astin should have at least had a Supporting Actor nomination (a sentiment he himself has stated).
Like its predecessors, the action is thrilling, the music flawless, the performances perfect and the story engrossing for its full, lengthy run time. While a lot is made of the multiple endings being overly long and sentimental, for me it’s needed. It’s clear Jackson didn’t want to say goodbye to these characters, and neither did I. 
Return of the King is a film that almost always manages to make me cry, or at least choke up. What’s interesting is that it never seems to be the same point. Whether it’s Theoden’s speech at the Pelennor Fields, Frodo setting sail for the Grey Havens, Aragorn telling the hobbits they “bow to no one” or countless other moments in the back half of this film.
For what it’s worth, it was Sam’s delivery of this that set me off this time: “Rosie Cotton dancing. She had ribbons in her hair. If ever I was to marry someone, it would have been her. It would have been her.”
These films mean so much to me - my ultimate comfort films, as I know they are for many of you. The magic of cinema on full display - being able to switch off and disappear into Middle-Earth for a few hours is sometimes exactly what you need.

Title: Silent Friend
Comment:
Singapore International Film Festival 2025 Film #8

As someone who loves cinema I usually leave movies with countless thoughts (+ and -) banging around in my head. On occasion, a film will be so powerful that it renders me speechless. Silent Friend has had that type of impact on me. From the moment I entered the screening to the very last moment of the film, I could not stop thinking about how beautiful and masterful the use of artistry was in each and every frame of this film; the level of emotional maturity and intimacy that was shown throughout is something that many filmmakers will never be able to achieve. The life that the film gave to all of the plants throughout the movie is one of the reasons that I connected with the film on a personal level. It shows how deeply and intimately plants are able to participate in the creation of our environment and how they are able to communicate with us just like we communicate with other humans. After watching this film, I completely understand why my neighbor talks to their plants, why Hirayama from Perfect Days takes the time to spend with trees, and why the earliest people of the world considered nature to be their gods. This film even inspired me to practice shinrin-yoku when I return home to Japan.
Man, I love film festivals for giving me the chance to see films like this, ones that I feel can only be experienced on the big screen. On a small screen, I think much of its emotional resonance and visual poetry would be lost. I hope everyone who loves arthouse cinema gets the chance to experience this beautiful film.

As a man grappling with severe grief and his thirst for vengeance, Mel Gibson's psychological problems and struggles are skillfully written. The fighting war style, the horrific bloodshed, the acting, the villain, the appropriate use of the musical soundtrack to set the scene's tone, the location shots, and the depiction of the colonists conflicting views on the battle were all outstanding.
