Comment:
“you’re on their side, aren’t you? so, who will you bet with?”
paul and his damn stupid slutty shorts, and those tragic cry-for-help pink ankles jammed into those tight ass shoes forged in the ninth circle of hell, had me clawing my own face off in a rage so pure it could peel paint off walls !!! people have been hooting and hollering about this movie since the dawn of time apparently, so i walked in thinking i’d walk out with a new all time favorite, but boy oh boy was i wrong, painfully wrong, embarrassingly wrong. ain’t shit funny about this damn movie, i was steaming mad the entire time. i’m not even angry about what happened to the rich kids, i’m angry because how are you that useless as a human being. no survival instinct, no basic logic or reasoning thoughts, not even the bare minimum of knowing the police number. WHAT DO YOU ACTUALLY KNOW !!!!!! what skills do you possess. what brain cell is running the operation in there. goodness lawd. watched nearly twenty minutes of this before i was lucky enough to come across a big knife and stabbed myself to death 
i’m sorry, but as a thriller this barely drew a breath of suspense. peter lumbers across the screen, his gestures clumsy, his charm so staged it feels rehearsed by a puppet who already knows the script, and you start to wonder if the film ever actually wanted you to feel tension, or if it’s too busy winking at the audience with smug little nods. it flirts with danger only to yank it away, folding the plot into a meticulous little origami of predictability, every twist flashing on a marquee you weren’t supposed to notice. nothing is left to the imagination, the possibilities are sliced so cleanly that anticipation dies before it can even form, leaving you waiting for clicks and cues you’ve already guessed. maybe it’s trying to critique the genre, to lampoon its clichés and tear back the curtain with a self satisfied “look how silly thrillers are!” but it never plunges deeper, never lands a single piercing insight, content instead to preen in front of the mirror, patting itself on the back for pointing out truths everyone has long known. what’s so wrong with a thriller following well worn rules? what crime is it for an audience to expect the familiar rhythm of tension and release? we’ll never find out, because the movie refuses to leap into actual commentary. it just struts around, preening and posturing, highlighting the genre’s “failings” while denying us even a single pang of satisfaction. and it’s such a shame, because sparks of brilliance still managed to slip through the cracks. fleeting flashes of promise, tiny shards of the twisted cat-and-mouse games peter and paul play, moments that could have been clever, cruel, intoxicatingly smart. and you mourn them, because the film keeps dragging you into a dull limbo instead. crashing the one true gift of a thriller, which is the delicious and exquisite terror of not knowing what comes next, and replaces it with one long, smug FUCK YOU aimed straight to the audience. and well, guess what, movie? i don’t like your torture porn, and i don’t like your hollow “message” so FUCK YOU TOO. Title: Lisa Frankenstein
Comment:
"When I said I wished I was with you, I didn't mean that. I meant I wished I was in the ground, dead, because life sucks and people are jerk-offs."
I was seething with envy watching this. Yes, I know it's impossible and I'm all grown up now, but why can't I just have this incredibly handsome, Victorian-era man who plays the piano, is emotionally intense (even if his tears smell like ancient graves), is a gentlemanly kind, and most importantly, doesn't speak? And Cole Sprouse's gaze, with his soft, loving eyes, makes me feel like I'm 13. Yes I need help.
But the thing is Lisa is so me. She’s awkward, dramatic, delusional in the most endearing way and navigating life with main character syndrome as her only functioning personality trait. I respect her, I see her, I am her! And what's wrong with wanting to kick people who don't like you to hell, listening to The Cure, and dressing as gothic as possible?
Also, her obsession with Michael is completely relatable to me. He's the epitome of "not like other boys." He's "intellectual," wears a Nietzsche t-shirt (yes, that's a green flag for me), and quotes Oscar Wilde. No wonder Lisa lost her mind over him, I'd be worse.
So the whole movie was a neon-soaked mess of '80s chaos, with a touch of gothic glamour and a dash of campy romantic comedy. I loved the aesthetic and the Heathers vibe. And because it was the '80s, the music was epic, too. I especially enjoyed it when The Promise started playing. Interesting characters and good soundtrack, it's actually easy for me to enjoy a movie.

Title: The Beanie Bubble
Comment:
Galifianakis without his beard is such an uncanny-valley experience for me that watching the whole movie felt genuinely unsettling.
A time-jumping look at the Beanie mania, something I had zero prior knowledge of and honestly no real interest in, so a film like this has some pretty big shoes to fill if it wants to be an engaging package. The end result, however, is such a uniquely mediocre "celebration" of consumerism that nothing really sticks with me, except maybe the fact that Zach seems to be missing all his body hair.
Gore and Kulash’s structure is genuinely interesting, and I was ready for the way this film positioned its characters and story through constant time jumps. The problem is that it keeps going on like that for far too long without ever creating anything truly different with its own approach. This leaves everything in a kind of personal limbo that never manages to spark real interest in the story.
Visually, it’s good, there’s this shimmering American Dream aesthetic running through it, wrapped in the illusion of 90s power dynamics. But as a whole, it ends up being a somewhat disappointing experience.
So nothing really remains. It’s not a bad film, the acting is solid, but the conversations are a bit frustrating, intentionally shallow, yet that very shallowness ends up eating away at the film’s own core. The movie lacks the charisma it needed, that intoxicating pull that should have hypnotized those of us who actually want to enjoy something like this. It’s American allure that should have hit us hard with its experience, not just brushed us with its mediocrity. Meh.
53/100

Title: Big Eyes
Comment:
“walter never accepted defeat, insisting he was the true artist for the rest of his life. he died in 2000, bitter and penniless. he never produced another painting”
i think i might be one in a million who actually enjoys tim burton’s biopics, and big eyes just proves it once again. amy adams painting with lana del rey playing in the background is the closest thing to watching an artist pour their entire soul into a jar while another figure hovers beside them, waiting for the perfect moment to plaster their name across it the second it starts glowing and looks profitable. the story slowly shifts into a forensic look at how easily talent can be devoured by someone else’s ego. it shows how creation can be overshadowed and eclipsed by the person loud enough, or shameless enough, to claim it as their own. some people survive by making things, by leaving pieces of themselves in the world, and others survive by taking, by feeding on whatever light isn’t theirs. the more walter talks, the more obvious it becomes that the paintings matter less to him than the spotlight they attract. he wants the myth, the aura, the legend of being “the guy who makes big eyes” even if that title sits on a pair of shoulders that aren’t his. he stretches the truth like damp paper, bending reality until it fits the inflated version of himself he’s so desperate to parade around. every story he tells is a performance, and every lie a brick in the little kingdom he’s building out of borrowed talent. meanwhile margaret, terrified and hopeful at the same time, keeps shrinking and folding herself into smaller and smaller versions of who she used to be, a silhouette she barely recognizes anymore, just to keep the peace. she’s surviving the gravitational pull of a man who’s decided her brilliance looks better stamped with his name. he pushes her further into the shadows of her own paintings while he swells into this ridiculous and overstuffed balloon of self importance 
and that’s most definitely the most gutting part. a heartbreak that hammers through your chest, igniting blood into a wildfire that threatens to tear itself out of your veins. how someone can conjure something luminous, something trembling with their own fire, and still shy away instead of taking credit for it. while others, hollow and roaring, stride off draped in crowns stitched from sparks that was never theirs. vanishing is an art no one teaches, until someone with more magnetism, more audacity, more insatiable appetite reaches in and siphons the glow you never realized was yours to command, or yours to wield. the movie renders that power play into a portrait of manipulation, perfectly veiled in elegance. a canvas where devotion and domination blur. smiles curve over pressure like masks, praise drips with possession, and the marriage itself becomes a stage built for a solitary actor, where no other voice may rise. women compress into fragments of themselves, tucking storms and fury within just to be noticed, to stay married, to hold their ground, while men bloat and swell, puffing themselves past recognition just to maintain the illusion of feeling big and in control. and big eyes states it so plainly. empires are erected on the bones of other people’s labor, assembled by those blinded by vanity, desperate to appear greater than they are. and the most beautiful part is witnessing that fierce ember of selfhood, margaret’s talent, her terror, her unvarnished truth, awaken to its own power, realizing it can reduce an entire house to ashes if it wills. the film stretches that surge of self assertion into something jagged and ferocious simultaneously, a momentum that keeps gathering until it consumes the space that once denied her. from there, the story turns toward reclamation. breath, voice, authorship finally drifting back to their rightful owner. becoming, in itself, the act of stepping free from the man who tried to dim her out of existence, and who sought to make her invisible, only to learn that the world had always been drawn to her creations, not his theatrics. taking ownership of your work, your name, your creation demands a bravery most will never taste. hands reach fastest for what they never shaped, cheering for those who never lifted a brush, applauding the impostors, until the truth finally tears through the noise and stands where it always should’ve been

Title: I’m a Cyborg, But That’s OK
Comment:
“the vending machine says hi”
!!!!!!!!!!!!! CRYING. imagine crossing paths with a boy carved out of trouble inside a psychiatric ward, a small, improbable thief with palms trained to steal the intangible, and i ask him to pilfer the last piece of my capacity to feel. and the moment he takes it from me, that delicate trembling organ of tenderness, it flares open inside him instead, transforming him into the bewildered boy who now feels everything on my behalf. he then engineers a miraculous contraption that alchemizes food into pure luminescence, feeding me tiny detonations of light that keep my circuits from corroding, so i avoid gnawing on batteries in a desperate storm of metallic fever, letting my imaginary mechanism revolve in its own secret cadence. he intervenes and rescues me with the care of someone tending to a clockwork soul, never fracturing the consecrated scaffolding of my delusions, he simply crosses their threshold and dissolves into them, merging with their inner wiring, moving through my hallucinations as one moves through a sanctum wrought from flickering belief. an intruder turned acolyte in a cathedral stitched from invention and reverie. and all the while, he maps the strange terrain of my mind with an affection that could reorder the stars. at last, we find ourselves standing together beneath an uncooperative sky, asking the heavens for voltage instead of mercy. waiting for lightning to strike us, because in our mythology, love is measured in electric currents. a crackling conduit. a divine short circuit that arcs across our ribs and mutters, in its hush of static, that whatever strange machinary we are made of, we are destined to ignite and spark, again and again, without end. forever (!!!)
“i’m not a psy-cho. i’m a cy-borg”
i don’t think my heart has ever surrendered so completely to a film before. an almost alchemical seam opens with it, coaxing heat from my rusted, little shriveled fucked up evil heart until it kicks awake in a filament of molten unrest, quivering yet untamed, singing with its own untethered effulgence. here is a girl who starves, driven neither by vanity nor despair, but by the conviction that her stomach harbors a tangle of electric veins. a girl who chats with vending machines as if they were old confidants, who watches ladybugs fluttering through fissures in the air, who has slipped so far into her self invented circuitry that she can’t locate the doorway back to her own reality. she loses pieces of herself amidst familial wreckage and identity’s disarray. and so she does what many wounded people do, she becomes something utterly other. and then there’s him. a boy stitched together from absence and that hollowed out void of not knowing how to feel complete. instead of flinching at her oddities, he holds them in a reverent awe that seems to ripple around his fingers, as if each delusion were a rare specimen. he treads gently into her world, barefoot and careful, letting her logic be the gravity that anchor his steps. in his hands, her strangeness vibrates, a resonance only he can attune to. and he bends himself to it so she can eat again, so she can breathe again, so she can exist without tearing holes in her own spirit
here lies a tale that sees what most romances refuse to touch. love is the art of treasuring another’s peculiarities, allowing their eccentricities to become the very architecture of your shared world, and guide the rhythm of your hearts. the narrative treats mental illness as a stain etched deep into the human psyche, a visible shadow on the soul, yet one that coexists with resilience and refuses to define the person entirely. even inside the asylum’s walls, joy flickers in myriad crooked shapes, laughing and bleeding through the cracks. none of these characters are waiting to be “saved” from themselves, they’re simply learning how to live inside the lives they already have, with humor and companionship in whatever form it arrives. i’m worn thin and exhausted by stories where love triumphs despite the rough patches and the brambled depths of someone’s soul. what electrifies me most is surrendering to those very edges, letting them entwine with your own pulse until they form the lattice of desire, gathering them close when they shiver, pouring solace even when your own chest threatens to splinter. to love is to dive into their private tempests without expecting calm, to memorize the way their turbulence tastes, to cradle the parts of them that scratch and burn, and let them reshape your own skeleton in reckless gratitude. it’s knowing that the very quirks that would drive anyone else away are the strange magnets that anchor your heart, that every dissonant note they strike becomes a song you would never have imagined alone. and this film delivers exactly that and more. devotion sculpted from the unpolished truth of a person, and it is absolutely breathtaking (!!!) a sweet reminder that true healing begins with radical self acceptance, and giving yourself the gentleness you were never taught to crave. in a world fermented in cruelty and bitter days, we all hunger for a confection of embered comfort that spills endlessly with unblemished ardor. to meet someone who will sit beside you while you’re on your mission to end of the world, who will trace your cracked wiring and call it beautiful. that is what love, in its most incandescent, improbable form, can be <3

Title: Ran
Comment:
RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL
ACTION! - HEART OF AKIRA, BLADE OF KUROSAWA
Kurosawa returns with another masterful spin on Shakespeare, this time tackling King Lear in a film that also stands as the director’s final feudal epic.
And my man goes out with a bang!
Personally, I still lean towards Throne of Blood for its gripping story and performances, but when it comes to direction and technical brilliance, this one truly takes the cake. Right from the start, I couldn’t help but chuckle at the fact that someone finally gave Kurosawa free rein to unleash the carnage! Most of his earlier films in this genre portrayed violence in such a clean, almost bloodless way that it bordered on comical. But here… oh boy! That raid scene alone, with its mountains of bloody corpses, death lurking everywhere, and utter desolation, or that explosive blood wall splatter near the end—this is easily the bloodiest (and deadliest?) entry in Kurosawa’s filmography.
The rest of the film dazzles with breathtaking shots, immersive production design, and stellar performances, featuring yet another powerhouse turn by Tatsuya Nakadai as this version of King Lear—a man who essentially shoots himself in the foot by pitting his sons not only against each other but against himself. Nakadai brilliantly captures the anguish, the slow mental and spiritual decay, as we witness his life fading away, leaving behind a pale shell, like a wandering ghost. The writing is engaging, though I didn’t find it quite as gripping or thrilling as, say, Macbeth. Still, I appreciated the twists and turns.
All in all, Kurosawa hits another home run, cementing his place as one of the best in the genre and beyond, especially in the technical realm. It dragged a bit for me at times, but I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Title: On the Rocks
Comment:
Minimalist Coppola, small in ambition but wide open in soul… yet there’s something I can’t quite place.
Coppola is such a meticulous, precise director. You can feel how expertly she sets the story’s suspicion right in our laps, she’s subtly shifting the mystery so we never see anything too clearly. The central dilemma never becomes blunt or overstated, it just is in that same liminal space Jones’s character occupies, a gentle uncertainty you and I wander through together. And Coppola lets it all unravel in its own gravity, creating this built-in reflectiveness, a soft echo chamber in which the smallest gestures ring louder and louder.
But it must also be said that the film feels a bit “thin”. The resolution, when it finally arrives doesn’t quite settle with the weight or clarity it seems to be reaching for. At the heart of everything is a relationship that isn’t about the romance at all, but something else, a father–daughter bond. Jones is steady, controlled, never stepping beyond the emotional boundaries Coppola lays out for her. And Murray is his usual “charming” self, an old-school seducer, narcissist, with a smile that hides the fact that he’s been emotionally absent for decades. He’s the blueprint of a certain kind of man world overflows with.
So the past and present blur, and people who seemingly possess everything end up collapsing into the hollow space that no amount of wealth can fill. The vibe is gently selfish and broken, yet somehow overflowing with love in ways nobody doesn’t know how to show.
The film never really plays as a comedy, but it does contain these tiny pockets of humor, moments where life’s absurd coincidences become the joke. And what stays with me in the end is something slightly undefined, but also something warmth, a reassurance that maybe, just maybe, you’ll find your way.
So in the end, the Big Apple glows, neon promise, yet you can also sense a slow internal rot beneath the shine but it isnt never visible on screen, but present in the vibe, between the lines. Something new in a familiar place that feels strangely alien, reminding you that the ease of life sometimes deserves a pinch of hardship. And that hardship, along with a strange freedom, reveals itself every time someone steps into the doorway of your well-known, worn-in home🤔
Sooo, yeahhh four stars.
77/100

Title: A House of Dynamite

On a technical level the movie is well made and there are glimmers of greatness in here but overall it rings hollow. Title: Solaris
Comment:
Seven years before Andrei Tarkovsky created his milestone STALKER, which had completely broken free from genre constraints, he tried his hand at a story by Stanislav Lem. SOLARIS however only presents itself as a science fiction film, even though all the motifs point in that direction. this film as well is rather a philosophical voyage, a gigantic web of thoughts, a text-obsessed mental construct.
Similar to STALKER, the film presents a scenario that focuses on the differences between Tarkovsky's conceptual worlds. Right from the start, the film draws us into a magnificent, flowing natural landscape. Only within this space does the theme of family acquire a real form. The protagonist bids farewell and flies in a space bubble (Hello, Fountain!) to a space station. Even before this, we are treated to a remarkably dense, raw sequence, which Tarkovsky would repeat years later with the railcar ride in STALKER.
The industrial sea of metal condenses into a traumatic motif of alienation. The roads intersect, the noise level becomes unbearable, and the predecessor in space—someone who, thanks to his opposition to the civilization of science, has already been expelled from it—is caught in the dynamic current of the sea of lights. The film immediately contrasts this unnaturalness with the tranquil, organic flow of the river on the family estate in the very next shot.
Our protagonist arrives at the space station and finds a chaotic garbage dump. Something sinister is afoot, and the film takes on a truly eerie quality. The two survivors in this vehicle to nowhere represent the dualism that so often permeates Tarkovsky's work. While the somewhat deranged Snaut embodies a view of "letting things happen," of intuition, transcendence, and even the tragedy of life; Sartorius remains a stern, cold-blooded scientist, an explainer trapped in hubris. Someone who cannot be swayed. While the family sequences serve as a framework, primarily conveying warmth and security (including a sense of home), the philosophical levels collide here in the film's central section, within a very confined space.
The decisive catalyst for the plot is the emergence of imagination, of the repressed, of memory. His wife, who took her own life after their separation, appears and cannot be shaken off. Here the crucial driving force of the discourse merges with what is already statically given—it becomes almost tangible. To what extent does a person "construct" their life, their environment, even their fellow human beings? What happens when the repressed, anchored in memory, the painful recollection forces its way out? Who is subject, who is object, where is the point of view, who decides here at all?
This strange fog, primordial ooze, this entity that the spaceship constantly faces—this is the indefinable, uninvestigable mass that controls thoughts here. What can a person do then? What is chimera, what is real? Confronted with all these questions about life, the person becomes depressed and either commits suicide or goes insane. At least he changes his mind; our protagonist transforms from a devout progressive thinker into a searching believer.
Unlike STALKER though SOLARIS is not particularly aesthetically pleasing. The cramped sterility of the space station alone prevents this. The juxtaposed, organic nature scenes are all the more effective for it. Even more so than in STALKER, the film seeks contrast – the cold, misguided notion of progress versus the monumental power of the inexplicable, the guiding force, the one that thwarts the human mind. Tarkovsky must also accept the criticism that he basks his narrative in a belief in the supernatural, in religious mystifications, and ultimately allows a glimmer of hope to shine through, which Lem had not intended in his source material.
SOLARIS is also a film about the male loss of perspective. The woman, the unknown being; the woman as savior, as a constitutive element in the narrative of a man's life. child, lover, mother. The tangible connection to nature. As a self-born creation of the imagination, the woman on the space station escapes male desire, subconscious, memory, longing. She is still a constructed object, but becoming human is imminent, and the bond quickly becomes so close again that even future plans (tragically unrealizable, of course) are forged.
Behind all the destructive, depressive thought processes—love as an imagined, self-constructed pseudo-power—a search for cohesion has been found, and becoming human—and becoming a subject—is possible in true love. Hope never truly fades in this film, even if the final image seems to want to rebel against it one last time.
The utterly disillusioned faces of course always tell their own story. Despite all faith in belief, in humanity, in intellectual constructs and communication – Tarkovsky's films remain restless, contemplative and poetic, yet with a profoundly tragic gaze upon broken structures. As much as he might wish it were otherwise – no one here finds happiness. Except in his imagination.

Title: The Sword of Doom
Comment:
“The sword is the soul. Study the soul to know the sword. Evil mind, evil sword."
“Cruelty doesn’t to stop at your sword. It’s seeped into your mind and body, and it frightens me.”
RIP Tatsuya Nakadai who gives one of the all-time great soulless psycho-murderer performances here as Ryunosuke Tsukue, a nihilistic inversion of the wandering rōnin with a heart of gold/principled sense of honor and justice, the archetypal “man of action” as a cold-hearted killing machine. Kihachi Okamoto’s fluid formal precision effectively deconstructing this type of mythic hero, giving his empty animal instinct toward killing an unfeeling casualness, and an evil, enigmatic momentum towards hellish destruction. Hard not to be impressed by the sense of quiet stillness and patience right before each carnage-heavy setpieces begins, and the elegantly controlled long dolly shots that he chooses to deploy during all the slicing and dismembering choreography. From the opening scene of Ryunosuke gruesomely answering the prayers of an elderly man who no longer wishes to be a burden on his family by viciously striking him down atop a mountain to its frenzied, apocalyptic, half-imagined/half-real samurai massacre climax and hauntingly blurry and unresolved freeze-frame ending (that was apparently meant to imply sequels but in the absence of any suggests he may actually successfully kill the entire world), Nakadai sells the transformation from stoic shadow of death to maniacal demon swordsman whose lost all psychological connection to earthly reality. Trapping us in a labyrinth of fiery bloodlust, a ritualistic rumination on death, and a ghostly funeral for the trail of corpses left behind by this figure whose only purpose in this world is senseless violence. Shoutout to Toshiro Mifune who only has a few scenes as the more honorable master swordsman who is humble and regretful about committing acts of mass-violence, but whose snowy attempted-assassination rampage around the midpoint here would probably be the high point of a movie that didn’t have an ending as transcendent as this does.

Title: Dreams
Comment:
RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL
ACTION! - HEART OF AKIRA, BLADE OF KUROSAWA
Aka the film in which Scorsese plays Van Gogh
Ahh man, what can I say about this film that hasn’t already been said before? If I had to sum it up in one word, it would be “magical.” Yet, while the film dazzles with idyllic and breathtaking scenes—like the hauntingly beautiful ending, the mesmerizing Van Gogh sequence, and the captivating opening—it might just as well be called “Nightmares.” That’s because about 70% of the film plunges us into creepy, disturbing, and harrowing territory, especially everything surrounding the volcano and the nuclear devastation. Still, I adore the little details, like the delicate flowers—a bittersweet memory of a beauty that once was. Then there’s the unforgettable scene of people wailing and crying in pain, a haunting image that would linger in my dreams. So, thanks, Akira!
The performances are solid across the board, but ultimately, this film is more an exercise in visual storytelling. The dialogue serves to inform and sprinkle a few nuggets of wisdom—whether hopeful guidance or stark caution. Unsurprisingly, the cinematography ranks as some of the finest in Kurosawa’s entire filmography. The music also deserves special mention, perfectly building and setting the tone for every scene, whether joyful or ominous.
All in all, this film is like a beautiful painting—or should I say, a gallery of paintings—that I loved to gaze upon and appreciate. It conveys profound messages, many of which feel deeply relevant today. Yet, among all of Kurosawa’s works, I’m not sure this is one I’d return to watch repeatedly.

Title: Bugonia
Comment:
"Primarily, I'm not an alien."
Yorgos Lanthimos, how I missed you. Please don't let anyone stop this man because he works overtime with the muse and makes incredible work every time! Freak, weirdo, disturbing, uncomfortable, crazy, intelligent, confusing, surreal, critical, creative, colorful... I'm in love with Yorgos' style, and I'll always support directors like him. He's one of those who says "not when I'm still alive" to those who say modern cinema is boring. I already have my fingers crossed that wish him well for his new movie.
Having been exposed to Yorgos's films extensively, this wasn't hard to guess. But this familiar Lanthimos influence doesn't dampen the film's excitement—on the contrary, it plays with us with its subtle humor. Even the Andromedan aliens heard my laughter throughout watching this. I think even non-Lanthimos fans will love this—it has well-constructed plot. Gave me the freakiest version of fun and depression. My heart ached for Teddy and Don. Their experiences, traumas, beliefs, mentals. At first I thought they were just two isolated incels listened to too many podcasts—but as the veil they had slowly lifted from their past, I felt pity for them instead of resentment. The only way to save themselves was to save the entire world, and they sacrificed everything for it. Two simple men against a space ship full of aliens, that takes real dedication! Wish men would try to resolve some issues with therapy, but some men are more useful without therapy. For example, if Yorgos had "normalized" his mental state, we wouldn't have seen these masterpieces.
The dialogue sweeps you along like a river. Flowing, clear, intelligent. Michelle and Teddy are both smart. While their words remarks might sound like the opinions of a manipulative teenage boy trying to appear smart by using excessive jargon—their "respectful" discussions are the most important part of film's story. We get to know them both this way—both tough, strong, and determined. They don't give up, constantly trying to impress each other, engaging in a power struggle. Even though Michelle is chained in that basement, she has no intention of giving the charge to anyone. Coming from different backgrounds, one from upper class, other from lower, this duo competes for authority over each other. All we have to do is bite our nails with excitement until to see the winner.
I'm now on Jesse Plemons and Emma Stone's PR team this Oscar season! If they're acting, what do other actors do? They're not even acting—Yorgos creates a persona for them, and they become it. Give these two all the awards! Throughout the film, their characters battled for supremacy, and their acting was equally competitive. Every time I thought they couldn't do better, they upped the ante and shocked me. My favorite trio: Lanthimos-Stone-Plemons. Now I need hundreds more movies with them.

Title: Eddington
Comment:
Ari Aster's Taxi Driver? but make it way less grizzly & grim. consider me a double A fan up to now, and consider me raging about the fact his newest got its cinema start last week over here, pretty much as the last country on earth it seems.
having said that I should be relieved that Eddington is a huge letdown. but well, I'm not. the film feels very much like a draft written over the course of the covid pandemic, and wanting to forcefully reflect on the situation satirically. maybe that already sounds slightly antiquated?!
remember once the pandemic was over everyone was very much interested in forgetting the whole shebang (except the long covid patients and the angry anti anti anti internet mob). so the starting point of putting that on screen now - years later - might be already a step into the puddle.
the first half of Eddington is a surprisingly humor free drag, establishing lots of characters that will eventually fall out of the picture. no matter if starlets like Emma Stone, Pedro Pascal or Austin Butler, no one gets a proper treatment to work with. especially in the case of Butler's fishy cult leader that's a big miss out.
the second part then gets his literal guns out and therefore starts to become more entertaining. as dark as Aster's mayemish outlook gets, as slightly random and off it is though. especially the half-hearted explanation for what actually happened is another lackadaisical and desultory effort.
I fully understand the desire to make an all-embracing satire of those last five years - especially when this might be your last shot at putting something relentless individual on the big screen - but Aster delivers only a lukewarm, fade, evaporating dish here. expect him to re-enter the old "the horror genre is the new creativity sandbox" world soon again.

Title: Blade Runner 2049
Comment:
Blade Runner 2049 is an undoubtedly fantastic film and may honestly be one of the most beautiful films I’ve ever watched. The cinematography is phenomenal and it’s been so long since I’ve watched this that I’ve actually forgotten the story. As a result, it felt like watching this for the first time all over again. Also this is just absolutely mesmerising on an OLED TV. Every single scene could be a painting and I want it all up on my wall.
Ryan Gosling plays the role of a known replicant so well in this, and his ability to say so much without actually speaking anything really helps elevate the mood of this entire film. Honestly, I’d go as far as to say this is a major step-up from the original Blade Runner by Ridley Scott since I find the character journey to be so much more rewarding and it all feels so human. Not only this, but Denis Villeneuve really respects the original film in this and even Deckard’s return doesn’t feel like a fan-service trap as he is actually quite integral to the story. Blade Runner 2049 feels like a true sequel in that way, and it expands on the mythology explored in the first film expertly. It’s an aspect I didn’t truly appreciate the first time around however many years ago I’ve watched this, but it’s something I thought was really worth mentioning. 
I find the inclusion of Joi to be so interesting in this too, as she is an artificial intelligence that gives off the illusion of love and real connection, and helps encourage K that he is special. She calls him Joe, and it really helps show K’s longing for human connection even if he is a replicant himself. Her calling K “Joe” in the film is treated as a touching thing, until it becomes a tragic thing - and it is so damn manipulative. She is an illusion that highlights our vulnerabilities in wanting real love and wanting to feel special, and in this case she made K believe that he was the extraordinary one. She is also a product that capitalises on loneliness and need for affection and while watching the movie it really clocked for me that she exposes how easy it is for both humans and replicants to buy into illusions as long as it portrays (fake) emotion - and by extension, if it’s Ana de Armas, we’re vulnerable. This parasocial relationship is fascinating to watch on-screen and seeing K break free from her when she gets destroyed much later on in the film is actually a very positive thing for his character. He didn’t need a companion that listened and agreed with all of his decisions, he just needed his own agency.
Moving on from Joi, K’s choice at the end of the film I believe cements the whole point of the film really well. There’s a lot of talk about being born from 2 replicants and being special, but honestly that wouldn’t actually make K any more human. His ability to make the choice to save Deckard and then bring him to his daughter at the end is incredibly human and really highlights that he has his own control of his destiny. We all have our own control of our destinies. We don’t need a reason to be something more or have a program reinforcing our ideas, we simply need to make our own choices as our free will is what makes us human. 
In the film, we also see the replicant Rachel get replicated and yet she wasn’t an exact replica because as machine as these replicants are, Rachel still had her minor differences (for example, her eye colour). This small detail compliments the theme of humanity and identity so fucking well because it shows even a replicant can’t be replicated - at least not exactly and definitely not down to its own agency. I could genuinely go on and on and on about the depiction of free will and humanity in this film but I’d just keep repeating myself as I’m catching myself doing right now. It’s just so fascinating to see humanity not come from biology but instead our humanistic traits.
Where I think the first Blade Runner could have benefitted from being longer, I am very grateful that Blade Runner 2049 has the admittedly long runtime that it does have as it really does compliment the philosophical and visual storytelling on display. However I can’t quite give this the 5 stars treatment since I reserve that rating for my absolute favourites, and unfortunately I get depressed when I watch this. On that note, fantastic mood setting too.

Only my second time visiting Krampus but it has cemented its place as one of my go to winter watches, and it’s a for sure holiday horror classic. That is largely due to the masterful touch of writer/director Michael Dougherty, much like his celebrated Halloween anthology, Trick 'r Treat, Dougherty understands that genre films thrive when they nail the aesthetics and deliver a solid core narrative. Krampus is a genuinely great time, a wicked blend of dark comedy, holiday cheer gone sour, and effective monster horror.
The film immediately establishes a strong sense of place. The opening sequence, is a fitting slow-motion montage of aggressive Black Friday shopping.. those days are long gone now I’ve not seen a real Black Friday rush in some time, but this sets the stage so well.
The action then moves to the suburban home, this is where we see the weather and location work become a character in themselves. The sudden, suffocating snowstorm and the harsh sense of isolation create a chilling backdrop. The cinematography captures the eerie beauty of the frozen, abandoned neighborhood, intensifying the family's terror as the blizzard cuts them off from the world.
The cast is full of solid recognizable faces like Adam Scott and Toni Collette, and the ensemble is B-tier in the best possible way; populated by excellent actors committed to the absurdity. They play the dysfunctional family dynamic with a surprising amount of sincerity, which makes their increasingly desperate hell fest feel grounded. David Koechner and Conchata Ferrell are particularly awesome and provide some necessary comedic relief. 
The tight narrative keeps things snappy and running smooth. The pacing is excellent; the film doesn't waste time on excessive exposition, quickly moving from an uncomfortable family gathering to a terrifying siege, maintaining a relentless momentum up to its darkly satisfying and highly memorable ending, I haven’t forgot it since I watched it for a first time last year. 
The film truly shines with its creatures and monster design, which is a testament to the fact that Dougherty prioritized wicked practical effects from the talented heads over st Weta Workshop. From the demonic holiday elves to the unsettling Angel Doll, the monsters are imaginative and outrageous. The design of Krampus himself; a horned, cloaked figure with a monstrous waddle. These physical creations enhance the horror and give the film a vintage, tangible quality that CGI can often lack, it no doubt helped the actors on set too, those creations are nightmare fuel. 
The sound track is fantastic, full of a range of Christmas songs. The score by Douglas Pipes, who also worked on Trick 'r Treat, takes familiar holiday tunes and warps them with an unsettling edge, perfectly complementing the films atmosphere and tone.
Ultimately, Krampus is a delightful, lawless antidote to overly sentimental holiday fare. It works because it respects both of its genres: it's genuinely scary, often very funny, and deeply steeped in the look and feel of Christmas. It’s a must-watch for anyone who appreciates the naughty side of the holidays.
I can neither confirm nor deny whether that backdrop is from this film or not, you simply have to watch it to find out.

Title: A Streetcar Named Desire
Comment:
‘I don’t want realism. I want magic! Yes, yes, magic. I try to give that to people. I do misrepresent things. I don’t tell truths. I tell what ought to be truth.’ 
Based on the play by Tennessee Williams, A Streetcar Named Desire follows troubled former schoolteacher Blanche DuBois (Vivien Leigh), as she moves in with her sister Stella (Kim Hunter) in search of solace. However, her uneasy presence stirs tension like greased lightning, leading to even greater conflict in the household — especially with her brother-in-law, Stanley (Marlon Brando). 
Elia Kazan clearly had a great eye for casting when he choose Marlon Brando to play the contemptible and objectionable Stanley. His crude yet magnetic performance leaves you speechless — even more so once his actions fully unfold in the film. It’s no surprise it earned him his first Academy Award nomination. 
Speaking of which, Vivien Leigh won her second Oscar for her performance as Blanche DuBois. Leigh, who was well-known for her troubled personal life, left everything behind here and gave us an awe-inspiring performance. She was a hell of an actress. Kim Hunter doesn’t fall behind — she’s also outstanding too. In fact, most of the cast is! 
‘Straight? What’s straight? A line can be straight, or a street. But the heart of a human being?’ 
‘I never met a dame yet that didn’t know if she was good-looking or not without being told, and there’s some of them that five themselves credit for more than they’ve got.’ 
The remarkable storytelling and master-class performances make this film stand out by the test of time.

Title: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
Comment:
A raucous Hong Kong-style martial arts action movie mixed together with an otherworldly Chinese-mythology-inspired fantasy movie. And most importantly, amidst all the larger than life goings-on, it grounds itself in an engaging human story, delivering a nice message about striving to find your purpose rather than simply gliding through life.
The cast, as usual with the MCU, is top-notch: Simu Liu is a charismatic and intelligent leading man, Tony Leung makes for an imposing and three-dimensional villain, and the rest of the cast provides the needed humor, menace, and gravitas. Destin Daniel Cretton’s directing is imaginative and eye-catching. And the Asian-infused score from Joel P. West is surprisingly strong; how does this guy not get more work?
While the big finale drags on just a little too long — I’d have been happy if they’d cut the last ten minutes with the second dragon — this is still better-than-average Marvel. I’m disappointed that we haven’t seen more of Shang-Chi and his world in the years since this came out. Here’s hoping they remedy that soon.

Title: Late Fame
Comment:
Singapore International Film Festival 2025 Film #11

You ever sit through a movie and walk out feeling absolutely nothing? Like it didn’t make any changes in you or any particular feelings were received. that was my experience here.

The story itself deals with poetry, missed chances, nostalgia, and the weight of an unlived life. Usually these themes present some natural emotional charge, yet this movie explores these themes in such a distracted, detached manner that there is nothing that actually draws me. It simply floats by with no interest or demand upon the audience. There is no emotional engagement, nothing to be connected to, everything is presented with a sort of emotional detachment.
While the film included a lot of things that could be thought-provoking it left me feeling as though they were simply thrown at me instead of creating any sort of feeling of being deeply involved or reflective. Title: Wicked: For Good
Comment:
As someone who flew to New York for Wicked’s 20th anniversary on Broadway, it gives me no pleasure to report that like its titular song, Wicked: For Good is changed — but probably not for the better.
Fair warning: this is a review for fans of the show and the film. It is going to be lengthy and riddled with spoilers.
I’ve always admitted that Act II of the stage show mainly gets by on the strength of Act I — and that its more melodramatic choices feel right at home on a theatre stage. The problem with For Good is that the performances never quite rise to that level. Scenes on-screen have more space to breathe than they do live, so paradoxically, everything feels less intimate, less emotionally close, and far more restrained than what us Wicked purists are used to.
There was a lot of buzz after the pre-screenings about Ariana Grande’s Glinda blowing early watchers away. I think her vocals are good, but the performance reads oddly one-note — mostly pouty and sad throughout versus her arc in the first film. Cynthia Erivo’s Elphaba gets to have some range, and that contrast shows. I preferred Elphaba’s new song “There’s No Place Like Home” over Glinda’s “Girl in the Bubble,” even though neither added much value. (I get it, Stephen Schwartz — go for that Original Song Oscar.)
And while “There’s No Place Like Home” sets up Elphaba’s connection to animals, the film never directly pays it off. There’s not an ending scene where she’s leading the animals off to a new land where they can thrive together, when it would have been so easy to, or even a symbolic gesture. Even on a small scale, say for example, with Dr. Dillamond: early on, we see she’s kept his broken glasses in her grotto, and then later we see him back in his classroom — suddenly intelligent again — but without addressing the earlier reference. Imagine having his glasses repaired and returned, with a poppy beside them, so he knew it was Elphaba. It would have taken seconds and landed much harder emotionally.
More broadly, some of the film’s structural revisions just don’t work. “Thank Goodness” is overloaded with new material that didn’t need to be there. I get that they wanted to fill in gaps from the stage show, but sometimes you don’t need to. I know I’m in the minority, but I’d rather have the songs as originally written.
On the other performances: Cynthia Erivo and Jeff Goldblum are fine. Ethan Slater’s Boq is one-note as a sad, trapped Munchkin, but once he becomes the Tin Man, he gains real depth — sadness, rage, and a compelling physical change. Michelle Yeoh, though, is still the clearest misfire. She’s the main reason I couldn’t give the first movie a full five stars, and here she’s expanded even more. Madam Morrible isn’t a massive singing role, but she still needs someone who can actually inhabit the character. Let’s be honest: Michelle Yeoh just plays Michelle Yeoh. It never feels like she understands the world or the tone, and everything I heard from interviews suggested she didn’t know the material beforehand. Giving her extra scenes and song lines just magnifies the issue. For my own sanity, I also won’t address “Wicked Witch of the East” and my hopes that the soundtrack recording is an improvement on the version we got in the film. 
In all fairness, some things are done quite well. “As Long As You’re Mine” is still emotionally effective, even if less intimate than the stage show. “No Good Deed” is the standout song — powerful, sharp, and performed with real grit. “For Good,” despite the choppy added dialogue, is beautifully sung and still lands emotionally. I also liked how Dorothy and the trio were handled — backgrounded but present. We know the story. They don’t need more context. The melting scene was especially great.
What doesn’t work are the constant flashbacks. We don’t need a view of Glinda’s childhood to understand her desire to be liked — she has an entire arc across the first movie that tells us that. And the Wizard’s moment with the green bottle hits the audience over the head with information that could have been expressed with smarter cues or imagery. The stage show is literal about it, too, but here it feels even more clumsy.
In conclusion: I love the source material. I love the show. I love the book that inspired it. I love the first movie. I wanted to love For Good. Instead, I ended up somewhere lukewarm. It feels to me that first movie was made for fans of the stage show — through thoughtful additions, not revisions. This one is mostly revisions: filling blanks that didn’t need filling, smoothing edges that didn’t need smoothing, and tinkering with material that was already strong — for the benefit of people who became fans of the first movie. 
To end on a reference for the fans: I hope a rewatch changes my mind. I doubt it will.
Update: If you’re reading this, I’ve since re-watched and re-reviewed For Good. My feelings may have changed for the better… or at least slightly-better-than-before.

HORROR MOVIE #356:
It felt like torture watching this damn movie on an airplane with nothing else I could’ve possibly watched instead. It was either this movie, music, or pure silence, and I was so tempted to turn this off 15 minutes in and enjoy the plane’s engine noise for the next two hours.
Until Dawn got better as it went, but by god this had one of the worst sets of characters and dialogue ever. It almost like they were given a list of cliche catchphrases like “guys you might wanna see this” and then used one every 5 seconds. The dialogue was honestly the most irritating since it seemed so unnatural and unoriginal. It almost seems satirical; that’s how bad the acting was. Like I said, it started off on a really bad foot. If I had anything else downloaded for the plane, I would’ve left immediately and gone to watch something else. But since this was the only thing I had on my phone, I was held hostage by this movie. The concept is derived from the game which came 10 years earlier (which I didn’t even know about until the end. It’s a Happy Death Day and Five Nights at Freddy’s fusion with a few decent scares and tension building. I think that if the characters were written better and if the dialogue and acting were past bare minimum, this could’ve been pretty good, because the concept is creative.
I will likely forget about Until Dawn in about a month. It’s really nothing special, and maybe since I never played the game it doesn’t hold much emotional value to me. I’ve already forgotten the characters’ names, and pretty much everything that happened. I think the one memorable scene was the clown scene, which even that was a bit of an anticlimactic letdown.
Lesson learned: download at least two movies for the plane, even if you only have time to watch one.

Title: No Other Choice
Comment:
A história se organiza como uma espécie de panorama do desejo, mostrando como laços humanos criados sobre confiança podem se fortalecer ou ruir conforme as pressões externas se intensificam. Quando esses vínculos são cortados, até podem brotar de novo; porém, se o núcleo que os sustenta é frágil e sustentado por uma falsa sensação de clareza, a possibilidade de crescimento real se torna duvidosa. É nessa situação que acompanhamos Man-soo (Lee Byung-hun), um veterano com 25 anos no setor de papel que, de repente, vê sua trajetória interrompida ao ser dispensado junto de outros colegas. Sua estabilidade desaparece de uma hora para outra: a casa confortável, os filhos bem criados, a rotina tranquila ao lado da esposa, tudo começa a parecer ameaçado. Conforme os dias passam, a situação financeira se complica, mas ele insiste em manter o padrão, recusando-se a vender bens ou cortar despesas. Até que deposita todas as esperanças em uma nova oportunidade dentro do mesmo mercado, ainda que isso implique eliminar rivais de maneira literal.
Park desenvolve a narrativa, daqui para frente, com sequências de violência, situações tensas e momentos inesperados e divertidos. O resultado é um filme afiado, inventivo, cheio de pequenos detalhes e conversas reveladoras, em que personagens e subtramas se cruzam num ritmo imprevisível e deliciosamente absurdo. Ao longo da narrativa, fui me ligando cada vez mais ao que era contado, especialmente quando, no fim, o protagonista decide não insistir mais em agir com todos ao notar que aquilo não serviu para nada. Não interpreto isso como uma crítica à mobilização conjunta, de forma alguma. Enxergo mais como uma leitura sobre como o discurso vazio do universo corporativo corrói tudo ao redor, desfaz relações e atrapalha até as menores tentativas de união. E faz isso de um jeito direto, mas isso não chega a ser um problema, ainda mais com o humor despretensioso que conduz a história do início ao fim.
A disputa por um emprego deixa de ser apenas uma questão de renda e passa a significar pertencimento, posição social e, acima de tudo, uma masculinidade que precisa ser continuamente reafirmada. A impossibilidade de sustentar a própria família corrói o protagonista por dentro, e No Other Choice evidencia o absurdo de suas ações sem ignorar o peso emocional que o move. Os contrastes exagerados pelos quais o personagem transita, da euforia comprada à queda em um delírio impulsivo, revelam um retrato distorcido e frágil da figura masculina. O gramado impecável, as plantas cultivadas até na casinha dos cachorros e o abraço familiar emoldurado pelas folhas de outono que caem enquanto comem as enguias oferecidas pelo chefe dão forma ao ideal inalcançável que guia sua vida, sempre com um toque de artificialidade. Logo depois, o filme o empurra para o fundo do desespero, entre homens que travam o maxilar e acabam batendo a cabeça uns nos outros durante a terapia coletiva, que se afundam na bebida e fracassam em qualquer tentativa de afeto com suas esposas, numa sucessão de comportamentos que expõem o grotesco e o trágico da experiência.

Title: The Smashing Machine
Comment:
Once I got over seeing The Rock with hair and settled into this film, I found it a very compelling story of a man who was driven by a need to win and an innate need to dominate physically--a man with a urgency to prove he is the very best of what he does. And what he does is beat other men into submission (or unconsciousness)
What surprised me most was has generally friendly, open, and respectful Mark Kerr was outside of the ring. Of course, he had bumps in his life in dealing with relationships and opiate addiction, but he also built genuine friendships inside and outside of the sport and, in the end seemed to find his inner peace. It felt like finally losing released him from some sort of inner demon and gave him back his emotional freedom.
Whenever I watch a film like this, I wonder, how accurate and true is it. I did some digging. Here is a good article from Entertainment Weekly: Fact-checking The Smashing Machine: MMA legend Mark Kerr compares the movie to his real-life story. In the article, the real Mark Kerr says that the A24 biopic about his life and career is about as close as it can possibly get to the true story. That's good enough for me.
The structure and direction of the movie were very good. Director Benny Safdie kept the film grounded while managing to build tension throughout. I was a little surprised that the actual fight scenes were as short as they were---but the film wasn't really about the fighting, it was about the fighter.
I have to talk about Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson is his first real dramatic role. The man can act. In his past films, mostly light comedies or action thrillers, he has done well using his high charm and charisma to overall any acting shortcomings. But in this film, he really acts. I was impressed. Now, of course, he was fully in his element--the world of wrestling, but it is still a big dramatic step forward. I'd like to see him in a non-sports dramatic role. Emily Blunt is a star, she was great.
Overall, the Smashing Machine was a good film, but might have limited appeal. For those who are not interested in fighting sports, they may find this film a bit boring or pointless. Mark Kerr is a legend, but a legend in a sport some people just do not care about.

Title: Harold and Maude
Comment:
sounds funny but I think I have a valid take here: Bud Cort is the unofficial brother of Malcolm McDowell's Alex! look at his face, at his eyes, at his mimic. look at his forlorness in this god forsaken society. look at the fascination with death (although it's more of the intrigue of violence towards the outside with Alex vs the tendency for self-destruction with Harold). look at the eyes again - they are literally the same. it's the eyes of boys crushed by this world that's not made for them to catch a breath in.
it might be no coincidence that Kubrick's Clockwork Orange came out the very same weekend as Harold and Maude, ironically the one before christmas 1971. always fascinating to see what an influence the Vietnam war had on the US society and how it shaped the film industry back then. by today's standards it's unthinkable that this type of a vivid civil society tackling the industrial military complex could be possible nowadays, never mind Hollywood would have such a focus on it.
Maude meanwhile choses a hippie-esque, free floating, society mocking, life affirming lifestyle not out of free will but necessity and lack of alternatives: she witnessed the biggest horrors causing the biggest traumata leading to a life-or-death scenario and now she's gonna handle the aftermath. she confronts herself with the morbid playfully, and denies reality as good as she can (fascinatingly successfully when it comes to social restrictions; an utopia if you think about it). essentially though she's not only lonely and trapped in this world (her monologue about cages is coming to mind), she also needs the permanent contention with death up to the point of total control of her own.
there's tons of wonderful side gimmicks in here: the terribly cold, controlling, aloof mother, whose surrogate Maude has to become naturally. and speaking of Oedipus: the psychoanalyst in his prime position of the oversized, monstrous, black leather chair hiding his humanism gets his come-uppance as well as the priest and his pedophile desires hiding behind a fake moralism; not to forget the uncle as a comical joke of a soldier*. everyone stinks in here except Harold and Maude: the pretentious actress, the boring normies his mother tries to set up a marriage for Harold with, and of course all of the imbecile state authorities.
Hal Ashby fits his wildly ecstatic eccentricity into crisp 92 minutes, and you can easily see how this guy knows something about montage, not wasting a gram of fat on his way. Cat Stevens gives the endeavor the touch of a true 70s singer-songwriter bonfire experience, which fits the playfulness of Ashby's film very well, although underscoring the deep sadness it is oozing out. the big finale then leaves you pretty devastated there, in your cinema seat. as last mean move of the film it doesn't even give you any breathing room to reflect and spits you out of the comfy hall faster than you can say "did that really just happened?".
*the scenes between Harold and his uncle have an uncanny handle to it: the military as sensemaking community, war as ultimate extreme sport, the moment you can finally "feel" the ecstasis of living - something Harold can very much refer to, looking for something sparking some sort of fire in him. that's a great recourse on why such a death-loving, life-denying society as the militaristic one can blossom fresh as a daisy all through the existence of mankind.

Title: Lisa Frankenstein
Comment:
They say time heals all wounds. But that's a lie, time is the wound.
Where is my dead boyfriend? I need my goth, poet, pianist, mute lover.
Lisa was so freaky!! Totally crazy, has fire music taste, stylish outfits, fancy hair, dark humor, intelligent... This boring world don't deserve her. That girl who wanders around cemeteries, reads poetry, listens rock, has no friends, quiet and weird. In other words, the coolest one. Her mother's death and witnessing this tragedy devastated her. Now, she was trying to adapt her new life with her "perfect" stepsister, annoying stepmother, and passive father. She was lonely, and trying to get attention from her school crush Michael. And a lightning bolt brought her together with another broken heart. When The Creature, who had died years before, came back to life, she was no longer alone. She literally fixed him, took care of him, and shared her feelings with him. And The Creature punished those who made Lisa's life difficult—a little brutally way, but that's okay. I want what this deadly couple have. Accepting love, no matter what.
Lisa is so me, I get her well. I'd be in love with that Oscar Wilde-quoting, intellectual, long golden haired, cool music taste boy too. But these types are usually the same, just like Lisa says—they want to be the only cool one. Because they love to act superior to their partners while they have "simple" loves. But Creature is so understanding, kind, sensitive, and protective. Dream boyfriend! His tears are green and they smells awful, and he's a little pale from being dead, but he's better than a manipulative, toxic man.
I choked with laughter, felt incredibly good, time flew by, aesthetically satisfied, desperately wished lived in 80s, all these songs seemed to be playing exactly from my playlist!! This is what I call a comfort movie. I fell in love with its retro-neon vibe.

Title: Kill Bill: Vol. 2
Comment:
“EU VOU MATAR O BILL”.
 “Kill Bill, Volume 2, de Quentin Tarantino, é uma celebração exuberante da arte cinematográfica, deslizando com alegria desenfreada de um capítulo audacioso para outro, funcionando como ironia, sátira, drama e pura ação. Nesse longa-metragem, continuação direta do primeiro volume, claro, vemos o desenrolar do projeto de vingança de Beatrix Kiddo (Uma Thurman). Mas, para a surpresa de quem esperava mais do mesmo, ou seja, muita ação sanguinária estilizada, o segundo capítulo da saga de retaliação da Noiva é completamente diferente em praticamente todos os quesitos. Para começar, tudo é feito de maneira cadenciada e bem diferente do frenesi explosivo do primeiro filme. Essa mudança de passo estabelece outro ritmo ao Volume 2, quase uma ruptura total em relação ao que veio antes. A violência continua, mas em tom menos exagerado. O filme é uma destilação dos inúmeros longas de kung fu trash que Tarantino absorveu e que ele ama incondicionalmente. Quem reclama da superficialidade dos personagens na 1ª parte, finalmente vai calar a boca ao ver a profundidade que eles ganham nessa conclusão. Gostei ainda mais do que de " Kill Bill, Volume 1 "(2003)”. Não é uma sequência, mas uma continuação e conclusão, filmada simultaneamente; agora que conheço toda a história, a primeira parte ganha outra dimensão. "Vol. 2" funciona por si só, embora tenha uma ressonância mais profunda se você já assistiu à primeira parte.

Title: Deep Crimson
Comment:
Director’s Cut
When people talk about Mexican cinema on the global stage, the usual trio inevitably dominates the conversation: Alejandro González Iñárritu, Alfonso Cuarón, and Guillermo del Toro. Yet Mexico’s independent scene has long harbored filmmakers who’ve carved out their own signatures, and Arturo Ripstein is one of them. Experiencing Deep Crimson as my first encounter with his work felt like unlocking an entirely different lineage of Mexican cinema, one that rejects grandeur in favor of messy humanity, moral decay, and the strange, wounded tenderness that grows in the darkest corners.
Given that only around 5,000 people on Letterboxd have watched it, the movie feels like a genuine hidden gem. Set in 1940s Mexico and inspired by the infamous Lonely Hearts killers, Deep Crimson follows Coral Fabre and Nicolás Estrella, a pair of damaged souls who form a predatory romantic partnership built on seduction scams, emotional manipulation, and a desperate hunger for connection. It’s a noir in the most elemental sense: a story of doomed love, economic desperation, moral ambiguity, and the inevitable slide into darkness. However, Ripstein’s take on noir is uniquely his, with fewer slick shadows and trench coats and far more sweat-stained hotel rooms, peeling wallpaper, and the sad bravado of people pretending to be more than what life has allowed them to be. For Noirvember, it’s an inspired choice: a noir that doesn’t just look dark, but feels spiritually and emotionally scorched.
This might be an odd comparison, but watching Deep Crimson reminded me of “Love Will Tear Us Apart” by Joy Division because both share an almost uncanny emotional and thematic resonance. The song’s central paradox (routine, resentment, stagnation, and love’s slow erosion) fits Coral and Nicolás like a prophecy. Their passion is immediate, carnal, and consuming, but its foundation is cracked from the start: jealousy, insecurity, economic need, and a mutual willingness to exploit the other’s wounds. They latch onto each other not because love redeems them, but because love hastens their collapse. Ripstein captures this tragic contradiction with a brutal kind of tenderness, making their relationship both magnetic and disturbing to watch. By the time the movie reaches its final moments, you’re left with the chilling understanding that their love was never meant to heal. It was only ever destined to destroy.

Title: Punch-Drunk Love
Comment:
SHUT UP! SHUT THE FUCK UP! SHUT UP WILL YOU SHUTUP SHUTUP! SHUT SHUT SHUT SHUT SHUTUP... SHUTUP! NOW
For years this was my favorite PTA, and recently I started doubting myself, wondering if it’s still actually that good. The result? It’s even better than I remembered. One of the best rom-coms ever made, maybe the best. Here’s why:
In the 90s, rom-coms were at their commercial and cultural peak with Pretty Woman, Sleepless in Seattle, Four Weddings and a Funeral, Notting Hill, and 10 Things I Hate About You. However, in the early 2000s, the genre totally lost its spark. Studios kept recycling the same formula in films like Kate & Leopold, Bridget Jones’s Diary, and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days. They were still box-office hits, but creatively, visually and narratively, the genre was tapped out. And right at that moment PTA dropped this film. Rom-coms were fully formulaic and practically cry for help. PTA broke the genre’s basic comedy rules and proved there was still life in it.
Normally, girl meets boy or boy meets girl in the most cliche way possible. They don’t like each other at first, then there’s a spark, then the guy does something stupid and loses her, and finally he stages a big romantic gesture and happily ever after. That’s pretty much every rom-com, right? Except this one.
Barry and Lena meet “by chance” (or at least that’s what Barry and we think at first), but even that moment feels genuinely random, not fabricated like a fairy tale. And later we learn that she basically planned the whole “coincidence” because she already liked him.
Which brings me to the second cliche: The guy tries to win the girl over. Here, Lena is the one doing the work because Barry is socially awkward and defensive. His entire life he’s been shaped by how people see him. He grew up with seven sisters who constantly humiliated him by telling strangers embarrassing childhood stories. Barry has no private life. In a rare moment of vulnerability he opens up to his brother-in-law about his mental state and asks him to keep it between them, and of course, like everything else in Barry’s life, that boundary is violated too.
That’s why, both in his routine and even his relationship with Lena, he's angry, guarded, panicked, and always lying as a defense mechanism. Lena doesn’t care about any of that. She’s the first person who doesn’t try to judge or define him or force him to explain himself, and that creates one of the most natural, sweet, and genuinely interesting relationships I’ve ever seen in a film.
On top of all that, the film even dips into crime-thriller territory a bit. Even in its calm moments, the music and editing put us in Barry’s shoes, the jump-cuts, the anxiety, the sense that even a simple phone call can completely ruin his life. Watching Barry deal with all this while also growing through his relationship was amazing.
Sandman delivers a totally disarmed, vulnerable performance, and that’s exactly why this is still his best perfomance. It’s an incredible character study. Emily Watson is inviting, mysterious, and lovely. PSH had little screentime but iconic as always. The visuals are gorgeous, rom-coms never get this level of craft. The color grading, cinematography, lighting, everything feels so unique. The Hawaii scenes might be my favorite part of the whole thing. There Will Be Blood (which I'm excited to review one day, years ago I gave a presentation on it for an international relations and cinema course in college) is better and more monumental, sure, but honestly, this is favorite and 2nd best PTA. With this excuse I made a new list:
Top 50 Rom-Coms of All Time - Ranked: PTA

Ziehen wir einmal meine vorläufige und noch nicht vollständige Liste zu den Top 10 der Erstsichtungen 2025 heran, sehen wir sowohl Filme aus den 60er, den 70ern, den 80ern sowie aus den 90ern und mit einem Eintrag einen aus den 2010er Jahren mit „A Hidden Life“. Sehen wir uns einmal meine Bewertungen zu Filmen, und ausschließlich Filmen Made in 2025 an, kommen wir zu einer vorläufigen Höchstwertung von einer 3,5/5 bei fünf Filmen vorzufinden (sofern ich keinen unterschlagen habe). Ausgesprochen sehen wir: das Jahr 2025 bei vorläufigen null Kinobesuchen (ein persönlicher Minuswert) ist, soweit auf Filme bezogen, verdammt enttäuschend.
Warum jetzt die ganze Vorrede:
Weil wir hier eben und erstmals einen wohlmöglichen Kandidaten für besagte Top 10 der Erstsichtungen 2025 Liste haben der sich gut als Vergleich nimmt. Ein antretender Vergleich der sich weniger auf die Inhalte folgender Filme bezieht, schließlich ist Geschmack, gerade inhaltlicher, sprich bezogen auf die Geschichte und auch auf die Inszenierung, die Subjektivität in Person, sondern auf den technischen Aspekt der selbstredend und ebenso wenig wie ich selbst nicht ohne den erzählerischen auskommt und ihn einfach, ob bewusst oder unterbewusst, mit einfließen muss und wird.
Im Heranziehen der Vergleich zwischen „Train Dreams“ und, und hier beziehen und wir uns nur auf vergleichbar erzählte Filme, „The Long Walk“ wie „Frankenstein“, sehen wir eine verdammt große Diskrepanz (was die Vergleiche anbelangt und die mögliche Unfairness gegenüber ihnen: erstens sah ich mir die oben genannten Filme erst kürzlich an, und zweitens hätte ich, wohlwissend, auch das positive Beispiel aus dem Jahre 2025 mit „One Battle After Another“ nennen können, mach ich aber nicht, schließlich überwiegen Filme wie „The Long Walk“ und „Frankenstein“ oder auch „Havoc“ – klar, die Produktion hatte so einige Probleme –, und weil mir gerade „Dracula: A Love Tale“ einfällt, nenne wir auch „Dracula: A Love Tale“, das heutige Kino um ein zigfaches).
Die offensichtliche Diskrepanz zwischen ihnen ist, und hier mögen wir uns vergegenwärtigen, sind sowohl „The Long Walk“ wie „Frankenstein“ oder auch „Dracula: A Love Tale“ wie eben auch „Train Dreams“ klassisch erzählte Geschichten die mehr oder weniger auf einem Dreiakter und jenseits der Gegenwart beruhen, gar Jahrhunderte in ihrer Erzählung von heute weg in die Vergangenheit überspringen und darauf bauen ganz ihre etliche Jahre und Jahrzehnte alten Vorlagen gerecht, der technische Einsatz der verdeutlicht, wie die heutige Technik bzw. deren Einsatz einen Film sowie dem eigenen Geschmack zuwiderhandelt und damit das (eigene) Seherlebnis torpediert und mir immer wieder das Vergnügen einem madig macht und gar raubt (soweit, neben der Einfallslosigkeit Hollywoods und dem Meta-Dreck bzw. dem Franchise-Gedanke hinter egal welchem Film oder egal welcher Produktion mein größter Dorn im Auge).
Kamen bereits zuvor, und dass in Dutzenden, Adaptionen der Klassiker Dracula oder auch Frankenstein ohne selbige penetranten wie offensichtlichen Computereffekten bzw. CGI-Effekten daher in meinem Wissen um deren fehlende Möglichkeit bzw. dessen Wissensstand und Wissenschaftsstand, ich hier gerne als positives Beispiel „Bram Stoker’s Dracula“ (91) und auch „Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein“ (94) heranziehen möchte und gleichsam gestehen, wie schwammig die Erinnerungen an der 94er Frankenstein-Adaption ist, ist und bleibt es mir ein Rätsel, warum die jüngsten Adaptionen der gleichnamigen Romanvorlangen nicht darauf verzichten konnten oder gar aus Eitelkeit wollten. Stattdessen lassen sie eine Symbiose zu, die nicht funktionieren will und mit den fehlenden Mitteln (Engagement in Form von Zeit und Geld) es auch nicht kann, stört wie eine zu kleine Unterhose im Abdrücken der Hoden oder einer zu großen die, gerade während und unter der Arbeit, den Kronjuwelen zu viel Spielraum zulässt für Spiel, Spaß und Schmerz.
Selbiges Unverständnis beinhaltet auch „The Long Walk“ mit seinem CGI-Einsatz (Sicherheit hin oder her, geh ich über die Straße, steig in ein Auto ein, arbeite auf der Arbeit und ich potenziere die Gefahrenquellen um ein hundertfaches im Vergleich einer wohlmöglich scharfen Waffe am Set) aus Mündungsfeuer und CGI-Blut der mir einfach die Illusion raubt und mich aus der Immersion herausnimmt.
Gänzlich anders, also wie es positiv geht, mag der Vergleich nicht ganz gerecht sein, sehen wir einmal den Produktionsaufwand der Geschichte an sich an, zeig uns „Train Dreams“.

Clint Bentley erzählt eine kleine Geschichte. Eine kleine Geschichte eingefangen und dargestellt im 4:3. Die kleine Geschichte um den Holzarbeiter Robert Grainier der Anfang des 20. Jahrhunderts Gladys kennen und Lieben lernt die er ehelicht und später mit ihr ihre kleine Tochter Kate zeugt.
Eine Geschichte und eine Inszenierung die von Minute Eins nach Terrence Malick schreit, auch wenn die Kamera hier weit ruhiger, geerdeter daherkommt und Träume eher Mangelware sind. Wie Malicks Arbeiten, kommt auch diese von Bentley durch und durch traumwandlerisch daher ohne zu sehr in die eine oder die andere Richtung abzudriften was, zugegeben, zu einem Film führt, der die richtige Stimmung verlangt, die Akzeptanz seiner Inszenierung und seiner Geschichte die nur selten, aber wenn, groß ausschlägt.
Kurzgefasst wie gesagt: eine Produktion die weiß was sie will, in der Geschichte verankert ist und auch bleibt und sie nicht mittels offensichtlichem, und deswegen störenden CGI-Einsatz unterwandert, weil auch nicht nötig, wie selbiger Einsatz auch bei meinen Beispielen nicht nötig wäre, bekommen habe ich ihn dennoch. Dahingehend besticht, einfach großartig auszusehen, großartig gespielt zu sein samt mit einem nicht minder großartigen Drehbuch aufzuwarten das zu einem Film und einem Erlebnis führt, dem ich gerne eine weitere Stunde mehr beigewohnt wäre.
