Let's take a look at my preliminary and still incomplete list of the Top 10 First Viewings of 2025. We see films from the 60s, 70s, 80s, and 90s, and even one entry from the 2010s: "A Hidden Life." Looking at my ratings for films, and exclusively films made in 2025, we arrive at a preliminary highest rating of 3.5/5 for five films (assuming I haven't omitted any). In short: with a preliminary total of zero cinema visits (a personal low), the year 2025 is, as far as films are concerned, incredibly disappointing.
Why all this preamble?
Because here we have, for the first time, a likely candidate for the aforementioned Top 10 First Viewings 2025 list, which serves as a good comparison. This comparison focuses less on the content of the following films—after all, taste, especially regarding content, meaning the story and the direction, is subjective—but rather on the technical aspect, which, of course, just as I myself cannot do without the narrative element, and which simply must and will be incorporated, whether consciously or subconsciously.
In comparing "Train Dreams" with, and here we are only referring to comparably narrated films, "The Long Walk" and "Frankenstein," we see a tremendous discrepancy (regarding the comparisons and their potential unfairness: firstly, I only recently watched the aforementioned films, and secondly, I could have, knowingly, also cited the positive example from 2025 with "One Battle After Another," but I won't, since films like "The Long Walk" and "Frankenstein" or even "Havoc" predominate – sure, the production had its share of problems – and since "Dracula: A Love Tale" just came to mind, let's also mention "Dracula: A Love Tale," which represents today's cinema many times over).
The obvious discrepancy between them, and here we should bear in mind, is that "The Long Walk," "Frankenstein," "Dracula: A Love Tale," and "Train Dreams" are all classically told stories based more or less on a three-act structure and set beyond the present day, even leaping centuries in their narrative from today into the past and building entirely on their source material, which is several years and decades old. The technical application illustrates how today's technology, or rather its use, contradicts a film and one's own taste, thus torpedoing the (own) viewing experience and repeatedly spoiling and even robbing me of the pleasure (this, along with Hollywood's lack of imagination and the meta-filth or franchise concept behind any film or production, is my biggest thorn in the side).
They've already appeared before, and in dozens of adaptations of classics like Dracula or Frankenstein, without these pervasive and obvious computer effects or CGI effects. Knowing that such effects aren't feasible, given the current state of knowledge and science, I'd like to cite "Bram Stoker's Dracula" (1991) and "Mary Shelley's Frankenstein" (1994) as positive examples, while also admitting how vague my memory of the 1994 Frankenstein adaptation is. It remains a mystery to me why the most recent adaptations of the novels of the same name couldn't do without them, or perhaps even chose to do so out of vanity. Instead, they allow a symbiosis that simply doesn't work and, lacking the necessary resources (commitment in the form of time and money), can't. It's as jarring as underwear that's too small and leaves a mark on your testicles, or underwear that's too large and, especially during work, allows your crown jewels too much room to move around, play, and pain.
The same lack of understanding extends to "The Long Walk" with its use of CGI (safety aside, I cross the street, get into a car, go to work, and I'm multiplying the potential dangers a hundredfold compared to a potentially live weapon on set) of muzzle flashes and CGI blood, which simply shatters the illusion and breaks my immersion.
To put it another way, and perhaps not entirely fairly, let's consider the production value of the story itself; take "Train Dreams."

Clint Bentley tells a small story. A small story captured and presented in 4:3. The small story of woodworker Robert Grainier, who at the beginning of the 20th century meets and falls in love with Gladys, whom he marries and later fathers their young daughter, Kate.
A story and a style of direction that screams Terrence Malick from the very first minute, even if the camera work here is far calmer, more grounded, and dreams are rather scarce. Like Malick's work, Bentley's film has a thoroughly dreamlike quality without drifting too far in either direction, which, admittedly, results in a film that demands the right mood, the acceptance of its direction and its story, which only rarely, but when it does, reaches a powerful climax.
In short, as I said: a production that knows what it wants, is firmly rooted in the story and stays that way, and doesn't undermine it with obvious, and therefore distracting, CGI. Because it's not necessary, just as such use wouldn't be necessary in my examples, yet I still got it. Its appeal lies in its simply stunning visuals, superb acting, and equally superb script, resulting in a film and an experience I would gladly have stayed for another hour.

PS: I'll eat my hat (provided it had a theatrical release) if it doesn't get an Oscar nomination for something (cinematography) and thus has a legitimate chance of winning one.

I love that despite the overwhelming sadness, Grainier lived a full life. His persistence, his quiet resilience, and his capacity for love are sacred qualities, it urges us viewers to cherish our own moments and the people who give our lives meaning. 
I’ll only be speaking on the final minutes of the film; where it culminates in Grainier's biplane ride. It essentially functions as a rapid, powerful montage of his entire existence, from the tragic moments; the loss of his soulmate and daughter, the ghosts of past violence he witnessed, and the decades of profound solitude, all brought back in flashes.
These tragic flashes don't appear as individual painful events, but as essential parts of a complete tapestry; this culmination makes sense because his life story is not only his tragedy but the shell in which he wears, and ultimately he’s defined by what he has survived and lost. 
In the wise words of the narrator, Grainier misplaces all sense of up and down, and he felt, at last, connected to it all. This connection transcends his individual grief, suggesting that the tragedy was not a punishment; but the price of admission to a grand, universal experience. That’s something we are all trying to manage and understand, it’s why I think the ending is so universally powerful and resonantly felt.
What an experience, the narrative is tragic and profoundly full; you feel the weight of every dialogue, and the connection to the world and people who truly matter is a priceless reminder, especially in these trying times, it’s a slice of cinema that we all need. Makes matters even more rewarding when the cinematography, acting and original score are all next level, bravo Netflix.

I’m so happy this didn’t fall under the “sequel curse.” It was turbotastic fun from start to finish, and I was incredibly pleased—I genuinely loved it. 

It’s visually dazzling, a much-appreciated, energetic return to the high-speed streets of the animal metropolis, and in so many ways it delivers everything you’d hope for from a follow-up to the beloved original. The animation is stunning, from the vibrant colors and intricate textures, to the beautifully crafted environments, that make the city feel fuller and more alive than ever. The new neighborhoods are packed with clever references and tiny visual gags, and every corner of Zootopia feels thoughtfully expanded. Chase sequences whip up exhilarating thrill, and the water-tube transport scenes are not only creative but also breathtakingly fluid. You can tell the animators had fun because I had fun watching it. 

The character animation is another standout, as every expression, twitch, ear flick, and gesture is so meticulously rendered that you feel their emotions and thoughts every second they are on screen. Their faces radiate real feelings—joy, fear, confusion, longing—and it turns the whole film into a visual feast that pulls you in completely.

And of course, the humor. The jokes land often, sometimes subtly, sometimes with perfect timing; the filmmakers clearly remembered what made the original so charming. The story gives us a masterful blend of mystery, action, and heartwarming moments that create something special. 

But the real heart of the film—the thing that absolutely destroyed me in the best way—was them admiting they are the most important thing to each other (🥹). This sequel is definitely a triumphant and heartfelt film that expands its world, respects its characters, and brings the energy, humor, and emotional weight we all expected. Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
Comment:
Going into the second film was such a different experience to me than the first - when I first saw The Fellowship of the Ring I was 10 years old - I’d never heard of hobbits, orcs or Middle-Earth. I didn’t know that films could be so magical, or grand in scale. By the time The Two Towers was released, I was a year older, wiser - and crucially, had read the books and had watched the first part almost daily since getting it on VHS - I was practically shaking with excitement.
It’s amazing that Jackson was allowed to film the trilogy all at once - something a studio would never allow today, especially not something as risky, grand and expensive as The Lord of the Rings - the advantage is that the cast all still have amazing chemistry, no awkward aging between films, less continuity issues, and only a year wait between releases - it’s especially satisfying watching them all back to back.
The Battle of Helm’s Deep is the undeniable highlight of this film. While Return of the King has bigger battles, with higher stakes, there’s just something about Helm’s Deep that I love more than any of the other battles in the franchise. If I had to say why, I’d say it’s simply the atmosphere. The dark night, the resignation of the men and elves that they will lose, a heroic last stand - and a last minute cavalry charge to save the day.
Mostly, I think it’s the sound of heavy rain hitting the Uruk-Hai armour.
11 year old me thought Legolas jumping onto a shield, sliding down the steps shooting arrows was the coolest thing ever. 23 years later, I still don’t think I’m wrong.
This film also has some of the series’ best monologues:
Elrond’s speech to Arwen about Aragorn’s mortality - “He will come to death, an image of the splendour of the kings of men in glory undimmed before the breaking of the world. But you, my daughter, will linger on in darkness and in doubt.”

Theoden’s iconic lament - “Where is the horse and the rider? Where is the horn that was blowing? They have passed like rain on the mountain, like wind in the meadow.”

And finally, Sam’s incredible speech to Frodo - “But in the end, it’s only a passing thing, this shadow. Even darkness must pass. A new day will come. And when the sun shines it will shine out the clearer.”
And yet despite all of the brilliant action and writing, I’d still say this is (marginally) the weakest part of the trilogy - while still being a masterpiece.

You can start by wiping that fucking dumb-ass smile off of those rosy fucking cheeks!
All time classic this one. Steve Martin and John Candy probably had no idea they were making one of, if not the greatest Thanksgiving film of all time. It’s a chaotic 90 minutes of pure entertainment; a rollercoaster of a narrative following a couple of knuckleheads on a surprising venture of passion, laughs and the brewing of a lifelong friendship, it’s a priceless film and one that deserves its high status.  
The dynamics between the two leads, Steve Martin and John Candy are the heart and soul of the film. You’ve got Steve Martin’s Neal who is this high strung, impatient and stressed executive who has already had it up to the brim even before the chaos ensued. Compared to the eternally optimistic, talkative, and overwhelmingly friendly shower curtain ring salesman, Del. It’s the perfect example of a comedy duo who complement each other, going way beyond a tight and great script; which this film also has, but even without the script these two would of turned water into wine. 
The hardships and chaos sculpt them into having this very sweet and genuine bond, it’s part of the reason the ending scene is so special. That scene is so special for a multitude of reasons though; the acting from both Candy and Martin captures the essence of the situation so beautifully, Candys heartbreak and hope, and Martins realization is poetic cinema. Partner that with the methodical filmmaking and grand score work and you have a perfect ending scene to cap off a joyous hour and a half of the most entertaining cinema. 
I mentioned it in my first review but this film screams the feeling I get from watching the first two Home Alone’s, Hughes was clearly a master at crafting that specific kind of frantic, yet ultimately heartwarming, holiday story set in the suburbs of Chicago. It’s that mix of trying to get home, the power of kindness and that cozy, yet occasionally chaotic, atmosphere of upper/middle-class suburbia that works wonders for a narratives structure and makes the whole film flow with ease. 
The film really has a strong visual identity that sets the mood for their chaotic journey. I love the massive scope of the country, with expansive wide shots and a constant reminder of the grueling conditions of Winter in the Midwest. The visual cues; the flat, empty highways, the small-town motels, and the wide-open countryside, all instantly recognizable as the American heartland. The flawless combination of location scouting, color palette, and lighting design is what makes the film feel like a real odyssey across the wintry American landscape. 
I’ll cut it here for this one, Thanksgiving is off to a flying start with the best Thanksgiving film already visited, I may have to say screw it and chuck Spider-Man 1 on.. we all know that’s up there as the best Thanksgiving film too. Anyway, Planes, Trains and Automobiles is a film we should all be watching this time of year, whether you watch it today or closer to Christmas, just make sure you get it watched this year, all time classic with yet again another couple of legends leading the way. Happy Thanksgiving to those who celebrate!

Title: Frankenstein
Comment:
HORROR MOVIE #355:
Frankenstein matches the gothic caliber as Crimson Peak, solidifying Guillermo Del Toro’s reputation for making goth people proud. I’m not goth myself but if I was then I would only assume that Del Toro is their savior.
The movie itself was not my favorite Del Toro work, but I’m still very impressed that he brought an old tale to life in the most Del Toro way that you possibly could. Frankenstein was always depicted to me as a brain dead monster, but I’m quite satisfied with how this notion was turned around where “The Creature” feels more human. Even when Victor insists on referring to the creature as “it”. It has a Robert Eggers Nosferatu feel to it where it’s a much more gothic remake of an otherwise old entity.
I’m not sure how accurate this movie is to its Frankenstein novel predecessor. I have a rough understanding of how the story goes, but not fine tuning on any of the character arcs. The extent of my contextualization is: mad scientist make monster, monster alive. For a movie made by the same guy who made insanely great fantasy movies like Pan’s Labyrinth and Crimson Peak, I knew that Guillermo Del Toro could make this a monumental hit.
I think fantasy and gothic horror isn’t my favorite genre, so I would be lying if I said I was fully locked in the entire 2 and a half hour duration. But this is still undeniably one of the best looking Netflix movies of recent times. Then again, the bar is in hell for Netflix. It’s not necessarily anything against Guillermo Del Toro’s quality of direction, but it just didn’t pique my interest as much as a traditional supernatural or psychological horror movie would.
Frankenstein deserved a better fate than ending up on Netflix. But Del Toro hits again with this breathtaking portrayal of heartfelt rays of humanity shining on a misunderstood character.
In light of Thanksgiving, I’m thankful for goth people now.

Title: Magnolia
Comment:
"This happens. This is something that happens."
Magnolia is a P.T.A. film that I have managed to overlook for the majority of my life, and I don't understand why. It's messy and indulgent. It's way too much and that's exactly what makes it phenomenal. 
I loved this.
Even way back in 1999, P.T.A. was still young enough to be wildly ambitious and confident enough to build a three-hour mosaic such as this. How can one person have this much in them? It's beyond me.
Magnolia unspools over the course of a single day, but in Anderson's hands, time isn't a straight line. That's true for the character's lives as well as when you're watching it. He is one of the only directors that can make a three-hour film seem short. Characters zigzag into each other's lives, sometimes gently and sometimes violently.
As much as I don't like the man, this has to be one of Tom Cruise's best performances. Back then, he was still the clean-cut megastar that everyone loved. But, with Frank T.J. Mackey, he gets to be something far more volatile.
I'm noticing that Anderson has a knack for creating vulgar, hypermasculine bastards (looking at you, Sean Penn!). The real power though, I believe, comes from the slow, painful unmasking that happens in his interview.
Julianne Moore made me cry and I'm proud to admit that. Linda is a woman who married for money, cheated, lied, coasted and then at the very end, finds herself devastated by love she never expected to feel. I don't think Linda is necessarily a villain and I don't think Moore plays her that way.
Honestly, I think that she's someone whose heart has awakened just as it's too late to do anything about it. Her pharmacy meltdown is almost uncomfortable to watch because she's just so...unvarnished.
John C. Reilly, Phillip Seymour Hoffman, William H. Macy...on and on and on. There are so many big names in this film that it would take me forever to comment on all of their performances. Let me just say that none of them miss.
Probably my favorite moment in this was one that I wasn't expecting at all. When the ensemble joins in singing "Wise Up," it shouldn't work and yet it was really transcendent for me. Almost like an intermission about confession.
For nearly an entire hour, there is just tension-filled moment zooming one after the other. Jon Brion's score was making me extremely anxious. You're just waiting for the next bomb to drop or someone to say the wrong thing.
Magnolia is a film that reminds us about how meaningless (or meaningful) the gigantically complicated universe is in which we all live. All of these people are desperately trying to forgive themselves and wondering, or even hoping, that the universe hasn't entirely given up on them.
I felt this weight while watching Magnolia. I can't really describe it, but you really have to be in an okay mindset to watch something like this. There's a lot of suicidal depictions or thoughts and I think the film serves as one of P.T.A.'s most audacious works.
I'm not going to spoil the strange ending for anyone, but I will just say this: If you're willing to let Anderson guide you past reason and into the mythic, it hits. Coincidence and catastrophe often arrive hand-in-hand. 
I'll be feeling this one for some time.

Title: Before Sunrise
Comment:
“I like to feel his eyes on me when I look away.”
"Isn’t everything we do in life a way to be loved a little more?”
" If there’s any kind of magic in this world, it must be in the attempt of understanding someone.”
The amount of emotions I’m feeling right now is truly indescribable… endlessly overflowing inside me. I can’t explain how much I love this film or how deep my feelings for it are.
Before Sunrise is truly one of the most beautiful part of this trilogy, everything about it is beautiful.. it’s hard to even count all the things I love about it! Every time I watch it, I realize that almost all the topics and ideas they talk about are things I’ve thought about before. It’s as if they somehow knew exactly what I think about and turned it into a film in the most beautiful way possible.
The movie is visually beautiful and enjoyable in every sense, and it’s so simple. and honestly, that might be the most beautiful point in it, its simplicity. Just a girl and a boy on a train, she's heading to France and he's going to Vienna, She moves her seat next to him because a fight between a couple annoyed her. They exchange a spontaneous look and laugh about the couple, then suddenly they start talking. Then suddenly again, he asks her to get off the train with him, and she simply takes the risk and does it. They end up spending the most beautiful day of their lives together. Things like walking without planning in the quiet streets of a beautiful country, the small thoughs and small conversations that reveal their personalities without any masks or hesitation.. everything in this film is so beautiful that it makes you love it without even trying, and you never feel like a stranger among them.
What’s also beautiful about the film is that it’s not just about thinking logically, it shows that it’s okay to take risks sometimes. That risk might change your life, or at least leave a mark you’ll never forget. Not everyone you don’t know is bad or dangerous. Sometimes you just meet people by coincidence, and they turn out to be the best people of all.
Every scene and every idea in this film is so beautiful to discuss. It always makes me wonder.. why can’t people in real life talk like this? Why is there always restriction and attack even in discussions? That really bothers me. But what’s beautiful is that this film shows that people like this can exist in the world, that not everyone is constrained by limits they’re not allowed to cross.
The ending… one of the most beautiful endings ever. The shots of all the places they walked and sat in around vienna is now empty, it were so beautiful. As if the film was showing us that their spirits had filled those places, and their conversations and emotions had once overflowed there. And those gentle final smiles as each of them took a different path.. it was the perfect scene to close the film in such a beautiful way.
Honestly, no matter how much I talk about this movie, I’ll never be able to stop. So I’ll stop here but my love for this film will always be huge and deep in my heart. I’ll never forget it, and I will definitely watch it many more times in the future again <3

Title: If I Had Legs I’d Kick You
Comment:
Why do we bash “dead-beat” moms for not being there for their kids but we never question if the child has bad vibes? Or if they’re just unpleasant to be around?
Jokes aside, one of the more impressively abrasive characters + shooting styles/sound design gimmicks I've seen this year. Probably only works as well as it does because Rose Byrne is willing to be such a comical mess in such extreme fragmented close-up for such an unbearable duration (being sensory assaulted by outside noises), which is not to discredit Bronstein whose stressed-out, wine-drunk, rotted hole-in-the-ceiling domestic horror ambience filmmaking choices around her are so morbid they border on absurdist existentialism. Could not believe the hamster scene or the bit where Byrne mumbles to Siri in her drunk, sleepy Long Island mom voice: "What is movie... Babies... zombies.... 80s... mothers eating babies." The Safdie's producing and Bronstein coming from a similar NY mumblecore background might give the game away a bit in the sense that there's a similar Cassavetes inspiration to the rawness and proximity to the actors interwoven with "perception is reality" psychological subjectivity that suddenly feels surreal and cosmic without breaking the grounded indie fabric of the film. Which is why you're seeing a lot of reductive "Uncut Gems had a deformed baby with Eraserhead vibes", which is an easy way to explain how relentless and claustrophobic this feels formally, if not entirely getting at how specific and nonjudgmental this is regarding the psychological complexities and ambiguities of motherhood. The gruelingly sustained textural unpleasantness isn't just a cynical shock tool either, it feels like an entirely honest expression of frustration and empathy at the darker, dirtier things mothers are supposed to compartmentalize and hide from those around them. "This can't be it."
Shoutout to my mom who I probably gave a psychotic episode to at some point and don't remember.

ACTION! - FELLINI'S DREAMS
So earlier this month, I put up a little poll asking which Italian director I should focus on, and, to no one’s surprise, Fellini took the lead. Surprisingly, he didn’t dominate the vote but won with a modest 28%, followed by Pasolini at 17%.
We kick off this marathon with a charming little romcom that holds its own against Hollywood films of the era, brimming with colorful characters vividly brought to life by a delightful cast—including Fellini’s early muse and partner, Giulietta Masina. There’s also that one character who, whenever he appears, lets out an almost sinister laugh. Together, they deliver plenty of moments that spark genuine chuckles. I appreciated the whimsical tone throughout. While it’s nowhere near the brilliance Fellini would gift us later in his career, the cinematography here is quite impressive.
I feel—much like many others—that the film’s main weakness lies in its script. As I mentioned, there are solid moments of levity, but overall the plot is predictable and falls into the familiar melodramatic patterns of its time, offering little new. The cast and their performances do their best to elevate the material, but sadly, it’s not quite enough to fully engage me.
All in all, perhaps because Fellini had to share his vision or was still finding his footing, this early work lacks the magic and finesse of his later masterpieces. But if you’re ever in the mood for some classic old-school melodrama, this one’s definitely worth a look.

Title: Long Day’s Journey into Night
Comment:
Memory contains many mysterious aspects of our existence as human beings. it sways back and forth like a ping pong ball, changing based on how we perceive ourselves and how we currently view others and the world around us. Each time we bring something to mind, the remembered version of it shifts and in a way those objects, characters, or thoughts change color. Some grow brighter while others fade. Some details expand while other details minimize. There are so many different variations to how we come to remember things. We are left with a combination of both the truth and the imaginary and often times this memory is like a dream where past, present, and future are one. It is only when we view our memories from different angles that we will truly understand the value of our own memories.
How can filmmakers convey that subjective nature of how we remember things in a film? How can they visually portray the indescribable feeling of dreaming? by their very nature, films are not representative of reality, therefore, there will always be some limitation in terms of filmmakers being able to replicate those aspects of life through images on a film screen, regardless of how good the film may be at evoking human thoughts and feelings through stories.
This leaves filmmakers with three choices: remain safe and comfortable within the boundaries of accepted cinematic language, use experimental approaches, or use the limitations of the medium itself as a way to play with the viewer's imagination and create an experience that feels real in an abstract or symbolic way. The first option gives film professionals the greatest amount of creative freedom because they have established guidelines, while the second option allows them to find new ways to present an idea and achieve their artistic goals by reaching back and being creative. The third option, which is based on the limitations of filmmaking, enables filmmakers to be imaginative and creative with regard to the way they tell their stories and to express their vision artistically.
In this film, Bi Gan captures that subjectivity of memory. throughout the first half, we see how Luo Hongwu recalls his life and often struggles to reconstruct his past. Luo's attempts to derive meaning from his underlying trauma specifically, the loss of his mother (through disappearance) and the death of his father...add complication to the formation of his memories, leaving him feeling lost. Through memories from his earlier days which were shaped by these experiences, and longing for those days, Luo works to assemble his recollections into a coherent narrative, finding clarity in the truth that exists within them.
Bi Gan takes the second and third approaches simultaneously. He uses an unconventional approach to storytelling in the sense that instead of following a classic story arc or advancing linearly in time, he instead depicts the concept of timeline being "fluid." He creates scenes that evolve based on the associative leaps made within one’s thought process/memory. He again employs extraordinarily long takes, a technique he first explored in his debut film Kaili Blues. in that film, Bi Gan's long take sequences act as a kind of time travel, transporting viewers from the past to the present and back again, while making subtle critiques of the notion of time in a linear fashion as the main character travels through the country side. The long single take towards the middle of this film acts as a means of connecting the viewer with the way in which we perceive memories. While both films utilize long takes in a similar manner, the intent behind their use evolves slightly. In Kaili Blues, long take sequences show how time stretches and can unfold out of sequence, while in this, long take sequences demonstrate the surreal and confusing nature of our inner worlds. The extended shot sequences in both films serve a technical function, but they also serve to blur the line between memory, dream, and actual lived experiences.
In the final hour of the film, everything comes together or at least, that’s what I see. I already believe I'm watching a dream, a fantasy that could never occur in our physical reality, but as I witness the protagonist battling through fragmented memories to find them again, I see him coming to accept this dream-like vision of himself. Both he and I know that this cannot be real, but it does provide him with some sort of comfort. In this very long, almost hour-long unbroken shot, I was able to see how all of the different people and events from the character's past were woven together into one large story. When watching this shot, I felt as if I were experiencing how the different memory pieces flowed together, as memory flows in motion from one to another, creating a sense of satisfaction not found in the routine. As I continued to watch, I became drawn into the character's mind and the depth of his feelings (longing, grief or yearning) and his desire to connect the dots from the past with what could have been. The experience of watching this sequence was not only visually impressive, but it was also an experience of how we can bend the rules of time and memory to our will. During the time I was watching that part of the movie, my mind was able to forget the line that separates the real world from my imagination.
At the end of the movie, I find myself questioning whether I will feel satisfied with the ending of the film or whether I should continue to allow myself to be haunted by its mystery. The lingering effect feels like an extension of the characters thoughts, reaching into my own reality, my own mind. I realize I have to accept what I don’t know, just as the characters do, and somehow find comfort in the unknown.
The cinema has its limitations. It is not the exact same experience. Film cannot give us the real mental landscape of a character. The cinema lies to us and distorts reality. It is a tool of deception, but the artist, the filmmaker, can choose to create a false reality in any number of ways. Bi Gan has shown us that when you embrace the limitations of memory as well as the limitations of film, an audience can connect on a deeper level to a story. As humans, we are all flawed and our memories fail us. They distort over time or are interrupted and never formed. Our dreams can torment us, and when the flaws in our memories are combined with the artifice of film, it sometimes produces an emotion that resonates deeply with us. Plot resolution may not always be important to the audience or the creator. What matters is that the characters are asking the same questions we ask, and we are comforted by the idea that we are not alone, even if our companions exist only in memory and film.
"The difference between film and memory is that films are always false. They are composed of a series of scenes. But memories mix truth and lies; they appear and vanish before our eyes."

Title: Elevator to the Gallows
Comment: a film of daring self-possessiveness, refusing to commit to a single theme or conceit and instead embracing a loose correlation of characters who are all seeking an escape, whether that is a physical act of violence, a romantic gesture, or simply playing pretend. there is a strong sense of schadenfreude that celebrates the beauty of futility. no doubt antonioni must have taken some inspiration from this film when he has jeanne moreau somnambulently wander the streets of milan in la notte, and it shares the same angst-ridden precociousness as godard's early 60s films. henri decaë's work here with shooting in low-light environments is so gorgeous, the highway scenes in particular look exquisite. a great debut for a very young louis malle, this thriller is about the terror of being alone, of growing old, of only having the image of love to sustain you -- can one live with all that? or is anything else required? the impetuousness of the style draws us into our own introspection as the curtains fall upon each of these characters, that they commit their crimes out of fear of loss only to then be left with the lingering aroma of a passion we do not bare witness to. like breathless it is a work about the fitful frenzy of activity before the falling shroud of death, a romanticism you can only bask in briefly before you've been worn down by the waves of fate, years spent waiting in silence, listening to the music only your soul can hear.

Title: Knives Out
Comment:
⚠️92%
🔙Spider-Man🔙 
🔜Christmas Evil🔜
I forget just how insanely good Knives Out is, the way it operates as a meta whodunnit is brilliant. Johnson takes the deep familiarity with the mystery genre and uses that knowledge against us, and him showing the supposed truth of the killing within the first act, always tricks me. It’s genius honestly, and the tension immediately shifts from who, to will she be caught? Freeing up the rest of the film to focus on character, class commentary, and a second, deeper mystery. 
Johnson still populates the film with exaggerated, recognizable tropes; the suspicious family, the reading of the will, the eccentric detective, the dark mansion. But by centering the story on the genuinely kind and moral Marta Cabrera(the ‘good’ immigrant nurse who cannot lie without spewing her guts), he replaces the cold, calculated detective logic with a messy, yet extremely human empathy. It’s this shift that truly gives it a freshness, unbelievable work honestly.
The script structure is meticulously crafted with it essentially acting as a double-sided sword of plotting. There’s an outstanding balance to the narrative layers; first seeing the night of Harlan's death through the family's unreliable testimonies, then through Marta's accurate but incomplete perspective, and finally through the perspective of Benoit Blanc piecing together the true, third layer of events. It’s extremely rewarding and never falters when it comes to entertainment and keeping me engaged bell to bell. Not only that but the script manages to hide crucial information in plain sight without ever deceiving the audience, but rather just cleverly misdirecting our attention, its truly impressive screenwriting.
The commentary isn't just in the plot either, it embodies itself within the characters. The entire Thrombey family serves as a satire on generational wealth and entitlement, it’s honestly hilarious how they navigate the death of their late father and the change of will. The acting from the ensemble is incredible, the family dynamics were nailed and they create some wow moments throughout. The level of acting, when you look at the cast list, is to be expected, it’s still outstanding though.  
Especially that climax, with around 30 minutes to go I particularly lock in. That three-way dynamic between *spoiler*, Benoit Blanc, and Marta, is in my eyes the film's best moments. It’s not only Daniel Craig acting his heart out, but it’s a ridiculous narrative payoff that really does floor me every time, not to mention it’s absolutely hilarious when Marta chucks up last nights dinner, comedy gold. 
Daniel Craig as Benoit Blanc is as close to perfection as character casting can get, you can tell he loves the role. The American Southern twang is cherry on top, and not only is he stylish and well dressed at all times, but he carries a flamboyant, humorous, and delightfully eccentric manner to his highly theatricality and keenly observant character. 
Really enjoy the work of Ana de Armas in this film aswell, she has a purity and serves as the glue so well, her best role. This may be the only role post Cap that Chris Evan’s has actually sold me on, the rest of his work post MCU has been fairly dire. 
The Thrombey estate is such a stunning location and perfect setting for such a mystery. It acts as a character in itself, perfectly embodying the film's themes. It’s richly detailed with the house becoming a labyrinthine; a cluttered museum of wealth, full of unsettling artifacts, taxidermy, and secret passages.
It’s full of depth in terms of props and lush furniture, meticulously arranged and beautifully gathered to best appease the viewers, it manages to always have outstanding blocking and perfect framing, really a well shot film. Like that final image; Marta standing on the balcony, serenely sipping from Harlan's mug, looking down at the defeated and entitled Thrombey family outside, is such clever imagery, it’s the ultimate poetic justice. 
It’s been a couple of years since I last visited Knives Out but it’s certainly a film that rewards intellectual engagement without sacrificing entertainment, making it a truly enjoyable rewatch. As even 6 maybe 7 viewings later I’m still surprised by the twists and turns, a piece of cinematic gold that looks good, flows beautifully and maintains a high level of acting across the board, such an enjoyable film.

Title: Ida
Comment:
J'ai revu Ida : l'histoire d'une sœur d'un couvent en Pologne qui découvre son héritage familial.
C'est une plongée dans la Pologne pauvre et communiste via le regard de cette femme catholique qui découvre progressivement ses racines grâce à sa tante. Elles entament un road trip afin d'alléger leur deuil et trouver leur identité.
Pawel Pawlikowski utilise la dualité des personnages pour évoquer ce combat interne face à la foi entre judaïsme et catholicisme : doit-elle encore croire en Dieu ou succomber au pessimisme ? Elle passe du monastère silencieux aux bars de jazz bruyants et chaotiques, elle doit choisir entre sa croyance et ses envies sexuelles.
Pendant ce temps la tante juive se plaint du système communiste auquel elle participe en tant que juge et le manque d'appartenance qu'elle ressent dans sa vie suite la disparition de sa famille. C'est deux versions du monde qui s'opposent : Ida croyante et sa tante nihiliste. C'est à la fois la culpabilité d'un pays mais aussi d'une famille qui est examinée ici.
C'est un film très vide en termes de décors pour marquer l'absence de vie mais c'est aussi cadré uniquement avec des plans fixes qui mettent les personnages en petit dans le cadre. Le récit les dépasse et les enferme dans une prison politique et spirituelle.
C'est le conte d'une époque, d'une famille et du rejet d'un système imposé par défaut.

Title: Re-Animator
Comment:
'We all want to retain our personalities in some afterlife, we all pray for some miracle, drug, potion. Perhaps, though, it takes something else. Perhaps it takes desire, an obsessive desire.'
The recreation of life is a passion that can only be achieved when you leave your head on the chopping board, a loss of sanity stemmed from the numerous dead neurons in the brain which fear death. Life can only be brought back through the unnatural means of science and curiosity, an obsession, you could call it, an unusual passion project from the one who lost his mind to the smell of rotting insides.
'Who's going to believe a talking head?'
'You killed him!'
'No, I gave him life.'
A desk of red that splats blood not just over itself but also over the screen, it's another level of body horror that the likes of Frankenstein and similiar stories are too scared to utilise, peeling back the skin of safety and going all-in, a deep-dive of raw meat that sometimes goes too far. I've never been one that can't handle violence, I'm pretty tolerable for gore and body horror, but whenever there's pieces of violence towards animals or any type of sexual violence I just get extremely uncomfortable, especially in this film, where it's so explicit.
It's a bold potion, a sour ambition, but when there's no limits to doing what you want in a film, it can push past creativity and become exploitative and disgusting, torture porn disguised as clever violence 'for the arts', an injection of body-squirming danger and uncomfortable scenes that just don't work for me, but it has respectable writing and performances, just not my personal cup of tea.

Title: Predator 2
Comment:
2025 has been massive when it comes to rounding out franchises that I already love one or more films from. After finally watching its epic, Schwarzenegger starring first entry earlier this year, and also being a giant supporter of Dan Trachtenberg’s Predator entries, the universe has shot up my list of favorite action or horror properties. Further, as a minority fan of the only other Stephen Hopkins flick I’ve seen (shout out Nightmare on Elm Street 5) and with that added context aside, it was time I got around to Hopkins’ entry into Yautja lore, Predator 2. If Predator authored a series template, its sequel blasts through bullets, bodies and coke into its own raucous and welcome take entirely. 
Late 80’s/Early 90’s ensemble casts always bring a big ol grin, and that sentiment was absolutely nailed here. Predator 2 throws together Danny Glover, Gary Busey, Bill Paxton and more 80’s heavyweights, culminating in a near perfectly crafted cast for an all out 90’s action-exploitation sequel. It is a film powered by 90’s sleaze, yet it’s coupled with an almost LA noir meets horror-slasher stylistic aesthetic amidst its chaotic, battleground of a setting. And seeing a Yautja running across an imagined 1997 LA skyline from a 1990 perspective lit up my heart. 
Script wise, things certainly bounce around a bit more than expected, perhaps suffering from a case of bloat in its near 2 hr runtime and simple premise. And while that hacky writing and humor was critically panned in 1990, its self awareness and meta action has been contemporarily reevaluated and enjoyed for what it is: A hell of a good time that doesn’t take itself too seriously. 
Predator 2 is also an important little piece of Predator canon. There are more than a few powerful lore additions which helped shaped, and eventually rescue the heart of the franchise. Between the Xenomorph skull trophy, time-traveling Adolini pistol, and concept of Predators hunting for sport and ritual, Predator 2 is more than worth an Alien/Predator or 90’s action nerd’s time. 
Danny Glover you magnificent bastard.

Title: The Fabelmans
Comment:
"When the horizon's at the bottom, it's interesting. When the horizon's at the top, it's interesting. When the horizon's in the middle, it's boring as shit. Now, good luck to you. And get the fuck out of my office!"
Buenísima película, pero tampoco me conmovió como esperaba.
"The Fabelmans" narra de una gran manera lo que vendría a ser la vida de Steven Spielberg, a través de una historia con escenas memorables y muy bien interpretadas por un excelente cast, pero no terminó de emocionarme y no conecté tanto como esperaba en un principio.
Sinopsis: Tras ver la película "El mayor espectáculo del mundo", el joven Sammy Fabelman se enamora perdidamente del cine. Armado con una cámara y contando con la ayuda de su madre, Sammy trata de filmar su primera película en casa.
La historia es buenísima, un poco larga pero muy interesante en todo lo que cuenta. Estamos ante un coming of age donde vamos viendo la vida del protagonista mientras desarrolla su amor por el cine y a su vez los problemas familiares van afectando en esto. No suelo conectar del todo con éste tipo de película y con ésta, en parte, me pasó lo mismo, ya que al hablar tanto sobre el cine en general me terminó atrapando muchísimo y haciendo que se me haga bastante llevadera y pueda conectar con Sammy. Sin embargo, creo que falla en algunas cosas como todo el drama familiar, cosa que está bueno de ver cómo afectó en lo que aspiraba el protagonista, pero no me terminé de creer del todo algunas cosas y lo sentí todo algo ficcionado. Igualmente me parece que la trama destaca por algunas escenas fantásticas y muy bien realizadas, siendo la inicial (y todo el inicio en general) un gran ejemplo de esto. Por último, el ritmo es un poco lento pero eso no me molestó del todo, sino que se termina haciendo demasiado larga para algo que podría haber durado menos, recortándole media hora hubiera sido claramente mejor a mi parecer.
Los personajes me encantaron, la familia Fabelman es lo mejor. Sammy es un protagonista brillante y de los mejores personajes de la cinta, el desarrollo que tiene me parece buenísimo y está muy bien llevado, lo único malo es todo lo que mencioné antes del drama familiar, a pesar de que me gusta ver como esto termina cambiándolo bastante. Sus padres Burt y Mitzi son otros geniales personajes, muy por delante de los demás miembros de la familia que terminan quedando un poco de lado, siendo ellos el foco principal de todo el drama familiar junto a Bennie. Éste es un personaje que parece salido de otra película al tener mucha personalidad que encima se ve más marcada todavía por la interpretación de Seth Rogen, es un personaje que cae bien pero no me pareció de lo mejor.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente las actuaciones, Gabriel LaBelle, Michelle Williams y Paul Dano son los mejores del elenco, sin dudas una de las mejores cosas de la película por la enorme calidad que tienen las interpretaciones y lo mucho que llegan. También hay un grandísimo nivel, como siempre, en todo lo que hace Steven Spielberg acá, quien nos demuestra que a pesar del paso de los años todavía está intacto y puede seguir haciendo películas de buena calidad, incluso atreviéndose a contar la historia de su vida, algo que de por si ya me resulta interesante. Encima, como casi siempre, también está acompañado de John Williams, quien hace un trabajo sutil pero lindo en la banda sonora, con algunas melodías con la calidad que nos tiene acostumbrados.
En conclusión, una gran película que toda persona que le gusta el cine debería ver, no voy a entrar en comparaciones con cierta película porque las veo algo distintas por el tono de cada una, ésta me parece buenísima y encima tiene la mano de Spielberg que nunca me falla. La recomiendo.

Title: Frankenhooker
Comment:
Frank Henenlotter once told Joe Bob Briggs: “I’m a strange little man”. I think that quote just about sums up my personal love and adoration for the NYC art house-meets-sleaze master filmmaker. There are moments and sequences included in his movies that would make a decent amount of sensible people recoil, but they somehow feel purposeful and playful in his hands. At least for my own increasingly bizarre tastes. And dammit, especially as a Troma release, Frankenhooker is such a blast.
There are so many cheeky filmmaking staples encased within Henenlotter’s artistic expressions to adore. In this instance, how Henenlotter subtly infuses his films with a distinct color palette. In his absurdist drug allegory film Brain Damage, it’s deep, depressing blues, while in Frankenhooker, magnetic, electric purple & violet consumes its backgrounds. He always seems to bring an intrinsic touch of levity, humanity and humor to some of the most macabre and grisly moments I’ve ever seen on film. Like… I actually felt a slight wave of sympathy as “Dr.” Franken was having dinner and wine with the severed head of his deceased fiancée, waxing optimistically about their potential future. 
James Lorinz as Jeffry Franken does much of the heavy lifting, adding a thematic weight I didn’t think I’d feel coming into a movie with the title of Frankenhooker. But those subversions are exactly why Henenlotter has quickly become one of my go-to fun directors, and why I get so damn giddy around his movies. 
In a year that has included my favorite Frankenstein adaptation ever put to film, I’ve been searching for its companion. After recently viewing and adoring my first Henenlotter film earlier this month, coupled with the outpour of gentle urging from friends when I mentioned the possibility of covering Frankenhooker, I’m beaming having finally gotten a first watch.

Title: Arco
Comment:
Singapore International Film Festival 2025 Film #6

I'm so sorry that many adults view animated films as "just for kids" and unfortunately overlook the richness and depth that animation can uncover. animated movies are not just made for kids, many of the stories within animation explore complex emotional states of being, enlightened points of view, and lived experiences which children and adults share in an equally meaningful way. The ability of animated films to express this connection for both children and adults is something that I have seen repeatedly throughout my life, and it has left me with a strong sense of appreciation for the artistic abilities of the medium. This film encapsulated this to perfection, not only is it a beautiful representation of the power of childhood, it also highlights how childlike curiosity, wonder, and hope can inspire and motivate individuals to believe and see in themselves what others have long assumed to be impossible, all while giving a greater depth and impact to the emotional occurrence of innocence through experience and awareness that comes from being an adult.
I was completely consumed while watching this film with the amount of different emotions it creates among children and adults alike. The colors of the film are representational of what it has to offer, however, the message of this movie is about so much more than just the imagery, it’s about the reality of what we are experiencing with regard to climate change, environmental destruction, resource depletion and the impact of technological advancement on human relationships. I also appreciate how this story is woven into the fabric of our lives through time-travel, where we are reminded of the constant connection between the past and the future. Just because something is impossible, does not mean that it cannot be accomplished. I have viewed many stories like this in the past, and yet, here it never felt familiar in a stale way. The tenderness of this movie, and the way in which each moment is portrayed, really adds to the power of the message conveyed in this movie, and it is something that will be imprinted into my memory.
The film may not break new ground in how stories are told, but the way it brings to fruition the themes within the story through the visual medium was nothing short of breathtaking at various points throughout the viewing experience. I can safely say I cried throughout segments of the movie, as the stunning imagery brought me an overwhelming feeling of hope that if people choose to live in hope rather than despair, then a world that is desolate and broken could become a better place. In the same way that Studio Ghibli's animated films exude their own unique spirit and enchantment through stunningly detailed creativity, so does this film. However, this film does not simply imitate the style of Studio Ghibli, it uses the same principles of inspiration to tell a very individualistic story that combines whimsical adventures with very tangible processes and consequences. As a result, the scenery throughout the film gives the impression of being utterly fantastical while simultaneously feeling completely relevant to the viewer in a visceral way
There were moments when I stopped listening to the dialogue entirely, choosing instead to soak in the incredible animation. Each hand-drawn frame conveys raw emotion, from the flicker of a bird in flight to the stark devastation of landscapes ravaged by human neglect. Through these images, Bienvenu raises questions that hit close to home: what is humanity’s place in a world that is devouring itself? how do we coexist with nature when it reclaims its rights so violently? Shots lingering on the wreckage, while the children navigate the chaos, are both heartbreaking and illuminating, reminding me of the fragility of life and of the planet.
Although the film's intensity might seem overwhelming for younger audiences later on, the creativity, artistry, and inspiration throughout the film make it an engaging experience for all ages. Children may be drawn in by its whimsical, free-flowing energy, while adults will find deeper, more poignant themes within the film's storyline. The story culminates in a hopeful, profoundly moving note, encouraging its audience to carry on despite the challenges the world faces. It is my opinion that children should be encouraged to see this film, not only as a source of entertainment, but also as an opportunity to learn about our beautiful planet. If children grow up loving and respecting their home, they will be more likely to care for it when they grow up. Therefore, if children are not taught to appreciate the Earth, they will never develop an appreciation for it. If they do not develop an appreciation for the Earth, there is no way that they will be able to provide adequate care for it.

Title: Kaili Blues
Comment:
We usually perceive time as a path that moves from past through present to future. seconds turn into minutes, which turn into hours. As a result of that development, the past remains behind us, while the future extends before us.
However, time is everywhere. It is indicated by clocks, expressed through schedules, and used to define both memories and milestones. In spite of the strong presence of time in our daily lives, at best it is not what it seems, because our understanding of reality is primarily formed by how we perceive that reality. and that includes our understanding of time.
In addition to the perception of reality, our view of time is not the same as what a person perceives as time. Rather, time is more fluid than the way we perceive it. Time can appear to be either longer than expected or shorter than expected depending on the circumstances. An hour spent sitting in the traffic may feel as though it was an eternity, whereas, the same hour spent laughing and enjoying life with someone we love seems to pass in a matter of seconds. we view and account for time as if it is a constant and exists independently of ourselves, but the truth is, time is shaped by our perception, bent by our emotion, and filtered through the lens of our memory. What if the linear way we have been taught to understand time is incorrect? What if time is not shaped in a linear way? What if it’s more of a feeling than a fact?
And this is precisely what Bi Gan does with this film. He challenges the traditional or classical way of thinking about time. instead of perceiving it as a straight line in which everything happens in sequence, Bi Gan offers us the opportunity to reimagine time as something that can be reshaped, spread, crossed over, and played with. The different versions or understandings of time such as past, present, and future do not exist in chronological order to one another. All versions of thought bleed into one another, echo and repeat, and they also confront and reflect one another. The famous 40 minute unbroken single shot that follows the protagonist throughout several different places such as riverside villages and roads through mountains is much more than just a clever technical device. This single take is the representation of a type of time machine. As the camera pans down through space, the viewer can see that time has distorted. Everything that was, everything that is, and everything that may be exist within that same moment. The past, present, and future exist in tandem, where the memories of our experiences are intertwined with aspirations and dreams and where dreams become part of our reality.
The utilization of fluid temporal structures in the film creates an experience that feels more like wandering through the components of mind rather than assembling a traditional storyline. I am no longer tracking events as I normally would, but instead moving through feelings, memory, and dreams. I feel invited to step outside of traditional timeline conventions and allow time to exist on an emotional level, as an association between cycles. time becomes a tide to me, rather than a timeline.
I find a lot of meaning from this perspective. it reinforces my belief that as humans we often do not experience life as simply a series of chronological events, and the memories we have may represent multiple aspects of our life and connect in ways that may not be immediately apparent. A forgotten image, an old photograph, or a unique smell may stir up condensation inside me. Through this type of reflection, the film encourages me to reassess my perception of my past, present, and future and the nature of memory in relation to my own individual experience. Memory isn't an immovable object behind me. Rather, I believe that my recollections occur simultaneously alongside the other memories I create each day as I live through time and therefore may also extend beyond the map of time in a way that clarifies my understanding of the past and present, particularly the influence my past has on the current events in my life.
And what deepens this experience is how this film is laced with poetry, both in language and in image. The lines of poetry throughout the film function not as dialogue but rather as dream-like fragments, quiet confessions presented in between breaths. However, even when no dialogue is spoken in a scene, the film continues to speak poetically through visuals. Each moment in the film contains symbolism and metaphor, such as the vibrating reflection in a mirror, the slow moving silhouette of motorcycles through fog, and the dancing light cast from a spinning disco ball. In each instance, the film transforms ordinary activities and buildings into emotional spaces. Each surface remembers and every corner has a ghostly presence of what has occurred there before. Poetry is not used to decorate this film, it is inhaled by this film. Every shot is presented as a line of poetry and the imagery on screen is that of a poem being carried by the still air of a rural community
Finally, in confronting time as something fluid rather than fixed, the film speaks to fragility of identity, of memory, of the moment. It makes me think about what we might lose by believing that time is linear. What stories will never be told if we hold ourselves to chronology? There is potentially a beauty in allowing the passage of time to take place not in a road-like way, but like a river... unpredictable, winding, silent at times, rushing at others, filled with hidden curves.

Title: Secretary

“in one way or another, i’ve always suffered. i didn’t know why, exactly. but i do know that i’m not so scared of suffering now. i feel more than i’ve ever felt, and i’ve found someone to feel with. to play with, to love, in a way that fits for me. i hope he knows that i can see he suffers, too. and that i want to love him.”
my first logged movie in december feels weird to not be christmas related, but those types of movies are just so over joyful and not particularly interesting enough to watch for an entire month: and this was a really intriguing watch. unconventional, darker romantics about two complete weirdos are always some of my favourite things to watch, so it was pretty clear from the start that i would thoroughly enjoy this. it’s love story to its core is highly provocative and sexual: using a BDSM esque power dynamic between two leads. usually the sadomasochistic trope can come across as exploitative or even misogynistic, but here it’s really portrayed in a positive way. not only is the subject matter original and nothing the mainstream had really seen before within film, but is a journey of self discovery for both characters and their offbeat romance. with that all being said, i don’t think this movie would nearly be as good if the cast was any different. maggie gyllenaal was truly immaculate, with her breakout role as lee holloway, her character is performed with extreme vulnerability, dark humour and emotional depth to the point the character becomes an incredibly likeable, realistic protagonist. her counterpart, edward grey, is a nuanced, somewhat unlikeable character who has a charm that makes him enjoyable. both cast members and characters have an extremely strong chemistry which feels like the glue that keeps the entire structure together. the tone is highly unusual - it’s a dark comedy, it’s a psychological drama, it’s a bizarre love story. it blends really harsh elements with softer ones - which allows it to be sweet, just with an edge. this story has massive themes of self empowerment from start to end. the main character is struggling mentally - as she partakes in self harm to ease her inner pain, as she finds a consensual partner where she can act out her desires with a matching partner, allow her to accept herself as she is learns to accept the way she is, and removes her self destructive habits. it’s a must see love story that is totally different to anything else really, the ending feels a little too light and the whole ‘happily ever after’ trope is a little tired - this was still a memorable romance.

Luca Guadagnino did amazing work with Challengers last year, I really can’t believe both these films are made by the same director. The film lacks the palpable atmosphere and cinematic substance that made Challengers feel so unique and compelling, leaving its intellectual and thematic ambitions to fall flat. 
There’s an over reliance on Julia Roberts’s character, and she’s a bore so I never really get invested in her story. The sidelining of the younger student, Maggie and the complexities of her accusation is such an odd decision, her story was more of a side plot. The themes in turn felt underdeveloped and confusing, failing to deliver on its thematic resonance. 
Garfield yelling fuck you at a bunch of kids was the highlight of the film without question. It’s a shame that’s pretty much the last scene we see of him, abit of a let down honestly. 
At times the score is pretty gripping and well balanced, but for the majority it’s doing far too much and just overwhelms the scene it’s accompanying, it’s just noise without substance come a point. Which is a shame as again the same composer for the Challengers worked on this film aswell.
I think the film will work for a specific audience but it completely failed to make me feel any sort of way, just a bore fest honestly. From its grey visuals to the bulk of the acting, it’s just a bit stagnant and never really takes off. Always love seeing the talented Andrew Garfield and still have high hopes for Ayo Edibiri, ultimately though I don’t think I’ll ever revisit this film.

Title: The Count of Monte Cristo
Comment:
RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL
One of the greatest revenge tales ever brought to the screen, told with the grand scale and depth it truly deserves. I’d heard so much about how incredible this film was, so I was eagerly waiting to finally dive in and watch it.
And it absolutely delivers.
There’s a reason the novel has maintained its status as a masterpiece over the years — it has everything you want from a story like this: backstabbing, twists, turns, action, melodrama, and redemption. Just when the story seems to lose steam, it picks up again with something fresh that reignites the excitement. I even got the audiobook, and I won’t lie, now I’m genuinely hyped to finally listen the book. The production here is stellar, perfectly capturing the epic scope of the novel with breathtaking locations, stunning cinematography, and a powerful score that masterfully amplifies the emotional weight of every scene.
Edmond Dantes is such a compelling and complex character. I really loved watching how he pursued his revenge, yet at the same time, I felt the sorrow of being consumed by a hate that was destroying him from within. Pierre Niney does a fantastic job portraying him, delivering a nuanced and layered performance. The rest of the cast shines as well; I especially appreciated how the villains never slipped into caricature—their wickedness felt human, driven by greed that poisoned their hearts and pushed them to harm anyone who stood in their way.
All in all, I haven’t seen every adaptation of the novel, so I can’t say if this is the absolute best, but what I can say is that it’s undeniably a darn great one.

I read this is based on a play, and there’s definitely something theatrical about it as he performs for an apparent live audience and for those of us watching from the comfort of our homes—a comfort that slowly slips away into unsettling territory.
All in all, a very NSFW film that won’t leave you indifferent. As the horrible crimes unfold, it crawls under your skin and unsettles you. Title: Before Sunrise
Comment:
What I found magical about Before Sunrise was precisely the way the dialogues are incredibly long and natural. Honestly, to me, Richard Linklater's film doesn't feel like a rehearsed work, but rather a fragment of real life, secretly filmed. It becomes difficult to believe it's a rehearsed dialogue and not a real conversation, captured by chance.
The fluidity and depth of the exchange between Jesse and Céline are the core of its genius. I felt like I was there, not as a spectator, but as a privileged listener, absorbing every philosophical thought and every intimate revelation. The film is a triumph of naturalness, proving that the greatest emotion can lie in the brutally honest intimacy of two souls.
I was totally captivated by the way the words unfold, almost without interruption, building a connection that I feel is truer than most interactions I see on screen.
And when the movie ended, I just wanted to get on a train. This desire is proof of the impact the work had on me. I felt an irresistible urge to put myself in motion, to embrace chance and maybe find my own unforgettable conversation on the way to somewhere. The train, in that moment, represented for me the hope of transformative encounters and the continuation of the existential journey.

Title: American History X
Comment:
This movie feels like getting grabbed by the throat and forced to pay attention. I knew the reputation going in, but I wasn’t prepared for how immediate it is. It’s aggressive and sometimes blunt, but it’s also weirdly precise about how hate actually works. Not as some abstract evil floating around, but as something learned, fed, rewarded, and reinforced until it becomes your whole personality. The way it flips between past and present makes it feel like you’re watching a bomb go off in slow motion, then rewinding to see who lit the fuse. And that ending is just brutal. You can feel something terrible coming, but it still lands like a punch and it sticks with you after it’s over.
Edward Norton is the center of it all, and he’s unreal here. The physical transformation is one thing, but what’s really scary is how convincingly he plays both versions of the same person. Early on he’s all certainty and swagger, and then once the prison section hits, you watch that certainty get stripped away bit by bit. It never turns into some clean, inspirational redemption montage. He goes from terrifying to exhausted to haunted, and you believe every step.
A few moments are definitely built to slam you in the chest, and you can feel the movie doing it on purpose. But I also don’t know if subtlety would’ve hit the same. This isn’t a story that should feel comfortable. It’s supposed to scare you, anger you, and leave you feeling sick about how preventable it all is.

Title: Central Station
Comment:
“TENHO SAUDADE DO MEU PAI. TENHO SAUDADE DE TUDO”.
Central do Brasil está entre as produções brasileiras que obtiveram maior repercussão pelo mundo afora. Dirigido por Walter Salles, o longa-metragem tem a simplicidade dos grandes filmes, mas é certeiro como uma flecha que alcança nosso peito e nos faz refletir sobre a vida, sobre as razões existências de pais e filhos, sobre o valor da amizade e dos nossos valores como seres humanos. O longa conta a história de Dora (Fernanda Montenegro), uma mulher que ganha dinheiro escrevendo cartas para analfabetos na Central do Brasil. Depois de escritas, as cartas passam pelo crivo da `censura` de Irene (Marília Pêra) e da própria Dora, que julgam quais deverão ser enviadas ou não. É quando a mulher se vê envolvida com o triste destino de Josué (Vinícius de Oliveira), um garoto de 9 anos cuja mãe é atropelada e morta em frente à estação onde Dora trabalha. Agora, Dora se vê irremediavelmente `presa` ao menino, com quem - e em função de quem - irá vivenciar uma bela transformação. A parte técnica do filme é impecável. A belíssima fotografia de Walter Carvalho, exibe paisagens áridas e hipnotizantes, trazendo um ar quase caseiro ao filme, mas que auxilia na convicção dos espaços onde a trama se situa. Além disso, a linda trilha sonora vai se tornando um plano de fundo sensível e muitas vezes angustiante que nos mostra toda a força que a película pode ter. O roteiro de Marcos Berstein e João Emanuel Carneiro conta uma história pungente, onde a maior riqueza está nos motivos que impulsionam os personagens. Cada um com seus próprios limites morais, seus dramas, suas angústias e seus desejos. A narrativa é bastante centrada na relação entre Dora e Josué, e em como estas duas figuras ainda desconhecidas uma para outra começam a se aproximar de forma inesperada. É uma relação complexa, mas tratada com bastante simplicidade pelo roteiro, sendo uma jornada literal e metafórica, onde os dois protagonistas centrais encontram no "apego" que desenvolvem gradualmente um para o outro, repletos de ambivalência, uma maneira de reparar os danos que sofreram anteriormente em suas vidas. E o elenco não faz por menos. Fernanda Montenegro tem uma performance simplesmente absoluta neste filme. Sua atuação como a sofrida Dora é impecável, rica em sutilezas e detalhes, onde a atriz consegue dizer muito através de seus olhares e expressões tristes, duras, típicas de alguém que já apanhou bastante da vida. Vinícius de Oliveira, que interpreta José, também se sai surpreendentemente convincente para um ator mirim ainda em início de carreira. É impressionante o talento deste garoto. Ao final da obra, temos o desfecho iminente que se anunciava durante a jornada dos personagens. Fica a dor, a saudade, mas também a certeza que ambos ensinaram mais um a outro do que qualquer outra pessoa poderia ter feito em suas vidas. Eles jamais se esquecerão um do outro. E pra finalizar, reescrevo aqui as tocantes palavras de despedida de Dora: “O dia que você quiser se lembrar de mim, dá uma olhada no retratinho que a gente tirou junto. Eu digo isso por que tenho medo de que um dia você também me esqueça. Tenho saudade do meu pai. Tenho saudade de tudo.”

Title: Moments in a Stolen Dream
Comment: It’s an out-of-town experience to feel disembodied from your city-life self. No husbands nor fathers to think of, no futures to worry about, only a concern for what’s happening in the present. Joey (Christopher de Leon) and Ana (Hilda Koronel)’s unorthodox meetup reignites a flame long extinguished by the societal pressures put upon each of them: one from being successful while the other is to sit still. In a way, the fog is but a cocoon that clouds the mind from the responsibility that has kept them chained for ages; the city of Baguio becoming a fleeting haven for each of them to experience a spectrum of emotions they never knew were possible. To be seen, heard, touched—to feel like a full-fledged entity beyond the expectations of those around them. De Leon’s Kung Mangarap Ka’t Magising (Moments in a Stolen Dream) perfectly captures what it means to feel as though you are in a dream where everything moves according to your desires, albeit only temporarily. Though it may have been for the best; memories, after all, won’t ache if the love contained isn’t at least persevering.

Title: Dinner Rush
Comment:
I've been diving into some Thanksgiving pressure-cooker movies lately, and it finally got me to check out *Dinner Rush.* This film does an amazing job capturing the crazy energy of a restaurant on a busy day while weaving in a mob story.
Creating a gripping movie with lots of characters in one place isn’t easy, especially on a tight indie budget.
*Dinner Rush* isn’t about flashy scenes. As I've gotten older, I lean more toward the build-up of tension rather than just jumping straight to the action. The dialogue is quick and lively, the characters are well-defined, the stakes feel genuine, and everything moves at a solid pace.
What really kept me interested was the bold filmmaking. I felt the madness of the packed kitchen, empathized with a waitress juggling demanding customers, and totally got sucked into the authentic vibe of the restaurant—it really felt like a real spot.
The relationships between characters—whether it’s lovers, a father and son, an artist and gallery owner, or a critic and a chef—were relatable and pulled me in.
The main storyline is pretty simple, focusing on an aging restaurant owner dealing with mob pressure over a gambling debt. The real charm of *Dinner Rush* lies in the day-in-the-life storytelling. It’s packed with low-stakes moments that draw you in.
The life-of-the-party bartender is just as intriguing as those caught up in dire situations. For some, it’s the worst day ever. For others, it’s just another Tuesday. This mix creates a tragicomic vibe that makes it a breezy watch.
There’s just so much going on with the characters; *Dinner Rush* is a rich experience for anyone who digs sharp dialogue and character depth.
I’d label *Dinner Rush* as a postmodern or neo-mob film. Danny Aiello’s character breaks away from the typical tough-guy role—he’s an Italian American who's over the mob life and just wants to enjoy being the king of his corner table, keeping an eye on the family restaurant. He wishes for the simpler meals his late wife used to make instead of the fancy dishes his son whips up.
In the indie film scene, the script and performances are key, and this movie nails it in both areas. Danny Aiello delivered an incredible performance—right up there with his best work in *Do the Right Thing*!
It might not be life-changing, but *Dinner Rush* is a clever and well-made film that celebrates great characters, almost like a stage play.
Plus, who doesn't love a little food eye-candy now and then?
