Title: Phantom Thread
Comment:
ladies, is your man noncommittal? i have just the cure for you. side effects include excessive sweating, nausea, and betrothal!
i'm still stunned i stumbled onto this. Phantom Thread felt like something made precisely for me as a lover of fashion, breakfast, and any story of human connection. tailor-made for my perversions. from the first frame it was overwhelmingly elegant: gorgeous costuming, immaculate production design, a score that floats like silk, and performances that are nothing short of spellbinding. i was obsessed with Daniel Day-Lewis' face — raw, peremptory, feral, more heady than intensity itself. this was a rather middle-of-the-road reversal of the ‘age-gap love affair’ trope but he made every scene absolutely enthralling to witness. Vicky Krieps was incandescent. effervescent with melodrama, as per the genre, but anchored by real weight and depth.
this film is a great example on how to make characters come alive. it is serene, yet tense. sweet, yet dark. gentle, yet belligerent. the performances are theatrical, yet natural. i adore when it is inherently obvious that the filmmaker knows the ins and outs of characters and fully understands how to elevate and perfectly craft dialogue to make something like this work. PTA is pure magic because he manages to do romanticism in a way that is neither naive nor cheap—he simply makes you fall in love, or want to, desperately. there's a softness to this film, despite all the conflict and aggression, that made for quite an emotional viewing experience from the beginning right until the end. 
“Kiss me, my girl, before I'm sick.”
if you look past the fucked up parts and squint a little, this film is incredibly sweet. there is something so awfully poetic about the soft violence in their love. knowingly digesting poison, watching a loved one tailor something for you with a needle sitting gently on their lips, indulging in a twisted perverse love affair. Freud would be so horny for this, an Oedipus complex with a touch of Munchausen by proxy. Phantom Thread reflects a kind of adoration that is undeniably sacrificial and divine. i, too want to be a muse and mutually torment my lover! maybe it's because of PMS but this film was so jaw-droppingly wholesome and lovely that i started crying after 15 minutes and didn't stop until i went out for a cigarette. for a film where so little happens, the love is kept at a constant, tender, steady simmer and warms the heart. there is a possibility that i will be thinking about the shot of them dancing every single day of my life.
i understand both of them so deeply. i am both Alma buttering my toast with no regard for the person concentrating next to me, & i am Reynolds becoming unreasonably upset at the sounds of chewing— the dichotomy of selves! i think learning how to sew has made me at least a little sympathetic to the obsession that Reynolds has for his craft. measuring someone, moulding fabric to fit them, going through fittings are very intimate things even outside of a romantic context. i remember apologising to a friend over the phone the other day about getting impatient, wanting immediacy when it comes to working on anything i’m passionate about, and making people feel as if i don't value their time. i may be biased as a fellow perfectionist but i’ve never seen this kind of personality captured so well in cinema. it’s painful to see him crave love and attention yet push it away once he has it in his hands. Reynolds is an insufferable little control freak and ugh i GET HIM! 
“I want you flat on your back. Helpless, tender, open. With only me to help. And then I want you strong again.”
something in me can’t stop ruminating about this gorgeous film. a beautifully intense relationship, a contradiction of love, a character driven explanation of over-romanticism. pure acceptance of the most ugly parts of themselves. their relationship was toxic, yes, but what i absorbed is something i struggle with myself; the inability to let the darkest parts of myself go, the feeling of just accepting you are nothing. not only that, but romanticising the parts that disgust me. i have grown away from this I think, but it is still there. perfection is unattainable. i’m the most fragile i’ve ever been in my life and this story was the warmest hug and the most delicious meal; it made me realise i’m not alone!
careful, pristine and gorgeous. the score alone could bring me to tears. there must have been moments where there wasn’t music but i don't recall. it came and went so dreamily, like waves slowly rolling onto a moonlit beach. this film had a v similar feeling to Barry Lyndon — at first glance, boring and self indulgent, but had me hooked within minutes. 
“if he didn’t wake up from this, if he wasn’t here tomorrow, no matter. For I know he’d be waiting for me, in the afterlife or some safe celestial place. In the next and the next one after. You see, to be in love with him makes life no great mystery.”
i have watched more romance this week than i have in the past 3 months…. but this! best of them all. a film about intimacy in its purest form. elegant, delicate, pure, filthy, meticulous, restrained, intimate. PTA you are so fucking chic. am i terrible if i want what they have?

Comment:
"So what are you waiting for huh? What are you waiting for!?"
Call her Gabriette she's so inspired 💚. OF COURSE they had to play a song by Reneé Rapp during the sapphic kissing scene 😌. Jonah Hauer King and the sea are just synonymous with each other at this point 🧜‍♀️. I wish i had a bathtub so i could use bath bombs like that 🩸. As someone who calls everyone "diva" and is also losing hair due to stress i felt SEEN by this movie. Lots of Helen homages, a Brandy A.K.A Karla cameo AND Summer Forever by Addison Rae playing over the credits!? This movie was made for me ya'll! 😆.
Oh I Know What You Did Last Summer, you're never not reheating Scream's nachos, yes i know Halloween (2018) kick started this whole re-quel boom we've had in the late 2010s and early 2020s but i noticed a lot more similarities between this and Scream (2022) and as someone whose third favorite Scream movie is that one i ate this tf up 😝.
I was very excited when i learned this was written and directed by Jennifer Kaytin Robinson, the same woman behind Do Revenge (one of the better teen movies/chick flicks in recent years). She already has such a distinctive narrative style very much trying to appeal to young Gen Z women and queer people which is a very niche demographic so i can totally understand why she won't be for everybody. I was very surprised to see a lot of people my age say they felt the script was way too brain rot/made for the TikTok generation which... yeah that's literally what we are lol. Personally i thought it was very fitting to apply it to a movie that's part of a franchise that's never been taken too seriously, i think it isn't trying to appeal to us as a generation so much as it is trying to make a parody/satire of how we are with all our usage of AAVE and therapy talk, it reminded me of Bodies, Bodies, Bodies in that sense.
Just like I'll Always Know What You Did Last Summer the story of this one is basically a retread of the original just with new characters and updated to more modern times. I really appreciated how this one ACTUALLY takes place in Southport and how both Julie and Ray were implemented, they were used sparingly as to not alienate new audiences but enough to satisfy original fans. Most of the callbacks and homages felt a little forced like, we don't HAVE to go over EVERYTHING that happened in the first movie but stil they were cute, i just found it funny how much fan service Sarah Michelle Gellar/Helen got while Ryan Phillipe A.K.A Barry basically got nothing 🤣.
The new cast members were very good, all being up and comers with the surprise stand out being Madelyn Cline as Danica. At first i thought the humor in this movie wasn't gonna click with me and i feared it was gonna clash with the more serious moments but her line delivery and comedic timing were so in point, clearly she was supposed to echo a more modern version of Helen Shivers and i think she executed it flawlessly. Chase Sui Wonders as Ava was also very good, all the new characters were all very well developed and compelling, we get to spend enough time getting to know them that when they all start going down one by one i actually felt bad for at least 2 of them 🥲.
The kills in this weren't exactly great or all that memorable but the gore honestly made up for it. As for the killer reveal i also heard there was a lot of controversy as to who was behind The Fisherman trench coat this time around so i already had an idea of who could it be and me personally, i welcomed the idea with open arms. It's a very BOLD swing but it didn't bother me for many reasons i'm not able to discuss since it veers into spoiler territory but all i'll say is that part of the reason horror grew in popularity was because it broke the mold in ways other genres weren't willing to do so and i think that was best exemplified here 👏🏻.
I have nothing left to say other than this was a great legacy sequel, i look forward to Jennifer Kaytin Robinson's next project and since it's left open ended i actually wouldn't mind if this ends up getting a continuation 👀.

"Nostalgia is overrated."
Overall score: 9.5/10
P.S: The marketing team would've been on their A game had they named this I Remember What You Did Last Summer 😪.

Title: The Running Man
Comment:
“YOU SHIT-EATERS!!”
Slightly disappointed with this. Genuinely thought we were in for something great, better than the original film but no, I prefer that one. Wild, loud, and neon-charged dystopian chase story that bursts in with big ideas about media obsession, exploitation, economic desperation, and how far people will go when the world leaves them behind but kinda misses the mark. The problem is that despite Edgar Wright’s name on the poster, it rarely feels like his film. The usual crackling wit, rhythmic flair, and visual personality are mostly missing. The comedy barely shows up, the substance only comes in flashes, and the style never fully pops even though the world itself is a cool reinterpretation of the original concept. The cinematography is serviceable without being memorable, as generic as it comes. For a story that should feel breathless and dangerous, there’s a surprising amount of dead air and not enough of Wright’s trademark energy to fill it.
“Stop filming me.”
The cast, on the other hand, absolutely shows up. Glen Powell is fantastic as Ben Richards, easily giving a stronger and more layered performance than Schwarzenegger’s version ever had. Colman Domingo continues his unreal run this year and chews up every scene like he’s having the time of his life. Josh Brolin brings a ton of personality, and Michael Cera steals entire chunks of the movie with ease, delivering some of the most entertaining moments. The performances aren’t the issue. The real problem is that the movie struggles to stay exciting across its entire runtime. The third act feels oddly chopped together, and that is where most of the film’s problems hit hardest. We rarely see her struggle with her baby; instead, we watch her battle with herself, against the slow erosion of identity, autonomy, and connection.
I was most compelled by the way it examines marriage, the quiet unraveling that occurs when parenthood magnifies every fault line, fundamentally altering the landscape between two people and pulling them into strange, often painful territory.
Jennifer Lawrence is extraordinary, going completely feral, fearless, and heartbreakingly human in her descent into madness. The film can be a little too abstract for my taste, but its rawness and intensity are undeniable.

What I really think seems to work is characters. Real people played by really great character actors doing real-people things with only slightly exaggerated consequences for their actions. Like, he and I talked some about the Mike Yanagita scene in this movie. I started the convo, but he was into it. We talked about how we both really loved that scene, but why is it in this movie? It doesn’t propel the plot at all. He seemed to dig it when I said, “but it does inform the themes, it informs the world that Marge lives in. How, outside of her house, outside of her cozy life with her husband Norm, who spends his days taking care of her and painting water fowl, the world is full of pain, lies, violence, mental illness, greed, and suffering, and so many people are lost to it. But not Marge. Marge knows who she is, and where she’s supposed to be.” And he seemed to clock with that.

Title: The Prestige
Comment:
That rainy day, oh, it will be etched in my memory. You know those days when all you want to do is sink into the couch with a generous slice of chocolate cake and turn on the TV with zero expectations? Well, that was exactly my state of mind when I decided to give "The Prestige" a shot.
I know Nolan has those colossal films, with time explosions and cosmic twists, but honestly, The Prestige has always been my hidden diamond—the one that seems to go unnoticed but shines the brightest on my mental bookshelf.
From the first click of the projector, I was hooked. It's not just the story of two rival magicians; it's a web of obsession, sacrifice, and the insane pursuit of perfection. The film grabbed me by the collar and said, "Pay attention. Every detail matters." And I did.
I felt like a voyeur, sitting in the shadows of a period theater, watching Angier and Borden destroy each other, penny by penny, trick by trick. The scariest part is that the film has nothing to do with the cozy magic of singing canaries or bunnies popping out of top hats; here, the only thing that comes out is the truth, and it's always stained with blood. Their rivalry wasn't professional; it was visceral. It was about who was willing to pay the highest price, and with every scene, the price climbed in a way that made me hold my breath.
What destroys me in The Prestige isn't the special effects or the epic scale—it's its brutal honesty about what it means to be an artist. The way the film explores the "sacrifice" needed to create the perfect illusion is devastating. While taking another forkful of cake, the film made me question: What would I be willing to lose to be remembered?
And, of course, there's the final trick. Don't expect bad luck charms; the real "black cats" here are the protagonists themselves, crossing each other's paths solely to ensure mutual ruin.
I, being naive, thought I had figured it out. I was taking mental notes, trying to follow the three parts of a magical act: The Pledge, The Turn, and... The Prestige. But when the last card was revealed, and the music swelled, I felt a chill down my spine. It wasn't just a twist; it was a slap in the face. It was Nolan looking at me through the screen and saying, "You were looking for the key, but you forgot to look at the lock."
Five Stars. Non-negotiable. It's not just my favorite Nolan film; it's one of my favorite films, period. Not for being the biggest, but for being the most intimate and the most cruelly beautiful. It turned a rainy day into an experience that kept me thinking for days.
If you haven't seen it yet, or if it's gathering dust on your watchlist, do yourself a favor. Turn off the lights, grab your cake, and prepare to be deceived. You will love the pain.

Title: Crawlspace
Comment:
An elderly Nazi landlord (Klaus Kinski) only rents rooms to young and attractive women. He keeps one woman captive in a cage in his apartment. He keeps a collection of hungry and red eyed rats. He spends his time gliding though the crawl spaces of the booby-trapped building, plotting their murders while spying on them. 
This is a creepy horror movie elevated by Klaus Kinski. He’s already creepy as hell just playing normal people, so why not put some eyeliner and lipstick on him and have him do some “Heil Hitler” hand gestures. Yes, it’s as unsettling as it sounds. 
While it works as a creepy film, it’s not quite a slasher. Most of the kills are off screen and we see the after effects.
Behind the scenes, Kinski was a terror. According to director David Schmoeller, Kinski got into six fist fights with crew members in the first three days alone.
One day Schmoeller noticed that Kinski had a crush on one of the actresses Tane Mclure.  Kinski would actually behave on set if she was present (she only has a small part). The director had her stay on set during Kinski’s scenes to make him behave—it worked sometimes. 
Schmoeller actually made a short film about this experience. It’s called Please Kill Mr Kinski (1999). He talks about the shoot and how the film almost ended with the entire crew lynching Kinski.
I found this film to be slightly better than I expected. I was genuinely creeped out. I gave it an extra half a star for Kinski. It’s certainly not a great film by any means, but I was entertained and it clocks in at a brisk one hour and twenty minutes.
Recommended, if this is your sort of thing.

Title: The Shining
Comment:
The Shining is one of the greatest horror movies of all time because it does something most horror movies don't. Stanley Kubrick is a perfectionist and clearly believes in Gesamtkunstwerk, the idea that every element in a work of art should contribute to a cohesive whole. Everything about this film is meticulously detailed, from the steadicam cinematography, the color profile of the sets, the use of music, the performances, and so on. The use of wide-angle camera lenses gives the cast this distorted look, and we see their turmoil in full display. It's amazing how Kubrick gets these subtitles out of his actors. The gradual look of horror on Scatman Crothers' face continues to haunt me. Although controversially, Kubrick emotionally abused Shelley Duvall to get the traumatic performance he desired.
The Shining stands out from other horror films in how it terrifies audiences. We're all used to jump scares in modern horror movies, but what Kubrick does is linger on a character's reaction before showing something horrifying. We can see the scares coming, but it still unsettles us. Kubrick would also present something without context, and our brains can't process what we just witnessed. If you think about it, Kubrick's approach to horror is more terrifying than what we're used to.
The film is an adaptation of Stephen King's novel, and King hated it. He's been vocally critical of how much Kubrick deviated from the source material, notably in how it portrayed Jack Torrence as an irredeemable maniac, and removing more explicit references to the supernatural. Normally, I would criticize a film for betraying the spirit of the source material, but what Kubrick presents is too compelling. The film may deviate from King's storytelling intentions, but it presents intrigue that King didn't include. In the film, you can't tell if the Overlook Hotel is haunted or if the Torrence family is going collectively insane. Kubrick purposely leaves these mysteries so the film can linger in our minds. Why do you think he ended the film on that photograph? No wonder people are still interpreting the film in different ways 45 years after its release. It can be seen as a metaphor for Native American genocide, or Kubrick's coded confession to faking the moon landing. It haunts all of us.

Title: Wicked
Comment:
❤️‍🔥81%
🔙Train Dreams🔙 
🔜Die Hard🔜
Wicked is not my favorite song and dance but it’s still an absolute spectacle and it’s a film where you don’t necessarily feel the 160 minute run time. I watched this for the first and only time on New Years Eve last years with the family and we had an absolute blast, it’s entertaining from start to finish and if you can look past the glaring flaws in a visual sense you’ll have a good enough time. 
I get that the desaturated color grading and reliance on ‘natural’ lighting were intentional choices but it’s resulted in a mundane and washed out look, the whole time we spend at Shiz University is alarming. The use of intense backlighting and natural-looking light sources; like through the sun beamed windows, are overwhelmingly butchered. It felt like it overexposed the background and obscured details on the characters' faces and costumes, resulting in an amateurish look on many instances. 
The flaws are a shame as the world built is actually well constructed; utilizing massive, elaborate practical sets, like Shiz University or the Emerald City, all designed by Nathan Crowley. This dedication to physical sets is grandiose, it created a world with a tangible, lived-in feel. That stretches to the costumes and the architectural detailing, both possessing rich and expansive depth that can only be lauded. 
The songs were performed in spectacular fashion, but as far as acting goes I really wasn’t impressed with much. Luckily the film is a musical, so that’s okay, but the acting can be so one dimensional and stiff it’s hard to get fully invested, until it comes to that climactic boiling point. What I’m getting at is the dramatic moments don’t have that same punch as the songs and that’s a shame. 
Really though when you cast performers as iconic as Grande and Erivo, the focus naturally shifts to their singing, sometimes overshadowing the nuance of their dramatic performances. 
I will say the climax only gets me more invested in getting to the cinema to see part two, hopefully that will be before the week is over with. I do think the ending suffers from the same issues the MCU has though; the computer-generated flyovers and climactic sequence often resembled generic modern blockbuster CGI, it created a slight disconnect but nothing major, not where it hinders how much a spectacle the set up is for part two. 
Overall not as fun an experience as my NYE watch-a-long but still a mighty occasion and one where the 2 hours 40 minutes flew right along, an impressive feat but hard not to argue that it’s a tad overrated. Either way you look at it though, you can’t deny the talent in the musical sense and the grand scope of world building is masterfully executed.

Title: Mrs. Doubtfire
Comment:
Looking at the American Film Institute’s list of the Top 100 funniest films, you’ll notice that the first one is Some Like It Hot and the second is Tootsie. No need to be a film expert to know what these two classics have in common. Men dressed as women is probably one of the oldest — and curiously underused — comedic gimmicks. It’s an awkward intrusion into a forbidden world, carrying a strange mixture of voyeurism and self-questioning, capturing both the privilege and the curse of being a woman, while also teaching a lesson or two about being a man. You can play it for laughs, for tenderness, and sometimes even for poignant drama.
Chris Columbus’ 1993 comedy Mrs. Doubtfire belongs to this cross-gender film tradition and is rightfully listed at the 67th position on AFI’s list. And while it didn’t reinvent the wheel in the comedic field, the film bears a strong resemblance to dramas such as Kramer vs. Kramer. It seems obvious since it deals with divorce, but there’s more to it than that. I read that Roger Ebert criticized the film for being another showcase of Williams’ imitation talent, and while that worked for Aladdin, he believed it fell flat here.
His mistake, in my opinion, was misjudging the audience’s expectations: it wasn’t to see a man dressed in drag, but to see Robin Williams be that man — not because Williams would give the film an extra thematic dimension (kids and their parents didn’t know he had gone through a divorce), but because Williams was a popular, family-appealing actor. His role as Daniel Hillard embodied his personality: raunchy enough to appeal to dads, tender enough to create that awe factor for mothers, and full of mimics and vocal bits that would appeal to kids. Daniel is probably the closest character to Williams himself.
Williams can overplay his eccentric facets like Lemmon in 1959, but he can also break your heart when he talks about his kids or when he whispers something to his youngest daughter. And just as Tootsie dealt with unemployment and the battle of the genders, Mrs. Doubtfire is a film about divorce that shows the desperate extremes a father can be pushed to in order to keep seeing his children. I don’t understand how Ebert could overlook this aspect. That’s to say, the film has both the laughs and the heart, and while it would be a stretch to say that all the gags work (on that level, some bits are more predictable than others), Mrs. Doubtfire is something more than a film about a disguised Williams. And it’s a good reminder of a time when a good old-fashioned comedy could still win at the box office.
So, the story is about a family that goes through the harsh experience of divorce, a time when enough is enough and a husband and wife realize they’re heading in different directions. The setup is a bit awkward, as it leaves us wondering why this successful businesswoman, Miranda (played by Sally Field), married this goofball voice actor with the energy and temper of a teenager. When a man celebrates his son’s birthday by organizing a whole zoo party and dancing on a table, you have to wonder why he didn’t expect it would upset his wife — they were really totally different. What follows is a poignant argument in which Miranda finally asks for a divorce, and it doesn’t come as a surprise that she gets custody. I don’t even think the kids were surprised.
Daniel can only see his children on weekends, which is obviously not enough. He has three months to prove to the judge that he’s capable of taking care of himself — and therefore the kids — and one thing leads to another: he ends up working at a TV station as a janitor. (It seems a bit contrived that he suddenly couldn’t find anything in the entertainment field.) When he learns that their mother is about to hire a nanny, he goes to his makeup-expert brother (Harvey Fierstein) and asks if he can turn him into a woman. I guess the next scene probably upset Ebert, as it was another montage of Williams’ imitation talent — this one and the earlier interview — but while such a sequence would have felt out of place in a film like Dead Poets Society, it seemed natural that Williams’ character would do these things.
(If there’s one point this review is trying to make, by the way, it’s that once you realize Daniel is Robin Williams’ alter ego, you start watching the film with different eyes.)
So, Daniel becomes Mrs. Doubtfire, and although things don’t go quite well at first, he quickly impresses Miranda, surprisingly turning into a better father figure than he was as a man. This echoes the Tootsie situation: sometimes it takes acting like the mother to understand the father’s job. The film escalates from one comedic situation to another — I have a soft spot for the flirtatious bus driver, and for the little roasting the poor rival, Stu (Pierce Brosnan in his dashing pre-Bond years), has to endure from a jealous old hag. The hilarity peaks with two simultaneous restaurant dates, including one that puts Daniel’s professional future at stake. It’s easy to figure out where it’s going, but we follow Daniel’s troubles with excitement and fun.
The resolution the film offers is sweet and balanced, like in Kramer vs. Kramer — it’s something that appeases the mind and allows us to understand both sides. The emotional impact of the film reminds us that Robin Williams went through a divorce and didn’t have to act; the voices and antics that may have irritated Ebert were set against a very real personal experience. Watching the film after Williams’ untimely passing makes it impossible to view without shedding a tear. God, I miss Robin Williams…
—Chris Columbus: Ranked

Title: Frankenstein
Comment:
Frankenstein is a story that everyone already feels familiar with. There are countless adaptations, reinterpretations, and retellings scattered across literature, film, and pop culture. It’s probably one of the most adapted pieces of writing ever, and people have stretched its themes in every direction imaginable. Most of those adaptations end up being decent in their own way. This time, though, Guillermo del Toro takes the material and pushes it fully into his own territory. You can really feel how carefully he shapes this world. The whole film feels polished, considered, and fully realized, down to the smallest visual detail.
The story itself remains a classic tale about a man obsessed with creating life, eventually succeeding, only for the creation to reflect back the darker questions about meaning, responsibility, and what it actually means to be alive. It’s a fascinating allegory, especially in the way the film digs into Victor’s relationship with the creature and shows the irony baked into their existence. The thing that I like is how the film doesn’t flatten anyone’s motivations. You really see what drives these characters, what pushes them toward the choices they make, and how that ties everything together. Victor pours every last bit of his energy into bringing the creature into the world, only to find himself completely unequipped to nurture or care for the living being he fought so hard to create. That role ends up falling on Elizabeth, the film’s main female presence, who recognizes the creature as sentient and deserving of love. And that’s such a del Toro thing. In his world, the monsters almost always end up being more humane than the actual humans.
Gothic horror is a pleasure in itself, and this film leans into everything that makes the genre irresistible. The atmosphere is drenched in mood. The world feels lived-in, eerie, dramatic, and strangely beautiful. The costumes have that slightly exaggerated, almost theatrical quality that somehow just works on screen. Visually, it’s a feast. The whole film invites you to sink into its shadows and textures and let the story grow around you.

Title: Hamnet
Comment:
I’m literally passing out on the train trying to write this, so forgive me if the results are disorganized. Not that this movie—among the year’s worst, in a shitty year—rewards extended contemplation.
Bad news arrives before the first image: over the logos, a portentously pious choir backed by the susurrus of wind in the leaves. These sounds, which impersonate delicacy but in fact oppressively pervade the entire film, immediately reassure us that what we are about to see will be Profound, yet Hopeful. It’s like a grip on your arm. Then a title card explains the affinity between the names “Hamlet” and “Hamnet”, an affinity that would be obvious even to the biggest philistine in the room. First image: an imitation Malick low angle of trees, yet another cliché. Fake a shot every time one of these compositions shows up in this movie. They are there to assert the presence of nature and meaning: not in their particular dimensions, but as significations of significance itself. Thought is already being foreclosed.
What follows is a movie that makes, literally, the most hackneyed decision at every juncture. Buckley is a stock earth mother who cattily snaps back at all instances of patriarchal or religious oppression, like Mia Goth in Frankenstein. She has three tricks in her bag: wry smiles, po-faced solemnity, and yelling/bawling. There’s not much else going on with her performance. Mescal is doing his usual wounded sensitive guy shtick, but it’s more obnoxious than ever before, because here it’s fused to the abhorrent conventions of the writerly biopic. The screenplay 101 mandate by which every single narrative element must get its poignant callback late in the film, the stress placed on vulgar personal subtext over the manifest content of the work, and—most absurd of all—the spontaneous recitation of famous speeches all make an appearance. There’s one horrible prolonged scene of Mescal at his desk, struggling to write, while his wife implores him for understanding. And he yells and gnashes his teeth and cries between ostentatious pauses—all in the same flat, static, center-framed composition, held for minutes and minutes. The strain is painfully visible. Not the writer’s strain, Mescal’s. Same for Buckley in her big scenes, like her shaky cam close-up during the death of her child. In these moments, you do not see grief or struggle; you see Actors Doing Serious Acting, nothing more. It plays, as one friend observed, like a demo reel.
In the editing suite, Zhao manages the remarkable feat of making the movie feel treacle-slow while never actually lingering on anything. There are hardly scenes here, let alone drama. The impressionistic touches are quickly clipped so we can pick up the point without having to sit with it. The endlessly repeated cuts to black, meant to underscore intensity, are really just an easy shortcut out of having to develop intensity through action and staging. The camera position jumps erratically between handheld close-ups, Eggers-esque planimetric tableaux, and extreme high/wide angles. It’s very sloppy. Also as in Eggers, there’s a pronounced tendency to what I can only call pictorialism in the mise-en-scène, which does little to create a sense of a lived world but sure does draw attention to how carefully the set dressers have decorated the environment. Hence we must strongly highlight those lovely rows of apples in the background of the sex scene, etc. The actual image counts less than its conspicuous aura of prestige.
Throughout, Zhao evinces zero interest in the period, in Shakespeare himself, or in the theatrical tradition. (When Mescal’s on stage, he outrageously delivers his lines like an actor in a film: whispering, tearfully, with his back to the audience; a sharp contrast to the utterly wooden, high school theater deliveries of Noah Jupe, who nevertheless succeeds in moving the audience to rapt tears too.) She shoots the wind-up to the performance as if it’s a boxing match—Mescal roving backstage as if readying to enter the ring, blaring horns on the score as the audience mills into the Globe—then torpedoes the play straight into the base terrain of kitsch. The goal is ultimately just the gratuitous production of pathos, a safe, non-threatening pathos shorn of all friction and terror. It’s as bad as The Life of Chuck in that respect. But where The Life of Chuck, intentionally or not, reveals the solipsism of its own sentimentality, Hamnet passes itself off as, and has been received as, art. That renders it infinitely more pernicious. It wants you to cry so that your tears occlude its own emptiness.

Title: The Fury
Comment:
For his followup to Carrie, Brian De Palma stayed Carrie-adjacent, with another story about a teenage girl with psychic powers she doesn’t know how to control. But instead of a backdrop of high school drama, this one is centered around a shadowy government conspiracy. The horror/suspense/thriller story is twisty and fun, De Palma brings his signature style to many of the set pieces — Irving’s vision on the stairs and her escape from Paragon are both particularly strong — and John Williams contributes a lean but powerful score. 
The movie does suffer from not really knowing who its main character is. An action-horror sequence in the second half involving Andrew Stevens is especially hurt by this, because we’ve been focused entirely on other characters up to that point, and we don’t really know Stevens. 
But this problem and a few other minor ones don’t torpedo the movie. It’s not De Palma’s best work, but it’s still a really good time.
RANDOM NOTE: This is an especially good movie for before-they-were-stars spotting. Daryl Hannah and Laura Innes both have bit parts in this, and Jim Belushi can even be spotted lurking around the background of the Lake Michigan beach scene.

Title: A History of Violence
Comment:
“in this family, we do not solve our problems by hitting people!”
Cronenberg cracks the suburban calm to expose what was always underneath. The domestic sphere here is shown as forever rooted in a history of violence, compressed into one man and one family, making the metaphor as direct as it can be. It’s both a dissection of the American hero myth and a study of the thin line between ordinary life and the capacity for violence inside any person. Tom (Viggo Mortensen) tries to live as a father, a husband, a diner owner, but once he’s recognized, the facade quickly crumbles away. The supposed safety of this home was never separate from the savagery of the past and present, it has always been part of these walls.

“you’re the one who taught me violence.”

It’s a family drama built inside a thriller framework, and the thriller side is flawless – simple, tight, steeped in dread and punctured with bursts of violence that are jarringly real in their precision. Viggo Mortensen seems like the only one who can hold that kind of duality: the actual decency, even gentleness, and the tension of something buried, something unspoken, suddenly breaking through. Confronted with the overwhelming return of trauma and the repressed, the past forces its old coping patterns back into motion, cutting straight through the innocence of the present. Cronenberg shows what happens when love is forced to reorganize itself around a truth outside the narratives that hold, including the ones they use to fill the gaps in their story, like that early cheerleader fantasy, dirty but safe, fully contained. But now, it all spills over. The actors carry that displacement beautifully, each one shaped by the shock of what’s been uncovered.
The stairway sex scene becomes an initiation into the new truth between them. It’s a moment where damaged trust and alienation collide into something revelatory: the otherness that has entered their marriage now fully finds its place. As a struggle for agency, for a footing, inside a reality where the floor has dropped out. The power of that scene is how the wife (Maria Bello) stands as counterpart, not collapsing into this new truth or dissolving in his raw need for existing inside her, but holding her own ground. She meets him with everything she feels, refusing to surrender. It’s an amazingly shot and stunningly acted scene, a moment of brutal honesty, almost too real. It works because it’s the only way up from here.

“when mom brought you home from the hospital, i tried to strangle you in your crib.”
In the final act, the family drama folds into the thriller as Cronenberg leads us back to the closest source of that aggression – the sadistic brother Richie (William Hurt), the first to attack him, the trauma that never settled and shadowed every attempt at building a home that could hold the truth.
Well, not anymore. That shadow won’t return, at least not in flesh, not as a real person. Seriously, how did he fuck that up?! We’re all glad he did. Now there’s finally space for a first shared meal in this new home. Spoiler alert: it's not easy, but it's real.

Title: No Other Choice
Comment:
perfect nightmare burlesque about a guy so stupid that he's doing the work of his corporate masters by personally de-skilling the labor pool, and they don't even pay him for it. let's get real: there are other directors, who may have their virtues, and then there is park chan-wook, who makes everyone else look like tortoises at a race track. this guy cuts to the bone-marrow every single time -- the more frivolous you think he's being, the bigger the sucker punch he's got lined-up for you. decision to leave was this immaculate object of how and why it is more impossible than ever to communicate with other humans in the digital age, and now no other choice uproots the idea that human flourishing is at all possible today without at least somewhat being achieved at the expense of others -- there is no escape for the average peon, and no consequences for the successful few. this whole thing is built on dead bodies and the surrounding silence of society -- exploitation is fine, as long as it's happening out-of-sight, underground. your guilt won't change it, your desperation doesn't justify it, and the only thing that'll stop it is when the image we're sold of how things are 'supposed to be' ends up in the rest of the garbage heap, and we might be tossed in there too.
this is the new techno-feudal paradigm: you'll own nothing, be nobody, unless you're willing to abandon your humanity to join an inhumane system that wrings the last ounce of value from a resource-strapped world. no one made the single choice that had us arrive here, it was a death by a million little acts over the course of centuries -- now the great beast of capitalism is starving, and it will eat us before it expires. so i suppose you can't really blame yoo man-su for wanting to live it up a little in the fall before winter descends on us all -- the luxury of owning a home like his will be an ancient fantasy to the vast majority of those who come after, and it already seems like a mirage today. so smoke 'em if you've got 'em, and drinks are on the house.

Title: Black Christmas
Comment:
“These broads would hump the Leaning Tower of Pisa if they could get up there!”
I’ll start this review by making two points, firstly it’s December 1st and I felt it was the perfect time to kick off the Christmas themed films. Secondly, Black Christmas is perhaps my all time favourite slasher film. There’s very little blood and gore, what we do have is atmosphere and tension by the bucket load.
A party is going on inside a sorority house, we suddenly see somebody climb up a wall and into the attic of the house. The sorority girls start to receive incredibly bizarre and creepy phone calls, soon after the girls start getting picked off one by one.
Black Christmas is often referred to as being one of the first slasher films, it’s certainly one of the best. Bob Clark made one of the defining films of the horror genre with this film, he later went on to direct one of the first and best teen sex comedies with Porky’s and another quintessential albeit very different festive classic with A Christmas Story. Clark made several other great films such as Deathdream and Murder by Decree. Sadly Clark’s career went down hill dramatically after the ‘80s, his last two films were The Karate Dog and Superbabies: Baby Geniuses 2. Tragically Clark and his younger son, Ariel Hanrath-Clark, 22, were killed in a head-on car crash on the Pacific Coast Highway in Pacific Palisades, Los Angeles on the morning of April 4, 2007. His directing in this film was superb, from very early on there’s a constant sense of dread. The phone call scenes and a scene later with an eye peeping through a crack in the door are particularly effective. This is one of very few films that I find genuinely unnerving.
The acting is much better than in most horror films, horror in the ‘70s were able to attract pretty good casts, whereas today “horror movie” almost sounds like a dirty word to A-list actors. A lot of successful actors that started in horror films, tend to forget they were in them once they reach a certain level of fame. Olivia Hussey, Keir Dullea, Margot Kidder and John Saxon are the standout performers, Marian Waldman and James Edmond Jr also deserve mentions. Kidder is a particular delight as the foul-mouthed Barb who likes to hit the bottle a bit too hard. According to Bob Clark, Margot Kidder insisted on drinking real alcohol for the various scenes where Barb was to be drunk.
We never learn much about the killer (unlike the remake), which makes him all the more creepy. There are several funny moments early on, until the tone gets much darker. It was made in 1974 in Canada for just $620,000, it went on to make a little over $4,000,000.
Reginald H. Morris’ cinematography is superb, the tracking shots throughout the sorority induce fear and were a major influence on John Carpenter when he filmed Halloween four years later. Carl Zittrer’s music is wonderful, it’s never overpowering and again just superbly adds another creepy layer to this spectacularly creepy film. Zittrer said in an interview that he created the bizarre music score for the film by tying forks, combs, and knives to the strings of his piano so the sound would warp as he struck the keys. Zittrer said he would distort the sound further by recording audio tape while putting pressure on the machine's reels to make them turn slower.
During its initial release, the film garnered mixed reviews. A. H. Weiler of The New York Times called it “a whodunit that raises the question as to why was it made”. Variety called the film “a bloody, senseless kill-for-kicks feature, [that] exploits unnecessary violence in a university sorority house operated by an implausibly alcoholic ex-hoofer. Its slow-paced, murky tale involves an obscene telephone caller who apparently delights in killing the girls off one by one, even the hapless house-mother”. Gene Siskel of the Chicago Tribune gave the film 1.5 stars out of 4 and called it a “routine shocker” that “is notable only for indicating the kind of junk roles that talented actresses are forced to play in the movies”. Kevin Thomas of the Los Angeles Times wrote: “Before it maddeningly overreaches in a gratuitously evasive ending, Black Christmas (opening today at selected theaters) is a smart, stylish Canadian-made little horror picture that is completely diverting ... It may well be that its makers simply couldn’t figure out how to end it”.
Later reviews have been more positive. On Rotten Tomatoes, Black Christmas holds an approval rating of 71% based on 44 reviews, with an average rating of 6.5/10. The website’s critics consensus reads: “The rare slasher with enough intelligence to wind up the tension between bloody outbursts, Black Christmas offers fiendishly enjoyable holiday viewing for genre fans”. Heidi Martinuzzi of Film Threat called the film “innovative” and praised the leading actresses, Olivia Hussey and Margot Kidder. TV Guide awarded the film three out of four stars, writing: “Although strictly standard fare, the material is elevated somewhat through Clark’s skillful handling of such plot devices as obscene phone calls from the killer to the girls via the upstairs phone and a nicely handled twist ending, which provides a genuine shock”. Author and film critic Leonard Maltin gave the film two and a half out of four stars calling it “bizarre” but also praised Kidder’s performance as a standout. The Time Out film guide noted that the film “manages a good slice of old-fashioned suspense”.
Black Christmas has been included in multiple lists in various media outlets as one of the greatest horror films ever made. The film ranked No. 87 on Bravo’s The 100 Scariest Movie Moments. It was ranked at No. 67 in IndieWire’s The 100 Best Horror Movies of All Time, its entry stating that “the plot sounds formulaic, but Black Christmas remains timeless thanks to its terrifying and elusive killer, ‘Billy’, whose backstory is never revealed, as well as a foreboding ending that doesn’t offer much hope for the film’s Final Girl”. Paul Schrodt of Esquire placed the film at No. 23 in his list of the 50 Best Horror Films of All Time. In 2017, Complex magazine named Black Christmas the 2nd-best slasher film of all time. The following year, Paste listed it the 3rd-best slasher film of all time, while also placing the character Jess Bradford at #1 in their list of “20 Best ‘Final Girls’ in Horror Movie History”.
Olivia Hussey told Bravo during an interview about their 100 Scariest Movie Moments series, that when she met Steve Martin for the first time, he told her that she starred in one of his favorite films of all time. Hussey initially thought he was referring to Romeo and Juliet, but was surprised when Martin said it was Black Christmas and that he had seen the film 27 times.
According to Bob Clark the original script for the film featured murder scenes that were more graphic. Clark felt that it would be more effective if the murders were toned down and kept subtle on screen. Roy Moore liked the idea as well.
This was one of several films inspired by the urban legend “The babysitter and the man upstairs.” The legend involved a babysitter who kept receiving disturbing phone calls. When she had the police trace the phone calls, they realized that a killer was calling from within the house in which she worked. The urban legend inspired at least 6 different films in the 1970s, and several more in subsequent decades.
Black Christmas is one of the greatest, most atmospheric, creepy, well acted horror films ever made. A near faultless horror film. What a fantastic way to start December with one of the greatest horror films, one of the greatest slasher films, one of the best Christmas films and frankly just one of the greatest films ever made. Stunning.
One last note, Rob Zombie is on record as stating Black Christmas as one of his all time favourite movies and Quentin Tarantino even proudly claims Black Christmas is his favourite movie to watch during the festive season.

Title: Aftersun
Comment:
So hard to put words on this film — it didn’t exactly make me feel good, that’s for sure. It’s like: yeaaahhh? But also noooo… so many mixed emotions. Yeah, I get what is being done here — but nooo, you know what I mean?

On the one hand, it very much succeeds in making one feel like shit. In my case, it made me feel so selfish. It’s so selfish to be frustrated or sad about something so small when someone out there is depressed and suicidal. We take so much for granted, don’t we? That’s where films like this wake me up — they make me appreciate how fortunate I am.
In that way, Aftersun was excellent. Not a lot really “happens,” which makes the experience so much more raw. My own father has suffered from depression, and seeing Sophie sit there at the end, watching their old vacation tapes without a smile on her face… ugh. Just ugh.

But on the other hand… 4/5 of this film was just so boring. So incredibly boring. It tries its absolute best to be artistic and avant-garde, and while I usually appreciate directors going for something original, this just didn’t work for me.
I would never see this film again — it was too boring. And it’s funny, because I’m usually a big fan of simplistic, slow-paced films… but this was just too fucking boring haha.

All in all, while I wouldn’t replay this, it was still beautiful and insightful in its own way. What a tragedy… suffering from a depression and suicidalness that even the love of your own daughter cannot repair.

Title: Stay Tuned
Comment:
A couple (John Ritter & Pam Dawber) are on the verge of divorce over a TV addiction. One day after a mysterious and creepy man (Jeffery Jones) delivers a giant satellite dish, they are sucked into a TV universe and forced to fight for their lives. Meanwhile, their children must figure out how to get them back.
This was actually a little better than I expected. I was surprised to find that it was directed by Peter Hyams (Capricorn One, Outland). This director is really hard to pin down—he has lot of cult favorites in just about every genre. 
This film plays kind of like a sketch comedy as they hop into different TV genres, though each show is out to kill their characters. Standouts include a wrestling match, a western, an undead Wayne’s World and a Salt and Pepa music video. In between we see various satirical commercials for films like Driving Over Miss Daisy. 
In one sequence, they fall into a Warner Bros style cartoon. This very entertaining segment was supervised by the legendary animator Chuck Jones.  
Not every gag works, in fact most of them don’t. Yet, this was still pretty fun. The best gag involves John Ritter landing back in his Jack Tripper role in Three’s Company and then screaming in anguish. 
Jeffery Jones (Ferris Bueller’s Day Off) does good work here as a villain and brings a creepy vibe to the whole thing. Eugene Levy also stands out as a mysterious character.
Pleasantville does this concept way better. Yet, this is still entertaining if you’re looking for a light Saturday at midnight kind of film.

Title: Bugonia
Comment:
The first thing that I did as I prepared to write a short review on this film is to click the "Contains spoilers" box. You just can't talk about this film without talking about the big twist at the end. I feel quite fortunate that I managed to get to watching this without knowing the twist. If you have NOT watched the film yet, stop reading now. Come back when you've seen the film.




OK. so, in Bugonia, we have another very Yorgos Lanthimos film. He loves to challenge preconceived notions and established societal and cultural norms of life and the human experience. He loves to take those norms, twist them around, shake them up, put them in a blender, and then rebake them into something that vaguely tells a story about and conveys his somewhat alternative life view.
I really was loving Bugonia and grooving on what I thought the message was for the first two thirds of the film---and then, WHAM, the crazies were right all along about EVERYTHING. The mental image of donald trump standing in the Oval Office with a red hat with the words "Trump was right about everything" flashed into my mind. Surely, this could not be the message of the film: the conspiracy theorists are right about everything.
I don't think it was, and yet, my questioning that intent really make me dislike the ending of the film. But I loved the first two thirds so much that I still. overall, loved the film.
The first two thirds highlight the danger of the social media influenced world that we live in today. To quote the film, we live in "echo chamber danger. An internet induced autohypnotic feedback loop." This is the reality of 2025 and a primary cause of the group think tribalism that has a grip on America and other countries. (It happens on both sides, I admit, but on one side MUCH more than the other). The commitment to a "crazy" set of beliefs is taken to a extreme when Teddy and Don execute a plan to abduct a corporate alien figurehead (from Andromeda Galaxy) in the person of Corporate Girlboss, Michelle Fuller. In their minds, humanity as a species is at risk.
Michelle Fuller, of course, is not only an executive at a company trying highly experimental methods to save lives, but is also working to save the planet Earth as a living entity (as is part of the alien plan). Ironically, in the end, she does exactly that. It is, after all, the humans that cause nearly all of the problems that the Earth is having. The planet without them--full reset.
Let's talk acting and directing. Emma Stone should be nominated for another Best Actress Oscar. She is one of the best actors of our generation--but I don't think she'll win this time. Jesse Plemons should win for Best Actor. His performance was brilliant and nuanced--screaming with desperation and expression. A+++ Yorgos Lanthimos direction in this film was fantastic. This film is not as quirky as some of his recent films (seems odd to say about a film with aliens and conspiracy theorists) but still excellent directing. Nominated, doesn't win.
A few extra thoughts:
It is odd to me that all the people could suddenly die when the protective shield is "popped" but dogs and cats--perfectly fine. Other living things, perfectly fine. Perhaps all of humankind had been exposed to the genetic recoding that the conspiracy theorist talk about in the film and that was somehow activated to cause their instant demise.
You really have to stay and watch the ending and then listen to the credits to get the full meaning. First, of course, the classic folk song "Where Have all the Flowers Gone" which is all about vicious cycle of war can also be applied to our destructive natures and how they affect Mother Earth. Chirping birds, rain storms, no humans. It was a Earth reboot. The Earth can begin the process of healing, human free.
I loved the back and forth language and dialogue in the film. Corporate speak vs Crazy talk.
I have not completely ruled out that the ending was imagined or induced due to some calming treatment drug that would likely be given in the ambulance. A calming drug like Midazolam, often given to patients who have experienced extreme trauma, has a side effect of hallucinations. If she planned the who alien story in her brain to escape, it is quite likely that the story would continue in a lucid hallucination. However, director, Yorgos Lanthimos, in interviews, seems OK with the "she was an alien all along" storyline. I am just not sure if I trust his public interview answers.
Jesse Plemons is one of two current actors who should already have a shelf with a few Oscars. He has been so good in his last several films (and even in his Black Mirror episodes). (Colman Domingo is another actor who should totally have at least one Oscar by now)
Lanthimos did not write this film. It was taken from a film by Jang Joon-hwan and adapted by Will Tracy (who also did The Menu). His most twisted films tend to be the ones he wrote himself (The Lobster, Dogtooth, Killing of a Sacred Deer) but he can definitely find his vibe within other writer's works.
Kudos to Letterboxd for their CAPTCHA Easter Egg when posting this review.

Title: Wicked: For Good
Comment:
To the person whose phone alarm went off in the theater for the first 20 minutes: I hope your shower water is at a lukewarm temperature for the rest of the year.
I saw the actual musical of Wicked, but this was a while ago so I was lowkey surprised at some of the twists that I had forgotten. Long story short: I liked the first act better than the second act, but part of this is not the movie’s fault. Overall, I’m pretty satisfied with how they finished this out. After seeing the interviews of Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo, I was surprised to see that they weren’t touching all over each other throughout. But I think the storytelling and beautiful cinematography is on par with the first film.
I simply think seeing “Defying Gravity” was too good to make the second film better than the first. And even seeing it live on stage, just that one song was better than both of the films combined. There were just unfortunately no songs equivalent to Defying Gravity that absolutely blew me away in the second half, and that’s one of the primary reasons that I liked the first one better. Everything else was pretty similar to the first, so I think it’s just Defying Gravity which makes me think the first one is better.
Wicked: For Good is pretty similar to the first as far as quality of almost everything. It basically matches Act 2 of Wicked exactly and while I could predict most of how this movie unfolded, it was still nice to see how they finished off one of the best musicals that I had the pleasure of seeing. Like I said, nothing can really beat seeing the show in person, but these movies are solid and I’m glad the franchise was brought to cinema the way it deserved.
One final thing: I absolutely loved the last frames of the movie (I don’t wanna spoil it). I get the reference and that was an amazing way to end it.

Title: Pretty in Pink

Ok, yeah, I know.
5 stars? Look...I know it's not a perfect movie. Deep down, I know this.
But for me personally? One of my favorite movies of all time. Easily.
A lot of it can be attributed to nostalgia. I grew up watching this movie. I can still remember the commercials in between scenes on my tv recorded vhs of the movie. 😂
I watched this all the time. Reminds me of saturday nights with my older sister and mom. We would watch this and Dirty Dancing back to back, possibly my favorite movie of all time.
Just good memories and good times.
I know hes portrayed to be a loser...but Duckie was just the coolest guy alive in my eyes. Everything about him was what I wanted to be. He was outgoing, vocal, not shy...was exactly who he was, all the time. I wish I could have the confidence that he had.
And Andie, Molly Ringwald, was just one of the prettiest girls I had ever seen. Pretty in pink, if you will 😁
Second only to Jennifer Grey when it comes to my early celebrity crushes.
Not only is she beautiful, she is also an amazing actor. I just loved her and Duckies relationship in the film...and I STILL say they should have ended up together, like in the original ending. I don't hate the ending they went with, but man, Duckies and Andie should be together!
This movie has a loaded cast.
The legend himself, Mr. Harry Dran Stanton. A good man with a big heart in the movie. Doing the best he can with what he has got.
Annie Potts as the eccentric best friend.
James Spader as the rich prick, and god, did he play it perfectly. I still say his seasons on The Office is some of the best episodes of the entire show. Love Steve Carrell, but Spader is simply amazing.
Andrew McCarthy as Blaine. What a name...Blaine. Still one of the hottest guys ever, I don't care. I'm nt gay, but Andrew could've got it 🤷🤣
The soundtrack is phenomenal. I still listen to it quite often.
This movie is like a time capsule. I was only 3 when it came out in 86...but this movie perfectly captures the essence of the 80s. The rich kids, the poor crowd, the music, the cars, the outfits. Nailed it.
Even the Diceman makes an appearance, and in his short time, played the bouncer role perfectly.
Still to this day, one of my favorite movie scenes of all time is when Duckie is singing Try a Little Tenderness by Otis Redding. Absolutely love it.
Just a fun roller coaster ride through high school in the 80s. One of John Hughes best movies.
I just want to let them know they didn't break me. 💓

Title: Mickey’s Once Upon a Christmas
Comment:
Today, I finally put the last finishing touches on my Christmas decor! 🎁 My house is sparkling and filled with that magic only this season has. You know what it reminds me of? The Mickey and Minnie segment in Mickey's Once Upon a Christmas!
That scene where they exchange gifts – the case for Minnie's harmonica and the chain for Mickey's watch – is, without a doubt, an underrated adorable moment in Christmas animation. That sweet plot twist, where each gave up something valuable to buy a gift for the other, teaches such a beautiful lesson about love and sacrifice. It’s not about the object's value; it’s about the gesture's value. Mickey's line, 'You're all the music I need,' melts my heart every single time! It’s the true essence of Christmas: generosity, unconditional love, and the recognition that the person we love is our greatest gift. Absolutely beautiful! ❤️

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
Was unsurprised to discover that Rian Johnson was raised some type of evangelical Protestant (went to churches that “looked like a crate & barrel” growing up) and not Catholic after watching this. The bones were all there (the aesthetics, the systems) but the flavor of them was distinctly Protestant in a way that screamed someone who had heavily researched Catholicism but didn’t know the lived-in details of the religion. People will probably quibble over whether or not this is “allowed” (if you’re going to play in our pen then there are some rules) but then again, Johnson is using the setting as a conduit to a larger point about religious alienation in American society and cult of personality, especially the kind that he has witnessed and experienced as an ex-evangelical. It’s probably better to keep the themes less Catholic and more Protestant to appeal to the group with which you most wish to communicate, even if the over-emphasis on Jesus and the complete lack of Mary was a flag to me. 
Regardless of my accuracy quibbles, I really loved this. I’ll follow Johnson and Craig wherever they want to take this series. They could make one every 3 years until they die and I would love them all. But this one was so much more earnest than the previous iterations. Others have said it’s much more in line with the first, and it is, but even that doesn’t express the depth Johnson et al convey here. 
I ultimately don’t care about the accuracy to Catholicism because the emotions are real. How do you reconcile the concept of God’s eternal love with the hate and violence done in His name, in the name of His churches? And yet, when we are struggling most, we still reach for the divine for strength. There’s a moment in this movie where Josh O’Connor, intent on clearing his name, is in a funny tete a tete with another character. Suddenly, the other character stops. She forces O’Connor to stop too. He refocuses on her and in doing so remembers his purpose, his calling, why he chose the life he did. It reminded me of what I loved best about growing up Catholic. It made me mourn what I’ve lost in leaving the church. I don’t regret leaving. I don’t think Johnson regrets leaving his church either. But, in that moment, I felt that he understood the ineffable feeling of Catholics who have left the church, and why we call ourselves “lapsed” instead of some other adjective. It moved me to tears. 
This year has been hard on my family. A beloved family member has been in severe decline and, up until a couple of weeks ago, he was still living with us, completely reliant on us for his care and safety. His care is no longer our responsibility but the worry remains as does the guilt for putting his care onto others and the stress of financially maintaining his level of care. I haven’t been to church in years but, as I’ve struggled for grace, I’ve found myself praying more than I have in decades. It’s helped. I hope Johnson is finding grace in himself.

Title: Die Hard
Comment:
🌟95%
🎅🏼86%

🔜Planes, Trains and Automobiles🔜
Nine million terrorists in the world and I gotta kill one with feet smaller than my sister.
Die Hard remains a favorite of mine, actually getting better with each passing rewatch due to the endless quotes and elite performances from two icons of the industry. Whether you call it a Christmas film or not it’s a bloody fantastic action film and just so happens to be set at Christmas time, always gets a yearly revisit from me. 
Bruce Willis may just play my favorite action hero; John McClane, iconic beyond measure with style points for days. I can’t believe it was Alan Rickmans first cinema role, he was beyond made for the big screen; it’s one of the greatest first roles I’ve ever seen, and you’d think with how intense his villain performance was that he’d been doing this for years. 
The forever appeal of Die Hard is partly to do with its stupendously quotable dialogue, elevating it from a simple action movie to a cultural epic. I think a part of the appeal is the contrasting tone of our lead actors; the weary, sarcastic, and very American grit of John McClane is perfectly pitted against the chillingly cultured, eloquent menace of Hans Gruber.
McClane's one-liners are the peak of the piece, born from pain, exhaustion, and righteous fury, we get unforgettable outbursts like his signature; Yippee ki-yay, motherfer, or “Asshole? I'm not the one who just got butt-fucked on national TV, *Dwayne*. Now, you listen to me, jerk-off, if you're not a part of the solution, you're a part of the problem. Quit being a part of the fucking problem and put the other guy back on!”.. man I love the delivery on everything McClane says but that line right there.. perfection. 
There’s a great blend of practical old-school techniques and careful visual effects that make the action feel authentic and fluid, and is yet another reason for the film's lasting impact and appeal. From the stunts performed to the miniature model work used for explosion shots, it really helped in creating a spectacular action film that holds up with the best of them.
The Gruber vs. McClane dynamic is the heart and soul of the film, not only because of their extraordinary acting abilities but the characters are larger than life personalities. perfectly balanced with the actors themselves, it’s a joy watching this back and forth chess match, every great action film needs a rivalry like this to push it to that next level, something we are missing in a lot of modern blockbusters. 
Big fan of how even a mere side character like Al Powell was able to get such a compelling arc. Not only is he the one genuine connection McClane has to the outside world, but he's a cop paralyzed by his own past mistake; an incident where he accidentally shot a child. At the end of the film he’s able to confront this trauma and achieve a form of redemption, it’s rich storytelling and gives the film more emotional weight than the average action thriller.
One of the best in its genre, such a perfectly confined action thriller with an awesome soundscape, larger than life character personalities, with legends of the game performing at the top of their respective games and an overall craftsmanship we rarely see in these sort of films anymore. A film that lives up to the hype and then some, and if you haven’t yet watched it, you need to.

"They just fuck you and they fuck you and they fuck you, and then just when you think it's all over, that's when the real fucking starts!"
If you were shown The Game and was unaware of the director, you would probably still guess Fincher. For me, Fincher is a director who shoots his movies in a world where everything is always slightly off. Nothing is chaotic by accident and that's the trick of his films: you're meant to feel like you're inside a world that has been engineered. Whether it's in the rain-soaked dread of Se7en or the psychological destabilization of Fight Club, his style is unique.
I enjoy this film, but you really have to surrender to the story especially when it comes to the ending. For most people (me included), the ending seals the deal with this film. The scale of the "game" borders on miraculous and it stretches its credibility so thin, you can see through it.
Before you get to the ending however, The Game comes off as an old-fashioned thriller. I know I'm saying "old-fashioned" for a film that was made not even thirty years ago, but these type of films don't really get made nowadays. The pacing is taut but patient. Fincher weaponizes atmosphere in a way that is seen in his other films, yet combines it with so much doubt.
Even rewatching this, I'm questioning everything. And, that's exactly what Fincher wants you to do. Is this part of the "game" or is there something else going on?
With a lesser actor, this is a story that most likely wouldn't have worked, but with Michael Douglas, it's gripping. For a character like Nicholas Van Orton, the entire movie hinges on our ability to believe in his unraveling. At first, Nicholas is very minimal in his expressions, almost bordering on frozen. 
He's not necessarily rude, just profoundly uninterested in human life. Then the "game" begins and thus starts the downward spiral. I just love how incremental the unraveling of Nicholas is. He doesn't go from stoic billionaire to screaming paranoiac overnight. It's these tiny gestures and fractures that make the descent impactful.
Throughout the film, Fincher builds the world of CRS as this malevolent ghost that somehow infiltrates every corner of Nicholas' life. It keeps escalating and escalating and personally, I was waiting for some grand finale. 
And, it is, but not in the way that I had hoped. Everything has been planned down to the second. Emotionally, I guess it lands, but logically? 
I'm raising several eyebrows.
To accept the ending at face value, you have to believe that CRS pulled off an operation of impossible precision. They predicted Nicholas' every move, despite him being a man famous for doing the unexpected. They staged near-death events with pinpoint choreography and anticipated his psychological breaking point down to the moment. They arranged for actors to be perfectly synchronized despite Nicholas constantly deviating from the "script." Or, does he? 
Also, they assumed that he would jump from the EXACT rooftop at the EXACT time at the EXACT angle necessary for their safety measures to work. What the hell would happen if he hesitated for five seconds? Or jumped in the wrong direction? Or, idk. Reacted unpredictably as most traumatized humans often do? This is the main reason I'm giving The Game four stars. I understand it's not trying to be realistic and I understand that it's a movie. But, it still pisses me off.
Despite all of that, The Game is a fun film. It's a hypnotic psychological funhouse that bends rules with each rewatch. For all of its contrivances, this is one of Fincher's more daring adventures.

Title: Sentimental Value
Comment:
“It’s hard to love someone without mercy.”
Sitting across the dinner table from his actress daughter after sweeping back into her life with a high-concept plan for reconciliation, acclaimed filmmaker and absent father Gustav Borg (Stellan Skarsgård) offers that wisdom to Nora (Renate Reinsve) as if directing her on how to forgive him. And in the wake of his ex-wife’s death, that’s precisely what Gustav intends to do — not by apologizing for his decision to leave their family when Nora was still just a child, but rather by casting her in an autobiographical Netflix drama about his own life.
Exploitative as that sounds, Gustav isn’t just hoping to make Nora say the words he’s always longed to hear from his firstborn daughter in exchange for a cut of Ted Sarandos’ money. On the contrary, his plan — like everything else in the transcendently moving “Sentimental Value,” a layered masterpiece that “The Worst Person in the World” director Joachim Trier has been working toward for his entire career — is layered with a delicate sense of personal history. Because the (once) great auteur Borg doesn’t intend for Nora to play a version of herself in his movie. No, he insists on using her as a stand-in for his mother, who committed suicide in the sun-bathed Oslo house that has belonged to their family since at least the start of World War II.
Gustav has never understood the reasons why his mother took her own life after kissing him goodbye one morning — he was only a child at the time. Now a 70-year-old Volker Schlöndorff-type who’s been fading toward irrelevance in the 15 years since his last narrative feature (and has only found late-career success by entombing himself in a documentary about his life’s work), Gustav is convinced that the answers he seeks are still hiding somewhere in the Borg’s ancestral home. That home contains several generations of secret feelings that will only reveal themselves to those who know how to find the cracks in its foundation.
Nora — whose emotional avoidance has fueled the same acting career that it threatens to derail with stage fright, as we see in a funny and spectacularly fraught scene where she demands that her married lover (Trier mainstay Anders Danielsen Lie) either fuck or slap her before she greets the opening night audience of her latest play — has zero interest in helping Gustav look for where those cracks might be. She also vehemently rejects her father’s offer to star in his film. But as he charges forward with the project anyway (which he intends to shoot in the actual house that inspired its story, and still legally belongs to him), each of the surviving Borgs will be forced to navigate the resentful ocean of lost time that stretches between the truth of who their parents actually were, and the fiction of the characters they’ve created for them to play in their minds.
Few recent movies have reconciled the difference between those distant shores with the same tenderness that “Sentimental Value” achieves by the end of its soul-melting final sequence (though Charlotte Wells’ more haunted but equally poignant “Aftersun” comes to mind). Even fewer have so elegantly literalized how the love that parents are able to share with their children — and vice versa — can be limited by their ability to express it. Almost none have more beautifully explored the role that making art, which is to speak without talking, can play in facilitating that process.

Title: Game Night
Comment:
I’m glad that my game nights never involve faberge eggs and Bulgarian criminals. Most of the time they involve battleship or connect 4, my girlfriend, and an entire handle of whiskey.
Game Night was a fun time for sure. I remember seeing that this movie was rated R and was in theaters, and 14 year old me was intrigued by how a seemingly innocent trivia game based-movie could be rated R. Other than that, I haven’t really heard about this movie since 2018. The jokes were funny, and I liked what they did where they try and trick you as the audience by going back and forth from what’s real and what’s fake. Kind of a fourth wall breaking there considering that Brooks said that the players couldn’t distinguish reality from farce.
I was pretty invested for the first half of this movie, but by the end with so many twists, I began to lose interest. I know I just said that I liked the fourth wall breaking, but it just didn’t really seem to end and I was beginning to grow tired of it. The comedy in this was actually decent and made me laugh a few times, so even if it’s not the most perfect movie, it was entertaining at least. The characters were pretty familiar with the typical murder mystery plot: the main, invulnerable characters, the comedic relief/dumb one, and a couple who seemingly has recurring issues throughout the course of the movie. Even movies like Midsommar and Knives Out contain these stereotypes. Game Night seems familiar, but adds its own twist of creativity and messing with the audience.
I think this would be a perfect movie to turn on when there’s nothing else really to watch, and I mean that in the nicest way possible. It just seems like a movie that I’m never really itching to watch, but everyone is on board with watching it if we can’t decide on anything else.

Title: Lost Faith
Comment:
Haven’t we all found ourselves watching a shot-on-video action movie and thinking, if only it wasn’t missing a healthy dose of religious god-bothering it would be amazing? Well, thankfully this film has come along to fill that void.
An unintentionally deranged ode to martial arts and Jesus; whereby actor/director/producer/soundtrack singer/writer/stuntman Joel D. Wynkoop must fight bad guys, the police, a random larger bodied man and a crisis of faith. Yes, it’s a tale of a guy whose god and wife are missing, the latter thanks to some people traffickers and the former down to…crime?, and so he has to go to a secret island to fight the villains and his own atheism. Or something.
As with many of these shot-in-someone’s-backyard films, the plot or the lack of technical merits aren’t really what’s important here. No, the joy is to be found in the details, like: the main character renting a whole shelf of Chuck Norris movies, middle aged men doing unconvincing but high-energy martial arts, the unprofessional actors giving it their all regardless of whether that scene really needed it or not, jungle hair frizz, I think the man playing the car dealer was drunk, dialogue flubs and Jesus giving someone the strength to deliver roundhouse kicks of justice.
