Title: Monster
Comment:
I’ve never been thrown off by a film as many times as Monster did to me. I swear, throughout the whole thing I kept forming these little assumptions as I'm stitching together theories, trying to guess where the story was heading and every twenty minutes or so the film just smacked them down and left me quite wondering what the hell I actually knew. The questions pile up fast. You keep trying to get a grip on what’s going on, but the film offers so many perspectives, so many angles, that clarity becomes this slippery thing you almost catch but never quite hold.
The story itself is deceptively simple, but the film tells it in such an ingenious way that every beat feels layered. Each character is drawn with a kind of multidimensional care that makes you rethink them as the film shifts its point of view. Nothing is wasted. Every minute feels intentional. And when the final revelation lands, everything suddenly locks into place. It's like the gears in your mind finally start turning in sync and you see what the film has been building toward the whole time. We really gain a deeper understanding of the characters, their motivations, and the emotional ripples they cause. This is actually what I love most, on how the different perspectives don’t contradict each other and instead, they complete each other that's forming a fuller picture that you couldn’t have grasped from just one angle.
It’s an incredibly well-constructed film, especially in how it shows the weight that simple words or actions can carry. The story is basically about perspective on how easy it is to lose nuance when we only look through one window and assume we’ve seen the whole house. We miss everything happening just outside our frame.
And here’s the thing though, the story isn’t actually complicated once you reach the end and when you actually realized it. It’s the journey through each perspective that feels messy and emotionally taxing, the same way real life does. Life is confusing when you’re in the middle of it. Everything only makes sense once you’ve already lived through it.
The film being called Monster isn’t a coincidence. It’s a reminder that the real monsters are often our assumptions, the ideas we cling to without understanding the full picture. So, who’s the monster here? The easy answer is all of us. We jump to conclusions. We project. We fill in gaps with fear or bias. We decide who people are without knowing their whole story. And in doing so, we turn other humans into monsters in our minds.

Title: Wicked: For Good
Comment:
I don't have an exact count, but if I were guessing, I'd say I've seen over 120 plays in my lifetime--most of those musicals. Wicked is one that I saw in New York and touring. It is a favorite---but not Top 10. One thing that I can consistently say about Broadway musicals is this: the first act is always better than the second act. It has the better songs, the better story, and nearly all of the BIG moments come from the first acts. It is no different with Wicked--the two BIG showstoppers, Defying Gravity and Popular, first act. No One Mourns the Wicked, What is this Feeling?, Dancing Through Life. First act. The second act does have No Good Deed and For Good...but comparing the music and memorable scenes from the first and second act, it is, for me, not even close.
So, I was not surprised that I did not enjoy Wicked: For Good as much as the first Wicked (2024) films (act one). As in the first film, there were some things that were amazing technological film making wonder--full of sparkle, dazzle, and endless eye candy. The film is sure to be nominated for all of the Academy Awards that give the film its look: Production Design, Costumes, Makeup, Sound, Visual Effects, perhaps even Cinematography. It should win a few.
The singing was amazing--as good as Idina and Kristen (and I think they are perhaps the best singing duo in Broadway history). Adriana Grande and Cynthia Erivo and so vocally talented. The acting was very good too. Personally, I though Cynthia Erivo was better than Ariana Grande. Both might get nominated--I think only Cynthia should.
The film also made many changes from the Broadway production--which I am OK with. Two new songs were added, backstories were expanded, a wedding was added, and other parts of the story involving the animals were expanded. All of it worked for me, and, in some cases, helped clarify the overall story...but did not really improve the story.
Although I love Wicked, I have always had a bit of a issue with the story and its jumbled nature. It is as if the (original) author was trying to connect the dots and incorporate and explain all the major elements of the original 1939 movie story and the final picture is just somehow a bit off.
In my first review, I ranked productions of Wicked...but I would like to expand that in this review--since I have also seen the 1939 movie and read 3 of the Frank Baum OZ books, including the 1900 The Wonderful Wizard of Oz. (I've seen other productions too like the Rankin/Bass cartoons, The Wiz, and others---but I don't want to go crazy)

1.) The 1939 Wizard of Oz film
2.) Original Broadway Play
3.) Traveling Wicked Production
4.) Wicked film (2024)
5.) Wicked: For Good (2025)
6.) Frank Baum Wizard of OZ books
7.) The Gregory Maguire book, Wicked. (which would be lower, if there were a lower)

Title: After the Hunt
Comment:
I believe that this film has been somewhat misunderstood and unfairly criticized. Certainly, I too have my reservations about it, and during the viewing, I found myself frustrated multiple times regarding how this story, which addresses a very important theme, was handled.
However, by the end of the viewing, I realized that this film is ambiguous because it intends to be so. It does not seek to provide answers but rather aims to generate even more questions. It does not resolve the ambiguity, rather, it amplifies it, as what interests the director and the screenwriter is not the act itself, but its consequences: stemming from the complexity of the resulting situation and the characters' inability to navigate morally within a world dominated and marked by ambition, opportunism, and half-truths.
I still believe it is a very human film in this regard, and ultimately, it is up to us, the viewers, to provide the answers. Perhaps this is as it should be.

Father Jud Duplencity: "Here's what's gonna happen: Benoit freakin' Blanc and I are gonna ask you all some questions, and you all are gonna answer them, and we're gonna get to the bottom of who killed Monsignor Wicks and why, and then... that's it!"
Rian Johnson's third Benoit Blanc mystery is his darkest and most ambitious one yet. After the colorful chaos of Glass Onion, Wake Up Dead Man goes full gothic—we're talking candlelit churches, graveyards, and a murder that happens during a Good Friday sermon in a locked room. It's wild. Daniel Craig's back as the Southern detective we all love, but this time he's not just cracking a case, he's actually questioning his own reliance on pure logic when it crashes headfirst into faith and belief. The atmosphere Johnson builds here is incredible. Everything feels heavy and shadowy and, honestly, a little creepy, which is exactly what this story needed.
Josh O'Connor is the real MVP here as Father Jud, this former boxer turned priest who's trying to clear his name after the corrupt Monsignor Wicks (an absolutely menacing Josh Brolin) drops dead in what seems like an impossible murder. O'Connor and Craig have this fantastic back-and-forth where you've got the logical detective and the faithful priest trying to work together, and it's way more emotional than I expected. The rest of the cast is great too—Glenn Close, Jeremy Renner, Kerry Washington, Andrew Scott—but O'Connor's performance is what gives the movie its heart.
FAVORITE SCENE: The moment Father Jud realizes his calling as a priest is separate from Blanc's obsession with solving the mystery.
Release Date: November 26th, 2025
Distributor: Netflix
Production Companies: Netflix, Ram Bergman Productions, T-Street
Johnson's script is packed with twists and clues like always, though the first chunk of the movie throws a ton of info at you pretty fast. Steve Yedlin's cinematography is gorgeous, all those shadows and stained glass windows creating this oppressive but beautiful vibe.
Budget: $40M
Worldwide Gross: $2.5M (limited release)
Viewing Platform: Alamo Drafthouse Cinema
What I really dug about this one is how Johnson uses the mystery format to dig into bigger stuff about faith, corruption, and accountability without beating you over the head with it. He's drawing from those old-school locked-room mystery novels here more than straight-up Agatha Christie, and that puzzle-box structure is so satisfying when everything finally comes together. The movie takes its time getting there—maybe a little too much time in spots, honestly—but when that final act hits and all the pieces click into place, it's pretty damn thrilling. Johnson knows how to direct the hell out of these things, letting scenes breathe while keeping you on edge. Nathan Johnson's score is haunting as hell, too, adding this layer of dread that works perfectly.
DIRECTOR: Rian Johnson
WRITER: Rian Johnson
FILMING LOCATIONS: London, England / Church of the Holy Innocents-High Beach-Epping Forest, England
If I'm being real, the movie does get a bit too dense for its own good sometimes. That first half hour especially just dumps so much on you that it can feel like information overload, and I'm wondering if some parts might feel slow once you already know the ending. But honestly? That's a pretty small complaint when everything else works this well. This is definitely the meatiest and most thought-provoking movie in the series, and even though I think the original Knives Out is still my favorite, Wake Up Dead Man proves these two have a lot more mysteries left in them. I'm already hyped to see what comes next.
Be well, my friends.

Title: Hamnet
Comment:
What happens to a bond when loss teaches each person to grieve in their own isolated way? What makes Hamnet so affecting is not simply the tragedy itself, but the way it portrays the sorrow that stays in the spaces between Agnes and William. They are two people who love differently, who move through the world with entirely separate languages, yet they are bound by the same unbearable absence.
Agnes’ grief becomes an intimate act, one rooted in touch and memory. She mourns not only the child she lost, but the version of her life that will never return, navigating that emptiness with a kind of fierce, intuitive resilience. William, unable to sit comfortably inside his sorrow, retreats into work and distance. The movie shows how this divide doesn’t make either parent selfish or unreachable; instead, it highlights how grief can fracture even the closest bonds, redirecting love into different shapes. Their paths diverge not out of cruelty, but out of the simple truth that everyone breaks differently.
For William, creation becomes the only way he can process what he cannot speak aloud. The imagining of Hamlet is not a triumph of artistic genius so much as an act of self-reproach. Writing the play allows him to confront the guilt he carries for not being present when his son needed him most, turning that guilt into art that he knows will live far beyond him. Each line becomes a reckoning, a reminder, a refusal to let himself forget. The play becomes a monument not only to his grief but to his failure, a way of ensuring that the memory of his son exists in a form the world can never fully erase.
Yet Hamnet is not only the story of one family’s loss; it is also a meditation on the power of art to hold and transform pain. When our voices fail, we create. Art becomes the vessel for what overwhelms us: anger, regret, longing, love. It is both an expression and shelter. Whether you’re the one who makes the story or the one who receives it, art becomes a meeting place where grief can be understood, softened, or simply recognized. In this sense, Hamnet extends beyond its historical setting into something timeless: the idea that storytelling itself is a form of survival.
Hamnet absolutely floored me. Jessie Buckley deserves every bit of praise for her performance, but dare I say, Jacobi Jupe’s performance as Hamnet is just as good. This is one of those “remember the name” type of performances because he stole every single scene he was in. One of the best child performances in recent memory, and I would go as far as to say he should be in consideration for Best Supporting Actor. Lastly, this has one of the best endings I’ve ever watched and one I will be thinking about for quite some time.

i know you’re in there and that you’re suffering, even if you pretend to be okay. you’re probably wondering why there’s so much pain imploding on your chest, why you’re so sad, afraid anxious all the time, but the truth is that i still can’t find an answer. and please, don’t you worry and rest assured, because i know i’m going to find it. all i want you to know is that even if you feel lonely, you can count on yourself and your strength, because you’re the bravest person i’ve ever met, even if you don’t believe it. the things you’ve gone through… it’s so much to handle, but you did it all. you’ve made it and you’ve survived. and i know you’re scared, and you don’t know why. or maybe you do know, it’s just that you don’t want to admit it. you’re afraid that if you confess your fears, then the world will collapse on yourself, so that’s why you tried so hard to forget it all, to ignore everything. but sometimes escaping in your own little world is not the best solution, and you have to face this. asking for help is okay, it’s legitimate, and it will change your life for the better. opening up about your fears, your insecurities, your sadness, your anger, your pain, helps. but you never did so, perhaps because nobody ever wanted to listen to you or take you seriously. i’m sorry that i haven’t been there for you, to hold you in my arms and tell you that everything is going to be fine. but now i’m here, and i have no intention of letting you go, not even for one second. i know you feel like you don’t belong in this world and that you feel like an outsider, but i’m sure that you will find your place on earth, one day. we’ll find it together, even if it takes a lifetime, an eternity. one day we will finally be free, and we won’t be fighting anymore against what’s hurting us, but sometimes it’s just you, battling against yourself. one day we’ll be happy and free, i promise. i love you.
this is half of a letter that i've written to myself not too long ago, and i thought that it was just so fitting for this film, so that’s why i’ve decided to share it with you, hoping that it will resonate with anyone that has felt like me at some point in their life.
this is what the perks of being a wallflower is to me. it’s a long, emotional and heartfelt letter to myself, to my inner child, to the little quiet girl at the back of the class, observing everyone in silence and never made a sound. the little girl who used to take care of everyone, except herself. but this film is also a letter to my teenage days, when i was battling with severe depression and anxiety. those painful days when i couldn’t even get out of my bedroom. the perks of being a wallflower is a heartwarming poetry, a glimpse of light beneath a turmoil of darkness and despair. it’s a guardian angel looking inside your eyes, whispering to you all the things you’ve always wanted to hear, making you feel so happy and free as they’re holding your hand so gently, that you almost feel like you can touch the clouds with your fingers. the perks of being a wallflower is your imaginary friend, always standing beside you, tickling your shoulder to let you know that they’re with you all the time.
following charlie’s journey, the main character, just feels deeply personal and touching. charlie, sensitive and introverted, but he’s also profoundly troubled by a traumatic experience that is now culminating in ptsd, depression, anxiety, intense sense of guilty and mental breakdowns. he’s removed this memory from his brain, blocking it out, but that same traumatic experience, that same terrifying memory just keeps coming back for him, stemming in panic attacks and breakdowns. charlie is also quite devoted to music, reading and writing, probably as a way to escape reality and regain a sense of control over his emotions, over his life. and i see myself in him for this exact reason. without books, without writing and without music i would be lost.
“we can't choose where we come from, but we can choose where we go from there.”
watching charlie was like watching myself in third person, like an old distant memory where you don’t see it from your own eyes, but rather from up high, like you’re flying through it and just observing it as if you’re a whole other person. but you’re really not, it’s your story, and it belongs to you only. you’re just reminiscing your past, hoping it will follow you everywhere, because forgetting only makes it worse. you don’t have to ignore it, you just need to accept that this is where you come from, and it doesn’t cancel out the beautiful and strong person that you are. you came through pain, but from there it will only blossom an entire new soul, and it is only yours to choose what to do with it.
the perks of a wallflower is a tale about mental illness, repression and trauma. it’s about the burden of being an introvert, an outsider and an observer of life, because participating in it almost feels too scary and painful. this film is a journey through self-acceptance and healing, it’s about confronting your inner demons and that only through acceptance and the externalization of your pain, you can finally be free from it, because deep down you know that you’re the key to your own wellbeing and happiness. but this film is also a heartwarming hymn to friendships, to finding a second family in other outsiders just like you. it’s a bond crafted upon understanding. it’s a “home” where you can feel safe and sound, free, relaxed and at peace, because you know nobody will judge you here. it’s a safe haven built on trust, where all of you just help each other out, and finally come out of your shell. this is the magic in finding safety in someone who’s just like you. so, from being a wallflower, an observer, you’re finally blossoming in a beautiful white edelweiss; symbol of bravery and resilience, because through failing, learning and trying again, you will finally rise within yourself and be reborn, just like a flower, or maybe just like an edelweiss that you can find on the mountains. climbing, falling back, trying again, and then finally reaching the peak, only then you will find your edelweiss, and that flower is you.
“so if this does end up being the last letter, i just want you to know that i was in a bad place before i started high school, and you helped me. even if you didn’t know what i was talking about or know someone who’s gone through it, you made me not feel alone. because i know there are people who say all these things don’t happen. and there are people who forget what it’s like to be 16 when they turn 17. i know these will all be stories someday, and our pictures will become old photographs. we’ll all become somebody’s mom or dad. but right now these moments are not stories. this is happening. i am here and i am looking at her, and she is so beautiful. i can see it. this one moment when you know you’re not a sad story. you are alive, and you stand up and see the lights on the buildings and everything that makes you wonder. and you’re listening to that song and that drive with the people you love most in this world. and in this moment, i swear, we are infinite.”

Title: Blue Moon
Comment:
Blue Moon is a wonderful little film, an intimate work that aims to capture a man across two hours of his life. Told in real time it's a film of witty dialogue and constant performance, a hangout movie where everyone is putting on an act, as friends, lovers, and rivals. It's the story of a partnership ended and a new one rising, tapping into jealousy and desperation. We see into the world of Lorenz Hart, which seems so small, bitter, and vulgar. There is poetry too and moments of solace amidst the loneliness, making for a character study which is very well-rounded. Blue Moon is a film which interprets history into a condensed summary of emotion, tightly constructed yet feeling very loose and free. Ethan Hawke is completely submerged inside his character, given a tremendous performance. Blue Moon is brilliantly simple and elegantly executed. My favourite Linklater film.

Title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest
Comment:
I loved this so much. Like, not even 20 minutes in and I already knew it was going to end up as an all-time favorite for me. The performances are unreal across the board, but Nicholson is on another level. I'd even venture to say it's one of the best performances I've ever seen. 
The movie had me locked in from start to finish. It has this perfect mix of comedy and tenderness where you’re laughing one minute and tearing up the next, with basically no in-between. The ward feels full of real people, not “characters.” Everyone has their own little quirks and rhythms, and the film actually lets them be funny without turning them into a joke. That’s what destroyed me. You start caring about all of them, so every small act of control starts to feel personal. Those group scenes, the cards, the basketball, the trip out, feel like tiny stolen breaths of freedom.
And then the ending. It’s one of those final stretches that feels inevitable and still completely devastating. It doesn’t just make you sad, it makes you angry in that way you can’t even explain, you just feel it in your throat. I had high expectations going in, but I didn’t expect it to hit me like this. I’m already looking forward to watching it again.

Title: Zootopia 2
Comment:
The world of Disney’s Zootopia is not exactly an unspoiled paradise. The various animal species live in harmony — but only to a point. They still need a police force to maintain law and order. There’s still some form of a capitalist economy; the new sequel makes it very clear there are still haves and have nots. Really, the word “Zootopia” is less of a descriptor of the place and more of an accurate pun — because the only people who might truly feel like they have found utopia there are those who enjoy cheesy animal puns and knowingly corny dad jokes.
Let me put it this way. Let’s say there’s a world populated entirely by animals. Let’s say in this world there’s a road sign for a place called “Gnu Jersey.” If that gag makes you chuckle, then congrats, Zootopia 2 is for you.
Sure, yes, technically speaking Zootopia 2 is intended for your children. This is a colorful, energetic, and extremely busy animated film about talking animals. But while these critters’ adventures keep the kids occupied, a lot of the movie’s humor, tucked into its corners and backgrounds of the frame, is aimed squarely at their parents and guardians, at least those who love a groan-inducing play on words. As a certified dad (and certified dad joke teller), I must confess that while I would not necessarily describe Zootopia 2 as a watershed moment in the history of American animation, I will cop to chuckling quite a few times, and generally enjoying my return to this land of animals and animal-related wordplay.

Title: Riefenstahl
Comment:
“Anyone who thinks they already know the story of Leni Riefenstahl will quickly be proven wrong here.”
(English Version below ⬇️)
german version 
„Riefenstahl“ – komplex, verstörend, faszinierend
⭐⭐⭐⭐
„Riefenstahl“ ist eine dieser Dokus, bei denen man nach ein paar Minuten merkt:
Das wird kein gemütlicher Abend, aber ein verdammt interessanter.
Der Film nimmt sich Zeit, Leni Riefenstahl nicht einfach als Monster oder als verkanntes Genie abzustempeln, sondern zeigt sie so widersprüchlich, wie sie nun mal war – und genau das macht ihn so packend.
Besonders gut funktioniert, wie man Riefenstahl ständig zwischen eigener Selbstdarstellung und historischer Realität pendeln sieht.
Ihre Stimme, ihre Tagebuchfetzen, die alten Fotos – das wirkt manchmal wie ein Spaziergang durch ihren eigenen Kopf, bei dem man sich ständig fragt, was davon Erinnerung ist und was reine Selbstinszenierung.
Dieser schwebende, fast traumartige Erzählstil passt überraschend gut zu einer Frau, die sich ihr Leben lang ein Bild von sich selbst zurechtrücken wollte.
Spannend ist, wie der Film ohne großes Moralisieren deutlich macht, dass Riefenstahl weder so ahnungslos noch so unpolitisch war, wie sie später behauptete.
Die Brüche in ihren Aussagen, die Widersprüche, die Begegnungen, die sie nach dem Krieg lieber vergessen hätte – all das wird nicht laut angeprangert, sondern einfach gezeigt.
Und gerade dadurch wirkt es stärker.
Der Film greift auch einige der Vorwürfe auf, die Riefenstahl über die Jahrzehnte gemacht wurden – und manche davon wirken für mich absurd.
So etwa die Kritik, ihr Olympia-Film von 1936 zeige zu viele idealisierte, perfekt trainierte Körper und keine behinderte Menschen.
Ein Einwand, den man genauso gut den alten Griechen oder Römern machen könnte, die ebenfalls nur Statuen makelloser Körper schufen. Und der Logik nach müsste man dann auch Rafael, Michelangelo oder Botticelli anklagen, weil sie Schönheit und Idealproportionen feierten.
Der Film macht außerdem deutlich, dass Riefenstahl wohl genau das war, was ihr nach dem Krieg in typisch deutscher Manier sogar amtlich bescheinigt wurde:
eine Mitläuferin.
Keine Widerstandskämpferin, keine Heldin, aber eben auch keine offizielle Funktionsträgerin des Regimes.
Sie trat nie in die NSDAP ein und betrieb keine offene Propaganda im Parteiauftrag – doch sie profitierte von den Strukturen, bewegte sich bereitwillig in ihrem Umfeld und arrangierte sich mit den Machtverhältnissen, solange es ihren künstlerischen Ambitionen diente.
Gerade diese Zwischenposition, dieses bequeme „Dazwischen“, macht ihr Erbe so schwierig und so unbequem.
Was ich besonders eindringlich fand:
Der Film zeigt eine Person, die so sehr an ihr eigenes Talent glaubte, dass sie alles andere ausblendete –
bis zu einem Punkt, an dem sie selbst nicht mehr zwischen Verdrängung und Lüge unterscheiden konnte.
Das macht sie nicht sympathisch, aber definitiv interessant.
Fazit:
Sehr sehenswert, intensiv, gut erzählt – und eine Dokumentation, bei der man merkt, dass sie ihr Publikum ernst nimmt.
„Riefenstahl“ ist ein klug aufgebautes, forderndes Porträt, das noch nach dem Abspann im Kopf arbeitet.

“Riefenstahl” – complex, disturbing, fascinating
⭐⭐⭐⭐
“Riefenstahl” is one of those documentaries in which, after just a few minutes, you realize:
This won’t be a cozy evening, but it will be a damn interesting one.
The film takes its time and refuses to label Leni Riefenstahl simply as a monster or a misunderstood genius. Instead, it shows her in all her contradictions – and that’s exactly what makes it so compelling.
What works particularly well is how the documentary constantly shifts between Riefenstahl’s self-presentation and historical reality.
Her voice, fragments from her diaries, the old photographs – at times, it feels like walking through her own mind, always wondering what is memory and what is pure self-staging.
This floating, almost dreamlike narrative style fits surprisingly well with a woman who spent her entire life trying to reshape her own image.
What’s especially striking is how the film, without heavy moralizing, makes it clear that Riefenstahl was neither as clueless nor as apolitical as she later claimed.
The cracks in her statements, the contradictions, the encounters she preferred to forget after the war – all of it is shown without loud accusations.
And precisely because of that, it hits harder.
The film also addresses several of the accusations that have followed Riefenstahl over the decades – and some of them seem absurd to me.
For instance, the criticism that her 1936 Olympia film portrays too many idealized, perfectly trained bodies and too few disabled people.
It’s a criticism one could just as well level at the ancient Greeks or Romans, who also sculpted only flawless bodies.
And by that logic, one would have to accuse Raphael, Michelangelo, or Botticelli as well, since they celebrated beauty and ideal proportions.
The film also makes it clear that Riefenstahl was very likely exactly what post-war authorities officially classified her as: a Mitläuferin, a follower.
Not a resistance fighter, not a hero, but also not an official functionary of the regime.
She never joined the Nazi Party and never engaged in open propaganda on its behalf – yet she benefited from the system, moved comfortably within it, and adapted to the power structures as long as they served her artistic ambitions.
It is precisely this in-between position, this convenient “middle ground,” that makes her legacy so complicated and uncomfortable.
What I found especially compelling is this:
The film portrays a person who believed so deeply in her own talent that she blocked out everything else –
to the point where she could no longer distinguish between repression and outright lies.
It doesn’t make her sympathetic, but it certainly makes her interesting.
Conclusion:
Highly worth watching – intense, well-told, and a documentary that clearly takes its audience seriously.
“Riefenstahl” is a thoughtfully constructed, demanding portrait that lingers long after the credits roll.

Title: Steve
Comment:
"I really get it, and I just want to say to him, 'There’s so much, and it’s a lot, but hold tight, because you won’t always feel like this.'"
Doing a fair bit of teaching myself, I have always held a respect for the profession. I believe everyone should. You're underappreciated and underpaid. In today's world, you're blamed for most of society's issues. It's beyond draining and not everyone understands it until you've done it.
It's not just about the transfer of knowledge, but building relationships and letting kids know that they are not disposable. They matter to an adult who will not give up on them. This is what Steve does so well and it resonated deeply with me.
Steve and his small staff are dealing with teenage boys that society has completely given up on. Their behaviors are beyond abhorrent to most people, but to Steve, he sees something more. Cillian Murphy reminds me why he deserves an Oscar for everything that he's in. I adore how he approaches Steve as someone who is genuinely good, but also has issues of his own.
His philosophy is that the curriculum is the teacher-student relationship. Steve knows that having that consistency of showing up every day, setting boundaries without shaming them, noticing their strengths, and celebrating small wins teaches more than any worksheet ever could.
We see the progression of each boy acting out, sometimes by fighting and sometimes by sexual abuse. The film team that comes in sheds light on both sides of heralding something like this. On the one hand, it is incredibly noble and an immense undertaking. On the other hand, many view it as a waste of time and money on people who won't get better anyway.
Steve and the rest of his staff know however that when you look at behavior as communication instead of defiance, you can respond from curiosity instead of punishment. It may be a little jarring at first, but the staff members speak in almost the same manner as the teenagers do.
Tracey Ullman needs to be in more things. I love her. I feel like she is Steve's compass, always trying to guide him in a better direction. Watching the confrontations and the breakdowns of the boys got to me. Jay Lycurgo gives an outstanding performance as Shy as do each of the boys, embodying all of these faults in such a compelling way. The editing and look of the film is great.
There is one scene in particular where the camera is flying between the boys on the field and the staff in the conference room that caught me off-guard. I just wasn't expecting that. When working with teenagers like this, compassion is tested. When Shy begins to transfer his feelings to Steve, I could see the hurt in Cillian.
It's not supposed to be personal, though it can feel that way. But again, when you don't have the support systems in place and very little opportunity to rest and reflect, the job can kill you. Spiritually. Emotionally. And, unfortunately sometimes, physically.
Steve, to me, is a triumph of a film and a solid reminder of all of the work that teachers do. They refuse to accept labels for kids and can disrupt a negative trajectory. The final scene, when we're listening to Steve's tapes about the kids, is heartbreaking. He sees the child behind the behavior and understands that these are human beings who simply haven't had enough support.
Put me on the petition to award Cillian another Oscar.

Title: Blood for Dracula
Comment:
Obviously I’m not making the claim that this trashy, sleazy, ridiculous, crazy, excessive, joyful Dracula film is the best Dracula film of all time. That can be debated. I’m just saying it’s my favourite. How am I expected to resist a film with a sickly-frail Count, ‘wirgins’ and ‘hooers’ talk, communist farmhand and often shirtless Joe Dallesandro, blood vomit, limb hacking, tonal incongruity, sibling incest, unconvincing line delivery, mockable misogyny, and relentless unnecessary nudity?
Udo Kier’s passing is not my favourite reason for a rewatch, but when I heard the news, I just wanted to spend some time with him. The opening scene of him taking Dracula’s whited-out-level-of-pale-dead-face and applying make-up and hair-paint to it just to give him some colour, his big blue eyes staring at nothing, has always given this film an emotional heft it didn’t need, and it made me adore his presence, which cycles easily through camp and drama and horror pretty much in every scene he’s in in this.
He had a touch of the unicorn about him; a kind of magnificent otherworldliness he brought to everything I’ve seen him in so far. And with a filmography of over two hundred films, it’s cool that there’s the potential for me to get to discover and rediscover him for a long while yet.
RIP Udo Kier.

Title: Eternity
Comment:
This may be more my problem than the movie’s but: The rules of this afterlife baffled me and distracted me to me to the point where it took me a while to tune them out and concentrate on the characters. According to Eternity, when you die you need to commit yourself to one place and only one place for the rest of time, and once you choose that one place you never get to go anywhere else. Okay. But how do you define a single place? How big is one place? If I pick Walt Disney World, do I spend all of eternity in Magic Kingdom? Or can I go to Epcot too?
The notion of a woman forced to choose between her first and seconds husband as her partner in the afterlife is a really interesting one, and the less Eternity focuses on its arbitrary rules and explores that emotional dilemma, the better it gets. But, yeah, the whole one eternity forever thing is so arbitrary and so clearly inspired by a need to turn a thought experiment into a story with stakes and a ticking clock. Otherwise, the wife could just take her time deciding who to be with. Or maybe just decide to be with them both! It is heaven, after all.

Title: District 9
Comment:
"When dealing with aliens, try to be polite, but firm. And always remember that a smile is cheaper than a bullet"
Buenísima película, una cinta infravalorada.
"District 9" fue una grata sorpresa, una cinta sobre alienígenas con un mensaje y una crítica más que claras que en ningún momento me vi venir, una joya de la ciencia ficción que merece mucho más reconocimiento.
Sinopsis: Hace treinta años, los extraterrestres llegaron a la Tierra en busca de un refugio ante la muerte de su planeta. Separados de los humanos en un área de Sudáfrica llamada Distrito 9, los extraterrestres son manejados por Multi-National United, la cual no está preocupada por el bienestar de los alienígenas, pero hará cualquier cosa para dominar su tecnología avanzada. Cuando un agente contrae un virus que empieza a alterar su ADN, sólo hay un lugar en donde se puede esconder: Distrito 9.
La historia es buenísima, mucho mejor de lo que esperaba. Lo mejor que hice fue verla sabiendo sólo que iba sobre alienígenas, sin esperarme sobre todo lo que iba a hablar, tratando cosas como el apartheid de una manera espectacular y muy original, es algo que no vi en ningún otro lado y acá me parece que está ejecutado a la perfección, con un tono de ciencia ficción de por medio que le da un toque único. Además, también es original en el hecho de que por momentos sea un falso documental, viendo diversas entrevistas a personas conocidas del protagonista, opinando sobre lo sucedido y cada vez comprendiendo más lo que están diciendo. Otra cosa en la que acierta es en las escenas de acción y en general toda la ambientación que tiene, sobretodo por contar con un presupuesto relativamente corto y haciendo un brillante uso del mismo. Lo único que puedo criticarle son algunas conveniencias que tiene y que tarda un poquito en arrancar e ir a lo bueno, creo que los primeros 20/30 minutos son un poco lentos, pero no aburre para nada.
Los personajes me gustaron, en general son buenos pero me faltó un poco más. Wikus es el mejor personaje que se nos presenta, un tipo con un desarrollo fantástico donde podemos ver una gran evolución en él, haciendo que vayamos empatizando más con él a medida que avanza la historia. También es destacable la relación que entabla con Christopher, que si bien la noté algo conveniente porque en todo momento se cruzan, me parece que tiene un buen desarrollo y encima éste alienígena también resulta un gran personaje. Sin embargo, sacando a ellos dos no me parece que haya otro personaje tan bueno, aunque me gustó el hecho de que todos los humanos los presentan como los malos y terminemos empatizando mucho más con los alienígenas, siendo clave en el mensaje y la crítica que quiere hacer la historia.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente el trabajo de Neill Blomkamp en guion y dirección, nunca había visto una película suya y me sorprende la no tan buena calificación que tienen las demás teniendo en cuenta el excelente trabajo que hace acá, más para ser su primera película, inmejorable debut. También hay que destacar el trabajo en los efectos ya que para tener un presupuesto tan corto se ve realmente bien, si puede ser que no haya envejecido a la perfección, pero para la época no está nada mal. The Big Noirvember 2025
Prompt 30: Any film noir on your watchlist
This film is from Argentina. The Spanish speaking noirs are some of my favorites. They have a lot more darkness & drama/scandal than their Hollywood counterparts, & this one was no exception.
Alfredo Gasper (played magnificently by Carlos Cores), is not a good person. He wallows in self pity, & blames his circumstances for his dissatisfaction. It was interesting to me how his boss/colleague called him out on it. In most noirs it’s just a given that people are going to behave badly & they don’t get questioned (except by the cops). That’s why when Alfredo later starts to have a conscience, I thought… I’m not sure he would respond in this way? But then, from how he looked at his sister it was obvious he cared about her, so it made sense when she connected with Jarvis, that Alfredo would start to care about the murder.
I half guessed how this would end when the seeds fell in the ground, but I didn’t forsee all that would actually be happening! Guilt & avarice always destroy, as is proven over again in film narratives. They never satisfy as core motivators.
I loved the sets, the dream sequence, the score, the locations, & the clothes! Really well done! The restoration I saw was washed out, I’m assuming because of the degraded quality of the original? Surely when the film was first released, the cinematography looked amazing.

Title: Hamnet
Comment:
Adapted from Maggie O’Farrell’s 2020 novel of the same name, “Hamnet” is an emotionally pulverizing drama that imagines how the death of William Shakespeare and Anne (or Agnes) Hathaway’s only son might have inspired the creation of his greatest tragedy; think of it as “Shakespeare in Agony.” And yet the violent beauty of this film, which rips your soul out of your chest so completely that its seismic grief almost feels like falling in love or becoming a parent, is that it’s as much about the experience of having a child as it is about the experience of losing one.
More to the point, “Hamnet” is a wrenching story about how those two experiences — so unalike in dignity — might ultimately be catalyzed by the same process of emotional transfiguration. In the first, your heart is placed into someone else’s body. In the second, that body is subsumed into the world. To create anything, be it a person or a play, is to give a piece of yourself a life of its own; a life that you will never again be able to control or keep safe. It’s to risk the infinite potential of an offering over the unborn reality of an idea, and to accept how even something that looks just like you can grow to assume unimaginable shapes. The author dies so that their work can be reborn anew forever.
In that light, one of the great strengths of O’Farrell’s novel is how the lightly historical context it invents around “Hamlet” refuses to align with the play’s general plot and most obvious themes, and Chloé Zhao’s film — which she co-wrote with the author — respects how that 2+2=5 approach begs for a different kind of equation. Unlike “Shakespeare in Love” (a masterpiece), “Solo: A Star Wars Story” (not so much), or any other examples of modern day origin stories, “Hamnet” doesn’t reverse engineer its drama from the stuff of its ultra-familiar source material. Sure, there’s a brief aside in which Will (Paul Mescal) jots down the balcony scene from “Romeo and Juliet” after his first kiss with Agnes (Jessie Buckley), and a later moment where their three children roleplay as the witches from “Macbeth” on some gray English morning, but never does this movie rely on the lizard-brain thrill of recognition in order to stand on the shoulders of giants.
On the contrary, “Hamnet” derives its simple but overwhelming power from the disconnect between intention and response; it’s a film that plants its roots in the liminal space between them, and keenly observes how the same kind of no man’s land can form between a husband and a wife just as easily as it does between an artist and their work. By that measure, it would be hard to imagine a more fitting tribute to Shakespeare’s most widely interpreted play.

Title: Eddington
Comment:
2020 doesn’t even feel like a real year. I vividly remember getting groceries delivered to our house and then vigorously wiping them all down with disinfectant wipes. That and then also checking the Covid stat levels every other day.
Ari Aster remembers Covid a little differently.
How the pandemic is portrayed in this movie is pretty accurate, and how everyone argues over wearing or not wearing masks. But more importantly, the political takes in this and commentary on how the media cherry picks moments that could be out of context. I think Ari Aster was bold to bring recent political events instead of his usual traumatizing “Toni Collette climbing up the walls” scenes, just because you either love or hate the approach. I don’t really talk about politics in my reviews, but everyone can agree that bipartisanship isn’t really a big thing nowadays. So people are either gonna side with what Ari Aster decided to put in the film, or they’re gonna think it’s a gross misunderstanding of how the actual year played out. I personally overlooked the accuracy of the events and chose to focus on the content and how they were displayed.
Despite this being Ari Aster’s only non-horror movie, this was intense. There were still traumatizing scenes because there’s no way he could have a completely normal 150 minute movie and call it a day. The camerawork in particular was really fuckin cool, and especially at the end I felt as discombobulated as Joaquin Phoenix was. Transitions between scenes felt seamless. There isn’t an Ari Aster movie which has bad cinematography, to be honest.
I think Ari should probably stick to horror though, that’s where his expertise shines through. I enjoyed Eddington and it certainly has a similar feel to the rest of his movies, it just feels way less memorable than the other three that have happened, and I think it’s partly due to the inclusion of a more political standpoint rather than my personal interest: horror. Of course it’s hard to beat movies like Hereditary and Midsommar, so easier said than done.
I’ll probably end my review here because by now I’ve already said the name “Ari Aster” 50 times. I’m looking forward to another horror movie because I’m running out of good horror movies to watch and I feel like I need my man to save me.

Things Addie and I have in common:
1) Getting mistaken for boys multiple times when we were kids
2) Having lost our mothers
3) Scamming other people as kids (though I only traded fake Pokémon cards with my American neighbours for original ones — I’m sorry)
Things we don’t have in common:
1) I don’t smoke, she’s smoking at the age of 9.
Anyway, this was such a sweet film about a little girl (Addie) who has just lost her mom and goes on a road trip with a man (Moses), who ought to bring her to her aunt and may or may not be her father. In the end, it really doesn’t matter if he is, because they end up forming a genuine connection over the runtime of the film. Since I love found family and road movies, this was really the perfect film for me. 
The black-and-white cinematography seems simple at first glance but adds to the charm of the film by delivering beautiful images and shot compositions. That said, the dialogue is cleverly written and the chemistry between the leads feels genuine — which is probably because the actors are father and daughter in real life (which makes it even sweeter btw). 
The ending is so heartwarming and cute too, and underlines the tone of the entire film, which is always genuine and real but never feels over the top. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed every single thing about Paper Moon because it just has a unique vibe to it that I can’t quite describe.
P.S. Tatum O’Neal absolutely deserved that Oscar as the youngest winner ever!!!

Title: Knives Out
Comment:
"The family is truly desperate. and when people get desperate, the knives come out"
Murder mysteries inherently need tight plots, because part of the joy in watching them comes from finding out how all the pieces connect. still, writer/director rian johnson takes that need to another level, creating a mystery within a mystery. consequently, you hang on every line of dialogue, savor every shot, and wait breathlessly to see where things will go next. the film is pure entertainment from start to finish. noed mystery author harlan thrombey is found dead in his spacious mansion, his throat slit. private investigator benoit blanc is on the scene to figure out who did it. the suspects are numerous. was it his businesswoman daughter linda, her unfaithful husband richard or their obnoxious, entitled son ransom, was it his son/publisher walt, his gold-digging daughter-in-law joni, or his granddaughter meg? or could it possibly have been his in-home nurse marta?
Knives out does something interesting and unexpected. a little less than an hour in, it tells you what happened. with that knowledge, it seems like there's nowhere else for the story to go. then a second, more subtle mystery begins unfurling. In the final twenty minutes, the details of that mystery are revealed, and the ingeniousness of what johnson has crafted is immensely satisfying, knives out does a spectacular job of finding the right house to place a majority of the film, overflowing with small hallways, secret windows and book-filled studies. on top of that, the costume of blanc is spot-on. his suave suits of gray are as fitting to the noir detective as is thyme and butter to a nice steak, if they didn’t entirely commit to blanc as a character, including his wardrobe, he would seem a bit out of place and that slight distraction can be all the difference of whether or not he is believable as a piece in this game of modern clue. the lighting proves to set up environments of warmth and welcoming, but also rigidness and ice-cold temperatures. with the constant changes of perspectives in this film, the lighting needs to be as fluid as possible. otherwise, the equilibrium of the setting can be thrown off, and i applaud the fact that the lighting design used the playground of a house and all of its windows to showcase other aspects of this film. in terms of the cinematography, the angles are just as shifty as the lights, in the best way possible. there is this moment when walt, played by michael shannon, gives quite the monologue and the DP gave us an upward shot from the floor immediately putting shannon on a more powerful platform than he already sits; a perfect example of empowering characters through shot-selection; bravo.
The gothic mansion is filled with books and lavish trinkets. johnson gives us a fuller picture of the estate by adding quick shots of various props and knickknacks between scenes. there is little use of modernized technology. our detective relies on his trusty magnifying glass, while the police use their phones for pictures. there are no modern murder weapons or even a gun, instead, a simple knife is the weapon of choice throughout the story. the act of a modern-day mystery so rooted in past visual aesthetics of the genre creates an element of postmodernism that’s new to whodunits. a love of whodunits and murder mysteries are ingrained into the characters, the script, and the set. fran loves the hallmark movie deadly by surprise and talks about it often. marta’s mother is seen watching the show murder she wrote. harlan is a well-known murder mystery author. trooper wagner is a huge fan of harlan’s books. nearly all the characters have a love of the genre. the film, a murder mystery itself, nearly bursts with references and indications towards other works, creating a meta-ness to it as a film that feels both deeply rooted in the genre and acutely self-aware of itself as a genre film. this inherent awareness of the genre it exists within is a postmodern self-reflexivity that sets the film apart from other whodunits.
Knives out makes frequent references to the world of today, as it tries to bridge the gap between the generations. it tells how fast the world is changing when it comes to values, and what’s awaiting for future generations is that those who don’t feel entitled to wealth by privilege will have a better chance than ever of success in america’s future. caught in this change is the dysfunctional family, who all believe it’s their birthright to be rich and have entitlement. the film’s twist is in how brilliantly it moves from a murder-mystery to an examination of the current mores in society, even if its richly drawn character driven story might stumble somewhat in the second act with too much good dialogue. but it recovers fully in the third act to make this original whodunit a most memorable and enjoyable one!!
The light, cold and hard, pierces the bay window, upstairs, the heavy door. harlan thrombey is gone, the family arrives, shuffling in their expensive coats, a parade of entitlement, a new shape enters the frame: benoit blanc, he speaks of the doughnut. a perfect, beautiful ring, but what of the center? that empty space, that crucial missing piece. this case, he declares, is a doughnut with a hole cut clean out of the middle, he sits, observing the series of lies, the way the siblings avoid eye contact, and then there is marta, she becomes an accomplice to blanc, her honesty guiding his questions, blanc orchestrates the final confrontation in the very room where the book was closed, the family is left in ruins, she looks down at the shocked, abandoned faces of the thrombeys, the rightful owner looking down upon the undeserving, and the circle is complete.

Title: Zombieland
Comment:
A really good horror-comedy.
My favorite genre of movie is probably horror, second being comedies. So naturally, horror-comedy tends to be my favorite subgenres of both.
When done right, they're great. When done wrong, they are really, really bad.
This one is pretty well done.
Jesse Eisenberg can get on my nerves. Never really been a fan, just kind of annoying to me. Always saw him as a cheap Michael Cera rip off.
That said...I don't mind him to much in this movie. He's pretty annoying yes, but about as much as he is to Woody, which is the point I feel they're trying to get across.
I do love his list of rules, and when the zombies do finally rise, I will definitely keep his list on my mind. That is, if I survive the first few days.
I feel like a lot of people have a chance if they get past those first few days. A lot of deaths will just occur by not knowing your wife or husband, or kids, have been bit...and then you go to sleep to suddenly be awoken by your skin beaing torn off 🤷
I like that they actually refer to them as zombies in this movie. I mean, zombieland, duh...but the Z word isn't usually mentioned a lot in movies and shows about them.
I also like that the zombies are fast in this movie. Fast zombies are just scarier. When they're all super slow and dumb, it just kind of feels too easy to survive them. You could just power walk half the time.
A big downside for me about this movie is the sisters. Now, I realize that is literally half the movie. But man do they annoy me, and I would much rather have the movie just be about Tallahassee and Columbus.

Title: Wicked: For Good
Comment:
People who know the stage play knew the headwinds this was facing: All but one of the musical’s good numbers happen in the first act, and the second act is plotty, talky, bleak, and largely humorless. So the question becomes, how were they going to overcome the relatively weaker source material and match the quality of last year’s hit blockbuster?
I’m sorry to report that they didn’t. It’s the same cast, same costumes, same sets, same production design, and same lackluster CGI as Part 1, so no help there. I thought they might add in a big ensemble song-and-dance number or two as enjoyable as the ones in the first one, but sadly no. Instead they drag out the runtime of this one with unnecessary flashbacks to Glinda’s childhood, CGI action scenes, and a couple of bland original songs, one each for Erivo and Grande.
The staging of “No Good Deed” was eye-catching and fun. And there were a couple of brief moments where John Powell was able to cut loose and deliver some of his characteristically great scoring. But overall the whole 137 minutes (! Versus 60 minutes for the same material in the Broadway show) felt extremely slow-moving and plodding.
I’m still a fan of the stage musical. Here’s hoping that somewhere down the line someone does a tight 150-minute movie adaptation of the whole thing.

Title: Band of Brothers
Comment:
There is not a day that goes by where I don't think of the men I served with, who never got to enjoy the world without war.
_________________________

I never imagined I would willingly sit through a ten-episode war drama about WWII, yet here I am, left with a hollow ache in my chest. War, as an idea, has never made sense to me, and I doubt it ever will. World leaders sit comfortably on their fat arses in safety while sending the men of their nations to abandon their families and loved ones, ordering them to kill other young men who were given the same orders.
I understand the instinct to protect one’s country, but why do we, as human beings, carry such a barbaric impulse within us? They recruited boys as young as 17.... SEVENTEEN!!!! They hadn’t lived, hadn’t loved, hadn’t experienced a single moment of true liberation beyond school, and yet they were bound straight to the shackles of war.
I rarely give war films or series a perfect score, largely because so many of them reek of propaganda. But this one shows everything; the length, the exhaustion, the erosion of spirit. Some soldiers endured the full six years. Their marriages crumbled, their beliefs fractured, and after witnessing their comrades lying limbless in the snow of Bastogne, they were left to question whether any cause could possibly justify such suffering.
It takes only one nefarious leader to drag the entire world into a downward spiral. And the frightening thing is that leaders like that still exist today... we know who they are
And finally, the cast is unbelievable! Almost surreal when you consider how early some of them were in their careers: Michael Fassbender, David Schwimmer, Tom Hardy, James McAvoy, Colin Hanks, Simon Pegg, Andrew Scott, Scott Grimes, Stephen Graham, and the lead, Damian Lewis. Truly astonishing.

Title: Eternity
Comment:
"Well a lot has happened in a week. You died. I died. I've just been reunited with both of my dead husbands, and I have to pick where to spend eternity."
Is there a Middle Earth eternity? Because I would go there without a second thought. And no man ( Miles Teller and Callum Turner are worth considering) would be able to stop me.
But the hardest decisions I’ve ever had to make in life are things like “pizza or hamburger?” and I still take three business hours to decide. Meanwhile, women like Joan are making soul-shattering choices that will last for generations. I'm sure I'd have more fun if I weren't so adept at extracting life-altering messages from even the most ridiculous movies. But if Callum Turner ever looked at me the way he looks at her, I would absolutely surrender. Joan, you are the strongest woman I have ever known. Let him lock me into the eternity he desires. I'm just a weak, very weak woman, and I accept that completely.
But thirst aside, this film has such a gorgeous atmosphere. It gave me that soft, dreamy feeling of a 90s romantic drama you accidentally find and end up rewatching for the rest of your life. I may have said it a thousand times, but I prefer romantic movies that are full of clichés but really full of "feeling" rather than movies that are artificial for the sake of being "freaky" and extreme. And it was a lot of fun to watch two men like Miles Teller and Callum Turner grind for a woman. But I saw the potential, I need a version where they go to a completely different eternity together.
Still, the best part of the movie is unquestionably Anna. Every scene she appeared in had me laughing to the point of tears. She brings this sparkling, chaotic charm that just lifts the entire film. And I’d choose an eternity with her as my bestie over almost any man… except Callum Turner, because I'm unfortunately a terrible person with no self-control and zero shame.
If I have one tiny complaint, it’s that the ending felt a bit rushed like they suddenly realized they only had five minutes left to wrap up centuries of emotional baggage. But overall, it’s a beautifully atmospheric, strangely comforting movie with characters I would absolutely follow into the afterlife (again: Callum Turner please call me)

Title: The Long Goodbye
Comment:
What better way to announce my safe return home to Central Florida after spending a few days in Fort Myers than viewing one of Robert Altman’s most famous movies before it leaves the Criterion Channel after Sunday? Considering the noir and neo-noir I’ve viewed in my life, it seems like a misstep on my part that I’ve never tackled this until earlier in the day. Of course, I’ve viewed some other Philip Marlowe pictures before, but never one set in the 70’s.
Right away, I laughed that the movie opens w/ Marlowe’s forced journey to a 24-hour store to purchase cat food for his constantly-meowing feline. It reminded me of a previous journey to Kansas (this one with my father and late mother) when she helped out sis and fed one of the two cats she had at the time. It wasn’t 3 AM but feeding time was late; the kitty constantly meowed as mom prepared the food, much to my mom’s consternation! No, mom did not smoke constantly like Marlowe did here, nor did she act laconic like Elliott Gould’s portrayal of a man who deliberately felt out of lockstep with his surroundings… a 40’s or 50’s detective who lives right by a bunch of attractive young women who do yoga and love being topless.
Our private eye associates w/ a cad named Terry Lennox; much to his misfortune, Lennox is missing & accused of murdering his wife. The film had some interesting casting; Lennox was played by Jim Bouton… yes, the former baseball player who caused controversy by writing a 1969 book called Ball Four, where people at the time were shocked that pro sports players were human and thus did drugs, drank, and were womanizers. What innocent times back then. Anyhow…
It’s not my favorite movie involving the character nor my personal favorite from Altman-that said, The Long Goodbye was still a very good time. In fact, you might say that it was OK with me… the film was a satirical look at the life of a private eye involved in a convoluted case with various shady characters, some of them real reprobates. Marlowe was a jerk, albeit a funny jerk. It was a nice cast with several other recognizable faces… yes I did know that Arnold Schwarzenegger appeared in a scene as a hood, but not that an actor famous at the time had an uncredited part. I wasn’t familiar with Nina van Pallandt but that Danish actress did a swell job.
The biggest assets the film had came from a trio of legends: Gould’s performance as the lead, the jazzy score from John Williams, and the cinematography from Vilmos Zsigmond. The film was downbeat, although given the decade and its neo-noir style, this should not have been a surprise. I’m personally happy that in 2025, several famous 70’s pictures were finally partaken in by me.

It’s easy to imagine that the grass is greener somewhere else. I used to believe that too until life taught me that it’s not the place that makes things better, but the care you give to the life you’re trying to build. Moving to Japan gave me the chance to start over and build the life that a lot of my friends in the Philippines would love to have. a lot of them have asked me about living there, “kumusta diyan? ang swerte mo.” Some days, I agree with them. I am lucky to live in a quiet neighborhood, and I am lucky to have an ocean hundred meters from my front door. I am also lucky to live in a country where the streets are clean and safe, where I am able to access healthcare that works for me, and where I can see how my taxes are used to provide me with things I use every day. I have been fortunate enough to live in a place where I don't have to live in chaos and constant noise, lucky not to be surrounded by people with a 5 IQ. I live in Japan, where I can find peace, comfort, and order, things that I do not take for granted.
Even with all that Japan provides, there are moments when I am reminded of the Philippines and how different it is. I long for the noise and bustling streets of my hometown, I yearn for the sounds of laughter and commotion coming from a small sari-sari store. I crave the sense of being able to connect with people and know they will truly care for me, regardless of the hardships we face, and how they can make you feel less alone during these times. There is an indescribable warmth that exists in the Philippines that no amount of stability or comfort can replace.
Having lived in two extremely different cultures, I learned that every place we value or idolize tends to come with an equal and opposite shadow and that every place we tend to dismiss or judge has a lesser known equally beautiful side. Japan is often viewed as a place like Disneyland. Everything people talk about Japan is true, that the konbini food will make your day, the trains run on time, and everything is orderly and zen-like. However, there is also a deep sense of loneliness in Japan. People mostly do not engage or interact with other people. Japan has very high statistics of people who die alone. It is a silent epidemic of sorts that is hidden under the facade of Japanese culture of being very efficient. In contrast, when many people think of the Philippines they see it as a dirty, chaotic, messy, and a “third world” country. Yes, this may be very true about what is occurring within the Philippines, but the less visible side is that the people in the Philippines live their lives with a deep compassion for others. They seem to have an innate desire to help others, to stay with them, and to connect with them. In the Philippines, it’s rare for someone to die alone; family and even the community will care for you until your last breath. Also, Filipinos notice when someone feels lonely or left out. Even strangers will bring you back into the world with a simple, “kain tayo.”
That's why this film hit me personally. It showcased two places, equal parts of the home I come from and the home I have now, in the way they compare the two extremes of experiences... the isolation, calmness of Japan, and chaotic, warm, and emotional feelings through the people in the streets of Manila.
The film follows a traditional Japanese man late in life coming to terms with dying alone, a fate that is much too common for many japanese today. his journey to the Philippines becomes more than just a physical escape for him, it is a journey to find happiness and connections. The contrast between the two countries acts as a living part of this man's story. In Japan, his loneliness is silent. In PH, loneliness doesn’t disappear, but it’s drowned by motion, noise, community—people who weave themselves into your day whether you ask them to or not.
The way that the movie explores cultural conflict was very subtly done. The film avoids idealizing either country, instead it shows how the contrast between Japan’s quiet solitude and the Philippines chaotic warmth shapes the way people carry their pain, loneliness and pursue connection. The cinematograhpy of these two different environments captures the contrast perfectly, and I found myself drawn to the quiet, telling details seen through the eyes of a man navigating a country so foreign to him, yet so familiar and alive for those who call it home.
While the movie has its flaws, including a rushed conclusion and underdeveloped character dynamics, the heart and sincerity of the film remain intact, and I found myself charmed by it, and I related it to my own experiences, while also appreciating the subtle nature with which the movie showed how people connect with each other in different cultures.
This film really left an impression on me, and I feel its meaning will continue to grow as I spend more time away from my homeland. It sparked reflections and opened up realizations I hadn’t expected. In a way, it has become a meaningful addition to films like Past Lives and Didi, which helped me understand that asking someone if they’ve eaten isn’t just a childish form of affection “puppy love,” as my ex once tried to make me believe.

Title: Two Mules for Sister Sara
Comment:
An opportunistic mercenary (Clint Eastwood) comes across a nun (Shirley MacLaine) being assaulted out in the desert. He promptly saves her, but then finds he now has to babysit. And, even though he’s attracted to her, he finds her incredibly annoying. Soon, they team up to help a group of Mexicans fight off French invaders.
This is a very offbeat and somewhat unusual western. It’s more of a romantic comedy, which is definitely something we don’t see too much from Eastwood.
Eastwood and Shirley MacLaine have good chemistry together. It’s debatable whether they got along behind the scenes because neither has commented much on working together. 
This film can’t escape Sergio Leone, which can be a mistake because there truly can only be one. The very offbeat score by Ennio Morricone (it uses a mule braying as part of the melody) seals the deal.
Long time Eastwood collaborator and mentor Don Siegel is in the director’s chair. As always, he shoots a solid and efficient film, though he lacks a particular style.
Reccomended—this is a lot of fun.

Dasies has been described as dadaistic. Dada is when you dada all logic to criticize society. Is it so illogical? Butterfly collecting is just a Czech metaphor for sex. What else? Title: Being John Malkovich
Comment: Being John Malkovich is Charlie Kaufman's big introductory statement, establishing his creative brand through bold, original concepts. When you tell me the premise is about people occupying the mind of real-life actor John Malkovich, I'm hooked. I noticed that Charlie Kaufman's most successful partnerships tend to be with prolific music video directors. Spike Jonze does an excellent job of grounding Kaufman's high concepts and making them accessible to audiences. What makes Being John Malkovich so compelling is how Kaufman embraces absurdity and includes whatever crazy ideas he can think of. What would happen if John Malkovich occupied his own mind? How does role-playing as Malkovich affect one's relationship? Kaufman goes for it. Tying the entire film together is a sense of melancholy centered around unfulfilling relationships and the desire to be someone else.

Title: Nuremberg
Comment:
I will admit, I'm a bit of a sucker for a war film and especially one where I know little about the intricacies of the subject matter. And while "Nuremberg" does admittedly have some issues for me here and there, I thought this was pretty damn good really, certainly a more compelling, and informative experience overall than I expected going in.
It will probably come as no surprise that the main draw here is the trial itself. It's as informative, haunting and riveting as you'd expect considering what this is, with a script that shines and great performances. Crowe is particularly great as Hermann Goring in what may be quietly, one of his better roles... at least in a while anyway and that is where the majority of my rating here lies. So It's just a shame that it takes - at least in my opinion - a little too long to get to the trial. It decides to focus more on being a character study of Hermann Goring and his psychiatrist, which on paper - or execution actually - is absolutely not a bad thing, I just didn't think those scenes were as compelling or as meaningful as I'd want them to be. Plus, the few really weird comedy moments didn't help.
Importantly though, where this needs to shine it definitely does and if this is your type of thing, I don't think you'll be disappointed.

Title: They Call Him OG
Comment:
it’s a copy of a copy of a copy of a copy, nothing exists here except buildup shots and action scenes stitched together. being a pure no-brainer telugu mass masala built entirely as fan service for pawan kalyan, there’s no point digging into the story or screenplay.
the film shifts from a boat, to a port, to a police station, to a hospital, to a corn farm, in the first half itself, as if every possible cliched location had to be used once. and bits are lifted from kgf, salaar, and even daaku maharaj. characters exist either to hype the hero, oppose him, die for him, or be killed by him.
most scenes are edited like a trailer and every scene of pawan kalyan is treated like a hero introduction, silhouettes, slow-motion walks, cut like fan-made mashup videos. and it’s admittedly enjoyable at times because thaman’s music powers every frame like an adrenaline engine.
fans might disagree, but pawan kalyan himself has no aura here, his expressions land unintentionally funny, and the swag moments feel forced for me. loved his title card though. 
tbh acting across the board is overdone. shriya reddy’s character feels like an extension of her salaar role. prakash raj plays the same character he has played countless times. sudev nair gets a role similar to venky in kingdom, which he performs well. emraan at least brings some aura the film badly needs.
pam’s casting somehow solves the usual 'why doesn’t the heroine get more screen time?' question, since she can neither dance nor act convincingly, which also saved us from what could’ve been a forced dance number.
the only hope i had was the action scenes, but they decline in quality from the start and keep getting worse, and the aikido federation guy scene is especially ridiculous. instead of giving even one decent aikido move, it turns into a typical fight, made even funnier by pawan’s wannabe-swag choreography. ig no one in this film has seen aikido even on youtube.
the writing gets worse, which is obvious, shriya reddy somehow knows pam was killed and uses it to build up the hero, without any explanation. gambeera mysteriously knows omi’s explosion plan. the film tries to create impact by intercutting two parallel scenes, but ends up creating plot holes instead. and arjun’s subplot is completely pointless, an unnecessary addition that derails the movie every time it appears.
whenever a non-telugu character speaks, a telugu voice-over instantly replaces their voice, as if the film doesn’t trust the audience to read subtitles. and the funniest part: in the final scene, pawan kalyan gives a two-minute japanese speech, which may or may not even be japanese. 
the sequel gimmick is common now, but this film goes a step further by force-building a universe or a sequel that might not even happen, all just to cover up the limitations of the movie they’re actually making.
honestly, only the music works in this film, so you’re better off skipping the movie and just vibing to the album on spotify. thaman carried the whole thing on his shoulders.

Title: Bugonia
Comment:
🇺🇸 in english: Bugonia is a strange film in both the best and worst ways. It has the vibe of something bold and chaotic, a movie that feels like it’s about to explode into something wild at any second — but that second takes way too long to arrive. And that’s where my main issue lies: it gets stuck in its own concept. Lanthimos builds this delicious atmosphere of paranoia, full of contradictions and tension, but spends a huge chunk of the runtime just circling the mood without truly pushing forward. I didn’t need speed, but I needed purpose.
Jesse Plemons’ Teddy is the one holding everything together. It’s impressive how he plays this obsessive paranoid without slipping into cheap caricature. There’s a deep desperation in him, a genuine fear, an almost religious devotion to his own delusions — and that makes everything more disturbing, more human, more tragic. It’s the kind of performance that turns a ridiculous conspiracy theory into something so fully lived-in that you almost, against your will, start believing alongside him.
On the other side, Emma Stone once again proves she’s operating on another level entirely. Her portrayal of the kidnapped CEO is impossible to pin down: powerful and broken, calm and terrified, cold and emotional at the same time. Even tied up, wounded, shaved, thrown into bizarre situations, she dominates the frame with a hypnotic presence. She gives the character nuances the script doesn’t always offer — she builds layers on her own. She’s the one stopping the film from collapsing into its own artificiality.
And that’s the frustrating part: you’ve got two massive performances at the center, an aesthetic that blends sci-fi with dark comedy, strong visual ideas… but the film keeps spinning in the same gear for too long. Lanthimos seems enamored with the setup, but forgets the punch.
When the third act finally hits, then things take off. The movie fully embraces its insanity — the alien mythology, the cosmic reveal, the twisted fable about manipulation, paranoia, and destruction. Suddenly, everything that felt scattered finally clicks, as if we’re watching the explosion the film had been teasing all along. And that moment is great. Surprising, visually unhinged, and carrying that cruel, absurd energy Lanthimos handles so well.
But by then, you can already feel the wasted potential. Bugonia is a good film, sometimes a very good one, but it’s missing that punch — that cathartic absurdity that should run through the whole story instead of arriving only at the end.
It’s enjoyable, curious, filled with strong moments — but it never quite becomes what it promises to be. The potential is far more powerful than the final delivery.
———————————————————
🇧🇷 em português: Bugonia é um filme estranho no pior e no melhor sentido da palavra. Tem aquela cara de projeto ousado, meio caótico, onde parece que algo grande vai acontecer a qualquer minuto — só que esse minuto demora demais pra chegar. E aí já começa pelo meu principal problema com o filme: ele patina no próprio conceito. Lanthimos cria um ambiente de paranoia deliciosa, cheio de contradições, mas passa grande parte da duração só esfregando a atmosfera na nossa cara, sem realmente avançar. Eu não precisava de pressa, mas precisava de intenção.
O Teddy de Jesse Plemons é o que mais segura a coisa toda. É impressionante como ele interpreta esse paranoico obcecado sem cair na caricatura rasa. Tem um desespero dentro dele, um medo genuíno, uma convicção quase religiosa na própria loucura — e isso deixa tudo mais incômodo, mais humano e mais trágico. É aquele tipo de atuação que transforma uma teoria conspiratória ridícula em uma crença tão sólida que a gente começa, contra a vontade, a entrar na cabeça dele.
Do outro lado, Emma Stone simplesmente confirma que está em outro estágio da carreira. Ela faz dessa CEO sequestrada uma figura impossível de decifrar: poderosa e quebrada, calma e apavorada, fria e emocional ao mesmo tempo. Mesmo amarrada, ferida, raspada, colocada em situações absurdas, ela domina o quadro com uma presença quase hipnótica. Ela entrega nuances que o roteiro às vezes nem dá — ela inventa camadas sozinha. É ela quem impede o filme de se perder no próprio artifício.
E é isso que frustra: tem duas atuações gigantes no centro, tem uma estética que mistura ficção científica com comédia sombria, tem ideias visuais fortes… mas o filme fica girando na mesma engrenagem por tempo demais. Lanthimos parece apaixonado pela preparação, mas esquece do impacto.
Quando finalmente chega o terceiro ato, aí sim a coisa deslancha. O filme assume plenamente sua loucura: a mitologia alienígena, a revelação cósmica, a lógica distorcida de uma fábula sobre manipulação, paranoia e destruição. De repente, tudo que estava disperso encontra propósito, como se estivéssemos assistindo à explosão de algo que o filme só insinuava. E esse momento é ótimo. Surpreendente, visualmente insano, com aquele toque cruel e absurdo que o Lanthimos sabe fazer tão bem.
Mas a essa altura já dá pra sentir o potencial desperdiçado. Bugonia é um filme bom, às vezes muito bom, mas que fica faltando aquele soco, aquele absurdo catártico que deveria atravessar o filme inteiro em vez de aparecer só no finzinho.
É legal, funciona, tem momentos excelentes — mas infelizmente não passa disso. A promessa é muito mais poderosa do que a entrega.
