Title: Train Dreams
Comment:
“The dead tree is as important as the living one.”
🎬 Score: 9/10
What a delightful surprise this film was, I genuinely didn’t expect to like it this much. I had a few other movies lined up to review first, but I had to bump this one to the front of the queue so I wouldn’t lose any of what I felt while watching this spectacular piece of work.
Train Dreams, directed by Clint Bentley, takes us on a contemplative, poetic journey through the memories of a quiet, arduous life at the turn of the 19th to the 20th century. This is a story about the passage of time, grief and the marks it leaves on us, the intrinsic relationship between humanity and nature, and, above all, the celebration of what it means to be, to live, and to feel.
The film raises profound reflections in a very natural way, often through excellent dialogue accompanied by contemplative silences that allow everything to sink in. One of the elements that moved me the most is the dilemma so deeply rooted in this capitalist world we live in: the conflict between being present with your family or becoming absent so your family can live well. Enslaved by this system of exploitation, we don’t work to live, we live to work. And this film’s direct, almost sacred contact with nature makes me question how we live in such a beautiful world and yet barely have the time to enjoy it. This is something that affects me personally because it’s a recurring topic in deeper conversations with my parents, about how they wish they had had the chance to work less and spend more time watching my brother and me grow up.
Now it’s time for me to gush over the majestic work of the Brazilian cinematographer Adolpho Veloso who, in my humble opinion, delivered the best cinematography of the year. With breathtaking landscapes, stunning angles, and masterful lighting, the film captures perfectly the contrast between nature’s pure beauty and the brutality that unfolds within it.
Joel Edgerton’s spectacular performance as Robert plays a major role in the film’s deep sense of immersion, especially after the events in the first half. Even though he already had a solid grip on the character, it’s in the aftermath of those moments that he truly shines.
I’m someone who leans more toward the “show, don’t tell” side of storytelling, so I’m usually a bit hesitant when it comes to narration. Although the voiceovers here were clearly meant to keep the film from becoming too silent, I do think some scenes didn’t need them, particularly the more contemplative moments tied to Robert’s mental and emotional state.
Lastly, I’ve seen some reviews saying the film introduces certain events or social themes only to “abandon” them later. I actually think that’s intentional, because what we’re seeing are Robert’s memories, and even though some of those moments marked him forever, he never tried to go deep into them. If anything, he remains somewhat invisible within them. He simply tried to keep living, giving his attention to whatever mattered most to him in each phase of his life.
That’s all for Train Dreams! This director was an unexpected discovery, and I think we can expect great work from him in the future.

Title: Lady Vengeance
Comment:
“but what shocked us the most was her beauty. glamouring tabloids compared her to olivia hussey. that fall, the polka-dot dress became the hottest fashion trend.” ୨ৎ
being compared to olivia hussey has to be one of the biggest compliments a person can receive, and somehow i’ve been blessed with it — both directly, and both through being compared to minji from newjeans, who herself is often compared to olivia.
i’ve recently begun the journey of wanting to be a real writer and owning my own book, and it has made me inclined to write more and be more genuine about it, so pardon me if this review gets a bit too long.
i understood this film from the very first watch; i thought it was brilliant, stunning, one of park chan wook’s best, and one of south korea’s finest. but i was still a newbie to cinema then to fully grasp the magnitude of this film.
revisiting it almost three years later, i still stand by everything i wrote the first time, specially that you change after watching this film. but now i think that no matter how many times you re-watch it, it will always give you a new meaning.
now with more knowledge of cinema and south korea’s culture, i finally caught some details i missed — the dog scenes tied to the insult gae-saekki, which means son of a bitch in korean, or the quiet symbolism of tofu and purification. and some other technical and artistic choices.  
lee young-ae’s casting feels even more perfect now. she has always been south korea’s pure, national goddess — placing that purity inside this violent, sorrowful narrative makes her entire presence feel even more connected to its concept. the film’s plot is harsh, but it still has some silliness, making it unique even in its own type of genre.
୨ৎ  “in france, when there’s a break in the conversation like this, they say an angel is passing over.”
the ending of lady vengeance looks beautiful — the snow, a white cake — but it’s actually the moment the film admits there’s no real purification for her. the whiteness is a performance of innocence she can’t reclaim. even after orchestrating the parents’ revenge, she’s still contaminated by the years she lost and the person she became. her daughter’s gentle hug makes it worse, not better. it shows how badly she wants to be good again and how impossible that is. she ends exactly where she began — craving redemption she can’t feel.
i truly believe that korean thrillers are like sugar or other drugs. once you taste it, you’ll for sure get addicted to it.
thank you for reading this review.

Title: Train Dreams
Comment:
🇺🇸 in english: Train Dreams is the kind of film that arrives quietly, without fanfare, without grand promises — and suddenly you realize you’re completely under its spell. It feels like an act of gentleness from cinema itself: Clint Bentley directs as someone who listens, who observes a life unfolding without hurry, allowing the audience to breathe with the images and the music, as if every frame were a small confession of beauty the world still offers when we look closely.
The cinematography is the first invitation. It doesn’t try to impress; it simply flows, softly, across open horizons, across light that touches surfaces with an almost tactile sensitivity. There’s something deeply human in the way Bentley frames silence — not as emptiness, but as presence. And the score follows this rhythm like an emotional whisper: it doesn’t guide or manipulate, it just embraces. This is a film that understands that emotion isn’t extracted — it’s revealed.
Robert could easily be a familiar archetype — the man shaped by loss and hardship, trying to find a place for himself in the world — but here he becomes something more intimate. Bentley builds him through small gestures, lingering glances, brief hesitations that say more than exposition ever could. And within that space of subtlety, his connection with Gladys emerges: unhurried, unforced, almost as if we’re discovering it at the same pace they are. Their chemistry lives in what isn’t spoken, in that territory of quiet feeling that makes the bond even more genuine.
And maybe that’s the true charm of Train Dreams: it reminds us that cinema can also be calm, “slow,” contemplative — not out of weakness, but out of a deep sense of humanity. It’s a film that refuses to rush because it knows beauty happens precisely when something is allowed to simply be. It moves you not by reaching for tears, but by acknowledging what is fragile, ordinary, real.
In the end, it’s a film you don’t just watch — you share space with it. A cinema made of breath, texture, silence, and tenderness. A rare and thoroughly pleasant surprise. And honestly, I loved every second.
———————————————————
🇧🇷 em português: Train Dreams é aquele tipo de filme que chega de mansinho, sem fazer barulho, sem prometer nada — e de repente você percebe que está completamente entregue a ele. É quase um gesto de delicadeza do próprio cinema: Clint Bentley filma como quem escuta, como quem observa uma vida se desenrolando sem pressa, deixando o espectador respirar junto com as imagens e a música, como se cada plano fosse uma pequena confissão de beleza que o mundo ainda oferece quando a gente olha com atenção.
A fotografia é o primeiro convite. Ela não tenta impressionar; ela se derrama, suave, nos horizontes abertos, na luz que toca as superfícies com uma sensibilidade quase tátil. Há algo de profundamente humano na maneira como Bentley enquadra o silêncio — não como vazio, mas como presença. A trilha sonora acompanha esse fluxo como um sussurro emocional: não guia, não manipula, apenas acolhe. É um filme que entende perfeitamente que emoção não é algo que se arranca, mas que se revela.
Robert poderia ser um arquétipo familiar — o homem marcado por perdas, pela dureza da vida, tentando encontrar algum senso de lugar no mundo — mas aqui ele se transforma em algo mais íntimo. Bentley constrói o personagem com gestos mínimos, com olhares, com pequenas hesitações que dizem muito mais do que qualquer explicação. É nesse espaço de sutileza que ele cresce, e é nesse mesmo ritmo que a relação com Gladys surge: sem pressa, sem artifícios, quase como se fosse descoberta por nós ao mesmo tempo que por eles. A química entre os dois existe no que não é dito, naquele território da emoção contida que torna os vínculos ainda mais verdadeiros.
E talvez aí esteja o grande charme de Train Dreams: ele nos lembra que o cinema também pode ser calmo, “lento”, contemplativo — não por falta de força, mas por excesso de humanidade. É um filme que se recusa a correr, porque sabe que a beleza acontece justamente quando permitimos que algo simplesmente exista. Ele emociona não porque quer provocar lágrimas, mas porque reconhece o que é frágil, o que é cotidiano, o que é real.
No fim, é uma obra que você não apenas assiste — você compartilha dela. Um cinema feito de respiro, de textura, de silêncio, de afeto. Uma surpresa tão agradável quanto rara. E, honestamente, eu adorei cada segundo.

Title: Wicked: For Good
Comment:
I’m genuinely curious on whether these movies work for anyone who hasn’t seen the play. I would prefer to be in a wheelchair, get my heart broken, and a have an entire house comically fall on my head (in that order) instead of watching this again.
Something is missing… a lot is missing. I should care more about Elfaba and Glinda’s tearful goodbye, but I never felt the depth of their relationship. I should care that Elfaba and Fiyero get together, there’s a beautiful story in there about how love conquers all, but their relationship goes from straight crush to madly in love, without any of the romance that actually creates the sparks... they’re in love because the story needs them be in love. I should care more about these animals becoming free, but the land of Oz feels the same as it did in Part 1, the stakes are an afterthought.
Maybe it’s the lack of an interesting villain? It doesn’t help that Michelle Yeoh was hit with a horse tranquilizer during filming, sleepwalking through all her scenes. Maybe it’s the poor message of that Dark Knight-ass ending, with the people blind to the real facts while the hero goes into hiding and a white face shows up as the false savior. Maybe it’s how the film dances around the events from The Wizard of Oz — you want me to buy this retcon but you’re only half-committed! You don’t show us Dorothy’s face, the Lion is turned into a CGI mess (but thank you Colman Domingo for your 1 minute of service providing the “voice”?), the Scarecrow isn’t actually shown until the very end for some reason, and so the Tinman gets the spotlight? What are we doing here!?
I’m baffled by all this, how did we accomplish SO LITTLE across 2 movies and 5 hours of film? I tried turning my brain off just to enjoy the colors, sets, and costumes but I fell asleep... But hey, you have two solid performances from the leads, and managed to make this oddity of a story into something that had people in my theater hooting and hollering. I don’t get it, I felt nothing, but I’m happy for all of you.

But the emotions he does show, and just how perfectly cast he is—he’s excellent. The casting overall is spot on.
We also have Felicity Jones as the main character’s girlfriend. She’s great, even though she’s in the film very little. And Carrie Condon and William H. Macy appear briefly, but when they do, they’re excellent.
For me, the film is maybe a bit too poetic, too abstract, but I understand that for many people that will be exactly what they love about it. For me it’s a very good film, but not something I’d be eager to revisit.

Title: Killer Cop
Comment:
Poliziotteschi is a subgenre of crime and action films that emerged in Italy in the late 1960s and reached the height of their popularity in the 1970s. Influenced primarily by both 1970s French crime films and gritty 1960s and 1970s American cop and vigilante films, poliziotteschi films were made amidst an atmosphere of socio-political turmoil in Italy known as Years of Lead and amidst increasing Italian crime rates. The films generally featured graphic and brutal violence, organized crime, car chases, vigilantism, heists, gunfights, and corruption up to the highest levels. The protagonists were generally tough working class loners, willing to act outside a corrupt or overly bureaucratic system.
Police Inspector Matteo Rolandi witnesses a massacre in a hotel when a bomb explodes and kills dozens of civilians. The prime suspect, a young political activist escapes the scene and a manhunt begins. General Attorney Di Federico is brought in to solve the case. As Inspector Rolandi continues his own investigation to the annoyance of Di Federico, he soon discovers a terrifying conspiracy behind the act of brutal terrorism. Based on the notorious 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing.
The great Claudio Cassinelli is fantastic as Rolandi, it’s a far more interesting and subtle performance than I was expecting. He’s a really well formed character, he likes to set his alarm so it inches off a table and he has to jump out of bed to catch it, he always has his copy of Moby Dick nearby, always has to have a sandwich in the car, smokes like a chimney. Cassinelli tragically died aged 46 in a helicopter crash. All the characters have their little quirks in this, Arthur Kennedy who kills it as Di Federico is nicknamed “Minty” as he always sucks on mints when he’s thinking. The young activist has incredibly bad eyesight and a crippling drug addiction, a fellow cop called Balsamo has a habit of playing with things whether it be someone else’s lighter or pen and he shits himself whenever put into a tough situation. Even a tiny part for a drug kingpin slowly sucks on a lollipop. There’s so many interesting characters it really made the film a joy to watch.
The film itself was far more subtle than I expected, this is definitely a poliziotteschi but it doesn’t have many of the tropes I’ve come to expect. It’s more of a standard thriller/character piece than what I’m used to when watching a poliziotteschi. I think for many people the lack of those tropes will be a big positive, for me personally I like my poliziotteschi to have extreme violence, lots of car chases and cops that are prepared to sink lower than the criminals themselves to get the job done.
It’s wonderfully directed by Luciano Ercoli, he first rose to fame by directing a couple of Ringo films in the mid ‘60s, the Spaghetti Westerns A Pistol for Ringo and The Return of Ringo. In 1970 he directed the brilliant Forbidden Photos of a Lady Above Suspicion and followed that up with the back-to-back gems Death Walks on High Heels and Death Walks at Midnight. Ercoli was married to Spanish actress Nieves Navarro, who has appeared in several of his giallo films. Ercoli, described as “one of the first directors to jump on the thriller bandwagon”, retired from the film industry in the late 1970s after inheriting “a fortune”.
Marcello Gatti was the film’s cinematographer and he did a superb job, he’s perhaps most famous for shooting the brilliant The Battle of Algiers along with several other great films such as The Black Belly of the Tarantula. The score is a banger composed by the fantastic Stelvio Cipriani, one of the greatest film composers of the ‘70s. His thumping score here is outstanding and really sets the tempo and helps move the film along. I'm not sure if it was previously used for another film or re-used later but it seemed really familiar, although when you've watched hundreds of gialli and poliziotteschi the scores often seem similar or repeated.
I had a great time watching Killer Cop, although the original title was The Cops Have Their Hands Tied which I think is a much more apt title for it. Killer Cop makes it sound like the type of poliziotteschi I was expecting, the other title makes it sound like the much more subtle, interesting thriller it actually is. Definitely one for fans of a good police procedural, I just wish it had Cassinelli beating people to a pulp, car and bike chases and a lot more bullets and explosions. It does have some of that, the hotel explosion and aftermath is pretty ugly, there’s a cool car explosion, someone shot with a rifle disguised as an umbrella and a half decent shootout. Recommended.

Title: If I Had Legs I’d Kick You
Comment:
"I try very hard to be in control of her and everything, but, may as well not even be there at all."
This is a horror movie, we all agree, right? The annoying little girl who kept squealing "mommy" throughout this made me resent being a mother. For me, this was just as disturbing as We Need to Talk About Kevin. Despite not promising it, the film transforms motherhood into a body horror experience. The anxiety, the sleepless nights, the endless doctor's appointments, the constant fear of your child gnawing at you, and the growing hole in the ceiling as you try to cope with it all. The film succeeds in transforming these "invisible" burdens into tangible elements of fear.
Society's perception of motherhood often portrays a woman who sacrifices herself for her child, sacrificing everything, and shouldering all her problems single-handedly for their well-being. This image is often conjured up by those who aren't mothers. After all, a little reflection reveals that while striving to provide the best for her child, the desire for her own peace is clearly just as powerful a motivation as motherhood. It's not hard to see that this isn't selfish. What could be more natural than a mother wanting to find conditions that will benefit her before she can approach the "right" dictated by society? If she had a button that would pause her life, would pressing it, lighting a cigarette, or simply wanting to breathe for a few minutes really make her a bad mother? The film, with its surreal tone, points out that Linda is just a human being. Beyond her daughter, her husband, her clients or those who waste her time in daily life, she's anyone who wants to remember herself, someone who has the right to demand small joys. For me, she was the most relatable character in the film.
But without Rose Byrne's extraordinary performance, the film's entire purpose would be lost. It should definitely have received at least an Oscar nomination! Also ASAP Rocky what are you doing here? When I first saw him I said "oh this guy looks so much like ASAP" because I couldn't believe it was him.

Title: The Howling
Comment:
1981: the year of the werewolf! Besides The Howling, 1981 would also present us with Wolfen and the incomparable An American Werewolf In London. Based on the 1977 novel “The Howling” by Gary Brandner, The Howling can stand tall among the top tier werewolf films, though it is probably not the favorite for the majority of the genre’s fans.
“I hope these people aren’t too weird” - Dee Wallace, as Karen
The most memorable aspect of this film are the creature effects by the masterful Rob Bottin, whose name is more synonymous with the stellar work he did in The Thing (1982). Don’t overlook his signature style seen here, the character “Eddie The Mangler” in a lengthy scene transforming into a werewolf is THE highlight.
I’d like it more if it didn’t take so much time setting the stage. There is NO horror for the first forty five minutes. Uneasiness, suspicion, even dread, but you don’t see a werewolf for quite some time. Once it gets there it’s tremendously more enjoyable, right up to the fantastic ending. It’s also kinda fun to see the many smaller parts played by famous character actors including Dick Miller, John Carradine, Slim Pickens, Kevin McCarthy and Roger Corman.
Though it placed a distant second to the box office blockbuster An American Werewolf In London in 1981’s werewolf phenomenon, The Howling generated enough interest to garner a sequel, then another and another and another - SEVEN in all.

Title: Cyberpunk: Edgerunners
Comment:
Okay yeah wow this was really good. This is also the first anime series I’ve ever watched and the reason I chose this show specifically is because I absolutely love the video game Cyberpunk 2077 - one of my favourites for sure and the world is extremely interesting. If anything, this series inspired me to replay the game even after getting the platinum and 100% on Phantom Liberty, because it’s simply an awesome game with an awesome and beautiful and unique world.
Cyberpunk: Edgerunners has great and memorable characters and manages to develop the relationships quite well considering its rapid pace. I did find the first episode to be “eh” but after we see David go to the moon with Lucy in the BD, I ended up becoming very invested. I really did enjoy the characterisations on display and in my opinion it’s the strongest part of the show, which is great since I’d argue that good characters we can get invested in are the most important part of successful shows. And yes, Rebecca may honestly be my favourite character in this.
I also absolutely love the world of Night City, and hearing the ringing sounds or seeing the map in the finale etc. made me actually very reminiscent of my fun time with the video game. The music is very suitable too and I felt incredibly immersed every time I put an episode on. Also fantastic emotion.
There’s a lot of action in the show and I’d say it’s a pretty mixed bag for me personally - certain moments are quite terrific but then when it’s an all out explosive car chase, it kinda just goes over my head. But like I said, there are still segments here and there that have pretty great action that I really enjoyed.
On another note, and the one thing that kept bothering me, I found the constant nudity to be really obnoxious. The first episode had like 2 random sex jumpscares and then as the series progressed, I kept having animated boobies on my screen that didn’t really need to be there lmao! It doesn’t necessarily affect the fundamental quality of the show, but I just felt it was very unnecessary in most moments. 
However, this show was really great and as someone who really loved the video game, this was a really great watch and it really scratched my itch for more Cyberpunk content. I’m really glad I watched this, and honestly it convinced me to give more anime a try. I mean, I do have a few films (mostly Studio Ghibli) on my watchlist but maybe there’s a show or 2 that could hook me the way Cyberpunk: Edgerunners did.

Title: Frankenstein
Comment:
Wow. An absolute stunning piece of filmmaking, a movie I think Guillermo Del Toro was destined to make.
Firstly, the performances are incredible. Isaac and Elordi are both brilliant as the two leads, as well as a great supporting cast - Goth, Waltz and Kammerer all excel. Elordi in particular manages to relay so much emotion into his facial expressions and limited dialogue.
As usual with a Del Toro film it looks gorgeous - the set and costume design is immaculate, the creature design is great, the gore isn’t plentiful but the flashes of it are suitably gruesome, the cinematography is great and the soundtrack is beautiful.
The story is good - although unsurprisingly quite familiar - based on a 200 year old book that has already had countless adaptations. I don’t see that as a negative though, more of a testament to how much of a genius Mary Shelley was - I really need to get around to reading the damn thing.

Title: Lost Highway
Comment:
10! ABSOLUTE CINEMA!!
David Lynch’s Lost Highway is cinema as dream-logic, a film that refuses to operate on conventional gears but demands to be experienced. It begins as a noir mystery and mutates into something stranger, an existential loop of identity, jealousy, and violent fantasy. Rather than building toward clarity, Lynch dismantles it scene by scene. The result is hypnotic and maddening in the exact way his best work is.
Every scene plays like a memory collapsing into a hallucination, as if you’re trapped inside someone’s subconscious rather than watching their life unfold.
Lynch taps into his recurring idea that our minds rewrite reality when guilt becomes unbearable. This isn’t a movie about plot; it’s about psychology. Identities fracture, timelines distort, and characters become mirrors of emotional trauma. Lynch artfully suggests that we re-author our own narrative when the truth is too terrifying to face.
Lynch’s mastery of atmosphere carries more meaning than the dialogue ever could. The eerie blue lighting, empty spaces, slow pacing, and throbbing music create a sensory world that is seductive and suffocating. It’s a film you inhabit rather than interpret.
Angelo Badalamenti’s score, along with Trent Reznor’s industrial soundtrack, gives the film a pulse like a panic attack: metallic, rhythmic, threatening.
The Mystery Man stands as one of the most unique figures in horror cinema. He isn’t merely a villain, he’s a projection of guilt, a watcher of the subconscious, an embodiment of the fear that is always watching us from within. His appearance is a psychic rupture, the film’s most startling reminder that the monster is already inside the mind.
"I'm at your house right now."
That phone-call scene is pure cinematic horror.
It also stands as one of the greatest noir films ever made. A twisted heir to classic noir, but reimagined for a post-modern psyche. And yes, it’s also one of the most erotically charged films of its era. Lynch stages one of the most unforgettable and beautifully disorienting sex scenes in cinema.
Lost Highway isn’t a film for someone who wants answers. It’s for viewers willing to get lost, to feel cinema rather than decode it. The film’s final image is the perfect thesis: identity becomes a trap, desire becomes a spiral, and escape is impossible because you take yourself along.
"I like to remember things my own way."

Scream the tale of a bloodthirsty killer at work in a small town secondary school is witty, bloody and brilliant. Comedy and horror at their best is a glorious combination as bloodletting comes to the leafy environs filled with oversized CRT tv's, island benches, floral soft furnishings and Laura Ashley wallpaper: "what are you doing with a cellular telephone?" Shucks, such brutal interrogation.
Scream is suitably gory and delightfully deplorable, but it's silly and not particularly terrifying some 30 years later. Stu is brilliantly goofy, Billy is deplorably shallow, Sid is brave and Tatum is a national treasure. There's great moments of tension captured through rising apprehension, accusation and paranoia.

Title: After the Hunt
Comment:
You'll have to excuse me if this comes off a little harsh. Maybe it's the first snow of the year in Minnesota laying down its fresh carcass which has the buzzards of seasonal depression circling. Perhaps it's the fact that I just watched 2 bangers in a row coming into this (Train Dreams and Unforgiven), but this film is god awful. The Pelican Queef by Luca Guadagnino starring Julia Roberts and Ayo Edebiri in the Denzel role (for the record I am not going to rip on Ayo, she's the best thing about this film and the only one making an attempt at legitimate acting).
This film resides on the Blockbuster Video shelf that reads "the woke movement and the Gen X liberal Ivy League elites shall eat themselves" - sounds enticing no? If I went into Blockbuster and saw a title that read "After the Hunt" I would expect a 1991 film involving Steven Seagal in a loincloth hunting mutant javelinas for sport. Instead I got Spider-man in his boxers throwing himself at Pretty Woman's bad dye job. Funny! Humor! Ehhh.. give me the Seagal movie.
BUT
It happened at Yale…
Kierkegaard said…
I’m not contesting perceived existence…
When did offending someone become a cardinal sin?
Ok...I don’t hate that last angle, but Luca does absolutely nothing with it except put me into a coma with some haughty melodrama masquerading as relevant satire. It's so nice to see Michael Stuhlbarg in anything. Points for that, but JFC is this terrible dialogue. Nauseating “intellectual speak." I was exhausted by the 18 min mark and still had over 2 hours to go. I hate these people. Fucking Panopticon references? Who wrote this? Billy Corgan? At least Stuhlbarg can make just about anything sound coherent, but how dare they relegate the mighty Stuhlbarg to token house husband status! Decidedly NOT my jam.
Speaking of jams, this epic intellectual belly flop was soundtracked by the great soundtracking duo Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross. They use little Eyes Wide Shut Gyorgy Ligeti piano plinks here and there. It's obvious as hell, but somewhat appreciated. Just wish they’d ply their craft for directors who don’t stink on skates. Terrible Love by The National playing in the bar as Spider-Man kisses Pretty Woman? Very apt if not directly on the fucking schnozz. The Smiths on the jukebox at a college campus in 2025? Sure. Ok.
Garfield bellowing “FAAAHHCK YOUUU!” like Marty Landau in Ed Wood and “privileged coddled hypocrites!!” at a bunch of twee Yale students is kinda fun. It's just such a goddamn cliche that it saps any wee bit of joy I may have wrung from it. The Abe Simpson "old man yells at cloud" meme was more subtle. If this is satire, point me in the direction of an old Hee Haw episode so I can wash the stench off.
This movie makes me feel like an asshole. This movie makes me think Americans were justified in making Trump president twice. This movie makes me hate hand gestures and the people who film them. This movie has a series of never ending codas for a third act. Getting through this was a battle I was completely unprepared for. It’s totally insufferable. I hate every character and just about every sentence that comes out of their mouth. In Luca's world oversimplification is the way now. Annihilate the other and be free! Kids these days, amiright??
Worst film of the year and probably high in the running for worst of the decade.

Title: Scream
Comment:
Wes Craven’s genre revitalizing, meta-slasher Scream has been a personal favorite film at many different points in my life. Beyond the personal attachment, it’s also been a film that’s helped shape my entire relationship with not just horror, but media itself. At just the tender age of 9 sneaking in with my older sister’s teenage friends for a terrifying first watch on VHS, Craven’s literary horror flick shifted something in my being that has kept me coming back for over 25 years since its release. And with this being my first ever Scream log, I’m beaming. 
From its opening exterior shot through to the moment Drew Barrymore’s landline rings, something immediately comfortable and familiar enveloped my soul like lush black velvet. Every visual, narrative, and aural component of Scream feels intentionally mapped out to get the most out of its bloody climax. God damn, that third act still gets my heart racing too. There are so many beautiful elements to key in on when it comes to Kevin Williamson’s bulletproof script, and yes, Scream is the recipient of an insane amount of nostalgia points, but even with a critical gaze applied, everything works together perfectly. Its self referential humor flirts with parody, but manages not to pull away at all from its S-Tier suspense and bloody tension. I’m not sure another film can come anywhere to striking that balance.
I’ve probably got at least five more reviews worth of writing about Scream, so let’s just wrap it up. I love this film.

Title: Girl
Comment:
Singapore International Film Festival 2025 Film #1

Of all possible films, they decided to open the festival with this? I can’t wrap my head around what they were thinking.
There are several films I've seen where I can predict the trajectory of the story line, such as domestic violence, sexual assault or generational trauma. I have seen so many adaptations of the same wounds in movies that there are times when those films start to blend into one another. not because the same things are not important to me, but because they are the same tragedies that the world keeps having over and over. I always have a part of me that wants to see if the next film can take a different approach or takes that concept to a greater extent than other films have or goes into even greater detail so that I get a deeper level of understanding from the film as opposed to just repeating what I already know.
Watching this movie, I couldn’t shake the feeling that I’d been here before. Not a pleasant recognition, but a sense of disappointment from seeing the same scenario repeated over and over again. In spite of being somewhat formulaic in nature, I really didn’t think it offered much that would set it apart from many other films about similar subjects. While I didn’t enjoy the film specifically because of the narrative structure used to tell the story, I did find myself feeling sad about the fact that the movie chose to depict the story in this way.
The lack of character development was what had frustrated me the most throughout the movie. The entire time I was waiting and expecting to see more than what I had been seeing on the surface, but it never came. The running time of the movie was long, but even with that length there were so many things that could have been developed further and that I would have liked to see. on the other hand, some of the themes they attempted to display seemed very hollow. I wanted to connect with these characters and to be able to relate specifically to them. I wanted to feel something either very specific or very tender, but the emotional scenes landed with a thud. It seemed as though the expectation for me was to create all of the depth and emotional connection that was not being shown to me. You can only feel something if the film also feels that way about the characters and I did not feel this way about the characters in this film.
And that’s the saddest part. These stories deserve honesty, nuance, and a sense of lived-in truth. They deserve filmmaking that digs deeper, that risks complexity, that refuses to treat trauma like a template. But this film felt like it stayed on the surface, hitting the usual beats without reaching for the substance behind them. And like others who take on these stories, Shu Qi tends to keep the camera close to the abuse and crying, assuming that the repetitive showing of violence will do good, assuming the shock will be enough.
Upon leaving the theater, I had the feeling I had experienced a second-hand or third-hand experience of a tragedy/mistake that has gone before. The story as told was really incomplete because while the film touched base on some very important themes, it never met our expectations as to what could have been done. As a result, I felt disconnected, emotionally empty, and did not take away anything important from the experience.
Some stories repeat because the world repeats them. But some films repeat simply because they don’t try to go any deeper. This one, for me, stayed in that shallow space, never becoming more than an outline of a story that deserved far more. At worst, it becomes a kind of emotional fatigue, a feeling that I am simply watching the same nightmare in a different costume, adding one more depiction of violence to a pile already too high.

Title: Wicked
Comment:
“because i knew you, i have been changed for good.”
I’ll have to admit, this managed to move me in its strongest moments, and at the end even more, it overwhelmed me in the best way. Maybe it was partly due to the overlong runtime, but still I wasn’t prepared for how much it would rise up from the slight dullness that began to take over. They pulled a real punch there at the end. Unlimited, right? Agreed, everyone deserves the chance to fly, or at least emotionally soar for a moment. I'll take it.
But it’s actually more profound. What drew me in and kept me inside and yes, it was a close call was the stunning performance by Cynthia Erivo. So touchingly vulnerable and so, so powerful in the way she carries her outsider-ness. It genuinely intrigued me. She poured her whole heart and soul into all this, not just in her live singing. And for sure, Ariana Grande was outstanding in her own way. Her timing and delivery come with a self-aware wink that lands so well.
Together they’re a tandem that opens up a world where self-grandiosity and actual greatness echo through one another, shadowed by the self-doubt and humbleness underneath. A shifting, double-mirrored dynamic of self-discovery and resistance to the roles imposed on them, bound by the longing to be seen and the need to belong – one that sparks an unexpected connection and over time a mutual transformation. Even if Glinda doesn’t go with the wind and holds onto the reassurance of the world she knows, a regime she believes she must help hold together, her change is still real. That tragic turn deepens the truth of both characters. And it doesn’t erase their bond, it clarifies it. And that’s the brilliance: the connection between them still glows, leaving plenty of space left to grow from there.
Overall to me this was a better-than-expected Sunday afternoon blockbuster watch: delightfully expressive and with enough wit and nuance in theme and gesture that it has the power to stay with me.

Title: Deep Cover
Comment:
Hoooooly cow. I love (and rate higher)  more pictures than most discerning fans, but… I might’ve just found my favorite film. Longtime actor/director Bill Duke’s neo-noir take on the 90’s LA crime underground, Deep Cover, is an insanely gratuitous cinematic depiction with a pulsating, gritty edge. Within its core, a circular sense of raw violence, self-doubt, illegal thrills and vigilante comeuppance fuel a twisting, paranoid and drug fueled narrative into an underseen masterpiece that I wish more had on their “all time” lists. An almost mythic quality to Duke’s visual storytelling wraps its way around Deep Cover, yet it still somehow wields as grounded and tactile an artistic aesthetic as anything ever put to the silver screen. 
Lawrence Fishburne’s 80’s & 90’s acting roles always come off simultaneously so earnest and badass, and Deep Cover may be the biggest feather in his cap. The only comparisons I could conjure up on this level are that of a young Chow Yun-fat, in the likes of The Killer and City on Fire. Fishburne’s turn as Russel Stevens/Joe Hull fires equal parts kinetic energy and subdued empathy into a breathable, scuzzy LA underworld that had me glued to the screen. Also, I’m starting to understand the Jeff Goldblum thirst now. What a seemingly out of place yet perfect character fit he adds to Deep Cover. 
And how can we not touch on its epic sound design? The volume of gun shots and explosions in the mix are overwhelming but perfect. Each action sequence carries a bombastic feel, largely predicated upon its aural proclivities. Basically, shit goes boom exquisitely in Deep Cover. Further propping its tone is an epic soundtrack that peaked at #9 on Billboard’s US Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums. Well crafted and thought out music moves things for me as much as any imagery in film, and Deep Cover authors one of the more unique scores and most symbiotic soundtracks in action cinema. Instead of predictable strings and aural stings, 90’s hip-hop beats fuel tone and tension, while lending a slick edge of cool to every acting beat and action sequence. 
This movie has everything. High-octane Shootouts. A conflicted undercover officer who blurs the line between his two worlds. Visceral action gore and effects. A believable love story. Riveting car chases. Even a relatively happy ending that aims at a political takedown. Deep Cover is just absolute chaotic energy jumping off the screen, and I haven’t experienced anything close to it before.

Title: Frankenstein
Comment:
Idk I kinda hated this and upon more reflection I hate it even more. Don’t love the gaudy Disney ride aesthetics or Mia Goth’s utter lack of juice (Oscar Isaac could have chemistry with a fucking coffee pot but not with her somehow!) or the needless insertion of CGI wolf fights or Elordi in a dirty diaper for what feels like a billion hours. But mostly what irks me is how this just furthers the trend of recent gothic horror movies having (imo of course) the totally wrong grasp on the genre—or, probably more accurately, a grasp oriented around the most “duh” elements that they come off stately and staged when they should be bursting with messy batshittery! 
I’m not an adaptation purist at ALL but I feel like there’s so much lost in the sauce here, mostly due to the emphasis on physical excess—costumes and sets and the like—at the expense of the more existential sort. What makes Shelley’s novel so great is the slow ratcheting of dread mixed with Victor’s poetic melodrama (Isaac, bless his heart, really plays this up—he’s the only element of the movie that worked for me) and the intimacy of the locations and the fact that it’s a pretty straightforward fable about the dangers of having a god complex that’s made monumental for how she uses frustration (such a beautiful emotion to harness) to convey all of this. 
But GDT’s film feels totally reliant on ornate architecture and other BIG STUFF instead of doing the more exploratory character work that would actually get us there. Or maybe the character stuff IS in there somewhere but it’s so buried under swaths of showy design that you’re too distracted to notice. It feels like a movie made for people who like to play with toys and go on rides and dress up in costumes and not really for people with self-pitying despair in their hearts which imo is more the vibe for this kind of thing!!! Which, no shame to people who like GDT’s visual storytelling, I know I am outnumbered on this one, but to me his gothic horror movies all frustratingly zag away from the best shit this genre provides, like will touch on it but not get its hands dirty in the wretched emotion of it all: the agonizing turmoil of forced repression, the woes of being intelligent in a way that doesn’t mingle well with polite society, the big ideas you conjure and scrap in the fits of mania induced by the laws of the land and times. But mostly, the deep and unflattering perversion these thoughts and circumstances stir up in a person, and the gruesome consequences that come from healing them incorrectly. There ain’t a single perverted thing in this movie and I’m mad online about it!
And also, like, as a reminder, Frankenstein is a novel that contains quotes like “Every night I was oppressed by a slow fever… the moon gazed on my midnight labors, while, with unrelaxed and breathless eagerness, I pursued nature to her hiding places.” GORGEOUS, no? But in this movie that’s the kind of thing Victor might say but we feel none of in visual flourishes or sound design or the texture of the filmmaking. Everything is just kinda sitting there in frame and I felt a big load of nothing about it. Not ideal!
MOST annoyingly, at least to this hater, the movie ends with a Byron quote that quite literally made me LOL. Like what are we doing here??? Put some respect on Mother Mary!!! But hey, maybe it’s actually perfect to end this particular movie with a quote from a man more obsessed with the idea of the thing than with the blistering soul of it.

Title: Bugonia
Comment:
You can't beat me because you are a loser and I'm a winner and that's fucking life!
I am not gonna lie I unashamedly started vibing along with Emma Stone when Good Luck Babe started playing...
'The bees, they're dying, and that's the way they planned it. To make us the same as the bees. But it is not in control anymore. We are.'
A film that has both the buzz and honey, a hive of excitement and thrills combined with Yorgos Lanthimos' exotic direction-style, oozing with a substance that genuinely seems to care about what it's saying as Earth is wrapped up in a golden blanket of lies and conspiracy.
'Where's my hair?'
'Your hair has been destroyed.'
'Why have you shaved off my hair?'
'To prevent you from contacting your ship.'
'My ship?'
'Your ship.'
'What ship?'
'Your mothership.'
We should all be mixed up together like bees in a hive, a collective of social responsibility where we care for eachother, spreading the beauty of petals to help our world grow into something colourful and gorgeous, then bouncing off eachother's work, pollinating other stems to create a versatile and flourescent meadow of flowers for both humans and bees to enjoy, a utopia of peace, a utopia of equality. However the Queen divides the possibility of a utopia. She's the leader, a hornet among the nest of bumblebees, a hornet that all the workers mindlessly submit to as they unknowingly fall into the trap of hierarchy. They all believe they're important, they all believe that without them the colony wouldn't survive. But in reality their buzzes of protest are worth nothing more than how humans perceive bees to be in the first place, a pre-concieved opinion that they're useless creatures that have no purpose of being here other than to be annoying, like peasents we can keep in wooden houses for our entertainment, or food sources for the spread of our toast.
'I know who you are. I know what you are.'
'They want you to think it's you who made this world. But it's always been them.'
But even humans have to eventually come to realise that we are falling into the same trap, a blur of black and yellow fuzz we think we can sting our way out of. But there will always be a stronger stinger, someone stronger to kick us back down the ladder. We should be working on the daily, but our problem isn't that we don't work enough, but that we don't work in general. We whine, complain, suffer, but we don't push through. We just blame our struggles on someone else, on aliens, on a conspiracy, on the bees. When in reality, we can't complain about the honey when we're the ones pollinating it, too. And by the time we realise that we're the main players in a game we hate, it will already be too late, we'll be too far gone, we'll be wiped out by the Queen, like dead oxen in a meadow full of flowers.
But from that carcass spawns new life, a buzz from the rotting meat, a society ready to start over, a bugonia, with honey replacing blood as the violence of our Earth is glazed into a new, and better, social order, commanded by the bees, the 'peasents', the devils, the stupid ones we didn't think could ever outlive the smartest creatures on the planet. But the truth is, no matter how corrupt, no matter how depressing, we will always be able to create life from death, and turn an impossibly bad situation into something much better.
Life will always find a way.

Title: Glass Onion
Comment: I've softened my stance on this one a bit since my previous viewing but Glass Onion is still a significant downgrade on Knives Out. It's a fairly lazily plotted Agatha Christie style mystery focusing on an unlikely group of rich friends spending a weekend on a Greek Island owned by their billionaire sugar daddy. The film professes that the mega rich got that way by stealing ideas from talented people, and influencers got where they are via the backing of said talentless rich people. It could be true I suppose. The characters are generally one dimensional and irritating, though ably brought to life by a cast of memorable faces. What really saves this film is the central performance from Daniel Craig, who is absolutely magnificent as the overblown detective Benoit Blanc. He essentially becomes the defacto lead in the absence of any other character strong enough for the role and he's constantly entertaining and the source of most of the laughs. All the pandemic stuff is already looking tired, while the mystery itself lacks any real hook to make it as fascinating as it really needed to be. The dragged out pacing, especially in tje first half, doesn't help in this regard either. I'm keeping my fingers crossed that the new one will be better than this, and if it is then I hope we get more Benoit Blanc mysteries.

Title: Planes, Trains and Automobiles
Comment:
Having not seen Planes, Trains And Automobiles in forever, I’ve told myself for the last three years that I should watch it for Thanksgiving. I may be a few days late, but damn this is a really good movie.
I had mostly remembered it, but there were a few moments that still really got me. Lots of genuine laugh out loud moments, not surprising considering Steve Martin & John Candy are the stars, but while I knew this was also a heartfelt film, and I knew both actors were talented enough to pull that off, I was still a little taken aback at how well the sentimental stuff worked. I even got a little choked up one time. All of that is very important and it’s what elevates this one as a holiday staple for many, but it’s still the comedy that stands out. It really says something about how good Candy & Martin are that they can both play a couple of guys I’d hate being stuck with on along trip, but you become so invested in them getting home by the end.
It’s also been said many times that this one only gets the R-rating because of the one scene at the car rental desk. Title: Planes, Trains and Automobiles
Comment:
I didn’t love Planes, Trains and Automobiles the first, and only, time I saw it as a teenager. I am not the biggest fan of Steve Martin at the best of times, and I found his character’s martyrdom complex in the face of bad luck, worse weather and the sheer cosmic certainty that the universe hates him personally—and who could blame it?—a bit of a slog. And, to be honest, I found John Candy more and more grating with every spilled beer, every stolen cab and every pillow that is absolutely not a pillow. Yes, I was a real idiot back then.
Watching it as an adult, I think Planes, Trains and Automobiles works precisely because it understands that the people who annoy us the most are often the ones who carry the heaviest burden. The film’s comedy is very broad—and I can see why it turned me off—but its compassion is very precise. And now that I knew what was really going on beneath Del’s affable chaos, the gags quietly reassemble themselves into something far more tender and sad than I realised on that long-ago first viewing.
Perhaps Planes, Trains and Automobiles is a film that only fully works the second time, or perhaps I am more sentimental than I was as a youngster, but I love that it is ultimately about grace—the grace Neal finally learns to give, and the grace Del has been trying to offer through all the noise. And, yes, I also found it far funnier this time round. Most of all, though, I now see why it is such a beloved holiday movie, reminding us that travel is hell, people are complicated, and sometimes the family we find on the journey are just as important as the one waiting at home.

Title: Unforgiven
Comment:
"Now if they was giving over to wickedness in a regular way…."
This film is born of darkness and ends the same way. There’s no fancy street lights or glittery 4th of July pyrotechnics in Big Whiskey, there's only the fire that burns in the coal black hearts of men. It’s disgusting in its truth. The lighting is natural all the way, blacks crushed within an inch of their lives and daylight so blistering it will scorch your eyes clean out of their sockets. If Tombstone is the glossy version of a '90s western, this is matte finish all the way. A rhapsody in brown. We’re invited to wallow in the myopic pig shit of the era. We accept without reservation, so long as the reckoning comes.
“My wife cured me of drink and wickedness.”
To age with this film is to admit to our faults and frailty as a species. The infinite melancholy in me accumulates from the fact that Clint Eastwood looks younger and I look older every time I watch this. I’ve been every version of William Munny, at least in spirit anyway. I’ve watched this film as a reason to drink and a reason not to. I've watched it for hope in the midst of despair and as an injection of pure uncut nihilism. Quincy used to just watch all the time, scared. I’m just a fella now though. I've got three pistols and only one arm for Christ’s sake.
“What happens when someone comes to collect? Ya gonna hump 'em? Ya gonna hump 'em a thousand times?!”
Karma always comes to collect. Sally Two Trees knew the score. Spit on a rich fella? Naw it's far worse than that in the imagined nightmare of a broken down pig farmer. Our lives contain the greatest revisionism, we don’t need westerns or the duck of death to tell us so. Sally’s evil eye will suffice.
“Don’t tell my kids none of the things I done.”
There ain’t no hawk kid and you couldn’t hit it even if there was. It's been said before but it bears repeating, this film destroys every myth of the old west there ever was. The fastest gun didn't win the west, it was the ones who merely survived the onslaught through guile, guts and the dumbest of luck. If you're not "lucky in the order" you're crawling on the floor through the darkness praying for a scrap of light in the storm and finding only “snakes and such." Eastwood's Munny isn't just the most murderous, he's the cockroach that could survive a nuclear holocaust in spite of himself.
Eastwood was 61 here, still picking rocks and nervously flicking them at nothing in particular as America bleeds while asking for water. This is just as much about Eastwood as anything else, Sergio and Don be damned. The guy who plays the Schofield kid is actually really fucking good too. “It don’t seem real.” he whimpers. "We all have it comin' kid." says the wise old scowl. Greatest scene in movie history? Definitely. That's all Eastwood.
Then it keeps going back for more and more punishment until it seems so real that we don't wanna just get off the ride, we begin dry heaving over the side of the boat. The rage that flashes across Eastwood's face when he says “they got a sign on him in front of Greeley’s?” is the realest of the real… as is the way he slowly grabs Ned's whiskey bottle mid conversation and just starts chugging. Some of the best acting I’ve ever seen. I love HOO-haaa Al Pacino as much as the next guy, but that whole sequence should play on an endless loop on the garage door of every Academy voter that didn't vote for Clint that year.
Then there’s that ending with Hackman's Daggett at the saloon. A brutal killing that has stuck with me for over 30 years. It's not so much the carnage of that saloon shootout as the grimace Eastwood makes after he shoots Little Bill in the face. It's the look of a man who's seen some shit, and yet is still disgusted by the outcome. It's predator killing predator out of instinct rather than duty and then looking quizzically at the mess he created.
The thunder clap entrance prior to "Who’s the fella who owns this shithole?" is the most badass thing ever put on this earth. And we (the audience) are the wide eyed gleam in W.W. Beauchamp's eye. We root unabashedly for blood and once it's over we wear the same grimace Eastwood makes while we hide outside in the rain. W.W. better get those spectacles on straight because he’s watching the extinction burst of a T Rex. Thank God for dry goods.

Title: Zootopia 2
Comment:
🔙Zootopia🔙
🔜The Invisible Man🔜
I can’t believe it, it actually happened. A great sequel was made. Zootopia 2 is a very good film, even if it’s a bit weaker than the first one. This movie is excellent, really, it’s such a joy to watch. It’s a lot more fun than the first part. And what’s amazing here is that no matter how old you are, everyone will have a good time. In fact, older viewers will probably enjoy it even more.
When I went to the cinema, there were so many people — I’d say from around age 5 all the way up to 50. And honestly, the older audience, including myself, was having the best time. The more we laughed, the more fun we had. The amount of references to other films is incredible. I loved the nods to The Shining, The Godfather, and even the series Succession. The Ratatouille reference was also fantastic. There were references to other movies as well, but I don’t remember all of them.
Overall, the film feels a bit like something from the Knives Out series. It’s almost like a parody. At times it also feels like The Naked Gun, or even something from Mission: Impossible. The music seems inspired by the Mission: Impossible scores. For me, the soundtrack by Michael Giacchino is absolutely outstanding. I love the music, and it made the whole experience even more enjoyable.
The script, just like in the first movie, is excellent. This time the screenplay was written by Jared Bosch, and it’s truly great. The movie is the perfect length, and the script fits everything in — the funny moments, emotional moments, action scenes, quieter scenes. Everything is wonderfully balanced.
The film is once again directed by Jared Bosch and Byron Howard. They did an amazing job. It’s truly masterful direction for an animated movie. The editing by Jeremy Milton is also very good, the film is cut together in a really satisfying way. Technically, it’s a fantastic film.
I watched it in Poland, so I saw the dubbed version. Honestly, it’s one of the best Polish dubs ever. I have to praise the people responsible for dubbing in my country. I’ve heard that the voice cast is excellent and perfectly matched to each character. I can’t comment on the original voices since I watched it dubbed.
Today was just a great day overall. I watched Nuremberg in the cinema — a really good film that taught me a lot about history. And then I saw an amazing, entertaining movie - Zootopia 2, also in the cinema. Just perfect day.

Beliefen sich noch bei Film Nummer Eins, „Der Große aus dem Dunkeln“ oder eben „Walking Tall“, meine schlimmsten Befürchtungen, einen typischen 70er-Action-Reiẞer zu bekommen wo erst geschossen wird bevor es zur Verhandlung geht mit der daran verknüpften Erwartungen dürftigen Schauspiels, einem generischen Soundtrack, einer belanglosen Kamera wie einer ebensolchen, und die Produktion zusammenfassenden belanglosen Regiearbeit, ich selbige, mehr oder weniger, Erwartungen wie Befürchtungen bei meiner ersten Sichtung von „Ein Mann sieht rot“ aka „Death Wish“ hatte, zum unverhofften eigenen Glück jedoch einen beinharten, teils niederschmetternden, und einen wütend machenden, handwerklich top gedrehten Film bekam, nicht weniger ich selbige Attribute „Walking Tall“ zuschreiben möchte mit einem klasse aufspielenden Joe Don Baker von dem ich mehr und mehr ein kleiner Fan werde, bekam ich mit dem zweiten Streich aus der „Walking-Tall“-Reihe meine schlimmsten Befürchtungen.
Wo noch Joe Don Baker die Weichen zu einem Herzchen legte, die Produktion von Teil Eins hochwertig wie in der Tonlage bier- und bitterernst ist, ein Fundament der Glaubwürdigkeit auslegt, ganz der wahren Geschichte um Buford Pusser entsprechend, musste bereits mit dem Darstellerwechsel von Baker zu Bo Svenson die erste Enttäuschung hingenommen werden die sich leider fortsetzt.
Als hätten die Macher dahinter bewusst sämtliche Entscheidungen gefunden, eben nicht meinen Geschmack zu treffen, wird aus „Walking Tall 2“ die 08/15-Produktion mit einem Ablaufdatum von höchstens drei Tagen, und das auch nur, wenn ich einen Tag davon verschlafen habe. Plötzlich bricht „Walking Tall 2“ mit dem bierernsten Grundton seines Ursprunges und unterfüttert das mit einer Unglaubwürdigkeit bei der ich mir sicher bin, beinahe alle Geschehnisse innerhalb des Filmes, wurden frei erfunden oder dermaßen auf den Film angepasst, um eben dies zu suggerieren. Schraubten schlicht die wiedergegebenen Fakten um Pusser „Walking Tall“ auf eine Klasse über vergleichbare Filmchen, überholt sich hier Pusser wie der Film selbst, als befänden wir uns auf einer Abenteuerreise mit dem längst bekannten Ausgang der so endet, wie er erwartet wurde, ohne wirkliche Sorgen um unsere Hauptfiguren. Und als auch noch Actioneinlagen im Stile von Bond geschehen, hat er gänzlich jedwede Glaubwürdigkeit verloren so wie meine Geduld.

-------------------------------------------

While film number one, “The Big One from the Dark” or “Walking Tall,” my worst fears of getting a typical 70s action flick where they shoot first and negotiate later, with the associated expectations of poor acting, a generic soundtrack, an unremarkable camera and equally unremarkable directing that sums up the production, I had more or less the same expectations and fears when I first saw “Death Wish,” but to my unexpected delight, I got a hard-hitting, sometimes devastating, and infuriating film, masterfully shot, and I would attribute the same attributes to “Walking Tall” with a superb performance by Joe Don Baker, of whom I am becoming more and more a fan. With the second installment of the “Walking Tall” series, my worst fears were realized.
Where Joe Don Baker set the course for a heartwarming story, with the production of part one being high-quality, serious, and bitter, laying a foundation of credibility in keeping with the true story of Buford Pusser, the first disappointment had to be accepted with the change of actor from Baker to Bo Svenson, which unfortunately continues.
As if the creators behind it had deliberately made all the decisions not to suit my taste, “Walking Tall 2” becomes a run-of-the-mill production with an expiration date of no more than three days, and that's only if I sleep through one of them. Suddenly, Walking Tall 2 breaks with the deadly serious tone of its origin and underpins this with a lack of credibility that makes me certain that almost all of the events in the film were either invented or adapted to the film in such a way as to suggest this. While the facts presented in Pusser's “Walking Tall” simply elevated it to a class above comparable films, here Pusser overtakes himself, as does the film itself, as if we were on an adventure with a long-known outcome that ends as expected, without any real concern for our main characters. And when action sequences in the style of Bond are added, he has completely lost all credibility, as has my patience.

Title: Black Friday
Comment:
As you may or may not already know, I run an independent brick and mortar videogame shop in northern New Jersey, USA. Today was my store’s 20th Black Friday! I worked from opening until just before passing out (which happens earlier each time) and it’s my favorite day of the year. Sure, all of the extra shoppers help keep the business running, but honestly I feel I have the greatest customer base in all of retail.
My Black Friday is very different from what most retailers call Black Friday. Tradition dictates digging up a movie that refers to it whether by coincidence (Karloff’s Black Friday from 1940) or specifically, like this one which I’ll refer to as Bruce Campbell’s Black Friday. In a large toy shop overrun with infected humans, it is a metaphor for the plight of retail workers. I wouldn’t know anything about that, at least on this day.
Predictably, in this film the work day is horrible. The store is understaffed and has too many middle management try-hards and obnoxious customers. And that’s before the infected ones turn up and make things deadly!
Black Friday plays mostly like the pilot for a television sitcom produced by the SyFy network. It’s lighthearted despite the predicament, commonplace for a Bruce Campbell joint. Colorful, satirical, predictable, and each character is either relatable or like someone you know. Campbell is the standout as you’d expect, but neither he, the rest of the staff, or even the infected do anything over the top. It’s all just too safe. Too sitcom-ey.
“Gimme some sugar, baby” - Bruce Campbell, from a much better movie.

Title: Love at Second Sight
Comment:
Romcoms aren't exactly my go-to genre, and there are only a handful that truly nail both the romance and the comedy. This film is one of those rare gems where I found myself rooting for the couple to come together, all while chuckling at the eccentric friend who provides solid comic relief. Civil and Japy make an irresistibly cute couple, their chemistry electric, and both deliver great performances—especially Civil, who brilliantly transforms from a wildly successful writer to a bumbling professor almost overnight. The alternate universe concept didn’t bother me much, though it took some time to adjust; by the end, it seemed like he literally got trapped in his own story, which is quite an intriguing twist.
All in all, if you’re craving a warm, charming, and genuinely funny romcom, this one’s a must-watch. The on-screen chemistry ranks among the best I’ve seen in the genre, making this a quietly delightful film overall.

Comment:
A bounty hunter named Joe Kidd (Clint Eastwood) reluctantly takes a job from a rich landowner (Robert Duvall). He is to hunt down a Mexican (John Saxon) who is fighting for land reform. Kidd soon finds himself switching sides.
This is a pretty underrated western in that you don’t often hear too many people praising it. The plot is simple and straightforward, but it also has a an energy due to Elmore Leonard’s solid script.
Eastwood does what he does best—put holes in people while giving them the evil eye. Robert Duvall is excellent as the villain. It’s a lot of fun to see these two Academy Award winners have a bloody battle.
John Saxon does not believably play a Mexican. The second he spoke, I literally laughed out loud. I’m sorry, but but bad accents crack me up, and if some silly white dude says “son of beech” in these old Westerns—I will laugh. It’s ridiculous and racist. 
It is said that Eastwood and legendary director John Sturges (The Magnificent Seven) didn’t get along. Rumor has it that Sturges was drunk every day and that his assistant director shot a lot of the scenes. The whole thing feels very Sergio Leone inspired, though it certainly doesn’t get to that level of epic quality.
This was a lot of fun. Clocks in at a brisk one hour and twenty three minutes.

Title: Do the Right Thing
Comment:
It’s the hottest day of the summer. Mookie (Spike Lee) just wants to get through the day and make some money delivering food for Sal’s pizzeria. As the neighborhood swelters, underlying bigotry bubbles to the surface. 
This cinema masterpiece has not lost one bit of its energy or power in the 26 years since its release. It remains fresh and prescient in its indictment of America’s underlying racism. In fact, the culture has gotten worse as much of this anger and resentment is no longer simmering underneath the surface.
Spike Lee’s screenplay is a masterclass in writing. For a long time, this movie is a feel good comedy—but Lee slowly raises the temperature until things explode.  The neighborhood feels so real and lived in.
The opening credits with Rosie Perez dancing and boxing still burns brightly. We are introduced to this world with a bang. Public Enemy’s incendiary ‘Fight the Power’ sets the stage.
There are so many actors in this film who knock it out of the park, showing it is no accident that many of them are now superstars. The lineup includes Samuel L. Jackson, John Turturro, Giancarlo Esposito, Danny Aiello, Ossie Davis, Ruby Dee, Robin Harris,  Bill Nunn and Martin Lawrence. They all bring this colorful neighborhood to life in vivid clarity.
Ernest Dickerson’s cinematography is just brilliant. Is there a film in existence that makes you feel the heat more than this? His use of color to bring on the heat is masterful. Even the movie poster stands out as a perfect example of what Dickerson has achieved here. 
By the explosive climax of this film, all these perfect ingredients come together. If you don’t feel something during the last 15 minutes of this film, you are truly a fucking monster. The tonal change is such a shock, even though everything seemed to be slowly building to this point. It feels like a punch in the gut.
I am being purposely vague about what happens because part of the immense power of this film is the shock and surprise of the climax. 
There was a huge controversy around Mookie’s explosive decision near the end of the film. Some white viewers seemed to miss the point in 1989. In fact, some reviewers were claiming that this film would cause people to riot (how racist is that concept of thinking Black people couldn’t keep themselves together at the cinema?). If you don’t understand why Mookie makes that move, you might be part of the problem.
Highly highly recommended. If you haven’t seen this, please rectify that immediately.

Title: Drop
Comment:
"Yahtzee"
Buena película, una propuesta muy interesante.
"Drop" es de esas película que te entretienen de inicio a fin y encima se encargan de construir buenas escenas de tensión, todo con un guion que tienen sus claras fallas pero que termina quedando un poco de lado gracias al gran trabajo de Christopher Landon.
Sinopsis: Violet, una madre viuda, va a una cita en un restaurante con el encantador y apuesto Henry, pero empieza a recibir mensajes de una misteriosa figura encapuchada que amenaza con matar a su hijo y a su hermana a menos que ella mate a Henry.
La historia es buena, con un guion algo pobre pero muy entretenida. Es muy obvio que la película no aspira a mucho con su guion, tiene algunos diálogos muy absurdos y momentos que hasta pueden sacarte un poco de la experiencia, haciendo que no te termines de tomar todo en serio. Sin embargo, me encantó cómo construye la tensión en todo momento, tiene escenas de suspenso geniales que terminaron siendo de lo mejor, encima es un no parar donde la protagonista se encuentra en constante peligro. Esto, acompañado de un buen ritmo, hacen que la película se pase bastante rápido, aunque no puedo no mencionar que en ciertos momentos se me hizo un poco larga para que solo dure una hora y media, tiene un par de escenas donde simplemente se alarga.
Los personajes me gustaron, una gran protagonista. Violet es el mejor personaje que se nos presenta, es muy bueno todo lo que vemos de su historia y su pasado, cosa que la atormenta en todo momento y es algo que tiene que superar a lo largo de la trama. Si creo que se le podría haber dado algo más de desarrollo a su hermana, que termina siendo un simple acompañante. Por otro lado, Henry me parece un buen personaje que funciona como una figura en la que no sabemos si confiar o no debido a todo lo que está pasando en la trama, además de todos los otros personajes que se encuentran en el restaurant con los que pasa lo mismo.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente la dirección de Christopher Landon, me gusta mucho el estilo de éste director y ya hay varias películas de él con las que logré conectar a pesar de que el guion no sea la gran cosa, ésta es una más de ellas. Además del buen trabajo de cámara que hace, también es importante una banda sonora cumplidora en el tema de aportar tensión en ciertos momentos. Por último, las actuaciones son decentes, nada de otro mundo pero destacan Meghann Fahy y Brandon Sklenar.
En conclusión, una buena película que ya tenía ganas de verla desde que vi su tráiler y al final terminó gustándome como esperaba, para mi está lejos de ser mala y es completamente disfrutable. La recomiendo.

Title: Vertigo
Comment:
Out of the three Hitchcock films I’ve seen, Rear Window, North by Northwest, and now Vertigo, this one’s definitely my favourite so far. 
It has a hypnotic dreamy feel as it spirals deeper and deeper into obsession. And I can’t forget that warm Technicolor glow and the beautiful shots of San Francisco.
At the same time, there’s this innocence to it that sometimes gets in the way, especially considering the psychological territory he’s playing with, I understand that Hays Code was still in full effect at this time, so that’s not me wagging my finger at it or anything, I’m just acknowledging that it’s noticeable by my modern standards. And not towards my favour. 
Still, the influence is undeniable. You can clearly see how directors over the last 60 years have built off Hitchcock’s foundations, even when he was working with one arm tied behind his back. 
He’s definitely one of the best to ever do it. Even if he’s not exactly one of my favourites…(Yet)

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
"Damascus."
Rian Johnson has done it again, he simply does not miss. What a joy to see this in a theater with a crowd because it feels so tailor-made for that communal experience. Definitely has the strongest mystery of the three Benoit Blanc whodunnit's and felt like it had the most drama. Toned down the comedy from Knives Out and Glass Onion, but still has a levity. A couple scenes in particular really surprised me at how it took the time to slow down and sit in the moment and you really feel the effect religion is having on these people. Josh O'Connor is just sensational here, probably my favorite performance from him, which is saying a lot. Daniel Craig is great as always. Brolin and Close also great with the time they have. Has so much to say about faith and power and anger that really resonated with me. This film remains as biting as the previous two, but lays it on a bit less thick imo, not really a good or bad thing. What this film is absolutely the strongest at is the visuals. Johnson's direction paired with Steve Yedlin behind the camera create some truly dynamic sequences and overall stunning cinemtography. The blocking is just as good as Johnson's other films, he really knows how to place his actors in the frame and how to move around them, he has that down to a tee. Just total Rian Johnson and Steve Yedlin god mode from the first shot to the very last. As of right now, I would say this is my 2nd fav of these films, but on rewatches who knows, maybe this one is my favorite. All 3 are 5 Stars so it doesnt matter that much. Rian Johnson saved me once more and I know he will many more times in the future. I hope he makes more original films unrelated to Benoit Blanc, but I also hope he keeps making these whodunnits because they make my life better.
