Title: Blue Moon
Comment:
🇺🇸 in english: Blue Moon is Linklater doing what he does best: turning a confined space into a living universe, where every gesture, pause, and sideways glance carries the weight of an entire shared history. It’s a film that seems simple on the surface — a gathering, a celebration, a reunion meant to be polite — but gradually reveals layers of resentment, longing, memory, loyalty, and artistic tension. All of it contained within a single location, as if Linklater were reminding us that you don’t need to move characters across landscapes when what truly matters is moving what exists between them.
And within this tight emotional orbit, Ethan Hawke shines. He has always been underrated, maybe because his greatness never arrives in loud declarations; it comes from intimacy, vulnerability, and that quiet humanity he brings to every role. Here, as Lorenz Hart, he delivers something beautifully lived-in. Hawke seems to understand Hart from the inside out — his insecurities, his wit, his creative melancholy, that feeling of standing just slightly outside his own brilliance. It’s a performance full of cracks and light, and Linklater knows exactly when to let the camera settle on him, trusting the audience to recognize how deeply this actor deserves to be seen.
The film gains an extra charge with the brief yet magnetic presence of Margaret Qualley. She appears only a little, but when she does, the atmosphere shifts; Qualley has this uncanny ability to suspend the air around her, as if the film were suddenly breathing at her tempo. Even with limited screen time, she embodies that familiar Linklater muse energy — characters who linger far longer than their minutes on screen.
What’s most fascinating is how everything unfolds within that single location — as if the space itself were a sealed emotional chamber waiting to overflow. The celebration of a new musical, the reunion of old creative partners, the conversations that start light and turn revealing… Linklater uses the spatial limitation as dramatic fuel. The walls seem to witness more than we do, and every movement inside them feels precise, reminding us that human stories are, at their core, collisions between past and present.
Blue Moon is a film about creation, legacy, and the fragile dynamics between friends who once felt like brothers. It’s intimate, warm, and imbued with that gentle, aching melancholy Linklater wields so well. And with Hawke at the center — intense, vulnerable, quietly monumental — the title suddenly makes perfect sense: a rare glow, appearing only once in a long while, but unforgettable when it does.
———————————————————
🇧🇷 em português: Blue Moon é Linklater fazendo aquilo que ele faz melhor: transformar um espaço limitado num universo pulsante, onde cada gesto, cada silêncio e cada troca de olhar carregam um mundo inteiro de história. É um filme que parece simples na superfície — uma reunião, uma celebração, um reencontro que deveria ser apenas cordial — mas que aos poucos revela camadas de ressentimento, desejo, memória, lealdade e criação. Tudo isso confinado a um único lugar, como se Linklater estivesse lembrando que não é preciso mover personagens pelos cenários quando o importante é mover o que existe entre eles.
E nesse território fechado, Ethan Hawke brilha. Ele sempre foi subestimado, talvez porque sua grandeza nunca veio do óbvio; ele opera num registro de intimidade, de humanidade quase tímida, e aqui isso se traduz lindamente na interpretação de Lorenz Hart. Hawke entende Hart de dentro pra fora — suas inseguranças, seu humor, sua melancolia criativa, a sensação de estar sempre um passo ao lado da própria genialidade. É uma performance cheia de rachaduras e brilho, e Linklater sabe exatamente quando deixar a câmera repousar sobre ele, como se compartilhasse com o público a confiança de que esse ator merece ser visto, ouvido e levado a sério.
A dinâmica do filme cresce ainda mais com a presença breve, porém magnética, de Margaret Qualley. Ela aparece pouco, mas quando surge a atmosfera muda; Qualley tem essa energia que parece suspender o ar ao redor, como se o filme, por um instante, respirasse no ritmo dela. Mesmo em minutos reduzidos, ela captura o espírito instável e encantador das musas de Linklater: personagens que não precisam de muito tempo em cena para permanecer ecoando tempos depois.
O mais fascinante é como tudo acontece dentro desse único lugar — como se o ambiente fosse uma cápsula emocional prestes a transbordar. A celebração da nova peça musical, o reencontro entre parceiros antigos, as conversas que começam leves e terminam reveladoras… Linklater usa essa limitação espacial como combustível dramático. As paredes testemunham mais do que o público, e cada movimento dentro desse espaço parece milimetricamente desenhado para nos lembrar de que histórias humanas são, em essência, encontros inevitáveis entre passado e presente.
Blue Moon é um filme sobre criação, sobre legado, sobre a dinâmica frágil entre amigos que já foram quase irmãos. É íntimo, afetuoso e cheio daquela melancolia calorosa que Linklater domina. E com Hawke no centro — intenso, vulnerável, gigante na quietude — a lua azul do título parece finalmente fazer sentido: um brilho raro, que aparece pouco, mas quando aparece, é inesquecível.

Title: The Mummy
Comment:
"Beg your pardon, I dislike to be touched... an Eastern prejudice"
Decente película, esperaba un poco más.
"The Mummy" es una decente cinta de terror que para su época no estaba mal pero que hoy en día no resulta la gran cosa, aunque no envejeció del todo mal en cuanto a La Momia, que se ve bastante bien y no era lo que esperaba, pero me terminó gustando.
Sinopsis: En 1925, un grupo de cazadores de tesoros excava una tumba con 3,000 años de antigüedad y despierta la momia del sacerdote egipcio Imhotep, quien regresa con un solo objetivo: la venganza.
La historia es normalita, me esperaba mejores escenas y desarrollo en general. Lo que me pasa con la trama es que la noto demasiado simple y hasta predecible, no sorprende en ningún momento con su desarrollo, teniendo momentos de La Momia que destacan más por las actuaciones que por generar tensión, ya que solo resulta interesante las interacciones que tiene con otros personajes. Algo bueno es que dura sólo poco más de una hora, que no está mal para la simpleza que maneja, haciendo que se pase rápido y entretenga a pesar de que se sienta anticuada en ciertos aspectos.
Los personajes cumplieron, no hay mucho más allá de La Momia. Imhotep/Ardath Bey es el mejor personaje de todos pero sin hacer mucho, no es tan memorable como me esperaba pero es alguien que mejora por la actuación de su actor que hace todo lo posible para intimidar e imponer con su interpretación, ya sea por lo que hace o dice. Además, también destaca por el interesante vínculo que tiene con Helen Grosvenor, otro de los personajes decentes que tiene, quien resalta más allá de la relación con Imhotep. Los demás personajes lo sentí mucho más olvidables y realmente no hay mucho que destacar de ellos.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente la actuación de Boris Karloff, sin dudas el mejor del elenco, acompañado por un gran trabajo en el maquillaje que para la época estaba espectacular seguramente. También hay un correcto trabajo de Karl Freund, quien le da su propio tono a ésta conocida historia. De lo que si esperaba un poco más es de la banda sonora, aporta poquísimo a la historia, podría haber sido clave en muchos momentos.
En conclusión, una normalita película que esperaba un poco más al ser la primera adaptación de ésta historia y éste personaje tan interesante, no está mal pero podría haber sido mejor, me quedo con la de 1999. La recomiendo.

Title: Panic
Comment:
“why risk getting caught now?”
an individual whose existence doesn’t cross anyone’s minds — the lone wolf whose howls don’t make much of a mark, not even a dent, in the busy townsfolk’s lives. though, as he traverses out and around his fellow peers, whispers follow him — with rumours trailing his presence through and through. this person is revealed to be Monsieur Hire (Michel Simon), who becomes a suspect of a widespread conspiracy, an easy target to pin on and pursue — the blame for all things evil and unpleasant. 
Julien Duvivier’s Panique paints a story about mass hysteria, depicting a poor outsider who got caught up in wrong crowds. no one knows or even cares about M. Hire — yet the body of a woman shows up in town, wreaking havoc in the suburbs of Paris, and soon, folks have already made up their minds. 
“we’ve got nothing to hide. i want him to see me in your arms.”
M. Hire’s world is stalled by isolation — loneliness is all he knows… until he takes a liking to Alice (Viviane Romance), becoming fixated with protecting her. to be fair, he’s not exactly a good person — mostly, he comes across as a creep, spying into her life like she’s the only one for him. 
but, she’s not exactly the good girl he perceives her to be — you see, she’s gotten herself wrapped around Alfred (Paul Bernard), the bad boy, aka, the one M. Hire suspects (knows) as the real murderer. and like most young women who didn’t know any better, her naïvety is an asset to the boyfriend’s scheming & vicious nature. she loves him too much to let him go — for goodness sake, she even went to prison for him! this chokehold he held on her is tightly surrounded & under his control. and soon, her loyalty will inadvertently result in M. Hire’s eventual demise. 
“come on, it’s over. that’s the last thing i’ll ask you to do.”
in the end, i like to think Panique is actually a tale about how love can be dangerously brutal, broken by a false sense of trust & promise, and damaged by an unsympathetic power over the helpless & vulnerable. 
“oh, let him finish his last ride.”

Title: Jaws
Comment:
Not a single thought in my mind a shark movie could be this entertaining. I’ve watched 47 Meters Down, The Meg, and The Shallows, and I think what makes Jaws so much better than any of them is, the fact that they didn’t have the fancy tech we have now, and when you can’t rely on CGI or flashy tricks, you’re forced to write better, characters development, build the tension, reasonable events, and make the environment feel like actually matter to the story. And that’s exactly what Jaws does, it has three mc's, one is a shark nerd, one is a pain-in-the-ass who hunting sharks for fun, and one is a poor guy who hates boats, water, let alone sharks, and three of them facing an anomaly who's smarter, stronger, and the king in the territory. That's what I called a proper entertainment.
Most movies like this fall apart when they had to switch tones or settings drastically, like from “fearing the terror" into “facing the terror”, but Jaws has the strength to keep its quality and pacing. Even the investigating scene of them trying track the terror is still fun to watch. And I never said the shark is the reason why this movie is so great, because it's about as great as 70's could get. And I think It's more impressive for a mechanical device made from scratch even sometimes it shows clunky movements, than half the CGI creatures we get now. I love how the shark was rarely seen on the screen until the third act, it builds the tension way much better. You don’t watch this because you wanna see a big rubber shark chew people, you watch this to see these three completely different men deal with something way bigger than all of them. That’s why it still works today, solid story, solid characters, solid tension.
9.5/10 for legless Tralalero Tralala.

Title: Predator: Badlands
Comment:
Dan Trachtenberg loves the Predator more than most people love their own children, but that doesn’t quite explain why his “Predator” movies — of which there are suddenly now three — continue to be so much better than all of the series’ previous sequels, spinoffs, and reboots (let alone most of the IP-driven garbage that Hollywood churns out on the regular). No, Trachtenberg’s “Predator” movies are so uncommonly satisfying because his love for the franchise’s extraterrestrial trophy hunters allows him to celebrate how dumb they are.
No disrespect to the many different warrior tribes who may have inspired the Yautja, but there’s something fundamentally backwards about a hyper-advanced alien species that — despite having solved intergalactic travel — still only knows how to measure its own worth in murder and masculine aggression. ’Twas ever thus, on Earth as it is in the heavens, but Trachtenberg recognizes that the Predators are always just a bit more embarrassing than they are badass.
The genius of the franchise-reviving “Prey” and last summer’s utterly awesome “Killer of Killers” is that they both cast the Yautja as a foil first and an antagonist second. Now, the super fun and fantastically spirited “Predator: Badlands” takes that approach to its logical conclusion by making one of these creatures the hero of a story in which he gets deprogrammed of his culture’s “The Most Dangerous Game”-inspired approach to other species.
Yes, “Alien vs. Predator” struck a short-lived Yautja-human alliance out of situational necessity, but Trachtenberg’s latest hunt takes direct aim at the evolutionary uselessness of being the universe’s biggest assholes. The Xenomorphs aren’t smart enough to know any better, but these “ugly motherfuckers” have invisibility cloaks and triangulated laser sights! They’ve been around long enough to have T. rex skulls on their mantelpieces! They are — collectively — now the only performers in movie history who’ve ever shared the screen with Arnold Schwarzenegger and Elle Fanning, and they’ve held their own against them both!
And yet, for all of those accomplishments, the Yautja’s religious credo has never evolved beyond “Prey to none, friend to none, predator to all.” Congrats for surviving more than 65 million years on the hellish “Star Wars” concept art of a planet you idiots call home, but as someone asks at a crucial moment during the middle of “Badlands,” “Who would want to survive on their own?”

Title: Dial M for Murder
Comment:
❤️‍🔥85%
🔙Four Christmases🔙 
🔜Train Dreams🔜
Dial M for Murder wasn’t up next on my list but I saw it was a sub 2 hour film and I needed something in that ballpark to consume, perfect opportunity arose. I’ll start by saying it’s not my favorite Hitchcock film but it’s still a masterclass in contained suspense, demonstrating Hitchcock's genius to wring maximum tension from minimal resources. It’s a film that thrives on dialogue and atmosphere, palpable tension through nothing but storytelling and a meticulously claustrophobic setting. 
The film was set in the UK, shot in Hollywood though, it carries a certain sophisticated sensibility. It captures a particular mid-century English upper-class environment that contrasts sharply with the sour crime at its core. I did think the outside shots were a little peculiar and I guess that’s to do with them not actually shooting out on a London street, overall though the team did a great job bringing us to the UK despite not being shot there. 
The apartment acts as this singular elegant setting that amplifies the feeling of entrapment and high stakes. It’s full of perfect detailing that helps move the narrative forward, a brilliant place for this sort of murder mystery to be executed. With the help of crisp and deliberate dialogue, it all serves not just to advance the plot but to conceal and reveal the complex emotional dynamics and murderous intent of the characters. 
The performances are truly exceptional, and a cornerstone of the film's success. Ray Milland as the calculating, manipulative ex-tennis pro, Tony Wendice, delivers a performance of cold, sinister charm. His initial meticulous planning and later desperation are chilling, and so effortless. Robert Cummings as the American crime writer Mark Halliday, and John Williams as Chief Inspector Hubbard both provide strong supporting roles, with Williams offering a delightfully understated intelligence that ultimately unravels the perfect murder.
I’ve been meaning to watch another Grace Kelly picture and she stuns. She plays Margot Wendice, effectively portraying the transition from a seemingly guilty wife to a terrified victim of her husband's scheme. Potentially the most gorgeous lady in all of Hollywood, ever, she’s ridiculous. Anyway, enough of me crushing on Kelly, her costume design is telling stuff; progressively we see her move from more bright and colorful dresses to more contained darker tones as we move deeper down this rabbit hole of tension. 
The score is scoring, composed by Dimitri Tiomkin, it’s as elegant as it is suspenseful and enhances the thrilling atmosphere. There’s a good amount of weight added through the score and the suspense can be truly felt during key interrogations and the climax. 
Dial M for Murder is not as visually groundbreaking as some of his later work, but Hitchcock and cinematographer Robert Burks utilize the limitations of the stage play setting effectively. The film was shot in Vistavision, and uses tight close-ups to capture the anxiety and suspicion in the characters' eyes and dramatic lighting to enhance the mood. That one shot of Kelly in court is so ahead of its time, proving just how genius the man behind the lens really was. 
This is the first time I’ve spotted a famous Hitchcock cameo, this one was in the photograph on Tony's wall. I have come to find out he appears in all of his films, I have to pay a closer eye when watching his films so I can spot him some more, love when directors do that; Peter Jackson is another one who does great cameo work. 
What I love is that the film is a masterclass in suspense over surprise. We are made aware of the murder plot from the beginning, and the tension comes from seeing how the characters execute or fail their plans, rather than what will happen next, it’s quite a compelling plot to see unfold and adds to the intrigue. It’s a highly polished, supremely effective thriller, but in my eyes not as deeply resonant or cinematically innovative as classics like Vertigo, Psycho, Rear Window, even Rope for me is a personal favorite I enjoy a little more than this. 
Still though, Dial M for Murder is a film many directors could only dream of making, so far ahead of its 1954 release date, it’s an essential viewing for any fan of the thriller genre. It’s a tightly wound clockwork of a film that proves crime and punishment can be utterly compelling even when confined to a single room. It's a testament to the power of a great script, great performances, and a master director's command of suspense, even if it sits just a notch below his absolute masterpieces.

I get it.

Title: Glass Onion
Comment:
Glass Onion • 2022
Directed By: Rian Johnson
Directed by Rian Johnson, comes Glass Onion released in 2022, starring Daniel Craig, Janelle Monáe, and Edward Norton in this mystery comedy, distributed by Netflix 
The film follows Benoit Blanc as he unexpectedly arrives on tech billionaire Miles Bron’s island for the weekend, after receiving an invitation to his murder mystery party. As the weekend unfolds, secrets within the group begin to surface. It becomes clear that everyone has something to hide and that they all have complicated, messy ties to Miles. When the murder mystery gets ruined and someone actually ends up dead, Blanc must solve the case before the killer strikes again
Back in 2022, I had the chance to watch this at TIFF with some friends, and it was a great experience. My teacher at the time volunteered there and got us tickets, so it ended up being sort of a field trip. Nonetheless it was a fun time, and I remembered liking the film a lot. When it released on Netflix a few months later, I felt the same way. I didn’t review it then, so I’m happy I get to now. Having rewatched this, and watching all the Knives Out films, this is definitely the most lacklustre of the three. It’s still a very solid film, but compared to the other two it just isn’t as strong 
Even if the film itself isn’t great, the performances in these films always deliver. The casting is always on point, and they somehow manage to bring together people who match eachother’s energy. Some standout roles for me were Daniel Craig, Janelle Monáe, Edward Norton, and Leslie Odom Jr. Unlike Wake Up Dead Man, we actually spend time with the characters, exploring their personalities and what led them to this moment through flashbacks and some dialogue. However, what ruined the tension for me was the over reliance on exposition. There’s so much of it, and everything is being spelled out for you, you just wanna yell "STOP TALKING" It’s rare for the film to have a moment of silence, and since the focus stays mostly on three main characters from the friend group, the other plotlines get sidelined, even though they were set up earlier
The thing with these films is that when you put too many personalities into one story, it becomes difficult to decide who deserves the spotlight. Even though some characters do shine, they still end up getting pushed aside 
There’s a reason this is the lowest rated Knives Out film, and it’s because it leans more towards being a comedy than a mystery. The story is very predictable, and instead of trying to hide who the killer is, the film makes it so obvious during certain scenes, showing exactly where things went wrong. There’s also a million other subplots. I’m here for a mystery, yet all I’m hearing about is renewable energy and how it’s going to change the way the world works. That’s fine to a certain extent, but we need some setup for these characters. When the film focuses on these useless plot points for so long, it slowly loses its audience because nobody really cares about that. It works as a motive for the killer and that’s about it. What it really is, is just filler
I’m not sure when this was written, but I have a feeling it was in 2020 because the mystery itself was pretty disappointing. There are some clever twists, but as a whole it just didn’t feel like I was watching a Knives Out film. It felt more like an episode of 9-1-1 because of how ridiculous and cringe some scenes were. The pacing also feels very rushed, which is obvious from the way the film presents itself. That said, using Blanc’s idea for the murder is a fun twist. Dumb, yet brilliant in a fun way. I’m used to that level of comedy in these films. Subtle yet effective, not over the top. We’ve never seen this level of heightened realization before, so seeing it happen out of the blue feels very weird 
Unlike the first film, this one leans more into comedy. The first film had moments of humour that worked and felt earned, I could connect with these characters, and they were genuinely funny. That’s not the case here. Instead we have a billionaire acting like a manchild. To Edward Norton’s credit, it’s funny at times because you wouldn’t expect that from him, but eventually, that’s all he does, and it gets annoying. It’s like Mike Myers in The Cat in the Hat repeating the same laugh over and over, after awhile it stops being funny. Other characters who are meant to be serious are given funny lines that just don’t work. There are also random screaming moments from Kate Hudson’s character, and they’re just not funny at all. I found myself sitting there like Homelander in the theatre with a blank expression on my face because of how unfunny that was. I love her work, but without proper direction, the cast can seem lost and unfortunately many of them are, despite trying their best with what they were given 
All the talk about masks and the pandemic gave me flashbacks, especially that zoom call
The writing is unfortunately the films main problem. Rian Johnson is a talented writer, he’s done some very good work, aside from the eighth film in one of cinema’s biggest franchises. But with Glass Onion, it feels like he had too many ideas and tried to cram as many as possible into the story, thinking he could get away with it. When in reality, people will be comparing this to the first film, which people did, including myself right now
Daniel Craig as Benoit Blanc feels very out of place here. Compared to the first film, this version of the character seems like a completely different person. The southern accent is still there, but the writing and direction don’t support it
As much as it seems like I’m bashing the film, it does have the best visual style of the three. There’s a lot of different camera moments that are very striking and memorable. Placing all the characters on a single island was a great idea as well, because as the audience we feel trapped. Much like Wake Up Dead Man, it’s very claustrophobic and has this sense of terror, more from the atmosphere than the killer. The metaphor of the Glass Onion is also a fun concept, raising some interesting discussions. The cinematography is also very impressive, especially given the location. The setting adds a sense of realism, which heightens the fear factor 
Johnson also cleverly uses this film to deliver some social commentary on modern power and celebrity culture. The film critiques society’s tendency to mix wealth with intelligence. The other characters embody performative behaviours, showing how people will change their morals to stay close to money and status. He also takes aim at disruption culture, highlighting how reckless ideas are often glorified. The film suggests that much of the elite world is like the Glass Onion itself. Layered, shiny, and attention grabbing on the outside, but hollow and transparent once you look closely on the inside 
It was Miles Bron all along… And I killed Drax too…. Hahahahaha
I liked the way this film was structured, with the beginning in the present, the middle exploring the past, and the ending as the resolution. The other films don’t use this structure, and I love that it’s unique to this film. Having that reveal at the end of act one makes the rest of the story feel much more earned by the end. If the clues hadn’t been so obvious, the reveal would have been even more impactful 
Overall, Glass Onion is a visually striking film with clever moments and strong performances, but struggles with its story and use of comedy

Title: The Wizard of Oz
Comment:
I am back from my small break that I took to finish up school work. In preparation for Wicked For Good, I decided to revisit one of the most fascinating movies of all time. The movie that introduced color to television was the same that had a rumor of a hanging munchkin caught on footage, and the same that severely damaged actors who played the Tin Man from the aluminum in the paint. The list of incidents goes on.
About the movie itself, a good word to describe it is “vibrant”. It quite literally brought color to life, changing the scape of movies forever. Even still, it’s one of the most colorful movies ever, using exuberant shades of about every color of the rainbow. The backdrops were amazingly done as well. There’s no doubt that this is extremely recognizable from pretty much any frame. Its story and songs are quite nostalgic even for someone who was born when this was already 65 years old. Of all the movies that have come out in the 1930s, I would say this is probably the most known in even today’s generations.
I’ve watched videos on how many things happened during the production of this movie. Even if the rumored hanging munchkin thing was a hoax, there were still instances of toxic metals, asbestos, and makeup mishaps that happened. Of course these were all terrible things that happened, but it’s fascinating to me because a film as big as this has a lot more backstory to it than first glance. Plus, this is a very happy story, and so hearing that all these bad things happened makes this a little bit disturbing. The cast was surely mistreated by the studios in the name of making this movie.
It’s been a while since I’ve seen this, and this is my first time since hearing about all the stuff that happened on set, which makes this viewing much more interesting. Even hearing about Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo looking clearly underweight during Wicked makes me think that the entire world of The Wizard of Oz is cursed in general. I’m still seeing it on Friday with my family!

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
Wake Up Dead Man • 2025
Directed By: Rian Johnson
Directed by Rian Johnson, comes Wake Up Dead Man released in 2025, starring Daniel Craig, Josh O'Connor, and Josh Brolin in this new mystery comedy, distributed by Netflix
The film follows Benoit Blanc as he investigates a mysterious murder in a small community just outside New York City. A young priest named Jud arrives at the parish and quickly clashes with the fear driven leader, Monsignor Wicks. During a Good Friday service, Wicks is suddenly and seemingly impossibly murdered in what appears to be a locked room scenario. Everyone soon becomes a suspect, turning the case into something far more sinister 
I’ve been a fan of the Knives Out franchise ever since I saw the 2019 film. I thought the writing was incredible, and the sequences and montages were incredibly edited. I fell in love with the idea of bringing back the classic murder mystery in such a fun and creative way. I saw Glass Onion at TIFF in 2022, and I was so grateful for that experience. I’m even happier now to have seen this theatres, because I think a film like this deserves to be experienced on the big screen. I didn’t expect much having seen the trailers, but now having seen the film, I can confirm it’s a near masterpiece
The thing with these Knives Out films is that you’re always guaranteed incredible acting from everyone involved. In the other films, I was immediately convinced by the cast’s chemistry. I didn’t expect to find myself enjoying these characters interacting with eachother, but there are some very dialogue heavy scenes that make this film stand out among the other two 
The standout performances for me were Daniel Craig, Josh Brolin, Josh O’Connor, and Glenn Close. They stood out the most, and their characters are some of my favourites in this franchise, most notably Glenn Close as Martha. She’s such an underrated actress, and I’m tired of not acknowledging her as one of the greats. At 78 years old, she’s still delivering master class performances, and we’ll be seeing her again next year. She was a phenomenal addition to the film, and an overall delight to watch
As for the others they’re fine, they serve the plot and fulfill their characters motivations but there’s a lot of wasted potential. I think that’s the film’s main issue. Too many characters are sidelined, only appearing when the plot needs them to be there, rather than giving them any real personality. I was also a little disappointed with Jeremy Renner. I know he’s a talented actor, I should know I’ve seen him in other dramas, but I didn’t get a real sense of his character here. His role felt very cliche and I think he got lost in it
Speaking of Jeremy Renner, he looks a lot like this Dr. Nat Sharp guy… Coincidence? I think NOT-
The writing in these films always fascinates me because Rian Johnson not only directs these films, but he also writes them. The way he crafts these stories and gives each character a clear purpose is incredibly satisfying. The dialogue can feel very heightened at times because nobody actually talks like that, but you expect them to because his style has become so distinct in these films. The dialogue especially is important since much of the mystery is revealed through conversation. Certain clues slip out casually, and once they’re mentioned, they aren’t referenced again until the very end. It’s a classic blink and you’ll miss it scenario. Compared to the other films, the writing quality here is on par with the 2019 Knives Out film. Glass Onion was enjoyable, but now it feels out of place with this new third installment
The mystery itself was handled very well. I found myself trying to solve it as the film continued, paying close attention to every clue and every piece of information Josh O’Connor’s character shared. I won’t spoil anything, but if you follow all the clues carefully, you could solve the mystery on your first watch. A particular line in the second act made me put two and two together, which made the final reveal even more satisfying. I also think setting the story in this small church community added a claustrophobic feel. The close and personal environment added so much tension and created some truly memorable moments throughout the film
This film is a lot darker than the others, and by darker I mean atmospherically. The murders and overall tone feel much more sinister and hate driven. In the other films the deaths were sad, but in this, every kill feels personal and malicious. It’s explained later why that is, but shifting the usual narrative really helps this film stand out from the others. Even the atmosphere outside reinforces this, as it's always cloudy, and the sun rarely shines, unless some sort of divine intervention occurs, and that’s all I’ll say about that. It’s almost like a looming cloud of misery is hanging over the town
Setting this film in a church has its advantages, as the main theme revolves around faith and religion. Other themes, like morality, ethics, power dynamics, loyalty, and deception are also present, but faith remains the central focus. The characters discuss their beliefs and how these convictions shape their daily lives, with Josh O’Connor’s character in particular struggling and raising some thought provoking questions. The cinematography is also impressive, with some exceptionally clean and striking shots that help the film express its unique style 
Setting the film in a church also opens the door for jokes about religion, but I found them to be unfunny. Religion based humour is so overused that it just comes across as lazy or arrogant. If you’re going to include those kinds of jokes, they should be at least original. Don’t recycle ideas that have been done before
This trilogy is basically the better version of what Murder on the Orient Express, Death on the Nile, and A Haunting in Venice tried to be 
If you’re interested in watching this, you don’t need to have seen the other two films to understand the story, but watching them will give you a better sense of what this franchise is about 
Overall, Wake Up Dead Man is a strong and entertaining addition to the Knives Out trilogy, with a few minor issues, but nothing major

Title: Critters 3
Comment:
So I started my Critters journey with the fourth installment while completing an actor’s filmography. Now, I’m watching the third. I guess the logical order would be to continue with the second and then the original. Interestingly, the films seem to improve slightly with each one I watch in reverse. At least this one actually features more of the title creatures tearing, biting, and killing people around.
The creatures’ destructive humor isn’t nearly as memorable or funny as the Gremlins, but whenever they’re on screen, the film definitely perks up. The humor is very hit or miss— that scene with Blackie screeching and yelling was downright hilarious, but everything involving the humans felt kind of boring. It’s always wild to see major stars in these films; here, we have none other than DiCaprio making his film debut. Going from this to This Boy’s Life is wild—you wouldn’t guess you were watching a future star and Academy Award winner by seeing this, but hey, everyone has to start somewhere. He wasn’t terrible here, though his role isn’t very memorable. Again, the human stuff is mostly dull, except maybe Opper as this eccentric man.
All in all, the first half drags a bit, but once the Critters action kicks into full gear—especially in much of the third act—the film becomes more entertaining. I just wish the rest had been as cool.

Title: Singin’ in the Rain
Comment:
2025 Alphabet Challenge Letter S: Singin’ in the Rain
Previous: Rear Window
🎵What a glorious feeling, Im happy again!🎶
Singin in the Rain is pure cinematic magic, and a heartwarming tribute to the history and art of filmmaking in one of its most chaotic times. Its one of those perfect comfort films, an uplifting experience from start to finish, using the setting of the transition from silent films to talkies as a backdrop for some great music, fun drama, funny characters (love Cosmo, loathe Lina), and a heartwarming story from start to one of the most satisfying endings ive ever seen. All the characters and performances were fantastic, with all time great roles from Gene Kelly, Debbie Reynolds, Donald O’Connor and Jean Hagan. Jean Hagan as Lina Lamont is absolutely vile and the perfect hatable antagonist, yet i kinda couldnt help but feel for her as her entire profession is upheaved by the fact people dont like her voice yet shes made the villain for being upset at the fact the characters replace her voice entirely to make their musical. I think it kinda hit me that way since I watched Damien Chezelle’s Babylon before this which shows the darker more real sides of this era of filmmaking and how actors were treated whereas this is very whimsical and fun filled. Babylon also pays incredible tribute to this film, I think I felt what that guy felt watching this. This was so technically perfect in its production design, cinematography, musical choreography and song and script writing combined with incredibly endearing characters all make for a movie thats the perfect testament to why the art of film is so enjoyable. All the musical numbers were really fun and superbly well made, and jts clear theres a ton of talent on display on screen at all times.
Singin in the Rain is funny, touching, dramatic, heartwarming and incredibly immersive as its story and production sweep the viewer away in a way only the best movies do. I think it has something for everyone to enjoy, and even people who dont usually gravitate towards traditional musicals like me can find plenty of fun in the fascinating history of filmmaking it portrays and its heartfelt tribute it pays towards that. Its just about one of the most straight up happy and comfort food type of movies ive ever seen, and that Singin in the Rain song segment is absolutely mesmerizing and cinematic art in its purest form. A must see for all film lovers and a great time for casual audiences, one of the best and gets ny highest recommendation!

Title: Eternity
Comment:
Eternity is a long time to have regrets.
I wish I had to choose between Callum Turner and Miles Teller to live together forever. It's like heaven!
Sharing eternity with someone. I don't know about you, but I can't imagine it. Maybe because I'm still a boring bachelor, but spending eternity with someone is crazy. We fall in love with someone, break up, make up, we marry, abandon each other, desire, get bored... These things happen in a single possibility, in a single life, in a single heart. That's why they bring excitement, then peace that becomes a habit over time. But to experience all these infinite possibilities and memories with just one person, I don't know. It's actually romantic. Maybe that's what love is like—wanting to stay together forever despite all the monotony. I wonder which eternity I would choose? There are endless options. Maybe would choose cinema eternity and watch movies 24/7. Or I could be a badass detective from Victorian era. Or a vampire rockstar from 80s. I have so many options. I can't even decide what to have for lunch! And definitely want my twin by my side. No man has such similar tastes with mine, so don't need a husband who will live with me forever.
Joan's choice was difficult. She choose her magical, perfect, dreamy first love, left unfinished, or her simple but sincere life partner, with whom she had spent 65 years in life? The story is interesting, sweet, wholesome. It was full of surprises and felt good to watch. One of those movies that makes you believe in love, but I prefer the ones that make you depressive and hate love. This was too hopelessly romantic. Who would wait 67 years for someone? It's unfair to criticize this film seriously. Just walk into the theater and be sure to leave with a big smile. If you have a lover, definitely watch this with them. If not, don't worry there might be a Callum Turner waiting for you in other life.
Here's an alternative 5 stars scenario:
Remember when Larry and Luke first met. Larry saw him in that bar, and the first thing he said was, "who are you, an angel?" Then they will unable to resist their feelings for each other, and embark on the "bromance eternity" together. Joan, meanwhile, went to Paris with her best friend. Perfect scenario. I want a romcom starring Callum and Miles, now!

Title: Bicycle Thieves
Comment:
A simple concept, told with so much heart. What I loved most is how honest it feels. It stays in that gray area where good people can still make bad choices, and where surviving doesn’t always come with dignity.
What makes it hurt more is how the movie never tries to push your emotions with big speeches or dramatic music. It just lets you watch this man try, and try, and try again. There’s a dignity in how he keeps going even when things get humiliating.
And then there’s the kid. Honestly, he’s the soul of the movie. The way he watches his dad fall apart little by little is somehow more heartbreaking than anything the movie spells out.

Title: All That Jazz
Comment:
All That Jazz uses theatrical choreography to examine life, regret, and death in the shadow of show business. The plot follows Joe Gideon as his life of prescription drugs, multiple women, and his fixation on perfecting his craft eventually take their toll.
While I admit that showtunes and theater musicals are not my favorite subject, I was mesmerized by the direction. The production value is top notch and the frequent dips into dreams/hallucinations add a surreal element that complements the themes of mortality. Scheider is incredible in his most auteur role yet and shines in both the obsessive drive and inherent fallibility of this man.
The sound design and editing were also excellent. Whether it’s the elimination of noise to convey Joe’s floating psyche or frantic cuts to match his raising heart rate, the audience is placed inside Joe’s head and feels every downward trajectory that he does.
While I felt all of the musical numbers were well designed, some of them were a little long for my taste. The pacing also drags in the second half of the film while repeating a few of its favorite tropes.
It’s a story that normally wouldn’t be that interesting to me, but is done with spectacular execution. The final result is an enthralling journey that both embraces the faults in our lives while also accepting inevitable end that we all face.

Title: Materialists
Comment:
Amores Materialistas começa com um certo charme, aquele ar romcom moderna toda iluminada e com trilha animada, só que tudo vai perdendo força no caminho.
O primeiro trabalho da Celine Song foi tão cheio de personalidade que a comparação surge sem nenhum esforço. Quando alguém chega com um trabalho tão forte, é natural esperar que o próximo refine tudo aquilo que já tinha de bom. E aqui, isso não acontece.
A ideia até tem um brilho inicial. Falar sobre relacionamentos atravessados por desejos materiais, padrões de vida e expectativas sociais poderia render algo realmente interessante. O problema é que tudo é trabalhado de forma tão direta e previsível que perde qualquer interesse maior.
Eu queria me conectar mais com os personagens, mas senti que eles existiam muito mais como símbolos do que como pessoas. Falta profundidade nas relações e faltam camadas emocionais que sustentem tudo o que o filme tenta propor. Por mais que a estética e o clima tenham seus momentos, nada disso segura o peso do que ele pretende discutir.
O resultado final funciona de maneira leve, ainda que distante da profundidade que parecia possível no começo. A intenção da diretora é perceptível, embora isso não se traduza completamente.

Title: Daybreak
Comment:
On the surface, Marcel Carné's Daybreak is a heart-pounding, claustrophobic thriller built on a then-revolutionary use of a non-linear, flashback-driven narrative — and this was two years before Orson Welles' Citizen Kane. On that surface level, one can watch the film and find every reason to love it. But you also have to appreciate the existential poetry of Jacques Prévert's script, which unfolds like the raw and penetrating lyrics of a tragicomic symphony, speaking the deepest truths about life and rejection, as well as the fiery and haunting performance of Jean Gabin as François, a simple foundry worker who becomes, despite himself, first the immediate instrument and then the collateral victim of an unexpected killing.
“Unexpected” is the word, since it’s with gunshots that the film opens: a murder has just happened off-screen. We only see someone leaving the apartment, his hand on his belly, then tumbling down the stairs until landing at the feet of a blind resident — of all the witnesses. Honest people shout for help, the police come, but the man inside won’t give himself up easily. He’s armed, he can protect himself, and he has all the time he needs to figure out what the next step is. The irony is that there’s no possible escape. The siege begins immediately; he’s literally cornered, and the apartment becomes a temporary but fragile shell of safety. He has some cigarettes, but like most resources, they are limited. Time is all he’s got, and it works like the countdown of a ticking bomb.
Not only Gabin, but also Arletty and Jules Berry, give many reasons to appreciate the film — yet it’s Gabin who steals every scene. Gabin is both the subject and the object: he’s the one who sets the plot in motion by killing, and he enriches our experience by telling us why he did it. The film has always been associated with the poetic-realism movement, but the notion that immediately emerges is fatalism. There’s a sense of impending doom hanging over François’ shoulders, and we know it’s only a matter of time before he is lured into the fatal action. But the film isn’t interested in the fate of François — who has already lost by the time we meet him — so much as in the circumstances that lead him to that act, because obviously he doesn’t strike you as a “typical” killer, does he?
The use of flashback is crucial because what we see confirms our doubts: he’s a decent man — rather friendly, despite his tough façade — but he’s driven into a dark corner because of a rivalry with a man who is everything he is not: an older, more manipulative, smooth-talking, upper-class erudite dog trainer, played with classy sneakiness by Jules Berry. Both men are in love with the same delicate woman, and she is too shy to reject either of them. She wasn’t the prettiest or the smartest, but she was gentle, innocent, and too much of a beautiful flower to let some manipulative, smooth-talking pervert corrupt her.
There’s a subplot involving an affair between Berry’s mistress — played by Arletty — and François, but it never distracts from the core of the film, which is the rising tension between two men and two different versions of humanity. Meanwhile, we are taken back to the apartment, which seems to grow smaller as the plot advances, and the situation becomes similar to the media circuses showcased in films like Dog Day Afternoon. One of the emotional climaxes of the film involves an angry monologue by Gabin directed at the crowd: he can’t stand the hypocrisy of a system that will label him a criminal while other men commit far crueler acts than plain killing. This is Gabin at his finest — a sign that he is a tragic figure in the making and won’t fully realize himself until the final act.
There’s something so premonitory in a film featuring a French man caught in a lonely place and forced to commit suicide because he simply can’t face the ugly reality. The film dates from 1939, before the war would put thousands of citizens in similar situations. The dawn that was about to break was an ugly one, forcing people to transcend their nature and ethics and do things they would not be proud of. The question raised by Gabin’s rant is, “Who are we to judge?” — and this question resonates even more powerfully when placed in the context of the film’s making. The film hasn’t lost any of its relevance today, like many of Gabin’s classics.
Here, he is at his most complex and tortured, yet somehow this is also his most decent character, which makes his ending even more tragic — or, given what was awaiting France, perhaps not as tragic as it seems. After a second thought, maybe he was lucky to get the hell out of the place, to be the master of his own destiny instead of surrendering to mediocrity.

Title: No Other Choice
Comment:
Eu não consegui assistir este filme na 49ª Mostra Internacional de Cinema, mas queria muito ter ido, e posso dizer que valeu a espera. A obra apresenta uma visão satírica e contundente sobre a precarização do trabalho e a pressão constante por produtividade. A narrativa acompanha Yoo
Man-soo, que perde seu emprego depois de vinte e cinco anos dedicados à fábrica de papel e faz de tudo para manter seu sustento. Em um mercado apertado e dominado pela tecnologia, ele começa a enxergar seus concorrentes como ameaças que precisa eliminar.
A narrativa encontra força na união entre humor ácido e tensão psicológica. Park Chan-wook cria diálogos afiados, e a direção complementa com planos precisos e uma montagem que mantém a história sempre interessante. Entre uma risada e outra, sentimos o peso de acompanhar um homem que tenta se agarrar à própria dignidade.
O impacto do filme cresce ao focar no ambiente doméstico. Ali, Man-soo, interpretado brilhantemente por Lee Byung-hun, que é um ator muito bom na moral, se desfaz diante de seus papéis como trabalhador, pai e marido. A história revela, de maneira delicada, o peso de perceber que tudo o que construiu pode desaparecer de repente.
O ponto que menos funciona está na repetição dos crimes ao longo do segundo ato, que às vezes afasta o foco do conflito familiar, onde a narrativa realmente se aprofunda. Ainda assim, sempre que o filme retorna ao espaço doméstico, recupera sua força emocional e satírica. É um filme muito ousado, brutal e surpreendentemente engraçado, transformando o desespero de um homem comum em um espelho distorcido, mas totalmente reconhecível do capitalismo contemporâneo.

Title: Black Swan
Comment:
“It was perfect.”
🎬 Score: 10/10
Never underestimate the power of rewatching. I saw Black Swan for the first time a little over a year ago and I remember liking it, but not thinking it was anything extraordinary. Now that I’m binging Isabela Boscov’s list of the 100 best films of the century, and with a little more cinematic baggage, I decided to revisit it, and it simply became one of my favorites. This is a true masterpiece.
Black Swan, directed by Darren Aronofsky, portrays in a poetic psychological thriller the relentless and destructive pursuit of an impossible perfection. Nina, a ballerina, achieves the great feat of being chosen to star in Swan Lake, but she doesn’t expect that, in order to embody both Odette and the Black Swan, she’ll have to let go of what she has always clung to and chased obsessively: perfection.
Natalie Portman deserved every single vote for Best Actress. She delivers a spectacular performance not only as Nina, capturing all the purity and insecurity of the White Swan, but also in portraying the gradual transformation into the Black Swan. Her gestures and expressions throughout the dance sequences translate Nina’s internal conflicts with astonishing precision. It’s also clear how desperately the character struggles to free herself from the perfectionism that has dictated her every move, to the point that she tries to achieve perfection in the act of being imperfect. Portman is undoubtedly one of the film’s best choice.
I was so invested in the movie that I barely wrote anything while watching. If you’ve been following my reviews for a while, you already know I’m obsessed with descent into madness arcs, and Black Swan elevates that to a spectacular level. The film uses every audiovisual resource at its disposal to portray Nina’s deteriorating mental state, giving a true lesson in symbolism and metaphor as she begins to live out, in her own reality, the story of the ballet she’s about to star in.
The score and cinematography tell the story just as powerfully as the script. Constantly contrasting white and black, light and shadow, not only referencing the dual roles Nina plays but also her internal conflict, the artistic choices are impeccable and translate her inner world majestically. Alongside the breathtaking music, the sound effects of wings flapping that we sometimes hear faintly in the background show the meticulousness of this sound design. This exceptional direction makes the dance scenes, especially the final one, striking and absolutely mesmerizing.
Finally, something I find perfect is how the film tackles so many themes like excessive self-pressure, self-harm, abuse of hierarchy, sexuality, self-esteem, maternal narcissism, aesthetic expectations placed on women, and of course, perfectionism, and manages to develop each of them not only satisfyingly, but in a way that ties directly into Nina’s core conflict.
Well, that’s all for Black Swan! I definitely want to watch more of Aronofsky’s work.
See you in the next review, and always remember: take a break from chasing perfection every now and then and just live a little (and you don’t need drugs for that, ok?)

Title: Sorry, Baby
Comment:
There are very few films as awkward as this one. It's got that rickety first film fragility, but at the same time it lobs a bunch of stilited Yorgos cadence at you. At first blush it's like swinging at a knuckleball when you are expecting a fastball. It reminded me a lot of Train Dreams in that once you get on its wonky rhythm it kinda just falls into place and wins you over.
I don’t know what to think about all this, but I do know that writer/director/star Eva Victor has got a great eye for composition. Almost every scene is framed in a visually stimulating way and that's enough to hold your interest for awhile. Also, a dude says "ahoy" as a greeting and there are no boats around. I’m going to start doing that.
The story just wasn't grabbing me at all though at first. It was a struggle to pay attention at times. Then Sally Bugs from The Irishman shows up, something unexpected happens, and the film cracks into a million tiny pieces. We spend the rest of the film gathering these pieces and wondering which direction the character is going to go, but it turns out she's just on a neverending merry go round of self-hatred (aren't we all?). It's like the plug is pulled from the bathtub and we just watch the water slowly swirl down the drain. Maybe this film should have just been called "The Bathtub" because there is not one, but two incredible monologues given by the lead character while sitting in the tub. This dialogue is a lot more lacerating than when she talks to the cat she finds (movie poster) or her friend's baby (movie title).
However great Victor the actress is here, and she should probably be nominated for this, it's the "Yam with a mouth on it" speech from John Carroll Lynch that single-handedly ties the whole film together like the dude's rug. Wow is that guy good. He's in one damn scene and it totally makes the whole movie. I had to hand out a passing grade at that point for what is a promising, yet somewhat uneven debut from wunderkind triple threat Eva Victor.

Title: The Blair Witch Project
Comment:
I haven't seen this since it was in the theatres; scanning through streaming for something made before the year 2000 led me to impulsively put it on. On reappraisal, it's better than I remembered, but the primary features that irked me when I first saw it still irk me today - I just have a better vocabulary to express it.
Specifically, the repetitive nature of the arguments and the constant need to fill the silence with narration don't add to the attempted authenticity enough to overcome how much they detract from the atmosphere. Knowing that this is a debut film leavens the frustration, knowing what they are going for helps, but ultimately, this is still a work of fiction whose primary goal was to evoke horror, fear, terror, dread, creepiness, all the wonderful things that come with the genre, and it let its concept overwhelm its purpose.
Found footage has a lot of potential. The marketing campaign that went with this, much as the one with Cannibal Holocaust did, heightened the atmosphere of the film for those willing to buy into it. It was a fun gimmick; the sensation helped pack the theatres eventually. But the point of found footage and its attempts to convince you what you are seeing is real is to heighten the fear it evokes, and the marketing - the old "this is real, these people are missing!" canard - eventually and inevitably backfired, breaking the spell as much as it heightened it.
Similarly, its improvised dialogue works save for the omnipresence of it. It's not unrealistic - well, mostly - but in trying to remain authentic to how people in this situation would act, it ultimately distracts from the other aspects that make this work - the sounds of the forest, the encroaching darkness, the distant and unexplained noises. It's at its best when they shut up and let the atmosphere creep in, but this is often short-lived. It's a little bit of "show, don't tell" and a lot of "quit reminding us that you're there and we aren't". The power to scare us is to let us feel present with you.
I feel like when it first came out, it attained a mixture of mainstream success and cult status, as well as plenty of backlash and petulant press about its shaky cam nausea. Found footage has always been a frustrating genre when it comes to breaking its own premise, but this one did better than most at adhering to the concept. I am sure it's possible to nitpick it (when she's filming the bloody shirt fragment, for example, it just feels like she would pull away from it and lose focus more, see? nitpicking!) and find the spots where it doesn't work, but compared to many modern found footage films, it's a breath of fresh air.
Of course, this movie is beloved by millions; if it works for you, great. But it's hard to watch this and not want them to stop shouting for Josh or bickering and let the wooden symbols and eerie sounds dominate long enough to let us immerse in their environment. It's hard to watch this and not think it's almost perfect. How frustrating they didn't trust themselves enough to let us soak it in.

Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
This is the best one of the Knives Out trilogy! My biggest gripe with the last two entries is that I could figure out the mystery within the first act, but this one actually kept me guessing the whole time, which made it so god damn fun!
The cast in this one is also pretty on par with the first film. I do wish we got a bit more from Andrew Scott and Cailee Spaeny. We deserved at least 3 more scenes of Spaeny smoking a cigarette. Josh O’Connor is the lead of this film, and he is fucking excellent. I think this will be the film that opens many more people’s eyes to him and shows just how damn talented he is. Even though Craig’s Benoit Blanc is the heart and soul of this series, O’Connor matches his energy perfectly and doesn’t miss a single beat. I also loved how much fun Daniel Craig gets to have in this outing as Blanc. Yes, he lets loose in the previous films, but here he is completely unhinged and lays it all out on the table. Josh Brolin is excellent too. What a year he’s had. He is absolutely dominating every role he has taken on in 2025 and is one of the best parts of each film. He’s so funny yet menacing in this. I do think Jeremy Renner was miscast. He didn’t really do much for me in his role, but it was still nice to see him back on the big screen.
The cinematography in this film is really great too. There are plenty of beautifully crafted scenes that were so satisfying to see on the big screen. It really proves that these are films meant to be experienced in a theatre first and not at home. The pacing is incredible too. For an almost 2 and a half hour film, this absolutely flew by.
What a fun time out at the movies! I give this a strong 4 out of 5 stars, maybe even a 4.5 on a rewatch. I 100% recommend checking this out as soon as possible, and hopefully you can catch it on the big screen. For my American readers, this would be a great film to catch with your family over the long holiday weekend. This is easily my favorite of the series, and I hope we get even more entries. I really think we need one every 3-4 years. SCOOBY DOOBY DOO!

Title: The Seventh Seal
Comment:
A film I ended up enjoying way more for its look than its actual narrative. Every shot is so good to look at, haunting, calm, and gorgeous, like the director turned a medieval tale into a moving art gallery. The use of dark imagery and symbolism definitely boosts the film’s philosophical visualization, even if half of the actual meanings flew over my head. For some reason I thought the entire movie was just the knight and Death sitting on the beach playing chess for an hour, I mean that’s the only clip of a scene people keep talked on social media, so I assumed that was the whole thing. Anyway, the medieval plague setting actually gives the film this eerie, dreamlike vibe that makes it even prettier, some frames genuinely look like paintings.
Now the story, it's "intellectually stimulating" at some point, sure, but it can also feel pretty alienating(?), it will piss off some audiences, especially those who actually really tried to understand, like me. But the minimal using of soundtrack works tho, matching the somber tone and keeping everything quiet and personal. The whole point of the story is that the protagonist has lost his faith, one of few things I noticed, at the start he’s terrified of Death, desperately trying to find some deeper meaning to keep going, yet by the end, he just accepts his fate, whatever it is. Yeah, it’s heavy and philosophical, but it wasn’t emotionally draining or too depressing. Death as a character is fun enough, even if the roles don’t require huge acting skills in my opinion, just follow the direction. I agree it’s a great movie, just not something I’d voluntarily rewatch. Too deep and too much hidden things to dig up, and almost every conversations feels like a philosophical debates instead of normal human interactions. It doesn’t feel like a narrative, more like a big abstract idea turned into a film. Overall, it's still fun to watch.
8/10 for a proper homework for your film class.

Title: Frankenstein
Comment:
Based on Mary Shelley's iconic novel, Frankenstein is a gorgeous Gothic tale, oozing with elaborate costumes and sets. Del Toro's passion fuels the movie, creating an honest adaptation infused with sophistication and, like Frankenstein's monster, forged with heart and humanity.
Jacob Elordi's performance eclipsed all else; an almost impossible task to achieve, considering everyone gave outstanding texture and detail to their characters. Not only does he bring a great emotional depth, but it is also a very physically demanding role. It's been phenomenal listening to his praises centred around Frankenstein and the creature. He truly deserves the complimentary recognition. I was beyond shocked by his transformation.
I think we should discuss the movie's settings and just how stunning they were. I was particularly fond of the stone buildings; they have a classic beauty that modern architecture lacks. They are a testament to enduring quality, enriched with history. My latest dream is to eventually own a gothic home crafted from stone, and a cute little garden to grow vegetables and blossom flowers.
My biggest complaint is that I was robbed of watching Frankenstein on the big screen, with a bucket of popcorn. None of my local cinemas was playing it, so I feel incredibly envious towards those who were blessed with such an experience. However, I must say Netflix have been surprising me recently.

Title: Bowfinger
Comment:
“You wrote a great script, your accounting days are over!”
Bowfinger is a man of many promises. When you rock a pony like Robert K. Bowfinger, you are instantly shown to give no fucks. What a glorious silver fox tail stapled to the back of Martin’s head! Why did Martin not wear it for the whole film? Coward! My favorite cinematic prop, the fake ponytail, accept no substitutes.
"The white man takes all the best catch phrases."
Eddie Murphy is so good in this. This has to be top 5 Murphy. I don't think casual filmgoer remembers how fucking funny he is in this movie. Even before "Jiff" appears he is murdering everything in sight.
“KKK appears in this script 486 times!”
“Tell 'em the spear chucker said hello!” while shooting the cymbals on a random drum set that’s sitting in his office?
The whole "happy premises" mantra sesh with Terence Stamp at "MIND HEAD"??
“There is no giant foot trying to squash me.”
“I HAVE to show it to the laker girls.”
“Find me a script with a retarded slave!”
“They inhale your gonads!”
I'm dead. This film was kind of the last of the Mohicans for a certain type of mean-spirited comedy spoof. This thing runs like a Swiss watch. No dead spots.
“When you hit 50 they don’t hire you anymore, it’s like they can smell 50.”
Boy did that line sting this time around for old dad rock. Every movie costs 2,184 dollars cash in ‘Fingerland and everyone has the personality of a zip code in Kansas. Martin is great here, it might be the last time he was actually funny, but Jiff Ramsey might be Eddie’s greatest creation. Murphy’s performance towers over every other bit in the film. Just the voice alone is fucking crazy. 
Martin and Murphy put on a clinic during the whole "acting in traffic" sequence. “Your errand is to run across the freeway until I say cut.” Then Jiffs face when Heather Graham shows her boobs. Omg Lolol. And the whole “You actually have some plutonium?” scene with Kit (while Jiff sneaks around trying to hang a mic off the roof). I was freaking dying. I haven't laughed this hard in a looooong time. What do you think Charlie Murphy thought of Jiff? I'd have loved to sit behind Eddie and Charlie at a screening of this.
Bowfinger is light and airy like a really good SNL sketch that you don’t want to end, yet it still leaves you wanting more. There’s a bite and meanness to the satire that you just don’t see in farcical 90 min comedies anymore (the "romance" in it is the meanest and most nihilistic part of it). It's just really good writing that’s made to look bad. A very hard thing to do for a writer is to write bad on purpose and still have it come off as intelligent satire. Co-writer Martin still had the goods here. 
It's even harder for the actors to pull these endless bits off without sturdy, capable direction. Enter Frank Oz. Do we have to consider him an auteur? Bowfinger, Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, and What About Bob? are all world comedies. They actually should have let Oz make Fake Purse Ninjas for real. I am being serious. Let's go to Taiwan baby!

Title: Train Dreams
Comment:
“That day, as he lost all sense of up and down, in that moment he felt connected to it all”
Really impressive! What a random surprise for the 2025, but a welcome one. The annoying streaming monster that is Netflix has produced some of the best films of the year in Frankenstein, Wake Up Deadman, Kpop Demon Hunters and now Train Dreams
Train Dreams is easily one of the best looking movies ive seen come out in 2025. The cinematography is jaw droppingly beautiful and is filled with amazing scenic shots of north american landscapes. The movie goes beyond just showinf off natural beauty to display fantastic pieces of blocking and incredible intimate lighting. It makes for a movie that is just pleasing to see and to get emmersed in its beautiful setting even if the plot may not be the most fast paced or riveting. Id say the movies biggest hurdle for people to get passed is that it feels like “oscar-bait drama” type of movies that always come out this time of year, films that tend to be slower paced, character driven slowburns.  However, the movie is so technically impressive and effective in telling its themes that the slow pace works in its favour, as it is able to allow more time to build up the characters personalities. 
The slow burn story is one about men’s search for the American dream during America’s expansion westward and the greed fueled need to build railroads there. The story only begins here, and expands over 80 years of the protagonists life as he is witness to America’s many changes with technology and culture. The movie hammers home a feeling of futility, as the main character of this Robert Grainer constantly does his job well yet is unable to truly advance in life with constant setbacks and a feeling that life is always moving our goalposts in the ever changing world. The film has many references to the capitalistic machine that is America and its need to destroy land and places of nature that have existed long before humanity began ruining the world, and the movie goes on to show how this remains throughout all Robert’s life. Robert Grainer represents a sort of stocism in the face of lifes troubles, as he is searching to find some peace in his life even in the face of heartbreaking loss and tragedy. He is a witness to how the search for the American dream chews people and nature up and spits them out, and that most of us have little power to change it and all we can do is find out our peace and happiness within the time were given. Despite how dark much of the movie can feel, it also has this cozy vibe to it at times as its just a man quietly working and living on his own in spite of hardship and combined with the incredible camera work it makes for a strange but enjoyable vibe. Its also helped by the fact that Robert’s story is also about finding happiness and contentment in a life even through all the hardships we experience. 
Its probably the best performance ive ever seen from Joel Edgerton. Hes always been that great supporting actor to me whose always trying to do a good job when playing characters who are often unlikeable or uncharismatic. He was fantastic here, and gives a subtle and introspective performance in a character that really lends itself to his style. He plays Robert Grainier’s stern stoicism and quiet sorrow equally well, and its captivating to watch in both instances. The rare times you see him truly happy, he makes you feel it. Probably one of the best lead performances ive seen this year. The movie also has some stellar supporting performances from Felicity Jones, Kerry Condon and William H Macy. Also had some great narration to tie the story together done by 
Overall, didnt really have any hype for Train Dreams but the glowing reviews its been getting made me curious enough to give it a try. Its admittedly slow paced and not the most gripping film for how long it is, but it also uses that time to build a great character story of a man working to survive as America expands its territory. Its a story following a protagonist who makes every small thing he feels feel valuable and profound, and its endearing to see him struggle and survive in the face of a world that pushes against him in ways he can never understand. Some of the most beautiful cinematography with some of the most emotionally moving moments you will see this year, and honestly is worth seeing just for the amazing scenic views the movie provides. A slow burn but a very well done one, recommend!

Title: If I Had Legs I’d Kick You
Comment:
"Maybe I got rid of the wrong one."
Anxiety, nervous breakdown, panic attacks, stress overdose, humiliation, screams, depression. I don't know what I was expecting from this, but I didn't expect to experience all of these at the same time! I will NEVER EVER watch this again. I can't do this to myself. Huge birth control propaganda, and I fell for it.
Linda is caring for her sick daughter. She's tasked with feeding her child food and IV fluids so she can reach her weight goal and get rid of the tube in her abdomen. Her husband is working remotely, and he doesn't hesitate to issue "gentle" commands over the phone, as if he were remote control. While dealing with the hole in her daughter's abdomen, Linda is also shocked by the massive hole in the ceiling of her house. After their house is flooded, they check into a motel. Motel, her husband, alcoholism, depression, spoiled daughter, doctors at the hospital, her own patients... They all drive her crazy. I feel so bad for Linda. She has no life of her own. She only does what she has to do, not what she wants. The only time she has for herself is drinking in the dark motel garden after her daughter is asleep. She surrenders to alcohol, give the control to something else. She wants her thoughts to disappear, her responsibilities to vanish. No one helps her, not even her therapist. She has to take her daughter to hospital every day, feed her, be always kind to her, give her husband daily report, and do therapy for her patients. In the time she has left to herself, people call her an "alcoholic" or a bad mother. She already gives 100%, and they want her to give everything, to give her all for her daughter. But no one blames her husband because he works away. Women are treated as if they have to be mothers. And when they do, people are never satisfied with their "motherhood." Fathers occasionally care for their children, while mothers can't even get an hour of peace of mind. It's maddening! Why are men always the ones who want to have children? That's why. The only thing that will change in their lives will be a cute baby and a few expenses. Mothers' lives will be changed forever. Linda didn't deserve this and she held on so well. I could never.
Whenever I say don't want to get married because I don't want to waste my life doing housework, taking care of kids, etc, people say, "come on, your husband will help you." Excuse me, but help?? We should do these things halfway, not help. I know women are burdened with tons because they're so resilient and strong, and they can handle it, but I don't have to live with that burden. None of us do. Linda, I want to pay for your therapy and be your lawyer in divorce case.
P.s> The daughter was worse than Chucky. So annoying, scary.

Buenísima película, gran cinta de artes marciales.
"The 36th Chamber of Shaolin" es un clásico dentro de su género, una película con una historia de venganza buenísima con escenas muy bien realizadas donde se nota el talento de quienes las hacían.
Sinopsis: Un joven aprende duras lecciones de kung fu para vengar a su familia asesinada.
La historia es buenísima, para la época una locura. Es una trama de venganza con un desarrollo típico pero que tiene su encanto gracias a que se me hace muy original el hecho de ir pasando de prueba en prueba, viendo el desarrollo del protagonista para lograr su objetivo. Lo que más destaca son las escenas de acción a mi parecer, aunque también todo lo que vemos en las pruebas es muy interesante. Algunas como la pelea final me parecen grandiosas secuencias, mucho mejor realizadas de lo que esperaba. Eso si, la historia es un poco predecible y hay cosas como el final que lo sentí un poco abrupto, el montaje fue medio raro ahí. Por último, el ritmo que tiene al principio es un poco lento pero después remonta muchísimo a mi parecer, las casi dos horas se me pasaron rápido.
Los personajes me gustaron mucho, sobretodo el protagonista. Liu Yu-de/San Ta es un gran protagonista con un excelente desarrollo donde vemos toda la evolución que tiene hasta ser un maestro del kung fu. Después el otro que destaca es Tien Ta como el principal villano, quien está bien pero siento que podría haber sido mejor ya que no tiene tanto desarrollo, pero como rival final del protagonista y fundamental para la venganza que tiene que llevar a cabo me parece más que decente.

Por otro lado, la dirección de Lau Kar-leung es buenísima, no conocía a éste director y me sorprendió mucho, tengo que verme más de su filmografía si todas las películas tienen éste estilo. Para finalizar, la banda sonora es decente y no mucho más, podría haber sido un poco mejor.
En conclusión, una gran película con una historia genial y muy entretenida a pesar de que arranque un poco lenta, logrando sostenerse gracias al desarrollo simple pero efectivo de su trama donde hay secuencias de acción muy bien ejecutadas. La recomiendo.
