Title: Rogue Male
Comment:
In early 1939, with the Second World War looming, English aristocrat Sir Robert Hunter embarks on a ‘sporting stalk’ of the deadliest of prey: Adolf Hitler. Captured by the Gestapo and left for dead, Sir Robert soon becomes the hunted on a chase from the Bavarian mountains to the wilds of the English countryside, where he will need all his sportsman’s wit and guile to survive.
Peter O'Toole is wonderful in the lead as Sir Robert, he was just a class act and that’s perfectly carried over into his role here. An aristocrat, he’s extremely posh yet feisty and witty. He’s really put through the ringer in Rogue Male, he’s tortured, pushed down a cliff and left for dead, literally crawls his way to potential safety, is locked away in the bowels of a ship to get back to England, is mercilessly pursued by the Nazis and has to survive in horrible conditions. It’s a tour-de-force performance, he really conveys the stress, exhaustion and fear of a man on the run, all the while keeping a stiff upper lip and humour. John Standing is great as Major Quive-Smith, the man in pursuit. The two share several scenes where the dialogue is brilliant. The great Alastair Sim in his last ever film role is magnetic as The Earl, Sir Robert's uncle. He was close to death at the time, he literally climbed out of his sick bed, saying, "Peter needs me."
It’s exceptionally well directed by Clive Donner, despite being a made-for-TV adaptation shown on the BBC it’s incredibly cinematic. Although not explicitly shown, the aftermath of his interrogation is brutal, the film moves at a brilliant pace as Robert is caught, pushed down the cliff, escapes and then even back in England needs to go back on the run, the final 40 minutes or so despite never being boring, the pace does noticeably slow and for a while almost completely stalls. I don’t usually appreciate flashback scenes, in this they came at a time where they really felt welcome and really explains Sir Robert’s attitude and motivations.
Despite its low budget, the finished film was regarded by the BBC as being suitable for a cinema release internationally. This had the potential to cause legal and industrial problems in the UK, because the crew had not been paid at the rate applicable to cinema releases. The BBC decided to terminate screenings in the UK and disallow future screenings in the UK. In an interview with Francine Stock for BBC Radio 4’s Film Programme in 2007, Peter O’Toole named the film as his favourite among those that he had made.
The story was previously filmed by Fritz Lang as Man Hunt (1941). This was a very free adaptation – Geoffrey Household later said that Lang had “made a smashing film”, but it hadn’t been much like the book. This television version also took several liberties, but was generally closer in plot and it, too, won praise from the author.
Michael Byrne plays a Nazi interrogator in this film and would go on to play a very similar role, that of a vicious Nazi officer, in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989). Whereas Michael Sheard plays Adolf Hitler in both this and the aforementioned Indiana Jones film.
I had a really good time with Rogue Male, I adored the performances, the first half is sensational but unfortunately I did feel the flatter second half lowers the overall rating. Overall I still think it’s a really well made, incredibly entertaining, brilliantly acted film that would have been outstanding had it kept the momentum of the first half through to the end.

Title: Pinocchio
Comment:
After watching Del Toro’s rendition, we can only refer to this as a piece of trash, and as you can see even the film references itself as such.
Baffingly lifeless, a shameful reiteration that manages to drain nearly every ounce of charm, wonder, and emotional sincerity from the original classic. In its place, we're left with a soulless CGI-fest and a script so uninspired it would cringe if it read itself. A really washed Robert Zemeckis/Tom Hanks duo, empty visuals and weightless sequences add to the mix as well, preventing any attempt of genuine storytelling. Giving as result something that’s not just dull—it’s an cheap imitation of what should be magical.
Its bizarre pacing drags you from one scene to another with no rhythm or purpose. Moments that should evoke whimsy or heartfelt emotion instead fall flat, buried beneath layers of unnecessary flourishes. Sentiments come and go rushed, humor feels forced, and the characters themselves lack depth. Pinocchio’s journey, which ought to be a touching tale of morality and belonging, instead feels like a checklist of scenes the filmmakers felt obligated to include rather than genuinely care about. There's no real growth, no meaningful connections—just a string of glossy, overproduced set pieces that fail to mask a complete absence of creativity or spark.
By the time the credits roll, one is left not only questioning the why of its existence, but wondering how a story steeped in joy and nostalgia could end up feeling so disconnected from its own heart. More than being a disappointment, it’s genuinely disheartening. We’ll need to rewatch Guillermo Del Toro’s stunning rendition to erase this from our memory.

34/100

Title: PUNKS△TRIANGLE
Comment:
Eu li o mangá antes de assistir à série — e, por isso mesmo, comecei PUNKS△TRIANGLE com aquela mistura de ansiedade e expectativa que só quem já tem as páginas decoradas entende. Existe um prazer particular em ver uma cena que você já conhecia ganhar movimento, som e cor. E, para minha surpresa, a adaptação funciona justamente nesses momentos: quando algo que antes era só imaginação no papel finalmente ganha forma na tela.
A primeira coisa que realmente me prendeu na adaptação foi a maneira como trabalharam a dupla identidade do Enaga/AE. No mangá isso já funcionava, mas ver na série deixou a diferença entre eles ainda mais marcante. É menos sobre peruca, chapéu ou roupas largas — e mais sobre postura, olhar, ritmo. Enaga é o estudante desajeitado, tímido, quase escondido dentro de si; AE é o modelo sedutor, seguro, com aquela presença que domina qualquer espaço. O impressionante é que nenhuma dessas versões parece uma máscara. São duas versões sinceras de si mesmo, coexistindo em conflito — e o Yasunari Fujibayashi faz essa transformação parecer tão natural que, por alguns momentos, você esquece que está vendo o mesmo ator.
Chiaki, por outro lado… olha. Eu queria gostar dele tanto quanto gostei no mangá, mas a série realmente não facilitou. Aquele olhar eternamente assustado, sempre à beira de pedir desculpa por existir; os lábios trêmulos; a boca semiaberta como se tivesse acabado de lembrar que esqueceu o gás ligado… Em certos momentos, eu só queria mandar uma mensagem pra produção pedindo um close a menos. Depois, não sei se acostumei ou se meu cérebro simplesmente decidiu poupar energia, mas a verdade é que parei de esperar nuance e passei apenas a aceitar o que vinha.
E, apesar de tudo, quando os dois dividem cena… funciona. De um lado, AE com aquela aura de perigo elegante; do outro, Enaga todo torto e adorável; e, no meio disso tudo, Chiaki reagindo como se estivesse apaixonado por duas pessoas diferentes — e, de certa forma, ele está mesmo. A química muda de tom conforme a identidade aparece: mais fofa e caótica com Enaga, mais tensa e sedutora com AE. É quase um triângulo amoroso sem triângulo nenhum, só esse jogo de versões que se esbarram — e Chiaki, sem perceber, acaba se apaixonando duas vezes pelo mesmo homem, como se estivesse destinado a gostar dele de todos os jeitos possíveis.
No geral, a adaptação é surpreendentemente fiel ao mangá — fiel o suficiente pra eu sorrir antecipando falas, gestos e até enquadramentos inteiros. As pequenas mudanças feitas aqui e ali até fazem sentido, principalmente por causa da classificação indicativa, então nada que faça arrancar os cabelos. O problema é que nem tudo que funciona no papel sobrevive intacto na tela: algumas expressões ficam caricatas demais e, principalmente, a enxurrada de flashbacks (juro que lembro do que aconteceu há dois minutos, obrigada) pesa mais do que deveria no live-action.
No fim das contas, PUNKS△TRIANGLE me deixou com aquela sensação gostosinha de revisitar algo que já era querido, só que sob outra luz — imperfeita, mas agradável de acompanhar. No balanço geral, é uma série de três estrelas: tem charme, tem química — mas também tem o Chiaki fazendo expressões tão dramáticas que, honestamente, eu já estava pronta para lhe oferecer um copo d’água e perguntar se ele precisava sentar um pouquinho.

Title: Fireworks
Comment:
“you really shouldn’t feel guilty about it.”
beyond our deepest struggles and fears, we often wonder what life has left to offer. for Nishi (Takeshi Kitano, though credited as Beat Takeshi) though, he’s feeling drowned by his own actions and the trajectory of life: the death of his young daughter a few years past, his wife’s terminal condition, and his tragic incident during his time in the police force — which his partner died from the hands of the suspect, whilst his fellow men were severely injured, one even ended up paralysed and now uses a wheelchair for accessibility; the weight of it all, bringing him down, yet he remains conscious for the moment — keeping it together for his wife, devoted to spending as much time with her until she goes. 
ending Noirvember on a touching note — Takeshi Kitano’s HANA-BI (Fireworks) features a plethora of emotive sequences, a heavenly score all due to the legendary Joe Hisaishi, and Kitano’s pieces of art — drawn by his own hands and conceived by his own vision. this was a surprisingly simple yet powerful addition to the world of cinema; despite Kitano’s comedic roots, he managed to build a narrative surrounding the melancholic and hopelessness of one’s own existence.  
“can you wait? just for a moment.”
Nishi spends the entire film covering his eyes with his dark sunglasses — as far as i’ve seen, not once did he ever take them off, yet, he’s still able to express his true feelings. those may say that ‘the eyes are the mirrors to your soul’ — in this case, his soul traverses in a deeply profound way without having a clear look at his optical vision. on surface, his presence looks stoic as ever… maybe this is his way of mourning what’s soon to be gone. 
as we view the calming waves of the beach, or look up to see the fireworks in the sky — HANA-BI reminds us to always find the beauty in simplicity; the things we take for granted, can also be the moments we hope to experience once again. 
“thank you… for everything.”

Title: The Third Man
Comment:
I actually never really heard of this film before, but since I was in Vienna and there was a screening at a cinema we almost walked past every day, I needed to watch this. I think it’s amazing and a unique experience to watch a film in the city it takes place in.
As for The Third Man, I can definitely see why it’s a film noir classic. It starts with an American named Holly Martins coming to Vienna to visit his friend, who apparently has a job for him. As he arrives, he learns that his friend Harry Lime died in a car accident. Holly begins to investigate the cause and background of this incident since it all seems a little bit implausible. From there on, the plot slowly unravels with multiple twists until we learn the truth about it all. 
The atmosphere we get thrown into is very grim, dark, and shadowy, which is also due to the film’s setting in postwar Vienna. You can still see how the city is deeply affected by the aftermath of the war, and it fits the overall tone of the film perfectly. It’s hard to describe it without giving any spoilers, honestly, but it really fits the themes addressed in it, which are, among others, friendship, loyalty, and morality. Lastly, the cinematography, especially with its use of multiple Dutch angles, adds to the tone and atmosphere.
Of course, the storytelling is probably the strongest part of the entire film. The way the story is written and told creates a lot of suspense until it finally resolves in the chase sequence in the sewers near the end of the film — which is btw probably the most remarkable and iconic scene of the entire film.
That said, I don’t know what to think of the score. I really couldn’t take it seriously, if I’m being honest. It reminded me a lot of the score of SpongeBob or Pumuckl (a German kids’ TV show), and it sounded a little too uplifting and playful. So it’s a little bit ambiguous considering the rather dark tone. But it lowkey makes it iconic and memorable, I’m torn on what to think about it yet, but the more I think about it, the more I like it.
What definitely enhanced my watching experience was exploring some of the filming locations right after we watched it at the cinema — whether it’s the Palais Pallavicini, the Josefsplatz, the statue of Joseph II, the Prater with the Ferris wheel, the Zentralfriedhof, or any other location. If you’re ever in Vienna, I can recommend going to the Burgkino (cinema) and watching The Third Man. They offer English screenings most of the time. (Your travel guide carina 😭)
I wanted to yap about my Vienna experience a little bit here because it was lowkey a fever dream, but my review is already too long (so maybe another time haha).

Title: Tere Ishk Mein
Comment:
went in with zero expectations which probably saved me because the film works only in parts and pieces. The story constantly feels forcefully stitched together like it’s trying too hard to be emotional without earning it. But if they want to call this a “spiritual sequel” to Raanjhanaa, then sorry they’ve misunderstood what made that film special. The screenplay feels borrowed from everywhere, never settling into its own identity. Some dialogues hit hard, while others just float by without meaning. Music wise, only the title track Tere Ishk Mein works; the rest barely registers. The climax arrives rushed, leaving no emotional residue. And the biggest flaw? Scenes never breathe. Anand L Rai jumps from moment to moment with such hurry that nothing lands, no moment stays and no emotion deepens. A film with potential, but one that keeps slipping through its own hands.

Directed by Quentin Tarantino, comes The Lost Chapter: Yuki's Revenge released in 2025, starring Uma Thurman, and Miyu Ishidate in this animated short, distributed by Epic Games
The short follows The Bride as she continues her journey to kill the remaining members of the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad, all while being hunted by Yuki Yubari, Gogo Yubari’s younger sister
I never would’ve imagined in my wildest dreams that we would ever get a Quentin Tarantino collab with Fortnite, let alone a lost chapter from over twenty years ago that’s animated. Just saying it out loud sounds unbelievable, but it’s true. This all came together because of the new Fortnite season, and with The Bride being part of the battle pass, negotiations for more content naturally followed. Tarantino being the guy he is, sent over the pitch for the forgotten chapter, they approved it, and the rest is history
The original scene showed Yuki following The Bride back to the U.S while chasing her through a suburban street, seeking revenge for her sister’s death. But because of pacing and budget constrictions, the scene was cut and eventually forgotten…. until now. Don’t worry though, if you didn’t get a chance to watch it or just don’t play Fortnite, it will be available to watch during Kill Bill: The Whole Bloody Affair
The short is eight minutes long and fully animated, giving us an action packed continuation of the Kill Bill series. I personally would’ve removed the Fortnite characters because they ruined the vibe of the short, but I guess that was one of the conditions of the collaboration. But having it animated was a great idea, since animation allows for things you can’t pull off in live action. It was also a surreal moment seeing Uma Thurman return to the role, even if she’s only voicing her character
Going forward, this opens the door to a lot of possibilities, and I hope we see more shorts or even full films premiere this way. A whole new generation of people have now been introduced to Tarantino’s work, so who knows what this collaboration might lead to next 
Overall, The Lost Chapter: Yuki's Revenge was a fun and creative short. I’m looking forward to seeing the complete story next week when Kill Bill: The Whole Bloody Affair releases

Title: The Social Network
Comment:
Hollywood used to make stories out of nothing. Michael Mann made a story about 2 guys talking about confidentialities and whistleblowing and turned it into an absolute masterclass of filmmaking with The Insider. Fincher did it with Facebook. Fincher made a movie about paperwork and percentages and turned that into one of the, if not the most important film of the past 2 decades. I mean, the opening and final sequences itself puts The Social Network in that conversation.
We first see Mark Zuckenberg being an absolute asshole to his at-the-time girlfriend. Although I later learnt that character was complete fabrication which irritated me a little bit because it is essentially the core of the film. But, getting back to the opening. Erica rightfully breaks up with him. Then Facebook happens. A couple people sue him. And then comes the final shot where Mark is sitting alone in his chair repeatedly refreshing his Facebook page waiting for Erica to follow him back. The irony. What a beautiful ending. How did I forget about this ending?
Two of the more brilliant moments in the film are ironically the ones where Mark Zuckenberg is being called out for being an asshole. Firstly, his ex Erica absolutely insulting him when he tries confronting her in a public space. Secondly, the infamous scene where Eduardo breaks Mark's laptop. The film tries to make Eduardo a saint a bit too much and tries very hard to make Sean Parker a proper jerk. Maybe he really was but props to the terrific Jessie Eisenberg for making Mark Zuckenberg look like an annoying but still somehow charismatic nerd while Zuckenberg probably was probably a straight out annoying douche with 0 personality.
And the pacing on this. The movie does not let you take your eyes off for one fucking second. Some of the most incredible editing I've come across. Feels chaotic at times but makes perfect sense. And that soundtrack is glorious, too. You can see Michael Mann's influence so clearly here. What would Hollywood be if not for Michael Mann? Look at me shamelessly sucking Michael Mann off in a Social Network review but it is what it is. Michael Mann is the man.

Title: The Last Samurai
Comment:
“You have your honour again…let me die with mine”
🫡😢
How I miss the 2000s, when there was an epic, enthralling movie releasing basically every year.

The Last Samurai tells the gripping story of the american Nathan Algren played by Tom Cruise as he takes part in the final stand of the Samurai during their rebellion against the modernizing government of Japan. This movie is often lumped in with “white saviour” narratives and is also often compared to Dances with Wolves, an earlier film also covering the topic of a white American soldier finding peace by living with an ancient culture that his own is helping to destroy. I dont think either of these points are true. It just flat out isnt a white saviour movie, and it would be more correct to say its a “White Witness” trope as its an american man witnessing a culture in its final hours rather than being able to truly effect its outcome. Id say its also different from Dances with Wolves as in that the Americans are just outright destroying the Lakota Sioux whereas here the Samurai must contend with their culture being changed around them in a way that no longer needs them, and are instead confronted by the reality of a nation that has lost its use for them. Its a difference thats important in establishing the major themes of honour within the Last Samurai, as the honour bound Samurai must choose between dying for the traditions they hold dear or changing to survive in shame. Of course, i have to mention the obvious inaccuracies of the Samurai not using guns (they fucking LOVED guns) and the fact that the movie is somewhat of a romanticized version of the Samurai rebellion, as it portrays them as simply fighting to preserve their culture despite the fact that culture includes having the right to abuse and lord over peasants. To be honest though, if you watch this and your only takeaway is “well that wasnt historically accurate” i can only assume you have the soul of a machine as the story is so emotionally captivating and epic its impossible not to find some enjoyment in.
The title “The Last Samurai” does not refer to Tom Cruises character, it refers to Katsumoto played by Ken Wantanabe, in what may be his greatest performance. Katsumoto is portrayed here as the embodiment of true samurai nobility, as he thinks what is happening to his country and people are wrong but he must also uphold his duty to the emperor. It makes for an epic and inspiring character, the kind we rarely see in the modern age of anti-heroes. Its also a character that is by their nature of their internal conflict, doomed (“I will die by the sword, my own…or my enemies”) yet his personality is so captivating you cant help but see it through to its tragic end. His friendship with Algren is really touching and interesting to watch develop, as its the heart and soul of the film and represents the movies ideas of the potential for human connection beyond race, language and nationality. Tom Cruise does a great job, playing a man riven with internal torment over his crimes in the past, and has a yearning to do better as a result of it. The whole cast of the film does a great job, notably Hiroyuki Sanada whose always a pleasure to see. Its a technically flawless film, with fantastic cinematography showing off the beauty of Japan, immaculate production design, a great moving score by Hans Zimmer, and epic battle scenes brought to life with amazing practical effects and a host of extras. It has basically everything that makes movies great, and is another example of a bygone era of movies that we just dont see the same calibre of anymore. Like big epic movies are still being made, but they just dont look as good or arent as well written as the classic blockbusters of old like this.
The Last Samurai has 2 rare things that epic blockbusters lately dont have: characters with principals worth remembering, and heart. Its an epic story about brotherhood, honour, and integrity set against the backdrop of the end of a culture during one the many messy transitions of history. Sure some of its pacing could be faster, it romanticizes samurai history and tells a story thats been told in other films about other cultures, but none of that hinders its quality or make the films narratice points any less impactful. Its an incredibly moving and character-driven story filled with epic battles scenes, and if you dont shed a tear watching this i dont know what to tell you, im not sure we can be friends. A childhood fave that still holds up, and is probably my favourite of these types of white-witness/saviour movies. Highly recommend

Title: The Long Walk
Comment:
English Version below🟠🟢🔵

Dank dem kleinen aber gutsitzenden Anstoß mit dem vor einigen Wochen geschehenen Heimkinorelease besagten Filmes „The Long Walk“, beendete ich binnen zwei Wochen die gleichnamige Romanvorlage oder wie im deutschsprachigen Raum besser bekannt unter dem Titel „Todesmarsch“, Stephen Kings 1979 erschienen bzw. erst 1987 auch in Deutschland (bzw. im deutschsprachigen Raum) veröffentlichen Roman.
Schließlich, nach besagtem Beenden der Romanvorlage, sah ich mir heute bzw. gestern die meines Wissens erste Adaption von oben genanntem Roman an. Und im nun vorhandenen Wissen um beide Quellen, hier die Review.

Als jemand der unter der Direktive Bücher kauft, allen voran Romane, die immer über die Dreihundertseitenmarke hinausgehen, am liebsten eher an die Fünfhundertseitenmarke und darüber hinaus, hier den Hauptgrund darin sieht, einfach nicht genügend tief eintauchen zu können, so als würde die Länge eines Romans gleichbedeutend dafür sein, wie intensiv die Immersion und das Eintauchen für einen ist, was ich in meinem persönlichen Fall einfach dick und fett unterstreichen muss, war die Skepsis bei dreihundertdreiundachtzig Taschenbuchseiten und gerade bei den eigenen Erfahrungen mit Stephen King der eigentlich durchwegs für seine üppigen, zeitaufwendigen Werke bekannt ist, durchwegs groß. Eine Skepsis die sich auch bei den erste fünfzig Seiten nicht legen wollte, sondern sie untermauerte, mich wieder daran erinnerte, Konzepte (allen voran Kammerspiele) funktionieren in Filmform deutlich besser als in Buchform für mich, wozu hier Stephen King seinen großen Beitrag leistete.
Soweit auf den Roman bezogen, führt Stephen King die Welt in „Todesmarsch“ mit ihren Charakteren eher solide, das eigene Können herunterschraubend und dämpfend ein anstelle, wie sonst auch, deutlich tiefer einzutauchen und im Tauchen darin mehr herauszuholen als vom Leser wohl je für möglich gehalten. Die Charaktere bekommen, soweit auf den Beginn des Romanes wie des (Todes)Marsch an sich bezogen, nur das nötigste an Profil und Hintergrundwissen verabreicht, was gleichbedeutend für den Schreibstil ist, was für mich „Todesmarsch“ zu einem der einsteigerfreundlichsten Kings mach (hier fasse ich Kings altes Ego Richard Bachman und ihn selbst als Stephen King zusammen). Einhergehend mit den wenigen Eckdaten die wir zu Beginn des Laufes von unseren Läufern bekommen, so schnell und kurz werden auch die Bedingungen des Todesmarsch zusammengefasst
Teilnehmer: Männer zwischen 14 – 17 Jahren
Laufgeschwindigkeit: mindestens 4 Meilen pro Stunde (ca. 6,4 km/h)
Verwarnungen: max. drei
Ursachen der Verwarnung: unterbieten folgender 4 Meilen pro Stundegrenze
Folgen: sofortige Liquidierung
Versorgung: Trinkwasser und Nahrungskonzentrate durch die die Teilnehmer begleitende US-Army
Mit fortlaufender Dauer des Lesens jedoch, zeigt sich wie gut Stephen King damit getan hat, die Charaktere eher rudimentär einzufangen und es nur punktiert zu intensivieren, ihnen nur hier und da etwas mehr Fleisch auf den Rippen zu verpassen das, soweit meine Eindrücke, bei zu viel die Figuren über den Marsch gestellt hätte wie eher ihre Beweggründe über den Lauf und die damit einhergehenden Beschwerlichkeiten, worauf es schlicht auch nicht ankommt. So schnell die Regeln innerhalb des Todesmarsch zusammengefasst werden können, King auch abseitsdavon keine große Hintergrundgeschichte über den Marsch selbst erzählt, so intensiv ist das Beiwohnen und das Mitverfolgen und eben das Mitgehen mit den Figuren auf ihrem Marsch in die eine Richtung, und nur in die eine Richtung, nach vorne.
Im Nachhinein völlig aufgehend, zu Beginn noch einige Fragen aufwerfend, ist der Umstand, wie durchaus lange sich King Zeit nimmt, den ersten und sich mehrenden Schrecken innerhalb unserer Läufer zu schildern ohne ihn auszuschlachten, eher in der Realität verankert zu sein. Erste Krämpfe entstehen, erste Übelkeit, erste Kopfschmerzen, erste Rückenschmerzen und erster Schnupfen. Zuvor noch wirft er uns gleich einmal den ersten Schrecken mit den Verwarnungen voraus. Verwarnungen gleich dem über einem schwebenden Damoklesschwert. Verwarnungen die zum eigenen Tod führen – unausweichlich, emotionslos, geschehend.
Um hier auch die Romanverfilmung aufzugreifen und den Kreis hierzu zu ziehen:
„The long Walk“ beginnt, kaum sind unsere Figuren mit dem Marsch gestartet, recht schnell mit den ersten Verwarnungen und Liquidierungen. Viel zu schnell, viel zu eilig, viel zu überhastet im fehlenden Vorspiel und dem Beiwohnen unserer Läufer während ihres eigenen Beginns des Marsches und der daraus sich zeigenden Charakterpalette und der Wirkung und der unausweichlichen Auswirkung mit ihrer Teilnahme.
Unteranderem schleicht sich von Minute Eins ein großer Fehler in den Film bzw. in die Produktion ein was eher ein Schleichen mit der trötenden Trompete voraus ist:
Wie bereits geschildert, sind die Bedingungen an den Todesmarsch wie an die Teilnehmer ihr Alter zwischen 14 – 17 Jahren. Egal wie oft es die Macher und der Film an sich uns vormachen will, keiner unserer Teilnehmer und Darsteller fällt annähernd in dieses Altersspektrum zwischen besagten 14 – 17 Jahren. Was die durchaus berechtigte Frage erlaubt und zulässt, warum man, also ich, das besonders erwähnen und hervorheben muss. Weil die Diskrepanz zwischen dem vorgegaukelten Alter und dem tatsächlichen einfach viel von der Härte und dem Schrecken nimmt, zumal kein einziger der Darsteller weder annähernd wie jemand mit dem Altersprofil aussieht noch es ist (dank der schnellen Recherche bewahrheitet sich auch diese Annahme).
Erwähnte ich zuvor noch wie sehr „Todesmarsch“ in der Realität verankert ist, die Liquidierungen und den Horror während des Marsches nicht ausschlachtet, ihn eher durch die Teilnehmer ausleben lässt, also durch das Mitverfolgen des langsamen Zerfalles aller Läufer, fehlt dieser Umstand hier gänzlich, zumal und abermals und zum wiederholten Male es wieder erwähnt werden muss, wie unvorteilhaft doch dieser allgemeine digitale Look mit dem CGI-Blut wie dem CGI-Mündungsfeuer und die Folgen zerschossener Gesichter und Köpfe sind. Vulgär ausgedrückt: zum abkotzen beschissen hässlich was jeden Impact, jede Gewichtung einem raubt.
Auch stellen sich die fehlenden Sympathien mit den Figuren mit fortlaufender Dauer auch nicht ein, wie es die Romanvorlage durch kleine persönliche Hintergrundgeschichten, durch die Gespräche und Dialoge und das darin Offenbaren der eigenen Charaktereigenschaften und der eigenen Persönlichkeit und den gefundenen Freunden für den einen Moment und den einen Marsch vollbringt.
Und warum auch immer das Ende umgeschrieben wurde, das Fazit bleibt selbiges:
In allen Belangen enttäuschend!!!

Science-Fiction

-------------------------------------------

Thanks to the small but well-timed boost provided by the home cinema release of the film “The Long Walk” a few weeks ago, I finished reading the novel of the same name within two weeks, or as it is better known in German-speaking countries under the title “Todesmarsch” (Death March). Stephen King's novel, published in 1979 and not released in Germany (or German-speaking countries) until 1987.
Finally, after finishing the novel, I watched what I believe to be the first adaptation of the above-mentioned novel today or yesterday. And now that I am familiar with both sources, here is my review.

As someone who buys books on a principle of always exceeding three hundred pages, preferably closer to five hundred and beyond, and whose main reason for skepticism is simply not being able to immerse themselves deeply enough—as if the length of a novel were synonymous with the intensity of immersion and engagement, a point I absolutely must emphasize in my own case—my skepticism was considerable when faced with three hundred and eighty-three paperback pages, especially given my own experiences with Stephen King, who is generally known for his lavish, time-consuming works. This skepticism persisted even after the first fifty pages, only being reinforced and reminding me that concepts (especially chamber dramas) work significantly better for me in film form than in book form, a fact to which Stephen King contributed greatly.
As far as the novel is concerned, Stephen King introduces the world and its characters in "The Long Walk" in a rather solid, understated way, instead of delving much deeper, as is usually the case, and extracting more from it than the reader would ever have thought possible. The characters, at least as far as the beginning of the novel and the (death) march itself are concerned, are given only the bare minimum of profile and backstory, which is synonymous with the writing style and makes "The Long Walk" one of King's most beginner-friendly novels for me (here I'm referring to King's alter ego Richard Bachman and himself as Stephen King). Along with the few basic facts we get from our runners at the start of the march, the conditions of the death march are also summarized quickly and briefly.
Participants: Males between 14 and 17 years old
Running speed: minimum 4 miles per hour (approx. 6.4 km/h)
Warnings: maximum three
Reasons for warning: running below the 4 mph limit
Consequences: immediate liquidation
Supplies: drinking water and nutrient concentrates provided by the accompanying US Army.
However, as the reading progresses, it becomes clear how well Stephen King captured the characters in a rather rudimentary way, only intensifying them sparingly, giving them a little more substance here and there. This, in my opinion, would have overemphasized the characters rather than the march itself, or perhaps their motivations over the march and its associated hardships, which, ultimately, isn't the point. While the rules of the death march can be summarized quickly, and King doesn't provide much of a backstory about the march itself, the experience of witnessing, following, and walking alongside the characters on their march in one direction only—forward—is incredibly intense.
In retrospect, it makes perfect sense, though initially it raises some questions. King's considerable time in describing the initial and growing horrors experienced by our runners, without exploiting them, feels grounded in reality. The first cramps appear, followed by nausea, headaches, backaches, and a runny nose. Before that, he immediately throws the first chilling warning at us. Warnings like a sword of Damocles hanging over the head. Warnings that lead to one's own death – inevitable, unemotional, happening.
To bring the film adaptation of the novel into the discussion and draw a parallel:
"The Long Walk" begins almost immediately after our characters start their march, with the first warnings and liquidations. It's far too fast, far too hasty, far too rushed, lacking any preamble or opportunity to observe our runners during their own start on the march, and thus failing to reveal the range of characters, the impact, and the inevitable consequences of their participation.
Among other things, a major error creeps into the film, or rather the production, from the very first minute—a kind of sneaky, almost overt, error:
As already mentioned, the conditions for the death march, as well as the participants' ages, are between 14 and 17. No matter how often the filmmakers and the film itself try to convince us otherwise, none of our participants or actors even come close to this age range of 14 to 17. This begs the perfectly legitimate question of why I feel the need to mention and emphasize this. Because the discrepancy between the implied age and the actual age significantly diminishes the film's brutality and horror, especially since not a single actor looks or is even remotely resembling someone of that age (a quick search confirms this assumption).
I previously mentioned how deeply "Death March" is grounded in reality, not exploiting the killings and horror during the march, but rather letting the participants experience it firsthand, by witnessing the slow disintegration of all the runners. This aspect is completely absent here, especially since it must be mentioned again and again how unflattering the overall digital look is, with its CGI blood, CGI muzzle flashes, and the resulting shattered faces and heads. To put it vulgarly: it's nauseatingly ugly, robbing it of any impact or weight.
The lack of sympathy for the characters doesn't develop over time, unlike in the novel, which achieves this through small personal backstories, conversations and dialogues that reveal the characters' traits and personalities, and the friendships they find, even if only for a moment or a single march.
And whatever the reason for the rewriting of the ending, the conclusion remains the same:
Disappointing in every respect!!!

Title: Bye Bye Love
Comment:
Singapore International Film Festival 2025 Film #3

It’s ironic that this film, which is all about the various aspects of identity slipping away, whether gender, the true self, or love, would be lost for decades only to re-emerge later. Its disappearance mirrors the idea that things like identity, love, and certainty can never be held onto permanently. When I watched it, it felt ahead of its time. A movie that handles gender and identity and love with such fluidity and yet in the 1970s, when it was made, there was no way for these topics to be handled in this manner. Through a queer lens, its tenderness, its restlessness, and its fluid approach to desire serve as an early celebration of queer love and all its complexity long before such stories could be told openly.

I was gagged by this movie. Most of the other japanese films from that time viewed non-traditional desire as a joke or something to be solved, but this film shows its characters as complex, real people. The emotions are believable, the desires are real, and the film's depiction of love and identity cannot be simplified or moralized. Watching this movie has given me a sense of freedom that was extraordinary for that time. It shows that no human experience should be reduced to generalizations or cliches. The film contains a gentleness and a patience in dealing with emotion that separates it from the more cautious, judgmental depictions of people during 1970s japanese cinema. This film is an example of how to break the rules of traditional filmmaking and give the characters dignity and a depth that the audience would have never seen before.

Originally made in early 1970s Japan during a time still feeling the effects of the counterculture movement of the 1960s and the yearning for social and personal freedom, this film represents the rise of the independent feature as an alternative to the popular cinema of that time. it provides an outlet for experimental film artists that rejected all conventions of film. through its use of a surrealist road-movie format with psychedelic imagery and moments of spontaneity and violence and its portrayal of a generation searching for answers regarding identity, morality, and the rules imposed by society, it represents a time of great energy and excitement when the concepts of love, sexual attraction, and personal identity were able to be conceptualized outside the restrictions placed by culture and tradition.

The film presents a gentle bye bye to love that is both painful and inevitable. It is more than just an ending, it leaves a lingering sadness for all of the delicate, fleeting moments that the characters and the narrative have tried to capture. The uncertainty of identity, fluidity of desire, and impermanence of connection have not been neatly resolved. they remain as memories with a sense of tenderness, loss, and beauty for all that cannot be held or held onto. By the end of the film, it becomes apparent that in the endless cycle of life, death, resistance, and transformation, nothing else matters at all. Giko has chosen to not be a definition of himself, nor have the characters on their journey defined who they are, which prompts me to examine what identity, connection, and freedom mean when one steps outside of the traditional norms of society.

Title: Port of Shadows
Comment:
Jean is a man of few words, but his demeanor and his clothing speak loudly enough about his condition. He’s dressed as a soldier and aimlessly wanders somewhere outside the city; he’s at the edge of the world and at the edge of himself. Although the word is never uttered in the film, the innuendo is obvious: he’s a deserter. He isn’t proud of himself — certain circumstances might have pushed him to it: malcontent disillusion, some existential sickness — but the film doesn’t give him excuses or alibis. His desertion isn’t the end of the journey, but the starting point. Or is it?
Jean doesn’t say much, but he doesn’t refuse the cigarette a truck driver amiably offers. With the cigarette butt stuck to the corner of his mouth, he utters brief and laconic responses. “Not a talkative fellow,” comments the driver, who had expected to break the serene monotony of his own routine. But if Jean is stingy with words, he knows how to act without asking for permission: he suddenly grabs the wheel and pulls the truck off the road to spare a puppy from being crushed to death. How ironic that this seemingly careless man shows his first signs of interest in this frail little animal; there’s still a heart beating behind that tough façade. One’s strength can be measured by his reaction in life-and-death situations. Eventually, when the grateful puppy follows him, he coldly dismisses it.
There’s something in Jean Gabin that is inexplicably appealing. He’s a man who exudes confidence and charisma even in moments of apparent weakness or immobility. He never really acts and is rather static: he can endure as many provocations as possible, yet one word too many against a woman he happens to like and you’ll get the backhanded slap à la Bogart. Gabin is perhaps the first Bogart-figure before Bogart — a guy who acts and reacts but doesn’t talk much. When it comes to talking, it’s in the characters gravitating around him that his films find their philosophy — about life, looks, love, everything. Jean is too stubborn, too earthly to think about the meaning of his life; he just wants to get the hell out of here. In the Port of Havre, some talk the talk — he walks the walk.
But this is not just any port — it's a port of shadows and foggy atmosphere. There’s no clear visibility in either the future or the past; everything lies in the present, a present embodied in many shades of black, white, and gray, or embodied by the beautiful Nelly, played by Michèle Morgan. She is obviously not a lady of the world — she’s young and looks sweet, but she must have a past too. And she does: she’s also fleeing a nasty, infatuated godfather, played by Michel Simon. With his ugly mug, he could be a sensitive teddy bear or a cynical villain; he resents his ugliness but says, “better this face than no face at all.” The place Jean lands is populated with these gray-area fellows. One of them is a small-time crook, Lucien, played by Pierre Brasseur, who is looking for Nelly’s boyfriend — one of his men — who has disappeared.
This little world revolves around the Port of Shadows, and it’s so small that we expect the inevitable collisions — and not a happy ending. This is a film that takes such a somber departure that there aren’t enough pixels to carry a rainbow. I read that the film was called somber by The New York Times. This film is perhaps one of the first and finest examples of a pre-noir film, the kind of film where you know with certainty that this port of shadows is a nasty place that can be either an end or a start. Some ships sail to Venezuela, and some gangster matters are handled in the port, as in films like On the Waterfront. Meanwhile, Jean spends a pleasant evening with Nelly: they go to a café, then to the carnival, and this is where they share the famous exchange, when Jean, staring at Nelly, tells her, “You’ve got pretty eyes, you know.” Her answer is as sweet as it is perfect: she asks for a kiss.
This is the brief and enchanted parenthesis before the plot moves toward its tragic destination, and I suppose the film is so sad and dark that it’s no wonder the most remembered line is a happy one. That moment was the highest point of Jean’s life, before karma came back to him and made him the victim of his own principles. Some “heroes” just can’t win — because they’re doomed, because the ugliness of the world is too great to bear, or because there’s more poetry in losing and dying than in hiding somewhere like a rat. He couldn’t go full deserter; he had to redeem that ugliness never explained — and that’s the poetry.

Angelino lives in Dark Meat City, in the midst of a city of decay, slums, paint and wallpaper peeling from the walls, garbage and dirt piling up on the sidewalks, food thrown out of windows and its packaging hanging from the facades of houses, multiplying with the garbage bags that unite them, in a city of hanging signs from the video store to the snack bar and from the snack bar to the gambling den to the strip clubs and electronics stores and grocery stores in the unifying flow of goods, in the streets of potholes of careless behavior and the passing shrug of the traffic officer, in the abrasion of their rubber on asphalt left behind by vehicles coughing and dripping poison, the ghosts populating them, death pumped into their veins, exhaling life, staring back at tooth decay in the clouded rot of their decomposing entrails, the decay of their cells in potentiation too fast, too vehement, too overwhelming and unifying ...

A world depicted that could easily serve as a milieu study for directors such as Alejandro González Iñárritu, Alfonso Cuarón, Sean Baker, John Singleton, F. Gary Gray, or Fernando Meirelles, were it not for one major circumstance.
The world of Dark Meat City through which our Angelino wanders, doing his job as a pizza delivery boy, spending his everyday life in their run-down apartment with his best friends and roommates Vinz and Willy, is animated. Our main character Angelino is a thoroughly black body with a round head that only resembles a human being in terms of the number of limbs he has. his best friend Vinz is also only remotely human-like, with two arms and legs but a skull for a head, topped with a flame encircling his head, while Willy is a cat, a cat wearing braces. The dilapidated world of Dark Meat City provides a truly appealing framework, and here one cannot praise the animation highly enough for creating a perfect harmony between the thoroughly realistic, familiar setting and the supernatural, playing with both in equal measure, which is truly an achievement worthy of recognition. Title: Wake Up Dead Man
Comment:
I was initially going to make a stray observation how weird it is that in Glass Onion there were jokes about Jeremy Renner, and to see him in this one, and no one made any comments about how Dr. Nat Sharp (Jeremy Renner’s character) looks strikingly similar to Jeremy Renner. Then again, I also had to remember that Noah Segan is in every Knives Out film playing a different character. So I guess, I shouldn’t really be over analyzing that too much. Anyway, I kinda loved this film a lot, even though, this could be the one where I “figured out” the twists and turns. While I do more or less love the cast he assembled for this one, some of the actors really teleprompter their roles for me. There’s nothing wrong with that, but I was able to connect the pieces of this one because of who they got to play what. I also would say, some characters aren’t as well utilized as previous films. That being said, this could have my favorite lead in the trilogy: Josh O'Connor. 
To say that Josh O'Connor has been having a good year would be an understatement. This has been a total lights out year for him. It’s funny how I first noticed him when I watched La chimera at NYFF where he was there at the Q&A. I thought he was good in La chimera, but I was not prepared by what he had in store in the next two years. In 2025 alone, he’s in four films, all of which he’s in a prominent role, and all gotten good reviews, especially from him. And this one is no exception. Both his performance and character are the reason I loved this film so much, or give as high marks as I can. So it’s no secret that this film dives in on faith, what faith means to people and how it can even manipulate people. Before this film, I had expected this film to be a takedown or at least demystifying religion, or in this case, Christianity. There’s nothing wrong with that, and I do believe there have been enough evidence to show how corrupt and manipulative it can be. However, I can say that I was quite astonished how this film values religion without ever teetering towards the faith based crap. I also believe this film exemplifies how religion can be manipulative towards vulnerable people. In 2025, we have seen how religion can be used to influence power of politics. Josh Brolin’s character is a vindictive, mean, manipulating, conniving asshole, and he knows how to reach people in nefarious ways. When someone tells Brolin’s character that he could be the president in a couple of years, he’s not wrong. We have seen that hate has let people follow shitty ghouls whatever they go. And what is great about both Josh O'Connor‘s character and the film in general is that, it sees hate or anger as not an option. Josh O'Connor’s character has a dark past, but in that past he learns to forgive himself and be a better person. This isn’t a film as to why being religious is a great thing, but rather why people choose the path. 
I liked that this installment is a bit more on the serious side of things. The other two installment weren’t goofy, but there was less goofy stuff in this one over the others. I sometimes wonder if Rian Johnson makes these film in reaction to the Kenneth Branagh Hercule Poirot films, but I also know that Rian Johnson just loves the mystery genre so much. Seriously, this and Poker Face prove that he can stay in the genre for the rest of his life. There’s a part of me, that almost would like to see him do something else, but I just love what he bring to this series, and I hope this isn’t the last. And from how Rian Johnson says it, he doesn’t want to stop, he wants to keep going. 
I’ll just put some other stray observation or thoughts on this paragraph. If One Battle After Another wasn’t released this year, there’s an argument that this would be Glenn Close‘s year to win an Oscar. I find her final scene extraordinary or a great reminder as to why she’s one of our great actresses. And apparently, she shot all of her scenes in a few days!? Fucking insane. Cute of Rian Johnson to have a Star Wars reference. Sorry we will never see your trilogy, but it was never going to happen given the weird reception Last Jedi got. This film strangely does a good job as to how some people fall into the manosphere, or red-pill rhetoric. How one character is trying to appease one demographic without ever being genuine, and realize it’s easier to trick or get what you want if you fall into right wing ideology. Funny how Hot Priest (Andrew Scott) is in this. Really thought there would be a fleabag reference in this. Not enough Cailee Spaeny! Kinda felt her character was the least developed or had the least going on. Love that the title for this film is based on a U2 song from their album, Pop. Pop is not a bad album, and more people should give it a listen!! Can someone explain to me why this one isn’t playing in wide theaters like AMC or Regal? They did it for Glass Onion, but they couldn’t for this one? It’s so strange because I definitely saw Glass Onion at a regal theater, and then just putting this one in odd independent theaters is a choice I don’t fully understand. At least the screening I went to was very packed and the crowd was into the film. This also had my favorite final shot in the trilogy.
There’s something about Wake Up Dead Man that genuinely moved me, and I really loved Josh O'Connor‘s arc and where that goes. I was worried that this film wasn’t going to stick the landing, but it absolutely did for me. I’m not sure if I prefer this over the original Knives Out, but I absolutely loved this film. It almost 150 minutes and it goes by, and it keeps you entertain and on your toes and to what the reveal will be. I’m definitely looking forward to seeing this one again!

Even though it’s a film packed with many different elements, I love how One Battle After Another remains true to its comedy aspect. The story combines a bit of everything, yet doesn’t fail to be a humorous story. In my opinion, I strongly agree that every cinema lover should watch One Battle After Another. Title: Malcolm X
Comment:
I have to start by saying I didn’t really know much about Malcolm X going in. I obviously knew the name and the basic idea, but I’d never actually dug into his life. And this movie just scoops you up and teaches you, not like a history lesson, but like you’re watching a life unfold in real time. It made me want to read more immediately, even though the film does an incredible job telling his story on its own.
What hit me is how cinematic his life already is. Every chapter feels significant, like the movie isn’t forcing drama, it’s just following a man whose life kept colliding with history. I had that same feeling I got watching Schindler’s List, where it stops feeling like “just a movie” and starts feeling like a piece of history you’re grateful exists.
This is one of the best biopics I’ve ever seen, maybe the best. The performances are great across the board, but Denzel is on another level. He’s doing something unreal here, not just “great acting” unreal, more like the kind of performance where you forget you’re watching a movie and start reacting to him like he’s actually in the room.

Title: The Young Girls of Rochefort
Comment:
‘I must steer clear of dreary bourgeoisie art, I must be avant-garde and paint what’s in my heart.’
Twin sisters, Delphine and Solange dream of finding romance and leaving the ‘very quiet’ town of Rochefort, France. One falls for an American musician, while the other must search for her ‘ideal partner.’
I’m not usually very fond of musicals, but I have to admit that this one is something special. The Young Girls of Rochefort is a film about love at first sight, and the joy of living in a world in which you are happy and loved. That joy bursts out through its electrifying soundtrack and instrumental pieces — you can practically feel love floating through the air.
The cast is wonderful AND beautiful. While you shouldn’t expect the deepest, most dramatic performances, you will absolutely be entertained and engaged throughout. The twins, Delphine (Catherine Deneuve) and Solange (Françoise Dorléac) are naturally the centre of attention, and they shine hilariously shine in their roles.
‘We are a pair of twins born in the sign of Gemini, Mi fa so la mi re, Re mifa so so so re do [they are singing here, I am not nuts!]. We’re two demoiselles who took to the boys long ago.’ [sing again].
‘Our mama brought us up on her own, working herself all her life to the bone.’
‘To make sure our minds could expand, she’s spend all her time behind a French-fry stand.’ […].
There’s a certain je ne sais quoi that makes this feel unlike other musicals. I could spend hours explaining the why and how — but why not let you see it yourself? Better, hein?
And remember, if the person next to you suddenly starts singing, no matter where or when, join them. What’s the worst that could happen? Awkwardness? Arrest? A Karen? Don’t be ridiculous! Just dance!
‘I’m afraid I can never get out. I’m confined to this aquarium. Me, who was meant to live in the open air on the Pacific shore, listening to sweet music and reading poetry.’
‘Knowing she’s out there fills me with more desire than all the naked girls in my wildest fantasies.’
That last quote is very relatable. I’ll leave you on that note.

Title: Spotlight
Comment:
This says the word 'Spotlight' far more than I would have thought
I wanted to watch this movie because I heard a lot of great things and it won Best Picture but I wasn't sure on how much I would like it. This in still images doesn't look that interesting and the overly office set films don't often appeal to me, but this movie was just really great. It somehow never got boring and it remained interesting and frustating watching as more information is found and handled by this team. Visually it may not be that much but a more muted sense of colour and subtle approach was probably the better fit for this movie. There's still a lot of effective shots and moments of direction selling the drama of certain interactions. I like printing newspaper shots and a lot of the imagery highlighting how children are in these same spaces and the changed framing of Churches create such an impact. This movie can do a lot with little in a lot of areas with a story that once it starts, remains engaging. This team involved in uncovering the truth around the Catholic Church starting with 13 cases before going up to 90 in just Boston and going against the system that allows and hides this is a really shocking development. The montages looking up this and a lot of the interviews can be entertaining but it mainly feels very frustating just the scale this occurs in and time it took. While highly talked about now, this movie looks back to that time period of the early 2000s that really wasn't that long ago with these characters reactions and conversations. It's a great showcase of the effect and lengths of journalism with how much time this all took for just a small team and the power of certain institutions being hard to fight. The characters themselves on the team is probably the weakest aspect of the movie, most of the time they feel more like serving the plot as opposed to their own people. I normally like Mark Ruffalo but I wasn't liking this character most of the way through untill some scenes later on that were really strong. The progression between this being their work they take seriously to some of the toll it takes on them to hear and think about everything happening around them hits quite a lot. While narratively straightforward, this has a lot of interesting dialouge that leaves a lot to think about regarding this. The way that the Church is tainted by this and the regrets of those involved in some cover ups are expressed really well. The conflict around waiting or holding out untill they have enough is one that leaves a lot of thought. While that may have been the better decision, it still meant almost a year on this project and time for more victims that they have to little to do to stop. While this can feel hopeless and full of dread at times, it still has some themes around finally trying to put a stop to lowering this and an ending showing that so many more victims are free to speak their story. This feels like it is doing a lot more than just telling a true story in a movie that I think deserved the Oscars for Picture and Original Screenplay, even if I would have gave both to Inside Out with it actually getting nominated for the latter. Spotlight may be a lower 4.5 star rating, but it really succeeds as a really great thrilling biopic about this subject matter. I've been on a strong week with movies about Church corruption with this, Wake Up Dead Man and sort of the Miseducation of Cameron Post, it's also a solid start to Christmas season with Silent Night being in this.

Title: Superman
Comment:
This has to be Gunn at his most campy, right?
Every straight dude hates Superman because he’s the best boyfriend in the world and no one else can compete. Lex was just the one petty enough to do something about it.
Anyway, I’m glad Gunn showed up for that second hour because the first was a slog. But once it turns into a Mr. Terrific movie and we’re introduced to the pocket universe prison built for tyrant grievances it does start to get pretty fun.
Jimmy Olson and his storyline sucks and this is the least interesting Ma and Pa Kent ever. However, Lois flying Mr. Terrific’s Jet reminds us that Gunn really does understand superhero stories on a fundamental level. In general his handling of secondary characters like Metamorpho (Anthony Carrigan in the house!), Supergirl, uncanny valley Krypto, etc. are the best things about this. But they also really step on Superman, who isn’t all that well fleshed out and has mostly boring shit to do.
I like that the forces aligned against him are technofascist billionaires, dictators, and E-Sports drone operators instead of some crazy extraterrestrial threat. I know this is probably to be expected in our current moment, but I also feel it's warranted. And its funny, and probably good for culture, to see so much faith placed in a goofy ass journalist crew that has its own superhero team vibe about them once they assemble... though half of them don't have shit to do. It’s still hard to believe you could drop a bombshell article about Lex Lurther and it would actually change minds. But then Gunn depicts society as being completely manipulated by the media. World opinion sways so quickly, and so completely, from “Superman has a harem” to “Lex Luther is responsible for all of this crazy shit” that it makes me think Gunn has no regard for actual people at all and his messaging throughout comes off more like virtue signaling than any real adoration for humanity.
The action is, of course, entirely weightless. I guess we’re just cool with all action being completely, obviously animated now, but I miss the sense that the world is dangerous exactly because things have density and mass and engaging in struggle has consequences. These are cartoon fights, and I’ll never feel any impact Superman takes in my own body while watching them. A CGI action sequences simply cannot make me wince. I was raised on 80s movies, real people got hurt making that shit. I don’t want people to get hurt, mind you, but this all just looks like pixels to me and so I drift hard when we move from human beings physically performing to cartoons getting hammered. It really makes me think about how much the ’78 Superman managed to achieve by relying on character more than spectacle. Which is exactly the kind of shit someone my age would say.
Movie’s fine. Better than most Superhero stuff right now, I guess. I’ve seen Gunn do much better, but at least it’s campy as fuck... I can truck with camp.

Title: Planes, Trains and Automobiles
Comment:
I can't think of many Thanksgiving movies, but everyone cites Planes, Trains, and Automobiles as their favorite. It's a comedy written and directed by John Hughes, in which a pair of mismatched guys are forced to go on a misadventure to Chicago after their flight gets diverted. It reflects one rage-inducing aspect of the Thanksgiving experience, not the political arguments on the dinner table, but rather the absurd travel delays. Steve Martin and John Candy are endearing to watch together, and the comedy of errors in their odyssey is as ridiculous as it needs to be. But it ends on such a heartwarming note that reminds us of what we're thankful for.
Happy Thanksgiving!

Title: Zootopia 2
Comment:
Zootopia 2 • 2025
Directed By: Jared Bush, Byron Howard
Directed by Jared Bush and Byron Howard, comes Zootopia 2 released in 2025, starring Ginnifer Goodwin, Jason Bateman, and Ke Huy Quan, in this animated comedy adventure sequel, distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures
The film follows Judy Hopps and Nick Wilde once again, as their partnership at the ZPD is called into question after a series of recent failed missions. To stay together, they’re required to attend a therapy workshop in hopes of repairing their relationship. Meanwhile, a new danger emerges from beyond Zootopia. A mysterious and supposedly dangerous reptile named Gary De Snake arrives, causing havoc and mayhem. It’s up to Judy and Nick to solve the case and uncover the reason behind his arrival
Nine years later and here we are. If you think about it, Disney took about the same amount of time to make this as it took Stranger Things to wrap up. 2016 to 2025, think about it. I just wanted to put that into perspective before the review starts
With Zootopia 2 now released, what better way to review it than during a special advanced screening courtesy of Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures. There’s a lot coming out right now, so I appreciate Disney for the early access this week. I had the chance to watch it in IMAX, and I’m glad Wicked: For Good isn’t hogging all the screens unlike some films (Avatar) because animation deserves to be seen in the best format possible. This film isn’t as good as the first one, but it’s definitely a strong follow up, just with a bit less structure
I mentioned in my Zootopia review yesterday that there’s been a decline in quality when it comes to children’s media. I call it "the purge" because of how much damage it does to today’s youth. Zootopia 2 may be a beautiful and colourful film, but unlike the first one, this feels like it has corporate interference written all over it. However there is a takeaway here like in the first film, but it’s not delivered with the same level of maturity
This has become the kind of film you put on when your child is crying so they’ll calm down for an hour and forty minutes. It’s a shame, but I knew this would happen. Don’t get me wrong though, there is a lesson to be learned here, but it’s not handled the same way the first film did. It relies a lot more on comedy and feels a bit forced at times. There’s a lot of new characters, and that’s expected in a sequel. It’s supposed to expand the world and make the film feel bigger. But instead, this film solves everything for the audience early on, rather than letting us figure things out for ourselves. I predicted most of the film, and I usually don’t do that, but it was so painfully obvious because they copied the same formula they previously did in Zootopia. Maybe I’m looking too much into this, but watch the two films back to back and you’ll notice a big difference 
The film once again explores some interesting themes. This time it looks at trust and emotional growth, diversity, inclusion, identity, redemption, and most notably segregation. The story shifts from a mostly external conflict to more of an internal and social one, involving relationships, institutions, and society itself. I won’t go into full detail like I did yesterday since this film just came out, but there’s a plot involving segregation and a new species being marginalized for corporate reasons that benefit the new antagonist, and I never really thought about other species in the first film. I just assumed all animals live in Zootopia, so seeing that inclusion was a genuinely thought provoking moment
It’s clear Disney wanted to get their message across. It just feels like there may have been some interference towards how that message could be delivered, especially since the film reflects issues happening in the world right now. When freedom of speech is taken away or silenced, film is able to get one’s point across, even if it’s not entirely clear. As long as it has a network, there will be people watching 
We get some incredible returning voice talent, including Ginnifer Goodwin, Jason Bateman, Idris Elba, and Jenny Slate, along with new voices like Ke Huy Quan, Fortune Feimster, Andy Samberg, Danny Trejo, and even Patrick Warburton. I think the film does a great job not only expanding the world of Zootopia, but also deepening the relationship between our two main protagonists
Throughout the film, Judy and Nick struggle to cope with their different methods of doing things, and there’s obvious tension between them. Having Nick be more open, but not too open was a smart choice. He had a lot of development in this. Everyone else remains true to their characters. Nobody feels out of place. I also thought the snake character, voiced by Ke Huy Quan would’ve been annoying, but he ended up being fun, and he actually has less screentime than you would expect. I also really liked the inclusion of Fortune Feimster’s character, Nibbles Maplestick. Having an openly lesbian protagonist fits perfectly with Zootopia’s message, and I’m glad they weren’t sidelined like other characters have been in past Disney films
I love a good comedy, who doesn’t right? While the first film succeeded with its jokes, I feel like the humour here is much more safer and geared toward a younger audience, rather than appealing to both kids and adults. Every once in awhile, you get a genuinely funny moment, but it’s often followed by a very obvious pun. It feels like there are two directors at work here, almost like two different films clashing, and I prefer the one that’s genuinely trying to be good, rather than the forced one. Byron Howard returned to direct this, and his influence is noticeable. Jared Bush, on the other hand, seems to be behind many of the film’s mistakes. Instead of delivering funny jokes, the film rather cram as many pop culture references as possible
Take a shot everytime a pop culture reference is referenced in the film. You would have liver failure before the second act, and it only gets worse from there. That said, there is one reference in particular to a classic horror film that I did find funny 
Michael Giacchino returns once again to compose the film’s score, and while it isn’t as good as the first film, it still does the story justice. It’s not bad, it’s just lacklustre in comparison. Shakira also returns, and I had no idea she recorded a new single for this. I’ve heard nothing about it, nor have I heard it on the radio. Compare that to "Try Everything" which was on the billboard charts for several weeks
I think the difference comes down to the film’s marketing. I barely saw any promotional material for this, and the same trailer ran for so long that I got sick of it. I never even saw the final trailer. That’s good though if you want to avoid spoilers, but it’s bad for the film because there’s no anticipation built. Compare this campaign to the original campaign, there’s a massive difference, and it shows 
The animation has improved significantly, and I’m so happy to say that. I highly recommend watching this in IMAX if you can. The animation is beautiful and really leaps off the screen. I wish I saw it in IMAX 3D, but unfortunately that wasn’t an option, and just to clarify something once again, when I talk about the animation, I mean the actual visuals, not the story
Would Walt Disney be a furry? Who knows
With this world expansion, Zootopia feels so much larger than before, and I loved getting some backstory on the different districts and even some forgotten areas. There’s so much to take in, and I’ll definitely need a rewatch or two to really dissect it frame by frame
There’s a hint at a third film towards the end, and I think whether that happens or not will depend on this film’s box office. There’s so much more that could be explored now, especially with the new concepts introduced here. A trilogy is definitely possible if this film earns as much or even more than the first one did
I know it might sound like I hated this film, but I didn’t. I just felt it was a bit dumbed down and didn’t have the same impact as the first one did. That said, it’s still a really good piece of work, and I can’t wait to see the behind the scenes footage for this film. Disney+ better deliver
Overall, Zootopia 2 is an enjoyable film with great animation and fun characters. While it doesn’t quite capture the depth or charm of the first film, it’s still entertaining and worth watching

Title: Behind the Curtain: Stranger Things: The First Shadow
Comment:
Props to anyone who works in the theater business because, boy, it is a grind. There is so much hard work and dedication that goes into the craft that the show itself is the easy part; it's everything that happens behind the scenes that's so mundane and exhausting. I remember having to do the live sound for one theatre production at the Artscape a few years ago, and man, those were looooooooong hours.
While I’m eagerly waiting for the first few episodes of Stranger Things 5 to come out tomorrow, I’m scavenging every bit of lore I can find to prepare, and apparently the Broadway show plays a vital role in the plot of Stranger Things 5. As you all know, I don’t live in the UK, so I won’t be able to watch it live.... maybe next year if they’re still performing it (if everything goes to plan). I got a view of some of the play online and had to look up some of the plot points, and it’s just so damn good.
Everything about this show is so encapsulating and mystical that you can’t help but fall in love with it. The characters, the setting, and the beautiful synths that dance through your ear canals are diaphanous. I’m not prepared to let go of this show; I practically grew up with these kids, and now we’re all grown. Sigh. Here’s to hoping Stranger Things 5 will be a banger.

Title: Pocahontas
Comment:
You know those movies that, for some crazy, unexplainable reason, you simply must watch when the year is winding down? For me, that movie is Pocahontas. I know, I know, it might not be the most obvious choice for Christmas or New Year's Eve, but there's something about the autumnal color palette, the songs, and, of course, our princess that pulls me back to it every single year-end.
To be honest, it's a story with its issues, especially regarding historical representation (which makes me take a slight deduction in the rating), and the romance between her and John Smith is a bit rushed. But, seriously, I love this movie. Alan Menken's soundtrack gives me chills, with "Colors of the Wind" being one of my favorite Disney songs of all time—it's pure poetry about respecting nature and seeing the world differently.
And Pocahontas? Oh, Pocahontas! For me, she is, undeniably, one of the most beautiful princesses Disney has ever created. She has a unique strength and grace, a free spirit that is inspiring to watch. Her design is stunning, from the way her hair moves in the wind to the necklace she wears. She's not just beautiful on the outside; the way she carries herself, her wisdom, and the courage to be the bridge between two worlds... that absolutely enchants me.
Who hasn't wished, for just a second, to be there? Running freely through the fields, with their hair loose in the wind just like she does, and interacting with all those cute little forest animals, like Meeko and Flit. It's a simple desire for peace and freedom that the movie conveys beautifully!
It's a beautiful film, with breathtaking landscapes, but it carries the weight of a complex real narrative that Disney tried to simplify. That's why the 3.5 stars. It's an imperfect movie that I adore and that gives me a nostalgic warmth in my heart.

Title: The Big Boss
Comment: The Big Boss is most notable for the fact that it provided the great Bruce Lee with his first starring role. Lee plays a worker who moves to Thailand to take a job in the ice factory where his cousin works. He's sworn an oath to his family never to get involved in violence - but this is put to the test when other workers start to disappear and he finds out the factory is a front for a nefarious drug dealing operation. It's a pretty basic plotline really but it does just enough to get the job done. The characters are all rather one dimensional and of course it soon pans out into a fairly standard good vs evil storyline. Lee really makes his mark, however. His oath of non-violence means its around half an hour before we see his lightning fast fists and feet, but it's a real explosion when we finally do see it. The Cantonese cut features some unauthorised but well used Pibk Floyd on the soundtrack. Han Ying-Chieh is good in the title role as the sinister "big boss" smuggling drugs on the side. The bloody final conclusion is well done and worth the wait. It's just a shame that the whole thing wasn't a bit better paced and less clichéd on the whole.

Title: Sentimental Value
Comment:
A few stray thoughts. I’ll be writing about the film for my newsletter but I wanted to put something in this space too.
-I don’t have a sister and I have no relationship with my father. So this film didn’t affect me in some one-to-one way of seeing myself or my experiences acutely onscreen. The film moved me in a number of ways all the same. I saw a piece floating around about the film being about eldest daughter syndrome, which is such a wild misreading of the film and its characters especially given that Nora (Renate Reinsve) struggles with intimacy; it is the youngest sister engaged in the carework necessary to mend the family and look at its foibles honestly.
-I found the film gentle (visually and emotionally) and a bit cerebral in a way that sparked with me.
-But the film has a sense of humor. A little wry. Maybe even dark. (That Ikea chair moment!) 
-The three central performances by Reinsve, Stellan Skarsgard, and Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas interlock in a beautiful way.
-There is much to consider about how the film reckons with the costs of being an obsessive artist — on your sense of self and the loved ones around you.
-I made peace long ago with the fact that my parents have never and will never be the parents I need. Maturing is realizing the foibles of your parents — and acknowledging their humanity is just as complex and fraught as yours.
-All artists bring the personal into our work. But sometimes can’t see clearly how that manifests.
-The scene between the sisters at the end is indeed stunning and emotionally astute. But the scene I keep coming back to is the aftermath of young Erik’s birthday party, Gustav’s grandson (Skarsgard), in which Nora and her father have a tense conversation in front of others. His absence. Her lack of children and ostensibly lonely life is what he brings up before making a series of other cutting remarks about the state of artistry too. The tension in the room and what remains unspoken is piercing in the truths they carry.
-Yes, the film is about a filmmaker. But I think Trier smartly avoids the reverential ouroboros that a lot of films about filmmakers devolve into. Sentimental Value isn’t so much about film as a medium and defending its importance in a historical moment when the arts are under upheaval globally. Trier utilizes film to make a broader statement about the relationship between art and life.
-Can I be a bitch for a second though? I’ve seen comparisons on here about how the film evokes Assayas and Bergman. I totally get it and agree to a degree. And I am not inherently bothered by people using those comparisons as a way to critique or even lambast a film they don’t like. Totally fine. What bothers me is when people’s thoughts begin and end on such comparisons. It comes across as people posturing as smarter than the film in question, able to see its influences (perhaps) and conclude the film is lacking without actually engaging in the film itself. I don’t know. I think I have become increasingly disenchanted with the modern “cinephile”. Cinephiles, I am using this word very specifically, are sometimes obsessed with film in a way I find closed off, insular, boring, and completely divorced from the act of living. Am I interested in the history of film, its current moment, and how this medium still in its infancy can develop more boldly? Of course! I am a scholar of this shit. But what’s most interesting about a film isn’t what it has to say about film, but what it says about being human and alive.

Title: The Running Man
Comment:
"I'm still here, you shit-eaters."
When I first heard about it, I was sure I'd see a wildly funny and entertaining film directed by Edgar Wright, and a fiercely hot one starring Glenn Powell. It mostly met my expectations, especially during "that towel scene" where a fire breaks out in the theater, but things took a sudden turn in the second half of the film.
First of all, I loved the semi-dystopian atmosphere created by the movie. Horrific reality shows and their seemingly bloodthirsty audiences don't seem so terrifyingly surreal. Of course, watching murders unfold on screen is an extreme example, and the likelihood of it happening today is very remote, but if the world continues as it is, it will happen soon, and the "herd of sheep who accept everything without question" will once again accept it as normal. The film depicts an oppressive, subjugating totalitarian regime. In this stifling environment, it becomes clear that the only ones who truly stand out and feel some measure of freedom are the massive corporations that organize competitions like Running Man. I know this is a Stephen King adaptation, but I still love seeing famous directors using anti-fascist themes in their films these days. Long live anti-fascist cinema!
And Glenn Powell... This man is running, jumping, fighting, sweating, smirking it’s basically a two-hour montage of him being illegally charismatic. I don’t think I absorbed half the plot because every time he showed up onscreen my brain simply whispered, “girl focus be serious” and then immediately failed. And then… the towel scene. I just forgot my own name. If the film’s intention was to devastate me with one man casually existing in a towel, it also succeeded. But Glenn Powell wasn't the only star of the movie because Michael Cera was there for me! Despite his short screen time, he single-handedly carried the entire "Edgar Wright comedy" of the movie.
But after the second half of the movie, it completely loses touch with reality and moves to a point where you'll say "what the hell am I watching?" Every scene got louder, bigger, more ridiculous, as if the movie had suddenly decided to be as "epic" as possible and not in a fun way. I would have loved for the film to have remained in the rhythm it began with, and I would have even wanted to delete the private jet scene entirely.
P.s. The moment The Hunter took off his mask was the climax of the film. Lee Pace, you can hunt me too, and you can find me right away because I won't run away from you.
